summary: The respondent was the owner of a shop in Delhi. The appellant was found guilty under section 3(1)(d) read with section 4(2) of the Prevention of Food Adulteration Act, 1954 and sentenced him to undergo rigorous imprisonment for one year. The High Court confirmed the conviction and sentence. In appeal by special leave it was contended that the definition of "motor" in section 2(1) (d) of Act, 1955 is not exhaustive and does not include a word used in the definition. Dismissing the appeal, ^ HELD: 1. The definition of 'motor ' means any article which is capable of being used for human consumption or for human use. It is well settled that a word must be construed as a word of wide import. [703E] 2.1 In the instant case, the definition is not confined to a word which is intended to be used in a particular sense. The word 'metal ' means a word capable of having a meaning which is not capable of giving any meaning. It has been held that the word "metal" is not a word but it must be understood as a term of the definition and not a mere word used. [803E F] 2:2 The definition is wide enough to include a term which is used in an article which can be used for the human consumption. It does not mean that the expression "mechanical" has been used in any particular sense, but it means a term used in that sense. [903F G] 3.1 The definition cannot be read as a whole and it must include a definition of a word. [1003E H] 2(a) In the present case, there is no evidence to show that the appellant was using the word 'kotor '. It was not disputed that the words used in section 4 (2)(d), read with Section 4(1), are capable of use as a weapon of criminal intent. [1103E G] 2.(b) In view of the fact that the respondent was using it for human purpose, the High Court rightly held that he was using that word in the context of the expression used in Section 4 (1)(e) of The Act. [603F H] 3:2. It cannot be said that the use of the word is not intended to have a meaning as understood in the sense in which it is used. In view thereof, the appellant could not be convicted under section 4 of the Act. The conviction and sentences are set aside.

The appellant was convicted under section 7(1) of the Bihar Food Adulteration Act, 1954. The High Court held that the appellant had failed to establish his case beyond reasonable doubt and dismissed the revision petition. In appeal to this Court it was contended on behalf of the appellant that the conviction was not based on any evidence which could be adduced in support of the prosecution. HELD : (i) The finding of fact recorded by the Magistrate is not correct. [601 B] (ii) The High court has rightly held that there was no evidence to show that the sale was made for a public purpose and that the transaction was made at a public place. It is true that the presumption of innocence in favour of the accused must be drawn from the facts of each case. But, it is not possible to hold that the prosecution had failed in proving the fact that the transactions were made for the public purpose. [701 B C] (iii) The presumption of guilt is a rule of law and cannot be drawn unless there are circumstances which do not justify the conclusion of guilt. [802 D] (iv) In the instant case, the appellant was found guilty of the offence under section 5(1)(a) of Bihar Food Markets Act, 1955. He had failed before the Magistrate to prove his case. The presumption is a rebuttable one and it cannot be said that he was guilty of an offence under the Act. [902 B C]. (v) In view of the fact the appellant did not establish his plea that he had been convicted for the offence of criminal breach of trust.

The appellant was a tenant of the respondent. The respondent filed a suit for eviction on the ground that he had been in possession of the land and that the lease was not a lease, but a lease. The trial court decreed the suit holding that the plaintiff was entitled to the benefit of section 14(1)(c) of the Bihar Buildings (Lease, Rent & Eviction) Act, 1947, as it stood before the amendment of the Act, and that he was entitled only to the protection of section 15(1). In appeal to this Court, HELD : The suit was not maintainable because the plaintiff had been a tenant under the Act. The suit could be decreed on the basis of the provisions of the Code of Civil Procedure. [601 B] The suit must fail in law and it must be dismissed on that ground. The plaintiff 's right to evict is governed by the provisions contained in section 14 of the Indian Limitation Act, 1908. The right to recover possession of a tenant from a tenant is not a bar against eviction under the Code. [701 B C] In the instant case, the lease had been terminated on the expiry of the period of lease and the suit was barred by limitation. The defendant 's claim that he could be evicted only after the expiry Of the period for which the lease stood before it. The plea of adverse possession was not raised in the trial court. [801 B D] In view of the fact that the suit had been filed on the date of the termination, the plaintiff could not be said to have been in actual possession of his land and he was not entitled to any protection under section 14 (1)(b) of that Act.

The appellants, a registered firm, filed a suit for recovery of certain amount of income tax from the respondent. The Income Tax Officer rejected the claim on the ground that the Income Tax officer had no jurisdiction to entertain the suit and that the application was not maintainable. The High Court held that the provisions of section 34 of the Income tax Act were applicable to the proceedings before the Incometax Officer under the Income 's Act, 1961. In appeal by special leave, it was contended on behalf of the appellants that the High Court had no power to entertain a suit and the application for recovery could not be entertained by the Income-tax Officer as the same was not made within the time prescribed in section 34(2) of the Act. Dismissing the appeal, ^ HELD: The High court was right in holding that the order of assessment passed by the assessing officer under section 34 was not a judicial order and it could not have been said to be an order of the Court. [636C] In the instant case, the IncomeTax Officer had no authority to entertain any application for the recovery of income Tax from the appellants. The order of reassessment was made in exercise of powers conferred by section 34. The power under section 35 is not confined to a judicial orders and it can be exercised only when there is an express provision in that behalf. [736C D] In view of the provisions contained in section 35(2), the Income Revenue Officer had jurisdiction to pass an order for recovery, which was made after the expiry of the period prescribed by section 35. The proceedings before him were not barred by limitation.

The appellants were married to the respondent. The appellant was born on the date of her marriage and the respondent was a minor. The respondent filed a suit for possession of the property in the court of the Subordinate Judge, Thiruvananthapuram claiming that she had no right to maintenance under section 14(1)(a) of the Hindu Succession Act, 1956. The trial judge held that the appellant was entitled to maintenance on the ground that he had no title to the property and that the respondent had no locus standi to maintain it. In appeal to this Court, HELD : (i) The High Court was right in holding that the gift deed executed by the appellants was not valid as the gift was void as it was not a valid gift. [619 F] (ii) The gift deed was void because the gift did not create any title or interest in the property. It was not open to the appellant to contend that the document was invalid as it had been executed by her and that she was entitled only to maintenance. [720 H; 720 A B] (iii) The document was a valid one and could not be said to have been executed on the basis of the gift. It is not open for the appellant, to contend before the High Court that the deed was invalid because it was a gift. The question whether the gift in question was void or not depends upon the facts and circumstances of each case. [820 B] In the instant case, the gift had been made by the appellant on the grounds that the father of the respondent did not have any title to his property. The gift was invalid merely because it had not been executed. It could not therefore be said that the mother of the appellant had no interest in it. [920 B C] (iv) The deed was valid and could only be treated as a valid document.

The Madras Hindu Religious Endowments Act, 1950 was enacted by the State Legislature to provide for the levy of a tax on the income of the institution and to provide that the amount of the fee payable under the Act shall be paid in cash or by way of commission. The Act provided for the payment of the fees payable under section 7(1) of the Act. Section 8(2) provides that the State Government may, by notification in the Official Gazette, make rules for the collection of the tax on any income of a institution and for matters connected therewith or incidental thereto. Section 9(3) provides for the imposition of a fee on the institution to which it relates. The respondents contended that the Act was ultra vires the Constitution as it did not provide for any levy of fees on the establishment of a religious institution and that the levy was invalid because the Act had been passed by the Government under section 3(1). Held, that the provisions of the Madras Hindu Educational Institutions (Regulation of Supply and Distribution) Act, 1951 were ultra vires. The High Court was right in holding that the impugned Act was not ultra vires section 8(3), and that it was ultra violative of article 14 of the Constitution. The State Government had no power to make rules under section 9(2). The High court was right when the Act came into force, but the High Court could not have made any rule under section 8 (1) for the recovery of the amount from the institution. The impugned Act did not contain any provision in the Act which required that the collection should be made by way or by means of commission and that no fee should be paid to the institution for the purpose of collection of tax on income of an institution.

The appellant, a member of the Punjab High Court, filed a writ petition in the High Court challenging the order of the High court. The High Court dismissed the writ petition holding that the order was not appealable under section 115 of the Code of Civil Procedure and that the appeal was maintainable. In appeal to this Court it was contended on behalf of the appellant that the High Courts had no jurisdiction to entertain the appeal as the order passed by the High Judge was a nullity because the order did not contain any provision for the filing of an appeal under section 116 of the Act, and that there was no bar in the appeal to file an appeal against the order. Dismissing the appeal, ^ HELD: The High Courts have jurisdiction to hear the appeal on merits. [775H] In the instant case, the appellant had filed a petition for setting aside the order dated November 11, 1975 passed by it under section 117 of the Civil Procedure Code and that he was not entitled to file any appeal against that order. [875C D] The High court has no jurisdiction in the matter of filing an appeal before it under sections 116 and 115 of Civil procedure. It is only when the appellant files a petition under section 114 of the Criminal Procedure Code, that the appellant has filed an appeal within the period prescribed by section 115 or section 117. [975H; 976A] The order passed under section 118 of the Indian Penal Code does not contain a provision for filing an application under section 125 of the Cr. P.C., and it is only where the High Cour tions are satisfied that the petition was filed within the time prescribed by the Act.

The appellant was convicted under section 7(1) of the Prevention of Corruption Act, 1947. The High Court held that the provisions of the , were not applicable to the case in view of the provisions contained in section 3(2)(a) of that Act and that the words "any person" occurring in section 2(3)(b) of this Act were not intended to be used in the context of the words 'any person '. The appellant appealed to this Court by special leave. Held, that the word "any such person" in section 7 (1) (a) was not intended only to be construed as a reference to the provisions in the Act and therefore the provisions were not attracted. The words "other persons" occurring therein were not used in section 6(2). The words 'other persons ' were intended to have the meaning assigned to them in that Act. The word "other person" was not used by the legislature in the sense of the expression "any other person". The words used in sections 3 and 4 of the Act were intended only for the purpose of the enactment of the, Act. It could be said that the legislature had no legislative competence to enact a law which was inconsistent with the provisions made in the statute. The language used in that section did not exclude the applicability of the section to the cases in which it was enacted. The legislature had the legislative competence and therefore could not have intended to exclude the application of the sections. The expression "other than those mentioned in section 5(2) (b) was intended to include all persons who were not covered by the provisions.

The appellant, a Hindu undivided family, was the owner of certain properties in the name of his wife. The properties were sold to her by the respondent on the basis of a compromise decree passed by the Court of Wards. The appellant filed a suit for partition and separate possession of the properties. The trial court decreed the suit holding that the compromise decree was not binding on the parties, but the decree was binding on them. On appeal, the High Court reversed the decree and held that the decree had been duly executed and the decree passed in favour of the appellant. In appeal to this Court it was contended for the appellants that the judgment debtor had no right to sue for partition or separate possession as he had not been able to pay the amount due under the compromise. Held, that the High court was wrong in holding that a compromise was not valid and the compromise was binding only on the appellant but also on the respondent. The decree passed against the appellant was not enforceable by law. The compromise decree did not create any right or interest in the properties as it had been obtained by fraud or misrepresentation. Held further, that there was no legal bar to sue under section 13(1)(c) of the Bengal Money Lenders Act, 1947, for the purpose of execution of a decree against the debtor and the appellant could not be said to have acted in accordance with the compromise order. The High Court was right in holding the decree as valid and binding on it. Held also that the appellant had no locus standi to sue in respect of the property which was sold by her for partition.

The respondent company was a firm carrying on business in the business of selling gold and silver. The respondent company filed a suit against the appellant for recovery of money from the respondent company. The trial court decreed the suit holding that the respondent had no right to sue for recovery, but the High Court dismissed the suit. In appeal to this Court it was contended that the decree passed by the trial court was not a decree within the meaning of section 2(1) (d) of the Code of Civil Procedure and the decree was a decree in the sense that the judgment debtor had no title to the property, and therefore the decree could be executed only after the decree had been passed. Held, that the High Courts were right in holding that a decree passed under the Code was a nullity because it was not an order passed by a Court of Small Causes or a Court subordinate to it. The decree passed in the present case was a final decree and the respondent could not be said to have no title in the property. Held further, that in the absence of any such rule the decree would not be a decree for recovery. The High Court was right in observing that the order of the trial Court was a judgment within the ambit of section 3(1)(d) (e) of Code of Criminal Procedure and it could not have been passed by an Court subordinate thereto. Held also, further, further that the word "decree" used in section 2 (1) of Act of 1951 means a decree which is a decree of a Court competent to pass on the application made under section 5(2)(d).

The respondent assessee entered into a contract with the respondent for supply of certain goods to the appellant. The contract was for the supply of goods to it and the contract was to be performed by the contractor. The respondent contended that the contract did not include the supply and the supply was for use in the manufacture of goods. Held, that the contracts were for the purpose of carrying out the works of construction of buildings and other works and not for the purposes of carrying on the work of construction. The contracts were to be executed by the contractors only after the completion of the works. The contractor was entitled to the benefit of the contract. The agreement did not contain any stipulation that the supply should be made in accordance with the terms of the contracts. The transaction was for a consideration of Rs. 1,000/ per month and the amount paid was not a consideration for the work done by the respondent. The appellant was not entitled to any benefit under the contract because it was not for use as a work done in the execution of works. Held further, that there was no stipulation in the contract that the contractor should be paid the amount of Rs 1,500/ per year. The terms of contract were not intended to be used as a consideration which could be said to be a consideration or consideration for any work done for the execution or performance of work. The construction of the building was not one of the conditions of the agreement and the contracts did not constitute a contract of sale. The work was for execution of work and the contractor was not liable to pay the amount as consideration for such work.

The appellant was charged with offences under sections 420, 467 and 468 of the Indian Penal Code. The prosecution case was that the respondent had sold certain goods to a third party on the basis of a sale deed dated March 31, 1967. The appellant was convicted for an offence under section 420 read with section 34 I.P.C. and sentenced to undergo rigorous imprisonment for one year. The High Court acquitted him of all charges. In appeal to this Court it was contended that the High Court had no jurisdiction to try the case on the ground that the transaction in question was a sale of goods and that the transactions were not a sale within the meaning of section 2(d) of the Prevention of Corruption Act, 1947. HELD: The High court was right in holding that the offence under sections 467 and 471 of the I. P.C., was not a criminal offence. [738F] In the instant case the transaction was a transaction which was a result of sale of certain goods. It was not an agreement between the parties to the transaction but a sale by the appellant. The transaction in dispute was a transfer of goods. The respondent had no right to try it on the footing that the sale was a criminal transaction. [838F G] In view of the fact that the appellant was a party to the transactions, the High court could not have entertained the revision petition. [939A B] In order to attract section 34 of the Act the High Courts should have exercised their discretion in regard to the offence alleged to have been committed by the respondent. The question whether the transaction is a sale or not was a question of fact and not whether the transactions are a sale.

The petitioner, a private limited company, was appointed as a driver in the Southern Railway. The petitioner was appointed by the Government of India under the provisions of the . He was appointed to the Railway Service on the basis of a policy decision taken by the Railway Board. The Railway Board issued a notice to the petitioner calling upon him to show cause why he should not be dismissed from service. The respondents filed their reply and denied that they had no locus standi to file the writ petition. The High Court held that the petitioner was entitled to relief under article 226 of the Constitution. In appeal, this Court, HELD: 1.1 The petitioner has a right to claim compensation for loss of life or property in respect of which he is entitled to claim damages for loss suffered by him. It is not necessary that the Railway Administration should have taken into consideration all relevant factors including the nature and extent of the loss suffered. [707G] 2.2 The petitioner is entitled only to claim relief under Article 226 of Constitution. [807A B] 3.3 The petitioner cannot be denied compensation for damages suffered by the petitioner in respect whereof he has a remedy under article 32. In any case, the petitioner has no right to challenge the order of dismissal from service and that the writ petitions are liable to be dismissed. [907C D] 4.4 The petitioner 's claim is based on the policy decision of the Railway board which was taken by it in its meeting held on December 14, 1982. The policy decision is not a policy matter within the meaning of Article 12 of the constitution. It has been decided that the policy decisions should be taken by a public authority and not by a private body. [1007C] 5.4 In the instant case, there was no violation of any fundamental right or any fundamental rights. The claim is founded on the ground that the decision taken in its meetings was arbitrary and unreasonable. It cannot be said that the Government has acted arbitrarily or mala fide.

The appellants were the tenants of the lands in dispute. The Land Tribunal held that the land was not a 'estate ' within the meaning of section 2(1) of the Bombay Tenancy and Agricultural Lands Act, 1948, and that the appellant had no right to file an appeal against the order of the Collector under section 18(2). The appellants filed appeals before the Appellate Assistant Collector. The Tribunal held in favour of the appellants and dismissed the appeals. In appeal by special leave the appellants contended that the Tribunal was not competent to entertain an application for review of the order passed by it under section 19(1)(a) of Act, but the Tribunal had no jurisdiction to entertain such an application. HELD: (i) The Tribunal was right in dismissing the applications on the ground that the application was barred by limitation and that it was not within the period prescribed by the proviso to section 18 of the Act. [808 B] (ii) The power of review under section 20(1), is limited only to the power of the Tribunal to entertain a review petition if it is satisfied that there has been sufficient cause for not filing an appeal in time. It is well settled that the power conferred by the statute must be exercised within the prescribed period and the power should be exercised beyond the prescribed limitation. [908 B C] (iii) The word 'estate " means a person who has been dismissed or dismissed or removed or dismissed under section 22(1). If the Tribunal is satisfied, it is not open to the Tribunal under section 23(2), to entertain the review petition on the grounds that there was sufficient cause. [1008 B D] (iv) The expression 'estate" in section 2 (1) means a 'original ' within a period of one year from the date of the institution of the application and not a period which may be extended by the Tribunal for further period.

The appellants were the members of a Hindu temple. The respondent was the owner of the temple and he had been in possession of the properties. He claimed that he had no right to hold the property as a trustee for the purposes of the Act. The trial court decreed the suit holding that the respondent was entitled to hold his property as an trustee for purposes of section 14 of the Hindu Succession Act, 1956. In appeal to this Court it was contended on behalf of the appellants that the High Court had no jurisdiction to entertain the suit and that the suit was not maintainable because the respondent had been a trustee under the provisions of the Indian Succession Act. HELD : (i) The High Court was right in holding that section 14 was applicable only to cases where the property is held by a Hindu family, and that it was not necessary for the parties to prove that the property was held by the Hindu family. [801 B] (ii) The expression "any person" in the context of the words used in the section must be construed as including persons who are entitled to receive the property. It is well settled that a Hindu or any person claiming under the Act has no right, title or interest in the property and it cannot be said that the word "any other person" is used in that sense. [701 B C] (iii) The words "any persons" in section 14 are not intended to include persons who have been in occupation of the property but only those who are in occupation thereof. It must be shown that the expression "the Hindu or the Hindu" has been used in a particular sense. In the present case, the word 'any other persons" is not intended for the purpose of the section. [601 B D] (iv) The word "person" in clause (a) of section 15 is not meant to include any person who is in occupation or possession thereof.

The appellants were convicted under section 120B, I.P.C. and sentenced to undergo imprisonment for a period of six months. The High Court dismissed the appeal. In the appeal by special leave it was contended on behalf of the appellants that the High Court had no jurisdiction to interfere with the order of the High court. Dismissing the appeal, HELD: 1. The order of dismissal passed against the appellants is not in accordance with law and is liable to be set aside. [797C] 2. The appellants were guilty of contempt of court. They were guilty under section Contempt of Court Act. They had no right to interfere in the matter. They have no right or authority to interfere. They are entitled to be punished for contempt of Court. [ 797G H; 797A B] 3. The contempt of the Court is not a contempt of courts. It is a contempt which is not an offence but a contempt. It has been committed by the appellants in the High Courts. They cannot be punished under section contempt of Courts Act. [897C D] 4. The charge against the appellant was that he had committed contempt of a court. He was guilty of Contempt of courts and was sentenced to suffer imprisonment for life. [997G] 5. The charges against the respondents were proved by the High Judge who held that they were guilty. They did not show any cause or reason to believe that they had committed Contempt of court, nor did they have any right to be heard in the case.

The appellants, who were the respondents in a suit for partition of properties, filed an application under section 34 of the , praying that the award be set aside and the decree be restored. The trial court dismissed the application on the ground that the parties had not been represented by their counsel. The High Court allowed the application holding that the appellants had not complied with the provisions of section 34(1) of the . In appeal to this Court, it was contended on behalf of the appellants that the order passed by the trial court was erroneous and that the decree was not set aside. Dismissing the appeal, ^ HELD: 1. The award is set aside as it was made in accordance with law and the parties are directed to appear before the arbitrator within a period of six weeks from today. [697C] 2. The order passed under section 35(1)(a) of , is set out in the award itself. It is not necessary that the court should have recorded its reasons for doing so. [797D] 3. The parties are required to appear on the date fixed for hearing before the court and the arbitrator shall be entitled to take steps to serve notice upon them. [897C D] 4. The court has power to make an award in accordance therewith, but it is not open to the parties to do so. It cannot be said that the Court has no jurisdiction to pass any order under section 37(1). [799D E] 5. In the instant case, the High Court had committed a manifest error of law and was not justified in passing an award. The appeal must fail.

The appellant was a tenant of the respondent. The respondent filed a suit for eviction on the ground that he had no right to continue in possession of the premises and that the appellant was not entitled to continue the tenancy. The trial court decreed the suit holding that the respondent was not a tenant within the meaning of section 2(1)(c) of the Bombay Rents, Hotel and Lodging House Rates Control Act, 1947. The High Court held that the suit was barred by limitation. In appeal to this Court it was contended on behalf of the appellant that the provisions of section 3(1) (c) were not applicable to the case in hand. HELD : (i) The respondent had no locus standi to continue his tenancy and he was entitled to be continued in possession as a tenant under the Act. [808 B] (ii) The High Courts have erred in holding that there was no valid contract between the parties and the appellant could not be said to have been terminated by the respondent on the grounds of bona fide requirement. The appellant had no cause of action for the suit. The suit was therefore barred by time. [908 B C] (iii) The appellant was entitled only to continue as a licensee under the provisions contained in section 3 (1)(b). The High court erred in dismissing the suit on the basis that the contract between him and the respondent had been terminated on the terms of the contract. [1008 D E] (iv) The contention that the agreement between the appellant and the respondents was not valid because the appellant had not been able to continue it as a lessee under the agreement, was not correct.

The appellant was a student of the respondent University. The respondents were prosecuted for offences under section 161 read with Section 34 I.P.C. and Section 5(1)(d) of the Prevention of Corruption Act, 1947. The High Court dismissed the writ petitions holding that the charges framed against the respondents were not proved beyond reasonable doubt and directed the respondents to produce the relevant record before the Board for examination. In appeal by special leave, it was contended on behalf of the appellant that the High Court had no jurisdiction to interfere with the order of the High court in exercise of its revisional power under Article 136 of the Constitution. Dismissing the appeals, this Court, HELD: 1. The impugned orders are not based on any evidence or material which is not permissible in law. [797C] 2.1 The High Courts have no jurisdiction in interfering with the findings of the Enquiry Committee and the High Courts. They have no power to interfere in the matter. [ 797F] 3.2 In the instant case, the High Power Committee had no power under Section 5 (1) of Prevention of Money Laundering Act, 1988 to interfere or interfere with any order passed by the Board. The power conferred on the Board under Section 4(1) is not confined to the power of the Board to interfere. [897F G] 3.(a) In the absence of any material to show that the enquiry was vitiated by any error apparent on the face of record, it cannot be said that the impugned orders were passed without jurisdiction or in violation of principles of natural justice. [997G H; 997A B] 4.3 The High Power Committees have no powers under Section 15(1), and the power to take disciplinary action against the delinquent officer is not restricted to the powers conferred on them by Section 16(1). [998C D] (b) In a case where the enquiry is vitiated by an error apparent, it is not open to the High Committee to interfere only with the finding of the enquiry committee and the Appellate Court. [1097G] 4.(c) The High power under section 15(2) is confined to powers of the disciplinary authority in respect of any matter which is in the nature of a quasi judicial function. It is not possible to hold that the findings are based on some evidence or materials. [ 1097F H; 1097A C] 4(d) The power of interference under Article 226 is not limited to the exercise of such power by the High power. [1197G G] 5.(e) In cases where the High Commis sioner has no jurisdiction, it may interfere with an order passed in exercise thereof. But in a case like this, the power conferred upon the Board is confined only to the discretion of the Court and not to the extent of interference by the Court. The exercise of the power under sub section (1), is limited to those powers which are exercised by the disciplinary authorities.

The appellant was charged with offences under sections 120B, 420 and 471 of the Indian Penal Code. The trial court acquitted all the accused on the ground that they were guilty of criminal misconduct and that the prosecution had failed to prove that the appellants had committed the offence of criminal breach of trust. On appeal by special leave it was contended for the appellant that the conviction of the appellants under section 120B was not justified because the prosecution did not prove that there was a public servant in the matter of the commission of the alleged offence and that there were no public servant within the meaning of section 2(1) (a) of the Prevention of Corruption Act, 1947. Held, that the High Court was right in holding that the appellant had committed an offence under section 5(1)(d) of that Act. The conviction of a person under section 4(1), therefore, must be set aside and the conviction is upheld. Section 5(2) (b) of Prevention of Vigilance Act, 1946, provides that if any public servant is found guilty of any criminal breach or of trust, he shall be punished with imprisonment for a term which may extend to one year or with fine which may extent to one thousand rupees. The offence of the appellant was not proved by evidence. The prosecution did prove that he had committed a criminal breach and that he was guilty of such criminal breach. Held further, that there is no public servants within the definition of section 5 (1) of Act. Section 4(2)(d), therefore does not apply to an offence of which the public servant has been found guilty. The appellant was entitled to be punished under section 3(1).

The respondent Bank, a bank, was the guarantor of the appellant Bank. The appellant Bank had agreed to pay the amount due under the said agreement and the Bank had also agreed to accept the same. The Bank issued a notice to the appellant for recovery of the amount. The respondent Bank filed a suit against the Bank. In the trial court the appellant contended that the bank was not entitled to recover the amount from the Bank as it was not liable to pay any amount due to the Bank under the terms of the contract and that the Bank was not bound by the terms and conditions of the said contract. The trial court decreed the suit holding that the respondent had no right to recover it from the appellant. In appeal, the High Court held that the appellant had no locus standi to file a suit for recovery against the bank. Dismissing the appeal, ^ HELD: 1.1 The High Court was in error in holding that there was no contract between the parties and the appellant was not a guarantor of any goods. [601B] 2.2 In view of the fact that the contract was not one of contract and the respondent Bank had no authority to enforce it, the bank could not be said to have committed any breach of the terms or conditions of contract. [702C D] 3.3 The High court was in wrong error in allowing the appeal. [802F] 4.4 In view thereof, the appellant is entitled to get a decree for recovery from the respondent. [903G H] 5.5 The High Courts have rightly held that there had been no contract with the Bank and the bank had not acted upon it. [1003C D].

The appellant was a Hindu undivided family. The respondent, who was the owner of the land in dispute, filed a suit for possession of certain lands on the ground that he had been in continuous service as an intermediary and that he was not entitled to any benefit under the rules. The trial court decreed the suit holding that the appellant was not a 'intermediary ' within the meaning of section 2(1) (c) of the Bombay Tenancy Act, 1948. The High Court held that the respondent was not an intermediary within the definition of "intermediaries" and that the suit was barred by limitation. In appeal to this Court it was contended on behalf of the appellant that the High Court had no jurisdiction to entertain a suit under article 226 of the Constitution. HELD : (i) The High court was right in holding that there was no evidence to show that the lands were not "inter intermediary" within the ambit of section 3(1)(c). [601 B] (ii) The appellant was an intermediary in the land and was entitled to claim the benefit under r. 6 of the Rules. [602 C D] (iii) The respondent was a ' Intermediary " within the scope of section 5(1), but he was entitled only to claim that the grant was not in accordance with the rules, and that it was not open to him to raise any question as to whether the grant had been made by an intermediary or not. [702 C] (iv) The grant was in accordancewith the rules framed under the Act.

The appellant, a Hindu undivided family, was the owner of certain properties in the name of his father. The respondents were the sons of one of them and the other two of them were the heirs of the deceased. The appellant claimed that he had no right to claim partition of the properties in question as they were not entitled to claim any partition of their properties. The High Court held that the appellant was entitled to succeed on the ground that the respondents were not members of the joint family and that the properties were not liable to be partitioned. In appeal by special leave, HELD : (i) The High Courts had rightly held that there was no evidence to show that the property in question was not liable for partition. [601 B] (ii) The appellant 's father was a member of the family and was entitled only to claim the partition of his properties. He was not entitled under the rules of succession to the properties. [702 C] (iii) The respondents had no title to the property as they had no rights to claim that the estate in question had been partitioned. [ 702 B] In the present case, the appellant ' father had no interest in the properties and were not the heirs. He had no share in the property. His father was entitled under section 6 of the Act. The suit was barred by limitation. [803 C] In view of the provisions of section 5(1) of the Madras Hindu Religious Endowments Act, 1950, the respondents could not claim any interest in that properties. They were not parties to the suit. [902 B D] (iv) The question whether the appellant had no locus standi to file a suit for partition or for partition was not decided by the High Court.

The appellants are manufacturers of cotton yarn and cotton yarn. They were manufacturing cotton yarn in the factory of the respondent. The respondents were manufacturing the cotton yarn from which they were manufactured. The appellants claimed that the cotton fabrics were not excisable goods as they were not entitled to exemption under Rule 57A(1) of the Central Excise Rules, 1944. The Assistant Collector rejected the claim and held that the said cotton fabrics was liable to duty under Rule 56A(2). The appellants filed a writ petition in the High Court challenging the validity of the said rule. The High Court dismissed the writ petition holding that the impugned rule did not apply to the facts of the case. In appeal by special leave, it was contended on behalf of the appellants that the rule does not apply in the present case because the rule is applicable only to the goods manufactured and cleared from the factory. Dismissing the appeal, ^ HELD: 1. The rule does apply only to goods manufactured or cleared from a factory. It is well settled that the word "manufacture" has been used in the context of the rule which is not applicable to the case of the present appellants. [636C] 2. In the instant case, the appellants were manufacturing yarn and yarn from the premises of the respondents. They have also produced the relevant rules for their clearance. The said rules do not apply even to the factory where they are manufactured or removed from the factories. It does not mean that the goods are manufactured by the appellants. Therefore, the rule cannot be applied in the instant cases. [736C D] 3. In view of the above, the impugned rules are liable to be struck down as ultra vires and void. [836D E] 4. The contention of the appellant is that the rules do apply only when they are produced from a factories. They are not applicable in the case where the goods have been manufactured or sold by the respondents, but are manufactured and removed from a warehouse. Therefore the rule applies to the appellants as they are not excisable. [936C E] 5. The impugned rules do no help to the appellant because the appellants are manufacturing yarn from a place other than the factory in which they are cleared from their factory. They cannot be said to have been manufacturing the yarn from one place other and therefore, they cannot be treated as excisable goods.

The petitioner, a private limited company, was registered under the Uttar Pradesh Transport Corporation Act, 1976. The petitioner filed an application under section 151 of the Code of Civil Procedure for setting aside the order of the District Judge dated January 20, 1979 and for a declaration that the scheme of the State Transport Authority was not valid and that the petitioner was entitled to be impleaded as a party to the suit. The trial court dismissed the application holding that the petition was barred by limitation. The High Court held that the application under article 227 of the Constitution was maintainable because the petitioner had filed an objection to the maintainability of the petition on the ground that the objections were not properly considered and that no order of dismissal passed by the District judge was required to be set aside. In appeal, this Court, HELD: 1. The scheme of State Transport Undertaking is a statutory one and it is not a statutory provision but a statutory right. It is a constitutional right which has been conferred on the State Government under article 226 of the constitution. [723F] 2. The object of the Act is to provide for the speedy trial of suits, appeals and revisions in courts of law. The purpose of the scheme is to enable the court to decide whether the objections are properly considered or not. It has been held that no objection should be taken at the time of hearing of the suit and that it is open to the court concerned to pass an order on the merits of the case. [823F G] 3. The Act does not provide for any remedy in a civil court. The power of the court under article 136 is not confined to the jurisdiction of the civil court but only to the extent provided by the Act. It does not confer any right on the court or the court, as the case may be. [923F H] 4. The legislature has conferred a wide power on the Court to make an order for the trial of the suits and revisions. The jurisdiction of civil courts is limited to the powers of the Civil Courts under article 133. It cannot be said that the power of a civil Court under article 134 is not restricted to the power to decide all questions relating to the right, title or interest in the property. [1023F F] 5. In the instant case, the petitioner has filed an appeal against the order passed by District Judge on January 20. 1979 and the High Court has rightly held that it was not open to him to raise any objection at the stage of hearing. The petition is therefore dismissed.

The appellant was charged with offences under section 120B, I.P.C., read with section 5(1)(d) of the Prevention of Corruption Act, 1947 and section 5 (2) of that Act for having committed an offence punishable under section 5 of the Indian Penal Code, and section 6(3) of this Act was added to section 5A of the Act. The appellant was convicted by the Special Judge under section 3(1) read with s.5(1). He was sentenced to undergo rigorous imprisonment for a period of one year and fine of Rs. 500/ in default to further undergo simple imprisonment for two months. On appeal, the High Court held that the appellant had committed an act of criminal conspiracy and that he was not guilty of any offence punishable with imprisonment for more than three years. The High Court also held that there was no evidence on record to show that the act of the appellant was done by him in furtherance of his official duty. On further appeal, HELD : (i) The appellant had been convicted under section 4(1), read with r. 5(2)(d). [619 D] (ii) The prosecution case was that the acts of criminal trespass were committed by a person in furtherance thereof and that the offence was committed by him at the instance of another person in pursuance of his duty. The fact that the accused had been charged with an offence under section 6, was not sufficient to prove that he had been guilty of such act.

The appellant was charged with offences under section 120B, I.P.C., read with section 5(1) of the Indian Penal Code and section 5 (2) of that Act for having committed an offence punishable under section 5 of the Prevention of Corruption Act, 1947. The trial court convicted him on the ground that he had been guilty of a criminal misconduct and sentenced him to undergo imprisonment for one year. The High Court held that the appellant was guilty of the offences under sections 120B and I. P.C. and section 4(1)(a) of Prevention of Anti Corruption Act. In appeal to this Court it was contended on behalf of the appellant that the sanction of the Government had been obtained by a person who was not competent to sanction the prosecution, and that the Government could not have acted in accordance with the procedure prescribed by the Code of Criminal Procedure. Held, further, that the High Court was right in holding that the prosecution had failed to prove that the charges were proved beyond reasonable doubt. The appellant was entitled to the benefit of section 5 Of the Prevention Of Corruption Act and he was entitled only to the benefits of section 4 Of the Act. Held: (i) that the order of sanction passed by the Government under section 4 of the Act was not a valid sanction and it could not be said that the Magistrate had acted in conformity with the provisions of section 3 Of the Code. The sanction of Government was not necessary for the prosecution to prove the charges. The fact that the charge was proved beyond doubt was not sufficient to establish the charges against the appellant. (ii) that there was no evidence on record to show that the accused had been charged with an offence under section 3(1).

The appellant landlord filed a suit for eviction of the respondents tenant on the ground that he was in possession of the premises in question. The respondents contended that the premises were not bona fide and that the respondents had no right to evict them from the premises. The trial court decreed the suit holding that the appellant was in occupation of the property in question, and that they were entitled to eviction under section 14(1)(a) of the Tamil Nadu Buildings (Lease and Rent Control) Act, 1960. The High Court held that the respondent was not a tenant within the meaning of section 2(e) of that Act. In appeal by special leave it was contended on behalf of the appellant that the High Court erred in holding that there was no relationship between the landlord and the tenant. Dismissing the appeal, ^ HELD: (1) The High court was right in holding the respondents ' suit for ejectment under section 15(1) of Act. [601 B] (2) The finding of fact recorded by the appellate court is not correct. It is well settled that a landlord has no right or title to the property and he cannot be evicted from the property. [702 C] (3) In the instant case, the respondents have been in occupation for more than one year and they are entitled to evict the appellant from the said premises. They are not entitled to any eviction under the Act. The finding recorded by both the appellate courts is correct. [803 B] In view of the fact that the landlord has a right or interest in the property, it cannot be said that the tenant was in actual possession of it. [902 C D] (4) The appellant 's case is that the tenancy was not bona bonafide and therefore the respondents are entitled for eviction under sections 14(2)(a), 15(3) and 16(1).

The respondent was a tenant of the land in dispute. The respondent filed an execution petition against the decree holder for possession of the property on the ground that he had no right to hold the land as a tenant under section 3(1) of U.P. Zamindari Abolition and Land Reforms Act, 1950. The executing court held that the respondent was not entitled to hold it as a mortgagee under section 4(1). The High Court dismissed the execution petition holding that the decreeholder was not liable to pay any compensation for the land on which he had been declared as a mortgagor. In appeal by special leave, the appellant contended that the judgment debtor was not a tenant within the meaning of section 3 (1) and therefore, the decree holders were entitled to the compensation under section 5(1)(a). Dismissing the appeal, HELD: 1. The word 'owner ' in section 2(1), is wide enough to include a person who has been declared a mortgagee by law. [703 B] 2. The definition of "land" in section 3 of the U. P. Zamindari and Land Revenue Act, 1953, does not cover the entire area of land which is held by him as a lessee under section 6(1); but it does not include a tenant who has become an mortgagee under the provisions of the Act. [ 703 B C] 3. The expression "land", in section 5 (1), means any person who holds land as such and includes a person holding land as an mortgagee. It is well settled that the word 'land" is wide and it does include a land which has been held by a person to hold land as tenant under the Act, but only a land held by the person to whom the land is held is not a "land". [704 B] 4. The term "land " in section 6 (1)(b) means any land which may be held by himself as an owner of the holding. It does not mean any land held for the purpose of the Land Revenue Code, but includes any land in the holding and it is only a 'land '. [603 B D] 5. The words "land ' in Section 6(2) are wide enough. In the present case, the word "land' in section 7(1A), are wide and they include a 'lands '. It cannot be said that the term "lands" is wider than the land held under the U P Zamindari Abolition Act, 1951.

The appellants were convicted under Section 302 read with Section 34 IPC and sentenced to undergo rigorous imprisonment for life. The High Court acquitted the appellants of all charges. In appeal by special leave, it was contended on behalf of the appellants that the prosecution had failed to prove the charge against them beyond reasonable doubt and that the conviction of the accused under Section 304 Part I IPC was not sustainable in law. Dismissing the appeals, this Court, HELD: 1. The prosecution has failed to establish the charge of murder punishable under Section 34 of the Indian Penal Code. [601D] 2.1 The prosecution had proved the charge beyond reasonable doubts and that there was no evidence on record to show that the appellants were guilty of the offence punishable under Sections 302 readwith Section 34, IPC. [702F] 3.2 In view of the fact that the accused were charged with the murder of one of the deceased, the conviction under Section 201 Part I I IPC is not sustainable and the conviction cannot be sustained. The conviction under section 201 Part II IPC is set aside. [803G H; 804A] 4.3 The prosecution case was that on the date of occurrence the appellants had gone to the shop of one A1, A2 and A4. They were armed with a knife and they were armed by a knife. The accused were armed armed with weapons. They had also attacked the deceased with a stick. The injuries sustained by him were simple in nature. The injury was caused by a sharp edged weapon. [903G] 4:3 In view thereof, the appellants are entitled to the benefit of Section 34 and they are entitled for the benefit under Section34 IPC. The offence punishable is not one of murder but it is one of culpable homicide amounting to murder. [1004B C] 5.4 The prosecution failed to show any intention or intent to cause death in the course of the occurrence. The appellants were charged under Sections 307 and 302 read together with Section 149 IPC. They are also convicted under Sections 201 PartI, IPC and they have been sentenced to suffer rigorous imprisonment. [0904C D] 5:5 The prosecution did not prove that A1 had caused the death of A2. The trial court acquitted all the appellants on the ground that the injuries sustained were simple. The appeal is allowed. The judgment of the High Court is set-aside and the appellants be convicted under section 302 read alongwith Section 34.

The assessee company was a registered firm carrying on business in India. The assessee company had entered into an agreement with the foreign company for the supply of foreign liquor to its customers and the foreign companies. The foreign company was also liable to pay income tax under section 10(1) (a)(i) of the Income Tax Act, 1922. The Indian Income Tax Officer held that the foreign Company was not a registered company and accordingly the foreign exchange was liable to be taxed under section 11(2). The assessee filed appeals before the Appellate Assistant Commissioner. The Tribunal allowed the appeals holding that the Indian Income tax Officer had no jurisdiction to assess the income of the assessee for the purpose of assessment under section 16(1)(a) of that Act. In appeal, the High Court held that since the foreign currency was not an Indian currency, it could not be taxed in respect of the foreign liquor which was a foreign currency. The High Court also held that there was no evidence to show that the assessee had any income from the foreign country and that the amount received by the foreign firm was not taxable under section 8(1). In appeal to this Court, it was contended on behalf of the revenue that the income received by it was a revenue receipt and therefore the foreign bank was liable for assessment under Section 16(2) (b)(i), as it stood before the amendment of the Indian Finance Act, 1969. Dismissing the appeals, ^ HELD: 1. The word "income" in section 10 (1) of this Act means income received from a foreign company and not income received or received by a foreign Company. It is only when the foreign money is received by an assessee for his own use, that the receipt is made by him to the foreign foreign company. [797C] 2. The expression "income", in section 8 (1), means income which is received from any foreign company or other person. In the present case, the foreign sum received by foreign company is not a revenue receipts and therefore it cannot be taxed as income received. [ 797F G] 3. The receipt was made by the Indian Indian currency to the Indian Company. The amount received in the foreign India was not the income from which the foreign business was carried on. It was only when it was received by him that the money was received and received by his foreign company, that it was not liable for tax under Section 8(2)(a). [799F G; 797A] 4. The Income Tax officer had no power to assess income of a foreign country. The Appellate Assistant Commissioners had also no jurisdiction in respect to the said foreign currency as it was never received by any foreign Company and therefore, the Indian income received was not exempt from tax under the provisions of Section 8 (2) of Act. [897F] 5. In view of the fact that the receipts were made by foreign companies, the assessee could not have claimed deduction under section 7(1), as the foreign receipt was not received by them. The question whether the foreign amount received from foreign company in India or not is a revenue expenditure and therefore not a question of law. [997F H] 6. In this case, it is not possible to hold that the said receipts were not income from other sources. It may be that the payments were made to foreign companies only when they were received by their foreign company but were received in India and not by the assessee. The payment was made to the Foreign Company on the basis of the receipt. [1097F F] 7. In order to determine whether the Indian currency was an Indian Indian or foreign currency, the Tribunal has to decide whether the receipts received by its foreign company were income from foreign country or foreign companies and not whether the receipt was received in Indian currency.

The appellant was convicted under section 302 read with section 34 I.P.C., and sentenced to death. The High Court acquitted the appellant of all the charges. In appeal to this Court, HELD : (i) The evidence of a witness is not sufficient to prove that he had been guilty of an offence under section 34, I. P.C. but it is sufficient if the witness has been convicted for an offence punishable under section 201 read with s.34 I.T. and section 34. [601 B] (ii) The testimony of a person who is in jail is not relevant to the question whether he was guilty of any offence under the Indian Penal Code, but it must be shown that he has been guilty for an act which is done by him or by some other person. It is also necessary that the witness should have been examined before the court and the court should have regard to the circumstances of each case. [701 B C] (iii) The High Courts were right in holding that the evidence of the witness was not sufficient for the purpose of proving that he was convicted for any offence punishable with death or imprisonment for life. [802 D E] (iv) The statement of a man who is a member of a family of a deceased, cannot be relied upon as a witness against him unless it is corroborated by some evidence. [901 B D] (v) The fact that the appellant was acquitted for an alleged offence under s. 201 readwith section 34 does not make any difference in the position of law and the evidence given by the witness is sufficient to establish that he is guilty of the offence under which he is convicted.

The appellant was charged with offences under section 409 I.P.C. and section 5(1)(d) of the Prevention of Corruption Act, 1947. The appellant was convicted for an offence under section 420 I. P.C., and sentenced to undergo rigorous imprisonment for a period of one year. He was also convicted for the offence under sections 409 I .P. C. and s. 5(2)(d). The High Court held that the appellant was guilty of the offences under sections 467, 468 and 471 I.A. and S. 5 (1) (d) and section 6(1) of Prevention of Criminal Procedure. In appeal to this Court it was contended on behalf of the appellant that the provisions of section 5 (2)(a) were not applicable to the case in hand because the appellant had been charged with an offence of criminal breach of trust and that he was not guilty of any offence under s.5(1). HELD : The High court was right in holding that the word "public servant" used in section 5 of the Act must be construed in a sense which would include a public servant within the meaning of section 2(2) (a) of that Act. [620 H] In the instant case, the appellant did not have any connection with the work of the Public Works Department and was therefore guilty of an offence punishable under section 5. The High Courts were right in coming to the conclusion that the offence was committed by him within the definition of "public servants" as defined in section 2 (2) of Act. In the present case, there is no evidence on record to show that the public servant was charged for any offence punishable with imprisonment for more than one year and that the Public Service Department was not competent to take cognizance of the offence. [720 H; 720 A] The High 's decision in State of Punjab vs Ram Chander, ; , referred to.

The appellant was convicted under section 3(1) of the Bombay Prevention of Anti Social Activities Act, 1958. The High Court confirmed the conviction and sentence but acquitted him. In appeal to this Court it was contended on behalf of the appellant that the order of acquittal passed by the District Magistrate was not a judicial order and therefore the order was not an administrative order. HELD: (i) The order of conviction is a judicial one and does not require any interference under article 136 of the Constitution. [630 H] (ii) The High court has no power to interfere with the order passed by a District Magistrate. [730 A B] (iii) The appellant was not entitled to the benefit of section 3 of the Act. [831 C D] (iv) The District Magistrate had no jurisdiction to deal with the case in accordance with the procedure prescribed by the rules. [932 F G] (v) The power conferred on him under section 4(1)(a) is not confined to the power of the District Collector to dealwith the case. [1031 C E] (vi) The provisions of the Code of Criminal Procedure are not intended to be used in a particular manner and they do not intend to confer any power on the High Court to deal under section 5(1). [832 F H] In the present case, the appellant was found guilty of an offence under section 6(1), but he did not comply with the requirements of section 4. The District magistrate had no power under section 7(1); and the order made by the High court was not in accordance therewith.

The appellant was convicted under section 302 I.P.C., and sentenced to death for life. The High Court acquitted the appellant of all the charges. In appeal to this Court it was contended on behalf of the State that the prosecution had failed to prove its case beyond reasonable doubt that the deceased was a member of an unlawful assembly and that the accused were guilty of murder and that he was not guilty of any offence under section 304 I. P.C. and that there was no evidence to show that the appellant was a person who was responsible for the commission of the crime. Dismissing the appeal, ^ HELD: (1) The prosecution had proved its case against the accused beyond reasonable doubts and the High Court was right in holding that the offence under sections 302 I I.T.P., is not established. [601 B] (2) The evidence of the eye witnesses to the occurrence was not corroborated by any other evidence. The evidence on record clearly showed that the appellants were armed with a knife, and that they had been falsely implicated in the case. The prosecution failed to establish its case. [702 C D] (3) The High court was right when it held that the evidence of eye witnesses could not be accepted as reliable. [803 B] In the instant case, the evidence on behalf behalf of both the accused was not supported by any independent evidence. It is true that the High court had taken a view that the testimony of the two eye witnesses were not reliable and that it was not possible to hold that the two accused were responsible for murder. [903 B C] (4) The fact that the three accused were armed together with a weapon, does not make any difference in the evidence.

The appellant was convicted under section 302 read with section 34 I.P.C., and sentenced to death. The High Court acquitted the accused on the ground that he had been falsely implicated in the case, and that the prosecution had failed to prove that the deceased had committed the murder of his brother. On appeal by special leave, HELD : (i) The evidence of the eye witnesses was not reliable because they were interested witnesses. The evidence given by the eye witness was not sufficient to establish the charge against the accused. [619 D] (ii) The High court was right in holding that the evidence of eye witnesses could be accepted as reliable and the conviction of the appellant under section 34, I. P.C. is based on the evidence which was not corroborated by the medical evidence. [720 F G] (iii) The prosecution had not proved that the accused had committed murder of their brother. The prosecution did not prove that there were any other persons who were present at the time of the occurrence and that they were falsely implicated. [819 E H; 820 A B] (iv) The conviction under section 307 read with Section 34 I, P. C., is based upon the evidence given in the light of the evidence adduced by the prosecution. It is not possible to hold that the appellant had committed any offence and that he was falsely implicated on the basis of the medical report. [920 F] (v) The fact that the eye eyewitnesses were interested witness, does not make out a case against the appellant for his conviction under sections 302 readwith section 34. [1021 E H] (vi) The charge against him is based only upon the statement made by the accused in the Court of Session and not on the other hand.

The petitioner, a company, was registered under the provisions of the , and the Central Excise Act, 1944. The petitioner, who was a manufacturer of goods, filed a writ petition in the High Court challenging the validity of the assessment order on the ground that the petitioner had not been able to pay the duty and that the levy of interest on the amount of duty was illegal. The High Court dismissed the writ petition holding that the assessment was illegal and void. In appeal by special leave, it was contended for the petitioner that the rate of interest was not applicable to the case in hand. Dismissing the appeal, this Court, HELD: 1.1 The petitioner had been able only to pay duty on the value of goods imported by him. He had also been able by the Customs authorities to pay interest on such amount. [797C] 2.2 The petitioner was not entitled to any relief in view of the provisions contained in section 14(3) of the Act. [897D] 3.1 In the instant case, the petitioner was a dealer and he had been paying duty on goods imported. He was also liable to pay excise duty on such goods. [997C D] 2.(a) The petitioner could not be said to have paid duty on imported goods. He did not pay any interest on that amount. He could not claim any relief under the Act because he had paid the duty. [1097D E] 3(b) The question whether the levy was illegal or void is a matter of discretion and cannot be decided by the Court in exercise of its jurisdiction under Article 226 of the Constitution. [1197C F] 4.(c) In the present case, there was no dispute that the duty was payable on the goods imported and cleared. The question as to whether the petitioner could pay the excise duty or not is a question of fact.

The respondent was the owner of a property in which he purchased certain properties. The sale was confirmed by the Collector on appeal by the appellants and the decree was confirmed. In appeal to this Court, HELD : (i) The sale of the properties was not valid because the sale was made for a period of one year from the date of the sale. [601 B] (ii) The respondent had no right to sell the property in question. The suit was barred by section 14(1)(b) of the Bombay Land Revenue Code, 1879. [702 C D] (iii) The decree was not a decree for money and it was not open to the appellants to claim that the sale had been made for the purpose of the Act. [803 B] In the present case, the sale in question was made on the basis of a registered deed of sale dated March 31, 1946, executed by the respondent. The mortgage was not registered as a result of which the sale could be effected. The decree did not create any right or interest in the property. [903 B C] (iv) The suit for money was barred under section 14 (1)(a). The sale in dispute was made after the expiry of the period of limitation prescribed by section 15(1) (b) and the sale of properties were confirmed on March 31. 1946, and the suit was dismissed on that ground. [1003 B D] In view of the provisions of section 14 of the Code of Civil Procedure, 1908, the decree could not be executed in favour of the respondent on the ground that it was a decree of money and not a mortgage. The High Court was right in holding that the decree for sale was not properly passed. [1103 B E] (v) The judgment of the High Court is set aside. [1203 C D].

The petitioners were tried for offences under sections 302 and 120B of the Indian Penal Code, 1860. The petitioners were charged with offences under section 302 read with Section 34 of the I.P.C. and Sections 3(1)(a) and 4(2) of the Prevention of Corruption Act, 1947. They were tried by the Special Judge for offences punishable under sections 120B and 4 of the . The Special Judge held that the petitioners had committed offences under Sections 302 readwith Section 34 and 4 (3) of Prevention of Anti Social Activities Act, 1988. The Special judge also held that there was no evidence to show that the alleged incident took place in the course of the investigation and that the allegations made by the petitioners were false. In the writ petition filed by the Petitioners it was contended that the Special judge had not committed any offence under section 3(2)(a). Dismissing the Writ Petition, ^ HELD: 1. The provisions of Section 4(1) of Act are mandatory in nature and the same should be complied with within a period of six months from the date of receipt of the report. [615H; 716A] 2. In view of the fact that the charge sheet was filed on the basis of the allegations contained in the charge sheets, it is not possible to hold that the charges were proved and that there had been no evidence against the petitioners. The charge sheet could not be said to have been filed beyond six months. [716B] 3. In any case, the Special Court was justified in holding that the allegation made by petitioners were true. [817C D] 4. The allegations contained therein are vague and do not disclose any offence of criminal nature. It is also not possible for the Special Officer to hold a preliminary inquiry against the Petitioners. [917E F] 5. In order to find out whether the allegations in the charges are correct or not, it must be shown that there has been no material before him to show any such allegation. The report of the Special Committee is not based on any evidence. It may also be possible for a Special Officer not to hold an inquiry against a person who has committed an offence under Section 3(3) and Section 4 (2)(b). [918D] 6. In a case where the allegations are vague, it should be shown by the Investigating Officer that there is no evidence on record to show the involvement of the petitioners in the alleged crime. The Investigating Officer must have been given an opportunity to cross examine the witnesses and to make his defence. [1017E G] 7. It was not possible or desirable for a special Officer to find whether the allegation contained therein were true or not. [1117C E] 8. In such a case, it would be appropriate to hold the preliminary inquiry as directed by the High Court.

The petitioners were carrying on business in the State of Rajasthan. The respondent was a registered dealer under the Rajasthan Motor Vehicles Taxation Act, 1950. The petitioners were assessed to tax under the Act and the tax was levied on them under the provisions of the Act. The petitioner challenged the validity of the levy on the ground that the tax imposed by the State Government under section 3(1) of the Rajasthan General Sales Tax Act, 1958 was not a tax on the turnover of the petitioners. The High Court held that the levy was invalid because it was not in accordance with the provisions contained in the Act as it stood before the amendment of the Rules and the Rules were ultra vires. In appeal to this Court it was contended for the petitioners that the State Legislature had no power to impose a tax under section 4(1)(a) of Rajasthan General Tax Act. HELD: (i) The levy is invalid because the tax is imposed on the dealer in respect of goods carried by him and not on his turnover. [636 B] (ii) The tax is levied on the basis of the rate of tax payable under section 5(1). If the tax has been paid, it will be a tax which is leviable on the goods carried in the course of inter State trade or commerce. It is not necessary that the rate should be fixed by the Government. [736 B C] (iii) The Act does not provide for any levy on a turnover of a particular class of goods and the levy is valid because it is not in conformity with the rates prescribed under section 6(1), but it is only in accordance to the provisions relating to the rate at which the tax can be levied. [836 B D] (iv) The State Legislature has no power either to impose any tax on a particular goods carried on by him or on his behalf. It cannot be said that the Act does provide for levy of tax on such goods carried carried in other course of trade or business.

The appellant company was a registered industrial concern. The workmen were employed in the manufacturing process of manufacture of sugar and sugar. The appellant company filed an application under Section 33A(2) of the U.P. Industrial Disputes Act, 1947 for the grant of relief to the workmen. The Labour Court dismissed the application holding that the workmen had been retrenched by the management on the ground that they were not entitled to any relief in respect of their retrenchment. The High Court held that the appellant company had failed to prove that the retrenchment was illegal and void. In appeal to this Court it was contended for the appellant that the termination of the services of the workmen was illegal because the workmen were not given a reasonable opportunity to show cause why they should not be dismissed from service. Dismissing the appeal, ^ HELD: 1. The award of the Labour Court is set aside and the matter remitted to the Industrial Tribunal for fresh decision in accordance with law. [797C] 2. The order of the High Court is restored. The appeal is allowed. There will be no order as to costs. [ 797F G] 3. In the instant case, the appellant was not given any opportunity to lead evidence in support of their claim. The Industrial Tribunal has not considered the matter properly and has come to a conclusion that the workman had been guilty of misconduct or negligence. [897C D] 4. The question whether the termination was illegal is one of fact and law. It is well settled that the award of reinstatement is based on an erroneous appreciation of evidence and cannot be sustained in any manner. [697F H; 897A B] 5. In view of the above, the Industrial Court has not committed any error in dismissing the appellant from service because it was not a case where the workman was retrenched by reason of the fact that he had been dismissed from services. The Tribunal has also come to the conclusion that there is no evidence on record which would justify the award.

The appellant was convicted under section 302 read with section 34 I.P.C., and sentenced to death. The High Court acquitted the accused of all the charges. In appeal to this Court, HELD: (1) The prosecution case is that on the date of occurrence the deceased had gone to his house for a night at about 8 p.m. when he was returning home after the incident, he was in the house and was in a position to make a statement before the police that he had gone there for a day to come to his residence. The prosecution has not proved that the deceased was in an unconscious state. [601 B] (2) The evidence of the witnesses is sufficient to prove that the accused had committed the crime. The fact that the appellant had gone with the deceased at about 9 p. m. when the deceased came to his home, does not make any difference between the evidence of P.W. 1 and the statement of P P.Ws. 2 and 3. [701 B C] (3) The High court was right in holding that the prosecution had failed to prove the guilt of the accused beyond reasonable doubt. [802 D E] (4) The conviction of the appellant under section 34, I. P.C. is set aside. [903 A] (5) The sentence imposed on him by the High Court is modified and he is sentenced to rigorous imprisonment for life.

The appellant, a mortgagee of the properties in dispute, was the owner of the property. The mortgage was executed on June 30, 1947, and the mortgage was confirmed by the trial court. On July 1, 1947 the plaintiff filed a suit for recovery of possession of the mortgaged property. In the plaint it was alleged that the plaintiff had not paid the amount due to him as security for the loan. The defendant contended that the suit was barred by limitation. The trial court decreed the suit on the ground that the mortgage in question was not executed within the meaning of section 2(1) (d) of the Indian Limitation Act, 1908 and that the defendants had failed to prove that the mortgaged properties were sold by them as security. On appeal the High Court held that the defendant had failed in proving that the loan was advanced on June 31, 1947. The High Court also held that it was not a mortgage within the definition of section 3(1)(d) and that it could not be said that the debt was advanced at the time of the execution of the mortgage deed. In appeal to this Court it was contended for the appellant that the plea of limitation was not raised in the plaint, but was raised only after the expiry of the period of limitation prescribed by section 3 (1)(e) and the suit could be dismissed on the grounds that the transaction was not one of sale within the scope of section 4(1). Held: (i) The plaintiff had failed before the trial Court to prove the plea. The suit was not barred by time. The plaintiff was entitled to a decree for recovery, but he did not do so. The defendants were entitled to the relief claimed in the suit. (ii) The suit could not have been dismissed on that ground. (iii) The defendant had not filed any written statement nor did he file any written statements. (iv) The plea of time was not taken in the written statement and it was only after a lapse of more than one year from the date of the decree, that the plaint was barred. (v) The High court was right in holding that the defence raised by the defendant was not maintainable. (vi) The defendants had not proved that the sale was made on June 1, 1948, and that they were entitled only to a relief claimed under section 3. (vii) The trial Court was right when it held that there was no cause of action for the suit to be dismissed. (viii) The contention that the High court had failed under section 4 (1) of Act, 1963, was not correct. (ix) The question whether the plaintiff was a mortgagee within the purview of section 5(1), was not decided in the absence of any evidence to show that the amount advanced by him was not due to the defendant.

The appellants were appointed as Assistant Engineers in the State of Karnataka. The State Government issued a notification dated 30th April, 1985 inviting applications for appointment to the posts of Assistant Engineers. The appellants applied for the post of Assistant Engineer on the ground that they had secured more marks than the appellants in the written test and had secured less marks than those who were selected by the Public Service Commission. The said notification was challenged before the High Court by way of a writ petition. The High Court dismissed the writ petition holding that the appellants had secured lesser marks than their juniors, and that they have been discriminated against. Allowing the appeal, this Court, HELD: 1.1 The appellants were not entitled to any relief in view of the fact that they were selected for the posts in question. They had secured higher marks than others who were appointed by Public Service Commissions. [740B] 2.2 In the instant case, the appellants have been given more marks and have been deprived of their right to be considered for appointment as Assistant Engineer.
