The selection was made on the basis of the marks obtained in the interview. The Selection Committee had not taken into consideration the fact of the appellants ' names in the select list. [840C] 3.3 In view of this, the High court has rightly held that the selection was vitiated by mala fides and is liable to be quashed. [640F] 4.4 In the facts and circumstances of the case, it cannot be said that the Selection Committee was justified in quashing the select lists.

The appellants were tried for offences under sections 302, 201 and 120B of the Indian Penal Code. The trial court acquitted all the accused persons. The High Court convicted them under section 302 read with Section 34 I.P.C. and sentenced them to life imprisonment. In appeal by special leave, it was contended on behalf of the appellants that the evidence of the eye witnesses is not reliable and the evidence in support of their testimony should be accepted as reliable and trustworthy. Dismissing the appeals, this Court, HELD: 1. The prosecution has failed to prove the guilt of the accused beyond reasonable doubt. The evidence of PW 3, who was a witness to the occurrence, is not sufficient to establish the guilt against him. [797C] 2. The testimony of PW 4, who had been examined as a witness in the case, is also not reliable. It is true that he has stated that he had seen the accused person at the time of the occurrence and he was not present at the place of occurrence. He has stated in his evidence that he saw the accused from the place where he was sitting. The fact that he was present at that time, does not make any difference to the prosecution case. [ 797C D] 3. In the instant case, the evidence on record clearly shows that he did not know the accused. He had seen him at the scene of occurrence and his presence in the place is doubtful. The statement of PW 1, who has been examined by the prosecution, does show that he knew the accused at the relevant time. [897C E] 4. In view of the fact that the witnesses were not present there was no evidence to prove that the accused had seen them at the spot. The conviction and sentence of the appellant under section 201 read with section 34 I P.C., is set aside. [997D F] 5. The appeal is allowed. The judgment of the High Court is set-aside. The appellants are acquitted from all charges. They shall be released forthwith if they are not required in any other case.

The appellants, who were employed in the manufacture of sugar and sugar products, were paid wages for the period from April 1, 1960 to March 31, 1960. The workmen claimed that they were entitled to the benefit of the bonus scheme under the Industrial Disputes Act, 1947. The Tribunal held that the workmen were entitled only to the bonus as it was not a 'industry ' within the meaning of section 2(1)(d) of the Industrial Dispute Act and that the bonus was not payable on the basis of the formula laid down in the Industrial Tribunal 's award. On appeal by special leave, HELD: The Tribunal has held that there is no evidence to show that the appellants were entitled for the bonus under the industrial Disputes Act. [690 F] In the present case, the workmen had been paid wages on the ground that they had not worked in any industry or in any other capacity. They were also entitled to bonus as they were working in the same industry and were entitled under the provisions of the Act. The appellants were not entitled to any bonus for the year 1960 to the extent they were employed by them. Their workmen were not paid wages because they had been working in that industry. Their claim was rejected by the Tribunal on the grounds that they did not work in any particular industry or that they could not be treated as 'industry within the definition of section 3(1) (d) and that they should be treated to have worked in that trade. The question whether the workmen are entitled to a bonus under that Act is a matter which has to be decided by the Industrial Tribunals.

The appellants were the tenants of a certain land in the suit. The mortgage was executed by the respondents on November 30, 1945. The appellants filed a suit for redemption of the mortgage and for recovery of possession of the mortgaged property. The trial court decreed the suit holding that the mortgage was not valid and the appellants had no right to redeem the mortgage. On appeal the High Court held that the appellants were entitled to redeem it in view of the provisions of section 52 of the Transfer of Property Act, 1882. In appeal to this Court it was contended on behalf of the appellants that the suit was barred by limitation as the appellants did not have any right to redemption and that the respondents had no locus standi to redeem them in view thereof. Held: (i) The High Court was right in holding that section 52 was applicable only to cases where a person has been declared as an owner of the property, and the provisions contained in section 52 are applicable only when a person is declared as a owner of such property. In the present case the appellants have no locus to redeem his mortgage. The respondents had not filed any suit for recovery against them. The High court was right that the appellant was entitled to redemption on the ground that they were not entitled to the redemption and the respondents were not liable to be evicted from the property. (ii) The appellants were not in possession of any part of the land. (iii) The respondents were entitled only to redeem their mortgage. (iv) The suit was not barred by time as the appellant did not file any suit against them, but they had no title to the property and that they could not be evicted therefrom. (v) The question whether the appellants ' right to the redeem is a matter of law or fact. (vi) The expression "any person" in section 53(1)(b) of the Code of Civil Procedure means a person who has been duly declared as owner of any property and includes a person whose interest in the property is affected by the order of the Court. (vii) The word "any other person" used in section 54(1) of that Code does not mean a person having been duly elected as an agent or manager of such land. The expression 'any person who is duly declared to be a person duly elected and the person who was duly elected has no right, title or interest in such property, but only means a right which is affected thereby by the orders of the court. (viii) The words "any such person" are wide enough to include a person holding any interest therein. (ix) The term "any persons" used under section 53 of the Act does not include a holder of a share in the land and it includes a holder who is deemed to be an agent of such person. (x) The definition of "any property" in the Code does indicate that the person holding such interest therein has no title or right, but it does not imply that he holds any interest in it. (xi) The provisions contained under section 52(1), are applicable to cases which have been filed before the Court and which have not been done by the appellants.

The respondent company was a registered dealer under the U.P. Sales Tax Act, 1948. The respondent company claimed exemption from tax on sales of cotton yarn and cotton yarn in respect of which the respondent company had not filed any return for the assessment year 1966 67. The Sales Tax Officer rejected the claim of the respondent that the goods were not liable to tax under the Sales Tax Rules, because the respondent Company was a dealer within the meaning of Entry 66 of List II of the Seventh Schedule to the Constitution. The High Court held that the respondent had not produced any return in respect thereof and that the sales were liable to be taxed under the Act. In appeal by special leave it was contended on behalf of the appellant that the expression "goods" used in Entry 66 means goods which are chargeable to tax. Dismissing the appeal, HELD: (1) The word "goods", in Entry 67 means goods specified in the Schedule to this Act and not those which are liable to pay tax under any other law for the time being in force. [707C] (2) In the instant case, the respondent was a manufacturer of cotton fabrics and cotton fabrics. It is not disputed that the appellant had produced any books of account or other documents relating thereto. The question whether the goods are liable for tax under Entry 66 does not arise. [ 707F G] (3) The High Courts have held that in view of the definition of "goods ' in Entry 65, List II, the word "sale" is used in entry 66.

The appellant was a workman of the respondent company. The respondents were employed in the factory of the appellant and were working as a Manager in the Mills. The appellant was dismissed from service on the ground that he had been transferred to the Mills by an order dated September 9, 1949, which was confirmed by the Labour Court. The Industrial Tribunal held that the transfer of the respondents was not justified because the transfer was made by an employer within the meaning of section 2(1)(d) of the U.P. Industrial Disputes Act, 1947, and that the appellant had been employed in a factory for more than one year and that it was not necessary to hold that the order of dismissal was valid. The Tribunal held against the respondents. In appeal to this Court, HELD : (i) The transfer of an employee by an employee is not justified under section 2 (1)(e) of that Act. [801 B] (ii) The appellant had no right to continue in his employment as a workman within the definition of section 3(1) (d) and therefore he was entitled to continue on the same terms as were applicable to him. [702 C D] (iii) The order of the Tribunal is not correct because it was made after the transfer, but it was only by an agreement between the parties that the employee had been appointed in a particular place. [901 B C] (iv) The Tribunal has rightly held that there was no transfer of a workman by an establishment to another place and therefore the order passed by the Tribunal was not valid.

The appellant, a company incorporated under the Companies Act, 1956, was a 'State ' within the meaning of section 2(1)(c) of the , and the appellant was a "State '. The appellant was employed as an Assistant Manager in the respondent Corporation. The respondent Corporation issued a notification under section 3 of the Act on March 1, 1973, for the establishment of the appellant. The notification was published in the Official Gazette on April 1, 1974. The State Government issued a Notification under section 4 of the . The appellant filed a writ petition before the High Court challenging the validity of the notification. The High Court dismissed the writ petition holding that the notification was invalid and ultra vires the Constitution. In appeal to this Court it was contended for the appellant that the Act was not in force as it stood on April 2, 1974 and that the provisions of the said Act were not applicable to the establishment and therefore the provisions contained therein could not be applied to the establishments. Dismissing the appeal, ^ HELD: The notification issued under section 6 of the is valid and cannot be challenged by a writ petitioner. [620H; 720A] In the instant case, the appellant had been employed as a Assistant Manager on April 3, 1974, and therefore it was not necessary to make any provision for establishment of an establishment. The Act was in force on April 4, 1973. The scheme was not a 'National ' within meaning of article 2(2) of Part II of the Constitution and that it was a State ' within which the appellant could be said to have been employed. [720H] In view of the fact that the appellant is a "National ' under the Act, the notification issued by the Government under section 5 of the was valid and ultra. The question whether the notification dated April 2. 1974 was invalid or ultra vires was not decided in the instant appeal.

The petitioners are engaged in the work of mining operations. They were engaged as casual labourers and they were paid wages for the period from 1st April, 1988 to 31st March, 1988. The petitioners were engaged on daily wage basis. Their services were terminated by the Labour Court on the ground that they have been retrenched without giving them any opportunity of being heard. The Labour Court held that the petitioners are not entitled to be absorbed in the said work and that they are entitled to get the benefit of the Scheme. In the writ petition filed by the petitioners it was contended that the termination of their services is illegal and void as it has been done without giving him any opportunity to show cause why they should not be absorbed. Dismissing the writ petitions, this Court, HELD: 1. The High Court has rightly held that there is no evidence on record to show that the retrenchment of the petitioners was illegal and invalid because the petitioners have been paid wages in accordance with the Scheme and that the same has been made without giving any opportunity for being heard to them. [740B] 2. In view of the fact that the workmen are engaged on a daily wage, it is not possible to hold that they were retrenched without affording them an opportunity of hearing to show why they have not been absorbed in their respective posts. The question whether the petitioners were entitled to any relief under Article 226 of the Constitution does not arise. [ 740C] 3. In order to determine whether a workman has been retrenched, it must be shown that he has been paid the wages for one year and that he is entitled to the same. If the workmen have been given the benefit, they are also entitled to claim the same relief under Articles 226 and 227 of the constitution. [640C D] 4. The fact that there was no evidence to show any such evidence on the record to establish that the workman has not been paid any wages for two years or more cannot be said to be illegal.

The plaintiffs were the owners of certain properties in a suit for recovery of possession of certain lands. The defendants claimed that they had no right to claim any interest on the property and that they were entitled to the benefit of section 53(1) (a) of the Transfer of Property Act, 1882. The trial court decreed the suit holding that the plaintiffs were not entitled to any relief under section 53 (1)(a). The High Court held that the defendants were entitled only to the right of preemption on the ground that they did not possess any right to sue for recovery against them. In appeal to this Court, HELD : (i) The plaintiffs had no title to the property in question and the plaintiffs could not claim any right under section 54(1)(b). [801 B] (ii) The defendants were not bound by the sale deed dated March 1, 1946, executed by them in favour of the plaintiffs. They did not have any right or interest in the property. The plaintiffs were entitled under section 52(1), (a). [901 C D] (iii) The suit was barred by limitation. The High court had no jurisdiction to entertain the suit on the grounds that they failed to establish that the sale was void because they did so with regard to the interest of the defendants. The suit could not be dismissed on the basis of the evidence adduced in the case. [902 B] In the instant case, the plaintiffs had not established any right of preemption on the properties in question. They were entitled by section 53 of the Act. [803 C D]. (iv) The High Courts were right in holding that they could not have claimed any interest in it.

The appellant was convicted under section 302 read with section 34 of the Indian Penal Code and sentenced to death. The High Court acquitted him on the ground that the prosecution had failed to prove its case beyond reasonable doubt, and that the evidence of the witnesses were not reliable, and therefore, the conviction of the appellant under section 307 read with s.34 was illegal. On appeal by special leave, HELD : (i) The High court has rightly held that the appellant was guilty of the offence of murder and that he had failed in his examination under section 313 of the Code of Criminal Procedure, 1973, and the evidence on record did not show that the witnesses had been examined under section 342 of the Evidence Act. [808 B] (ii) The prosecution had not proved its case within reasonable doubt and the High Court was right in holding that the statements made by the witnesses under section 161 of the Criminal Procedure Code were not admissible to the appellant. [908 C D] (iii) The evidence of a witness under section 164 of the Cr. P.C., is not sufficient to prove the case beyond all reasonable doubt. It is only when the Court comes to the conclusion that the statement made by him under section 162 of the Act was admissible to it, and if the Court finds that the accused had failed, it would be open to the prosecution to prove that the witness had been given an opportunity to cross examine the witnesses. [1008 C] (iv) The provisions of section 313 are not applicable in the present case because the statements were made under section 165 of the Penal Code. [1108 D E] (v) In the instant case, the High court was right when it came to the finding that the appellants had failed before the trial court and the prosecution failed to establish its case against them. The appellant was therefore entitled to cross examination the witnesses in accordance with section 342(1)(a) of the code.

The appellant was a public limited company carrying on the business of manufacturing and selling of water in the city. The respondent was appointed as a Chief Engineer of the Municipality for the purpose of carrying out the work of the factory. The appellant was appointed by the Municipality under section 3(1) of the Act. The Municipality issued a notice to the appellant calling upon him to show cause why he should not be removed from the Municipality. The notice was served on the appellant on the respondent and the appellant replied that the notice had been duly served on him. The District Magistrate, however, refused to take action against the appellant. The State Government passed an order under section 4(1). The appellant filed a petition in the High Court challenging the validity of the notification. The High Court held that the notification was invalid and the notice was not valid. In appeal to this Court it was contended on behalf of the appellant that the order was invalid because the notice did not contain any provision for the removal of the water from the factory, and that the appellant had no locus standi to file the petition under article 226 of the Constitution. HELD : (i) The notification was valid and the Municipality was bound to take steps against the respondent. [838 B] (ii) The notice did contain a provision for removal of water from a Municipality. It was not necessary that the Municipality should have taken action against it. The order was not in accordance with law. The fact that the respondent had been removed from his Municipality by an order dated December 12, 1956, was not sufficient to show that the said notice was duly served. [938 B C] (iii) The appellant had not filed any affidavit before the District Magistrate nor did he state that the District Collector had taken action under section 5(1)(a). The District Judge was therefore right in holding that the public notice was a valid one and the order of removal was invalid. [883 D E] (iv) The District Court was right in taking action against a person who was removed from a municipality by an authority empowered to take such action under the Act, and the District Court had no jurisdiction to take proceedings against him.

The respondent was a railway servant in the State of Uttar Pradesh. The railway administration of the railway was charged with offences under section 3(1) (a) and (b) of the Railway Act, 1934. The prosecution case was that the railway had taken possession of the goods on the basis of a written agreement between the railway and the railway authorities. The trial court convicted the respondent under section 4(1)(d) of Railway Act and sentenced him to imprisonment for life. On appeal by special leave it was contended that the High Court was in error in holding that the Railway had taken delivery of goods on a written contract between the Railway and the Railway. Held, that the prosecution case did not fall within the definition of "goods" as defined in section 2(1). The railway authorities were right in coming to the conclusion that the goods were not goods within the meaning of section 2 (1) of Act. The High Court had rightly held that the respondent was not a railway employee within the purview of section 3 (1)(a) of that Act and that the appellant was not entitled to any compensation under section 5(1), because it was not proved that the articles were goods within that meaning. Held: (i) The railway authority was right in holding the railway property as a railway administration within the ambit of section 4 (1). (ii) The High court was in wrong in holding in favour of the respondent. (iii) The finding of fact recorded by the trial court was not correct and could not be sustained. (iv) The appellant had failed to prove that the article was goods within a meaning of the Act. (v) The evidence of the prosecution witnesses were not reliable, but they did not support the case of the appellant. (vi) The fact that the police authorities had taken the delivery of the articles on a public contract between them and the railways was not sufficient to hold that the property was goods in the course of inter State trade or commerce. (vii) The prosecution evidence was not reliable because the railway administration had taken over the railway premises on a private contract between it and the Railways. (viii) The respondent was entitled to compensation under sections 5(2)(a), 6(1A) and 7(1B). (ix) The trial Court was right when the railway authority took possession of goods in pursuance of a letter written by the Railway to the railway. (x) The defence had not been able to prove the case beyond reasonable doubt. (xi) The Trial Court was wrong in relying on the evidence of P.W. 1 that the consignment was not goods in respect of which the railway servant had taken action under section 6(2). (xii) The statement of P P.Ws. 2 and 3 that the delivery was made by the railway to the Railway was not admissible because they were not railway servants within the scope of section 5 (1A). (xiii) The burden of proving that the movement was made in pursuance to a letter given by the Railways to the railways, was on the railway which had taken place on a railway.

The respondent landlord, a tenant of the appellants, was in occupation of the premises in question. The respondent landlord filed an eviction suit against the appellants on the ground that he had not been let out to the appellants for any period prior to the date of the termination of his tenancy and that the appellants were not entitled to any protection under section 14(1)(e) of the Rajasthan Premises (Control of Rent & Eviction) Act, 1958. The trial court decreed the suit holding that the respondent landlord was in possession of the demised premises as a tenant within the meaning of section 2(h) of that Act and that he was not entitled for any protection from the provisions of the Act. The High Court held that the tenancy was not terminated by the appellants under the provisions contained in section 14 (1)(d) of Act, but only a lease of the tenanted premises. In appeal to this Court it was contended on behalf of the respondent tenant that the appellant had been let into possession of a demised premises and that since the respondent landlords were in occupation thereof, they could not be evicted under the Act as the tenancy had been terminated by them under section 13(1) (e) read with section 14 of the said Act. Dismissing the appeal, this Court, HELD: 1. The provisions contained therein are not applicable to a tenant who is let out for any purpose other than that which is in occupation or possession of any premises. [703F] 2. The definition of 'tenant ' in section 2 (h) is wide enough to include a person who has been let on rent and includes a person whose tenancy has been terminated under the terms of the lease. It is not necessary for the landlord to prove that he has been inducted as a lessee or a tenant in occupation, but it is also necessary for him to prove his case. [803F G] 3. The word 'tenant' in section 13 (1) of this Act includes a tenant whose tenancy is terminated under section 12(1). It is clear from the definition that the term 'tenant" has been used in the context of the expression "landlord" and not in the sense in which it occurs. [903F H] 4. The term 'owner ' means a person to whom the premises are let out, but does not include a tenant as defined in section 3(h). It does not mean a person for whom the tenancy is let or let out. In the context, the definition of "landlord ' in Section 2 (k) of Rajasthan Premises Act, 1959 is wide and it has been held that a person can be evicted only under the conditions mentioned therein. [0903F F] 5. The expression 'tenant " includes a landlord who has become a tenant under the Rent & Control Act, 1961 does not refer to a person in occupation. It does include a landlord whose tenancy was terminated by him under section 11(1), but does include any person who is liable to pay rent or rent for any other purpose. [1003F; 1003A B] 6. The words 'landlord ' includes a lessee who has let out the premises for any reason whatsoever. It also includes a lessor who has leased out the demised property for any specified period. In view of the definition, the term "tenant" in section 12 (1), as used in section 15(1A) is not confined to a landlord and only a tenant can be inducted into a tenant on the premises. The phrase 'landlord" in Section 13(2) of both the Rent and Control Act are wide enough and it does not exclude a person from being let out by him. [1103F, 1003G H] 7.

The appellant, a company incorporated under the Bihar Electricity (Supply) Act, 1948, was a public limited company. The appellant was a Government company and was not entitled to any compensation for the loss suffered by it in its business. The Board of Directors of the appellant company had taken over the management of the company and the Board of directors of the Company had taken the over management of its employees. The State Government issued a notification under section 3(1) of the Act on March 31, 1960, which was published in the Gazette on April 1, 1961. The notification was published on April 2, 1961, and the appellant was entitled to the compensation for loss suffered in its own business. On March 31. 1960, the State Government made a reference under section 10 of the Bihar Industrial Disputes Act, 1947, to the Industrial Tribunal, which held that the company had not taken over management and that the Board had no power to make any payment or other payment to it. The Tribunal held that there was no provision in the Act for payment of compensation for losses suffered by the appellant in its previous year. On appeal, the High Court held that it was a case of an employer who has been given the benefit of the notification and that it had not acted upon the same. In appeal to this Court, HELD: (1) The Tribunal was right in holding that the Company was entitled only to the amount of compensation which could be claimed by the company under section 11(2). [601 B C] (2) The Board has no power under section 12(3), and it is not open to the Board to make a payment or any other payment. It is not correct to say that the Tribunal was justified in holding so because the Company has taken over its management. [602 D E] (3) The High Court was right when it held that in the present case, the company was entitled for compensation under section 8(2), and that there could be no provision for payment or payment of any other amount to it in respect of losses suffered in the previous year, but that is not a case where the Board has taken the benefit. [702 D] (4) The question whether the Company should have taken over charge of its management was not raised before the Industrial Court and the Tribunal had no jurisdiction to make such payment or not.

The respondent was married to one Shri Rambhai, the appellant and his wife. The respondent was living separately in a matrimonial home. On the date of the marriage, the respondent was residing with her husband. She was also living separately. In the month of November, 1973, the husband filed an application under section 125 of the Code of Criminal Procedure for restitution of conjugal rights on the ground that she had been living separately and that she was not entitled to maintenance from the date when she was living in a separate house. The Magistrate rejected the application. On appeal by special leave, the High Court held that the respondent had no right to maintain her husband as she was residing separately for a period of two years and that the appellant was not liable to be prosecuted under section 13(1)(d) of the Act. In appeal to this Court it was contended on behalf of the appellant that the High court erred in holding that the order of the Magistrate was erroneous and that there was no valid reason for refusing maintenance. Dismissing the appeal, ^ HELD: 1. The High Court was right in holding the respondent guilty under section 14(1) (d) and (e) of Code of Civil Procedure. [797C] 2. The order of refusal passed by the Magistrate is not a nullity because it has been made without jurisdiction. It is well settled that the court cannot interfere with an order of a Magistrate unless there is a valid ground for refusing to grant maintenance. [897G H; 897A B] 3. In view of the fact that the husband had no locus standi to maintain his wife, the order passed by him was not a proper one and it could not be said that he had been residing separately in separate house for a long time. The appellant has failed to establish that she has been living together for a longer period than two years. [997C D] 4. In any event, the court is right in refusing maintenance under section 15(1), and it cannot be said to be an order passed without jurisdiction or without jurisdiction as the order was not one of the grounds on which the order could be made. [697G] 5. The question whether a person has been residing together for more than two decades does not arise.

The appellant was the owner of a land in the State of Gujarat. The respondents were owners of the lands in question. They claimed that they had no right to possession or control the lands on the ground that they were not entitled to possession of the land. The trial court decreed the suit holding that the lands were not liable to be acquired under the provisions of the Bombay Rents, Hotel and Lodging House Rates Control Act, 1947. The High Court held that the respondents were not owners of any land in question and that the suit was barred by limitation. In appeal to this Court it was contended on behalf of the appellant that the High Court had erred in holding that there was no evidence to show that the land was acquired under a scheme framed by the State Government for the purpose of the Act. Dismissing the appeal, HELD: 1. The question whether the lands are liable to vest in the Government or not is a matter which can be determined by the trial court and not by the High Courts. [697 F] 2. The suit was filed on behalfof the appellant under article 226 of the Constitution. It was not disputed that the State had no authority to deal with the land in dispute. The State had not been able to prove that the properties were acquired under any scheme framed for the purposes of the State. [797 F G] 3. The plaintiff 's suit was dismissed by the Trial Court and the High court was right in holding so. [897 A B] 4. The appellant was entitled to the possession of a portion of the property on the basis of the scheme framed under the Act, and the suit could not be decreed. [997 F H] 5. The respondent 's claim that the Government had no power to deal in the land on the date of the notification under section 4 of the Land Acquisition Act, 1894. The Trial Court was right when it held that there were no evidence on record to show whether the land had been acquired under an scheme framed or not.

The appellant was charged with the offence of criminal conspiracy under section 120B I.P.C. and section 5(1)(a) read with section 7(2) of the Prevention of Corruption Act, 1947. The prosecution case was that the appellant had been guilty of a criminal conspiracy and was convicted for an offence under section 5 (1)(b) readwith section 7 (1) (a) of that Act. The High Court held that the charge was not proved beyond reasonable doubt and acquitted him. In appeal to this Court it was contended on behalf of the appellant that the word "officer" in section 2(2)(a), means a person who is appointed as an officer or servant under the Government, and that the expression "officer", in section 3(1) of this Act includes a person holding any office or post in the Government. Held, that the words "officer " in section 4(1), were not used in the sense of "officer". The word "Officer" in the context of the definition of "office" in sections 2(1A)(a)(i) and (b) of section 5 of the Act was not used as a term of office. Held further, that in view of the provisions of the Indian Penal Code it must be held that a person appointed as a public servant under a Government, is not an officer of the Government but a person employed by the Government for the purpose of carrying on his duties and functions. The word 'officer" was used in section 5 Of the Act to mean "an officer or employee" in relation to which he is appointed. It was not necessary that a public officer should be appointed as such, and it must have been used in connection with the performance of his duties.

The Respondent No. 1, a tenant of the land in dispute, filed a suit for recovery of possession of the property on the ground that he was not a tenant within the meaning of section 2(1) of the Punjab Land Revenue Act, 1887 (Punjab Act), and that the said property was purchased by him from his father, who had no right to purchase it. The Respondent No 1 filed a civil suit for declaration that the sale deed dated March 20, 1977 executed by her in favour of the Appellant was illegal and void as it was not executed by the Collector under section 3 of the Act. The trial court decreed the suit holding that the property was not liable to be sold by the Respondent No 2, and that since the sale was effected by the State Government under section 4 of the Land Revenue Code, the sale could not be held to be void as the sale had been effected by a person who had purchased it. In appeal, the High Court reversed the judgment of the trial court holding that in view of the provisions of section 3(1), the sale of the said land was not valid and the sale did not amount to sale within the definition of "sale" under section 2 (1) (a) of Act. Dismissing the appeal, ^ HELD: 1. The High Court was right in holding that since there was no sale by Respondent No 3, the property could be sold only by a purchaser who had sold it to Respondent No 4. [601B C] 2. In view of section 4(1)(a) (i), the property is liable to attachment under section 6 of the Code of Civil Procedure and that in any event the sale would not amount either to sale or purchase, but only to sale by a vendor who had transferred it to another person. [701B D] 3. The sale was made by Respondent Nos. 1 and 2 on March 20. 1977 and the property in question was sold by Respondent no 4. The property in dispute was purchased from Respondent No4 on April 20, 1978. The respondent No 4 was not entitled to any recovery of the amount due under section 7 of the Revenue Code. [801C D] 4. In the instant case, the Respondent Nos 1 and 3 were not the owners of the suit property. They had sold the property to Respondent Nos 2 and 3 on April 21, 1977. The Respondents No.1 and 3 had no title to the property. The Appellant was not the owner of the premises in dispute. The sales were effected by Respondent nos. 2 and3 on April 22, 1978 and the same were made by respondent No. 4 on April 23, 1978, and the said sale was confirmed by the District Judge. [901C] 5. The appellant had no locus standi to file the suit for the recovery of any amount due from him under section 8 of the Civil Procedure Code. The suit was not maintainable as the Respondent nos 1 and3 were not entitled either to recover or recover the amount of the sale.

The appellant was the owner of a land in dispute. The respondent acquired certain lands from the Government for the purpose of acquiring the said lands. On the death of his father, he filed a suit claiming compensation on the ground that the lands were not agricultural property and that the properties had been acquired by the Government under the Land Acquisition Act, 1894. The Collector held that the land was not agricultural land and that it was not liable to be assessed under section 4(1) (a) of the Act. On appeal, the High Court allowed the appeal holding that the respondent had no right to claim compensation on account of the death or of his own. In appeal to this Court, it was contended for the appellant that the Collector had jurisdiction to assess the lands in question and that he had no jurisdiction to determine the market value of the land in question. Dismissing the appeal, ^ HELD: 1. The High Court was right in holding that there was no evidence on record to show that the estate had been purchased by the respondent for the purposes of acquiring it under the Act and that there had been a valid sale of the lands. [601C] 2. The question whether the Collector could have determined the market values of the properties in question or not is a matter which has to be decided on the basis of evidence on the record. [702D] 3. The expression "land" used in section 4 (1) of Act means any land which is acquired by Government under a Land Acquisition act, 1894 and which is not liable for payment of compensation under the provisions of the Land Acquiring Act. [803F G] 4. In the instant case, the Collector was right to determine market value on the date of the notification under section 5(1). The Collector had no power to assess or determine the value of any land in respect of which the estate was acquired by him under a land Acquisition act.

The appellant was elected as a member of the Maharashtra Cooperative Societies Act, 1960. The appellant was declared elected on the basis of an election held by him under section 13(1)(c) of the Act. He was elected on his own behalf. On the basis that he had been elected on a valid nomination, the appellant filed a writ petition in the High Court challenging the validity of the election on the ground that the appellant had not been elected and that the order of disqualification passed by him was illegal. The High Court dismissed the writ petition holding that the provisions of section 13 (1)(b) of Act were applicable to the case of an elected member of a society under section 14(1) (c) and that he was disqualified for being elected on any ground. In appeal to this Court, it was contended on behalf of the appellant that the High court had no jurisdiction to entertain the writ petitions in view of the provisions contained in section 13 of the Bombay Cooperative Societies Rules, 1960 and that since the appellant was not elected on that ground, he could not be declared elected. Dismissing the appeal, ^ HELD: 1.1 The High court has rightly held that the election of the member of an society under the Maharashtra Co operative Societies Act is illegal and void. [797C] 2.2 In view of section 14 (1) of Bombay Cooperative Society Act, it is not necessary to decide whether the appellant could be declared as elected on such ground or not. The question for consideration in this case is whether the order passed by the High Courts was illegal or void. It is well settled that the power of the Registrar under section 15(1), is not confined to the power to make an order of the President and it is only when he has made an order that the member should be elected on some ground or other, that the person who has been elected has been duly elected. [897C D] 2:3 The power of a Registrar under sub section (1), in the instant case, is not restricted to the powers of the State Government under sub sections (2) and (3). It is only if he has been disqualified on the date of the order that he has become elected. If he has not made an application for being declared elected, he must be deemed to have been elected. The power conferred by sub section(1A) is confined to a power exercisable under sub s.(2) of section 15 and it cannot be said that he could be disqualified on any grounds or other. [997C E] 2 :4 In the instant cases, the order was passed by an authority competent to make the election. The order of removal was not made in accordance with law. It was only when the appellant has been declared elected and the order is set aside by the State Board under sub sec.(2). [998C E; 997A] 2(a) In view thereof, the HighCourt had no power to issue a direction for the removal of the members of an association under section 16(1). The appellant could not have been declared as disqualified on that account. [1097D E] (b) The order passed in this behalf was illegal and invalid because it was made without giving any opportunity to the appellant to make his representation against the order. [697C F] 2.(c) In the present case, the Registrar had no authority to issue the direction for removal of members on the grounds mentioned in section 14 of the said Act. The Registrar had also no power under sub clause (1A).

The respondent was a Government servant. He was dismissed from service on the ground that he had been convicted of an offence under Rule 3(1)(a) of the Bombay Civil Services (Classification, Control and Appeal) Rules, 1965. The respondent filed a writ petition in the High Court challenging the order of dismissal. The High Court held that the respondent was not entitled to any pension for the period of his service as he had retired from service. In appeal by special leave it was contended on behalf of the appellant that the order passed by the State Government under Rule 4(1) (a) was illegal and void and that the State had no power to impose any penalty or to impose a penalty or impose a punishment upon him. Dismissing the appeal, ^ HELD: 1. The order of the State government is not in accordance with law and is liable to be set aside. [630G] 2. The State Government has power to pass an order imposing a penalty on the respondent under Rule 5(1). The order passed under Rule 6(1), therefore, cannot be sustained. [730C D] 3. The power of the Government to impose the penalty or imposing a punishment is not confined to the power of imposition of any penalty. It is only when it is found that the power has been exercised by the Government in accordancewith law and without authority of law, the order cannot be set down as illegal. [830C E] 4. The Government has no power under Rule 7(1 ) (a). The power to issue a direction to impose penalty or imposition of a punishment on the person concerned is not restricted to the powers of imposition or imposition or imposing any penalty upon the person charged. [930E F] 5. In the instant case, the respondent had been dismissed from services for the reason that he was not in service of the respondent and had been acquitted by the criminal court. The disciplinary authority has also not considered the evidence on record. The punishment imposed is set aside and the order imposing the penalty is set down accordingly.

The appellants were the tenants of a shop in which they had been let out to the respondents. The respondents filed a suit for eviction on the ground that the appellants had not complied with the provisions of section 13(1) (a) of the Act and that the respondents had failed to comply with the requirements of section 14(1). The trial court decreed the suit holding that the appellant had failed in compliance with the mandatory requirement of section 4(2) (b) of that Act. On appeal, the District Judge held that the provisions contained in section 13 (1) were not applicable to the case and dismissed the suit. In appeal to this Court it was contended on behalf of the appellants that the District Magistrate had no jurisdiction to pass an order under section 4 (2) of Act and therefore the order passed by the District judge was illegal. HELD : The District Magistrate has no jurisdiction in the matter of passing an order which is not a nullity as the District court has no power to pass such an order. [690 F] In the instant case, the appellants were not entitled to the protection of section 3(1)(a) and (b). The District Judge had no power under section 13 of the . The District judge had no authority to pass any order under that section. The District court was therefore right in holding that it was not a fit case for grant of relief under section 14 (1). [691 F] The District Court was right in dismissing the suit on the grounds: (i) that the order of the District magistrate was illegal and void as the appellants failed to satisfy the requirements. The High Court was wrong in holding the order under appeal.

The appellant, a member of the Indian Administrative Service, was appointed as a Member of the Punjab Public Service Commission. He was appointed by the Government of India under the provisions of the Constitution of India. The Chief Justice of Punjab & Haryana, who was the Chairman of the Commission, made an order dated May 5, 1982 directing the Chief Justice to appoint a person to be the Secretary of the State Civil Services (Judicial Branch) in the Public Service (Judicial Division) and to appoint another person as the Secretary. The appellant filed a writ petition before the High Court challenging the order of suspension. The High Court dismissed the writ petition holding that the Chief Minister was not competent to appoint any person as Secretary of State Civil Service, and that the order was bad in law. In appeal to this Court it was contended on behalf of the appellant that the High court had no jurisdiction to entertain the writ petitions. Dismissing the appeal, ^ HELD: 1. The order of dismissal passed by the Chief Judge is not a judicial order but a judicial act. It is a judicial function and it is not an administrative act. The Court has to see whether the order is bad in fact or not. [636C] 2. The power conferred on the Chief Secretary under Article 309(1) of the Code of Criminal Procedure, 1973 is not confined to the power conferred by Article 309. It must be exercised within its limits and it cannot be said that the power has been exercised arbitrarily or without jurisdiction. [737D E] 3. The powers conferred on a Chief Minister are not confined only to the powers conferred by article 309(2) of Constitution. In the instant case, the Chief Commissioner was competent to make an order under Article 311(1). The Chief Minister had no power to appoint the person as Chairman of State Public Service. [837E F] 4. The learned Judge has not given any reasons for his conclusion and that he did not act in accordance with the rules of natural justice. He has also not given reasons for such conclusion. [937F G] 5. The report of the Chief Chief Commissioner is not conclusive as to the nature of the inquiry or the manner in which the inquiry was conducted. It cannot be disputed that the report of a Chief Commissioner has been made by the Public Commission and it has no power under Article 162(2). [938E F; 939A B] 5.(a) The Chief Secretary is competent to take such evidence as he thinks fit for the purpose of conducting the inquiry. He cannot be expected to act in his own discretion. He can also take such steps as he considers necessary for the purposes of conducting a inquiry or to record the reasons for doing so. [1039C] (b) The report is not merely a judicial report but a report of an officer of the Public Services Commission. It does not mean that the Judge has no jurisdiction in his case. He must be given reasonable opportunity to cross examine the witnesses and to give evidence. [ 1039A C] 6.(c) The High court has power to take into consideration all relevant circumstances including the nature, character and conduct of the parties. [1140F G; 938E] (d) The order is not one of judicial orders but a quasi judicial order. It can be said to be an administrative order. [ 1139A] 7.(e) The power under article 309 is not restricted to the exercise of the power by the High Courts in respect of any matter which is in the public interest or in the interest of justice. [1240F H; 941C D] (e) In the present case, it has been established that the appellant was a member and was appointed to the service of the Government.

The appellants, who were the members of a public temple, challenged the validity of the order of the High Court. The High Court held that the temple was not a private temple and that the properties belonged to the public temple. In appeal to this Court it was contended on behalf of the appellants that the High court had erred in holding that the trust was a private property and that it was a public trust within the meaning of section 2(1) (d) of the Act. Dismissing the appeal, ^ HELD: 1. The trust is a private religious institution and not a public religious institution. It is a public charitable institution which has to be established by the provisions of the statute. [601B] 2. The object of the trust is to establish a public endowment within the definition of section 3(1)(d) and that is, to say, the public purpose is to enable the public to establish the public interest. It must be shown that the public trust is an institution which is not a religious institution or a public institution. The public interest is not merely a private character but a public interest in the public. [701B C] 3. The question whether the trust has been established by a public body or a private body, does not arise for consideration in this case. It was not necessary to decide whether the public should be held to have been established. The fact that the appellants were members of the public public temple is not sufficient to establish that the said public interest was a religious endowment within section 3 (1) of Act. [801C D] 4. In the instant case, the trust had been established and it was not proved that the Trust was a Public temple. The appellants were not members of public public institution nor were they members of any public public body. They were also members of such public public institutions. There is no evidence to show that the trustees were members or members of that public public charitable institutions. [901C] 5. In view of the fact that there was a common public trust, it cannot be said that the property belonged to a private institution and the appellants had been in possession of the same. The appellant was not entitled to any benefit under section 3 of the Hindu Religious Endowments Act. The respondent was not an individual member of the Public Trust. [1001C E] 6. In order to establish public interest, it must be established that the trustee was a Hindu religious institution, and that he was a member of a private trust. It may be proved that there were two or more trustees in the same public temple and the public had been given a public purpose. The mere fact that a public object is not an essential part of the community, cannot be held that it is a religious trust. [ 1001C F] 7. In this case, it was established by evidence that the respondent was a trustee of a Public Trust and that there are two or three trustees in a public public trust. The evidence of the respondent that he had been a member or members in the said Public Trust was not sufficient for establishing the public interests. [1101C G] 8. In fact, the High Courts have held that there is no public interest involved in the matter. It has also come to the conclusion that the appellant was a person who was a beneficiary of the temple and it had been proved that he belonged to any private institution.

The appellant, a contractor of the respondent, was appointed as an agent of the Government of India. The appellant was to be paid a sum of Rs. 2,00,000/ . The appellant filed a suit for recovery of the amount due from him under the contract and claimed that the amount was not payable by him. The trial court decreed the suit holding that the appellant had no right to sue for recovery against the appellant. On appeal the High Court held that the contract was not a contract within the meaning of section 2(1)(d) of the Act and that the suit was barred by limitation. In appeal to this Court it was contended on behalf of the appellant that the agreement was not an agreement within the definition of 'sale ' in section 2 (1)(e) of that Act and, therefore, the suit could not be dismissed. HELD : The High Court was right in holding that a contract is a contract for sale and not a transfer of property. [601 F] In the instant case the appellant was not entitled to sue under section 2 of the . The High court had no jurisdiction to entertain the suit. [702 H] The appellant 's suit was dismissed by the trial court on the ground that the transaction was an agreement for sale. The High Courts were right in dismissing the suit and the appeal must be dismissed on the grounds that the transactions were not a contracts within the purview of section 3(1) (d). [703 H] In view of the fact that the respondent had no authority to sue the appellant, it was not open to the appellant to sue it for recovery.

The assessee was a Hindu undivided family and the income of the assessee was assessed to tax under section 10(1)(a) of the Income Tax Act, 1922. The Income tax Officer held that the income received by the assessee from the firm was not taxable in view of section 2(f) of that Act. On appeal the Appellate Assistant Commissioner confirmed the order of the Appellate Tribunal and dismissed the appeal. In the appeal to this Court it was contended on behalf of the appellant that the High Court erred in holding that the Income tax officer had no jurisdiction to assess the income for the purpose of assessment under section 11(1) (a) (b) of Act, 1961. HELD : The High Court was right in holding the assessee 's income as a Hindu Undivided Family and not as a person who is liable to pay income tax under the Income Act. [619 D] In the instant case the income from the partnership business was taxable in the hands of the firm. The income received from the assessee did not fall within the definition of "person" in section 2 (f) (c) of section 10 of the Act. The High court was right when it held that there was no provision for the Income 's tax to assess income for purposes of assessment. [719 D E] In view of the fact that the assessee had received the income, the High court erred in law in holding in favour of the Revenue. [820 H] The High Courts were right in coming to the conclusion that the expenditure was not a "person".

The petitioners were owners of agricultural lands in the State of Bihar. The State Government issued a notification under section 4(1) of the Act to provide for the levy and collection of fees for the sale of cattle, and for the maintenance of public order. The petitioners challenged the validity of the notification on the ground that it was violative of article 14 of the Constitution as it violated article 19 (1)(g) of Part III of the constitution. The High Court held that the impugned Act was violative Of article 14 and was not violative of articles 14 and 21 of the articles 14, 19(1)(d) and 21. In appeal to this Court, HELD : (i) The impugned Act is violative of Articles 14 and 19(2)(g). [801 B] (ii) The State Legislature has power to make laws for the purpose of carrying out the purposes of the impugned legislation. It is not open to the State Government to make any law for the regulation or regulation of cattle in respect of which it is made. [802 C D] (iii) The Act is a piece of legislation and is not intended to be a piece piece of measure. It cannot be said that the Act is unconstitutional because it is a colourable piece of measures. [703 B] In the present case, the impugned notification was violativeof article 14. [602 C E] (iv) The petitioners were entitled to the protection of articles 19 and 21 as they were not entitled to any protection under article 19(3)(g), and they were entitled only to the benefit of articles 21 and 21, and they could not be denied the protection under articles 19 or 21. [403 B C] (v) The notification was valid because it was issued in exercise of its powers under article 14, and the petitioners were not deprived of their right to carry on their trade as cattle.

The respondent, a company, was employed in the appellant Company. The respondent, an employee of the respondent, was suspended by the Central Government on the ground that he had been dismissed from service under section 33(1) of the , and that the respondent had not been given any opportunity to show cause why his services should not be terminated. On a reference made to the Industrial Court, the High Court held that the order of suspension passed by the respondent was illegal and void as it was not in accordance with law. The High Court dismissed the petition holding that the dismissal of the appellant company was illegal. Held, that the termination of the services of the workmen was illegal because the respondent did not have any opportunity of showing cause against the order. The order of dismissal passed by a Labour Court is not an order of punishment and it must be held to be invalid. The fact that the management had taken charge of the company in contravention of section 33 (1) does not make any difference between the termination and the termination. The termination of services of a workman was illegal as it did not amount to dismissal or removal. The only question for consideration is whether the order passed by an employer under section 32(1)(a) is valid, because the order was made in contravention with the provisions of section 34 (1). Held, further, that in view of the fact that a workman has been dismissed or removed from service, it cannot be said that he was not entitled to any relief. The question for determination is whether an employer can be terminated under section 31(1), because the termination is illegal and invalid as it does not amount directly to dismissal, removal or removal of the workman.

The appellant company was a registered company carrying on business in the manufacture of its products. The respondent company claimed that the amounts paid by it were not 'in respect of the employees employed in the manufacturing of its product and that the amount paid by the company was not 'outstanding ' as defined in section 2(1) (a) of the Act. The Tribunal held that the appellant company had been engaged in the production of its goods, and that it was not liable to pay any amount on account of the working of the manufacturing unit. In appeal to this Court, HELD : (i) The word 'output ' means 'in relation to the manufacture or production of goods. It is not defined in the Act as a term of employment. The definition of 'outward ' means "in relation thereto" and it does not include any activity which is carried on by the manufacturing company. [401 B] (ii) The expression 'outoutput' means "output" in section 3(1)(a) or section 4(2). It is only when a person is employed in a manufacturing unit that he has been engaged for the production or production, that he is not liable under any law to pay the amount on which it was paid. [501 B C] (iii) The definition does not cover "outward" and the word 'in connection thereto means "any activity carried on in by a manufacturing company". It is also not defined as a "outstanding" or "other activities carried on for the manufacture, production or processing of goods". In the present case, the appellant was engaged in production or manufacture of goods and it was only when the manufacturing process carried on. [601 B D] (iv) The words 'outwards ' means any activity carried out by a manufacturer of goods which is carrying on for sale or processing. It does not mean that the word "outoutward", in section 4 (1)(b) means "other than those carried on with the production, manufacture or processing".

The appellant, a manufacturer of sugar, was carrying on the business of manufacture and sale of sugar. The State Government issued notification under section 3(1) of the , to the effect that the said product should be treated as 'manufacture ' within the meaning of Section 2(f) of The Act. The appellant filed writ petitions in the High Court challenging the validity of the notification on the ground that it was not a 'manufacture' within the definition of 'manufacture'. The High Court dismissed the writ petition holding that the product was 'manufacture within the ambit of Section 3(2). Allowing the appeal, this Court, HELD: 1.1 The word 'manufacture" in Section 2 (f) means "any process or process which is not manufacture within the purview of the Act and includes any process or operation which is capable of being used for the purpose of manufacturing sugar. [740F] 2.2 In the instant case, the product is 'manufacture". The word "manufacture" has been defined in Section 3 (f). It means "an process or processes which is manufacture within a meaning of the definition. It means any process which has been used for producing or processing of sugar and includes process or operations which are capable of manufacturing or processing. [640F G] 2:3 The word used in Section 4(1)(f) is not defined in the Act. In the absence of any definition, it cannot be said that the word 'process" has to be understood as a "manufacture". It means only a process or activity which is intended to be manufacture within its meaning. [840F H] 2 :4 The word is used in the context of the expression "manufacture", but not a mere process or preparation for producing, processing or processing and processing. In view of the fact that the expression 'process ' has been understood as including process or manufacture within it, it would be difficult to hold that the activity or process was not manufacture. [940F F] 2.:5 The word in Section 5(1), is used only in the sense of "manufacture ' and includes a process which can be said to be manufacturing within the scope of the section. It is also clear from the definition that it has been given in the definition, that it is not a process of manufacture. In other words, it is used for production or processing but only a processes which are intended to operate as a process and operation which are ordinarily carried on by the manufacturer. [1040F E] 2.(a) The word must be understood in its ordinary sense and not in its popular sense. It has been held that the term 'process' is used to mean "any other process or work which is incidental or ancillary to the manufacture of sugar". In the present case, it was a process carried on for producing and processing of sugarcane. [1140F D] 2(b) The expression 'manufacture " means any processes which has not been carried on in the course of manufacturing process or processing or preparation. It does not mean that the process or treatment is incidental to the manufacturing process. [1240G H] 3.3 In view, the word used is a process as understood in Section 6(1). The word has been interpreted by this Court in various decisions including the decision of this Court on the question whether it is 'processing ' and not 'manufacture. It cannot be held that it must be treated to have been manufacture within that meaning. In order to attract the provisions of the Central Excise Act, the expression used in section 2(g) has to necessarily be understood by its ordinary meaning. The word should be construed in its wider sense and it is a different thing as understood under Section 6 (1).

The appellant was a tenant of the respondent. The premises were let out to him by the respondent for his personal use and occupation. He was in occupation of the premises. He filed an application under section 13(1)(a) of the Andhra Pradesh Buildings (Lease, Rent & Eviction) Act, 1960 for eviction of the appellant on the ground that he had been using the premises for a commercial purpose. The Rent Controller rejected the application holding that the appellant was not a tenant within the meaning of Section 2(h) of that Act and that the respondent was not entitled to eviction under section 14(1). In appeal, the High Court held that the premises were not used for any commercial purpose and that it was not liable to be evicted under section 15(1) of Act. Dismissing the appeal, ^ HELD: The appellant was an employee of the State Government and was therefore a tenant in the premises as defined in Section 2 (h). [703 B] In the instant case, the appellant had been carrying on business for a long time and that he was not using the same for any other purpose. He did not use the same nor used it for any purpose. It was only when he was using the said premises for commercial purposes. The appellant could not be said to have used it in the business of the landlord. [704 B] The definition of "residential purpose" in Section 3(h)(a)(i) of Andhra Pradesh Building (Lease and Rent Control) Act is wide enough to include a residential building or a commercial building. It is well settled that the word "residential" in section 2(g) means a business which is carried on by a person who carries on his business for any purposes other than that for which it is carried. The definition does not include a business carried on in by a tenant and does not exclude a business carrying on by him.

The respondent was a partner of the appellant firm. The respondent filed a suit for recovery of Rs. 1,00,000/ as advance by the appellant to the respondent on the ground that the amount of advance was not due to the appellant and that the appellant had failed to pay the balance of the loan. The trial court decreed the suit holding that the respondent was entitled to the benefit of section 7(1) (a) of the Indian Income tax Act, 1922. The High Court held that the agreement between the parties was a contract of sale and not a contract for sale. In appeal to this Court it was contended on behalf of the respondent that the transaction was a transaction of sale as defined in section 2(d) of that Act and that it was not a transaction which was a sale within the meaning of section 2 (d) and that, therefore, the appellant was entitled under section 7 (1) of this Act. HELD : The agreement between parties was an agreement for sale and the contract was a document for sale as contemplated by section 7 of the Act. [719 F] In the present case the respondent had not paid the balance amount of loan to the appellants. The appellant did not pay the amount due under the agreement. The agreement was a mortgage deed. It was a loan agreement. There was no evidence that the money was advanced to the respondents. The transaction was an exchange of correspondence between the appellant 's husband and the respondent. The fact that the loan was advanced by the respondent did not make any difference in the amount paid under the contract could not be said to have been advanced to him.

The petitioner was detained under section 3(1) of the Foreign Exchange Regulation Act, 1947. The petitioner challenged the order of detention on the ground that he had been in custody for more than six months and that he was not required to be released on bail. The High Court dismissed the petition holding that the detention order was vitiated by non application of mind and that the order was passed without giving an opportunity to the detenu to explain his case. Allowing the appeal, this Court, HELD: 1.1 The order of preventive detention is a judicial order and it cannot be said that the detaining authority had applied its mind to the facts of each case. [703F] 2.2 In the instant case, the petitioner was in custody since May, 1986 and he was released on his bail. He was not entitled to be detained under the provisions of section 3 (1) (a) of Foreign Exchange Act, 1973. The order was made by the detaining authorities on the basis that the petitioner had been arrested on May 1, 1986. [803F G] 2:3 In the present case, there is no material on record to show that the detenu had been released on the bail. It is not in dispute that the grounds of detention were served on him by the authority concerned and he had not been released till date. The detaining authority has not given any reasons for his detention. [903F H] 2 :3 In view of the fact that the detenue was arrested on June 1, 1987, the order passed by the authorities concerned was vitiated. [1003G H] 3:4 The order made by this Court in the instant writ petition is set aside and the petitioner be released forthwith if he is not required in any other case.

The petitioners were employed as a casual labourer in the respondent department. They were paid wages for the period of their engagement. The petitioners were engaged on daily wage basis and were paid salary for the same. Their services were regularised by the Department. The respondents challenged the validity of the order of regularization before the High Court which allowed the writ petition. Dismissing the appeal, ^ HELD: 1.1 The petitioners are entitled to the benefit of the provisions of Article 14 of the Constitution. [697C] 2.2 The petitioners have been engaged on a daily wage and are paid wages in accordance with the rules. They are entitled for the benefit under the scheme. [797D] 3.3 The petitioners cannot claim that they are entitled only to the benefits of the scheme, but they are not entitled to any relief. [897C D] 4.4 The petitioners who have been working as casual labourers in the department and are entitled even to the same benefit under Article 14 is entitled to get the benefit which has been extended to them by the Government. [997D E] 5.5 The petitioners, who have worked for more than 240 days in a year, cannot claim any relief on the ground that they were not entitled for any relief under Article 19 of the constitution. [1097C F] 2.(a) The petitioners can claim that their services are being regularised by virtue of the orders of this Court. They cannot claim the benefit as extended to the casual labourers. [1197D G] (b) The respondents have not been able to prove that they have worked continuously for more 240 days and are also entitled to equal pay for equal work.

The assessee, a Hindu undivided family, was assessed to income tax under section 10(1) of the Indian Income tax Act, 1922. The Income tax Officer rejected the return and declared that the income had escaped assessment. He also held that the notice issued by the Income tax officer was not valid as it was not served on him within the time prescribed in section 10 (2). In appeal to this Court, HELD : (i) The notice issued under section 11(1)(a) of that Act must be deemed to have been served on the assessee. [808 B] (ii) The proviso to section 10 of the Income Tax Act, 1961 does not apply to a case where the notice was served on it within the prescribed time and the notice is not served within the period specified in section 11 (2), but the notice must be served on that person. In the present case, the notice did not serve on the appellant within the stipulated time. The notice was issued by a registered post with the prescribed date. [908 B C] (iii) The assessee had no right to file the return under section 12(1). [807 D E] (iv) The notices were served on a Hindu Undivided Family, and the notices were not served upon it within time. [707 A] (v) The Income Tax Officer was wrong in holding that the notices issued by him were not valid. [608 B D] (vi) The High Court was right in holding the notice under section 8(1), but on a reference made to it, held that there was no sufficient cause for the assessee to file a return under the Act.

The petitioners, who were members of the Indian Bank, were elected as Directors of the Bank. The petitioners challenged the validity of the said notification on the ground that it was violative of Article 14 of the Constitution and that the said Act violated Articles 14 and 16 of the constitution. The Central Government issued a circular dated 20th July, 1985 to the effect that the Central Government had no power to appoint an officer as Director of the bank in terms of the scheme. The Board issued a Circular dated 20 th July, 1984 to the extent it is inconsistent with the provisions of the Act and the Rules framed thereunder. The said circular was challenged by the petitioners on the grounds: (i) that the notification dated 20.07.1984 was violative Of Article 14; (ii) that it violated Articles 19 and 16; (iii) that there was no violation of Article 16 of Constitution; and (iv) that in view of the provisions contained in Section 10(1)(a), the Central Board had no authority to appoint a person as Director, and (v) that since the notification was issued by the Central Govt. it could not be said that the petitioners were members in the Indian Banks and the Regulations framed thereunder, the impugned notification dated 21st July,1984 is violative of Articles 14, 16 and 16. The writ petitions filed by the employees of the Reserve Bank challenging the validity and validity of Section 10 (1)(b) are allowed. The High Court held that the impugned notifications were invalid because it violated Article 14 and 19 of the . Allowing the Writ Petitions, this Court, HELD: 1. The impugned notification is violative Of Articles 14 & 16 of constitution. [703F] 2. The object of the Scheme is to provide for appointment of a person who has been elected as Director or Director of a bank in accordance with the scheme and to provide that an officer shall be appointed by the Board on the recommendation of the Central Advisory Board. The scheme is intended to provide a minimum number of persons to be nominated by the State Government. [803F G] 3. The Scheme is meant for appointment by the Reserve Banks and to ensure that the members of a Bank are not elected as director or Director. The purpose of the notification is to enable the Central government to appoint such person as Directors or Director, in accordancewith the scheme, to provide an opportunity to the members to participate in the election. [903F H] 4. The Act does not contain any provision for appointment to a post in the Reserve bank. It provides that the State Governments shall have power to make appointments of persons who are not members of such Bank. [1003G H] 5. The provisions contained under Section 10 of the , do not provide for an opportunity of being heard to the parties concerned. [1103F; 1103A B] 6. The question whether a person is a member of a Indian Banks or the Regulations made thereunder, does not arise. [1203G] 7. The power conferred on the Central Govern ment under Section 9(1) (a) is limited to the appointment by an officer of the Government. It is only when the Central Governments are unable to appoint any person as director and Director of such bank that they have no power or authority to make appointment in accordance therewith.

The respondent assessee was a dealer in the assessment year 1960 58. The Income tax Officer, on an application made by him under section 35(1) of the Act, assessed the income of the respondent for the assessment years 1960 59 to 1961 60 and directed the assessing officer to make a fresh assessment after giving an opportunity to the assessee to show cause why he should not be imposed with penalty. The Appellate Assistant Commissioner confirmed the order of the Income tax officer. In appeal by special leave, the Tribunal held that the assessment was barred under section 34(1)(a) of Act and that the order passed by the Appellate Assistant Commis sioner was not a final order within the meaning of section 34 (2). The High Court in revision held that section 34 was not applicable to the case. In this appeal by certificate, HELD : (i) The High Courts were right in holding that the Income Tax Officer had no power to pass an order under section 36(1), and that it was not open to the Appellate Tribunal to pass a fresh order under sub section (2) of section 35. [401 B] (ii) The power conferred by section 34 is not confined only to the power conferred on the Income ' Officer but also to the powers conferred by the Act. It is not necessary that the power should be exercised in a particular manner and not to the discretion of the Appellate Commissioner. [501 C D] (iii) The order passed under sub sections (1) and (2), are not final. The High court was right in setting aside the order under s 35(3).

The respondent was appointed as a Police Constable in the State of Uttar Pradesh. He was promoted to the post of Sub Inspector on January 1, 1953. On December 14, 1954 he was transferred to the District Magistrate, Lucknow. The respondent was posted at the district of Lucknow and was posted there. On November 15, 1954 the respondent was transferred from Lucknow to Lucknow. On October 10, 1954, the respondent filed a complaint against him under section 161 of the Code of Criminal Procedure for an offence punishable with death. The Magistrate held that the respondent had committed an offence under section 5(1) (a) of the Prevention of Corruption Act, 1947 and that he was not entitled to any relief in respect of his promotion as Sub Inspector. On appeal by special leave, the High Court set aside the order of dismissal and directed the respondent to be reinstated in service with effect from January 1. 1953. The State appealed to this Court. HELD : (i) The order of the District Collector was not based on any evidence or material before him. It was not open to the respondent, to contend that the order was vitiated by an error apparent on the face of record. [619 D] (ii) The High Court had no jurisdiction to interfere with the order passed by the District Superintendent. The order was therefore, liable to be set aside. [720 H; 720 A B] (iii) The respondent had been posted at Lucknow and he was posted in Lucknow. He had been transferred from Allahabad to Lucknow on January 14, 1953, and he had been working there. The High court had no power to interfere in the order under section 164 of the Criminal Procedure Code.

The appellant was appointed as a Medical Officer in the Central Government of India on January 1, 1966. He was promoted to the post of Assistant Professor in the Department of Health and Family Welfare on January 14, 1966, and he was promoted as Assistant Professor on January 15, 1966 on the basis of his seniority in the grade of Assistant Professors. The appellant was promoted on January 16, 1966 by a notification dated March 31, 1966 issued under Rule 3(1) of the Central Civil Services (Classification, Control and Appeal) Rules, 1965. He challenged the validity of the said notification on the ground that he had been appointed as Assistant Professors in the Ministry of Health & Family Welfare only on January 17, 1966 and that his seniority was not based on any principle of seniority. The High Court dismissed the writ petition holding that the appellant was entitled to be promoted to a post of Deputy Professor in Central Government service on January 19, 1966 when he was appointed on January 13, 1966 as Assistant Collector in the Union Territory of Jammu & Kashmir. In appeal to this Court it was contended for the appellant that the said rule was ultra vires and void because the appellant had been promoted to another post of Joint Director in the State Government of Jammu and Kashmir.
