Dismissing the appeal, ^ HELD: 1. The rule is ultra vires because the rule is not ultra vires. [630B] 2. The rules are ultra vires as it is based on a principle of equality and equal opportunity. It is well settled that the rule must be read in its entirety so as to give effect to the object of the rule. [731C D] 3. In the instant case, the appellant has been promoted as Deputy Director in Central Hospital on January 21, 1966 but he was not promoted to any post of Additional Director in Union Territory. The said rule is based upon a principle which is based only on the principle that the promotion must be made by direct recruitment and not by promotion. [831C] 4. The respondents have been promoted on the same basis as Assistant Director in Ministry of Home Affairs. They were promoted to different posts of Deputy Directors in Central Health Service on January 20, 1966 after the date of his appointment. They are entitled to the benefit of the rules. [932D E] 5. The promotion is made by promotion from the post to which he was recruited and not from the date when he joined the service. The post of Director in State Government is a post in Central hospital. The promotions are made on the footing that the post is a promotional post. The seniority of the appellant is based solely on the principles laid down in the rules and the promotion is governed by the rules framed under the Rules. [1031C E] 6. In view of the fact that the respondents were promoted as Additional Director, Central Hospital, the promotion of the respondents to the posts of Joint Directors was not justified. The order of promotion is set aside.

The respondent was a tenant of the land in dispute. The respondent was allotted a plot of land to him under the Punjab Land Reforms Act, 1950. He was also allotted a portion of his holding as a tenant. The appellant 's father filed an application for allotment of the plot on the ground that he had been cultivating the land and that he was not entitled to any benefit under the Act. The Collector rejected the application. On appeal by special leave, the High Court held that the respondent was not a tenant within the meaning of section 2(1) (c) of the Punjab Tenancy Act, 1948. In appeal to this Court it was contended on behalf of the appellant that the land was allotted to him as a result of his transfer and that the transfer was invalid because he had no right to hold the land as a whole. Dismissing the appeal, HELD: The High Court was in error in holding that the State Government had no power to make an order for allotment under section 2 (1) of Act. [630 H] In the instant case, the respondent had been allotted a part of his land and he was also entitled to the benefit under section 3(1). [631 A B] The High Courts have rightly held that since the transfer of the plots was invalid, the State could not be said to have exercised its power under section 4(1)(c) on the basis of the transfer. [730 H; 730 A C] In view of the fact that the High Courts had no jurisdiction to make a reference under section 5(1), it is clear that the decision in the case of State of Punjab vs Ram Chander, ; , followed.

The plaintiffs, who were the sons of one Ram Singh, filed a suit for possession of certain lands in their favour. The defendants claimed that they had no right to claim compensation under the provisions of the Madhya Pradesh Land Revenue Code, 1950. The trial court decreed the suit holding that the plaintiffs had no title to the property and that the defendants had no locus standi to file the suit. On appeal by the defendants the High Court held that the suit was not maintainable because the plaintiffs were entitled to claim any compensation under section 6 of the Act. In appeal to this Court it was contended on behalf of the appellants that the High court erred in holding that there was no right of the plaintiffs to claim the compensation under sections 6 and 7 of the Land Revenue Act, 1950 as they had not been able to claim a compensation under that section. Held: (i) The suit was maintainable because, in view of the provisions contained in the Madhya Bharat Land Revenue Rules, 1950, the plaintiffs could not be said to have acquired any right of occupancy under the rules of succession and that they were entitled only to claim an compensation under r. 6 of that Act. (ii) The High Court erred in dismissing the suit on the ground that the appellants had no legal title to them. (iii) The plaintiffs were not entitled to the compensation as they were not able to establish their right of ownership under the Rules of succession. (iv) The defendants were not liable to pay any compensation for the land acquired by them.

The appellants were the tenants of a hotel and the respondent was the tenant of the hotel. The respondent filed an application under section 13(1) of the Bombay Rents, Hotel and Lodging House Rates Control Act, 1947 for eviction of the appellants on the ground that the appellants had failed to pay rent within the time specified in the notice. The trial court decreed the suit holding that the appellant was not entitled to the protection of section 14(1)(a). In appeal by special leave it was contended on behalf of the respondent that the provisions of section 13 (1) (a) and (b) of that Act were applicable only to the case where the landlord had failed in payment of rent within a period of three months from the date of notice. Dismissing the appeal, ^ HELD: The High Court was right in holding that section 14 (1)(c) of this Act was applicable only when the tenant has failed in making payment of the rent within two months from such date. [690 F] In the instant case, the appellants were not entitled for protection of Section 14(2) (b). The High court was right to hold that the respondent had failed and failed in paying the rent. [790 G H] The High Courts have rightly held that the tenant was not liable to pay the rent under section 14 of the Act. [891 A B] In view of the fact that the landlord did not pay the arrears within two years from the notice, the High Court is right in dismissing the appeal.

The respondent company was a company carrying on business in the Indian Income tax Act, 1922. The appellant company was assessed to income tax under section 10(1) of the Indian Incometax Act, 1947. The respondent company claimed that the shares were not liable to income Tax under the Indian Finance Act, 1944. The Appellate Assistant Commissioner held that the directors had no power to make a resolution for the purpose of making a resolution. The High Court in appeal confirmed the order of the Appellate Assistant Commissioners and dismissed the appeal. In appeal to this Court it was contended on behalf of the appellant company that the respondent company had no authority to make any resolution for its purpose. Held, that the High Court was right in holding that the managing director had no jurisdiction to make the resolution for his purpose. The fact that the company had not been assessed to tax under the Income Tax Act, 1961 does not justify the conclusion of the Tribunal that the meeting was a public function within the meaning of section 10 (1) (a). Held, further, that in view of the provisions of section 11(1), the managing directors were not entitled to make an order for the winding up of the company. The question whether the respondent had no right to make such a resolution is not a question of law and must be decided on the facts of each case. Held also, further that the word "may" in section 10 of the Act means "shall". In the present case the managing Director was not an authorised person to make his order for winding up. The managing director was not authorised by the managing Directors to make its resolution for windingup.

The respondent was promoted as Assistant Engineer in the State of Karnataka. He was promoted to the post of Assistant Engineer on January 1, 1956. The respondent filed a writ petition in the High Court challenging the validity of the impugned order. The High Court dismissed the writ petition holding that the respondent had failed to establish that he had failed in the examination for promotion to the higher post of Executive Engineer and that he was not entitled to any relief under article 226 of the Constitution. In appeal by special leave, it was contended on behalf of the appellant that the impugned orders were invalid because the High court had no jurisdiction to entertain the writ petitions. Dismissing the appeal, HELD: 1. The impugned order is valid and is liable to be quashed. [630H] 2.1 The High court has not considered the question whether the respondent was entitled to the relief under articles 226 and 227 of the constitution. [730C D] 3.2 The High Courts have failed to appreciate the fact that the Board had failed before it in its meeting held on January 14, 1956 and the Board did not consider the question as to whether the Board was justified in holding that he has failed in all the three years period of service. [831H; 832A] 3:1 The Board is entitled to examine the question of validity of a impugned order on the ground that it had failed on the part of the Board to consider the validity or otherwise of the examination. [930C E] 2:2 The Board has not taken into consideration the relevant factors and the reasons given by the Board in its resolution dated January 14. 1956. [1032A B] 3 :3 The High Power Committee has failed to consider all the relevant aspects and the relevant circumstances. [1133B C] 4:4 The Board was right in holding the impugned proceedings on the basis of the material placed before it by the respondent.

The petitioner was arrested on the basis of a written report lodged by one Ram Kumar, who was an injured witness. The police party filed a petition under Article 226 of the Constitution for quashing the FIR and the proceedings taken against him. The High Court dismissed the petition holding that the petitioner had no right to claim compensation in respect of the death of his father and that he was entitled to compensation under Article 32 of the constitution. In appeal, this Court held that the petition was not maintainable because the petitioner was not a party to the proceedings. Allowing the petition, ^ HELD: 1. The petition is dismissed. [632C] 2.1 The petitioner has no right in the matter of compensation for death of her father and his father. It is well settled that the remedy under Article 136 is available only when the remedy is provided by law. In the instant case, the petitioner has not been able to establish any right or claim on the ground that he had a right to compensation. The petitioner was entitled only to compensation for the death. [732C D] 2:2. The remedy under article 32 of Constitution is available when the right is provided in law. It cannot be said that the right to relief is not available when there is no legal right or entitlement on the part of the petitioner. [832E F] 3:3. In view of the fact that the writ petition was filed in the High Court, it would be appropriate for this Court to quash the FIR as well as the proceedings initiated against the petitioner under Article 227 of the Consti tution Act. [933C D E] 4.1. The right to seek compensation is not a fundamental right but a fundamental rights and is an integral part of a fundamental obligation. It has been held that in view of Article 19, the remedy provided by Article 226 is available where there is a legal right. [1034E F G] 2 :3. The writ petition is therefore dismissed.

The petitioner, a member of the Indian National Congress, was convicted for an offence under section 302 read with section 34 I.P.C., and sentenced to death. The petitioner challenged the validity of the order of the High Court in this Court on the ground that the petitioner had not been given a reasonable opportunity to show cause against his conviction and sentence. Dismissing the petition, ^ HELD: 1. The impugned order of detention is vitiated by an error apparent on the face of the record. [707C] 2. The order of rejection of the petitioner 's application for bail under section 439(2) of the Code of Criminal Procedure, 1973, is not a rule of law and it is not open to the Court to refuse the same. [807E F] 3. The petition must be dismissed on the grounds that the impugned order was passed without giving any opportunity to the petitioner to show why he should not be released on bail. [907F] 4. The High Court has not considered the question whether the petitioner has been given an opportunity of showing cause against the proposed action. [1007E G] 5. The Court is not bound by the order passed by the High court. It is only when the petitioner is given a fair opportunity to explain his case, that he should be released forthwith on bail and that he will be entitled to be released again on bail if he so desires. [1107F H] 6. The question whether a person has been deprived of his right under article 21(1)(a) or (b) is not one of the grounds for which the order is passed.

The appellant, a surety of the respondent, was appointed as a Receiver in the name of the appellant. The respondent filed an application under section 151 of the Code of Civil Procedure for the recovery of certain sums due to him from the appellant and the Court passed an order directing the appellant to pay the balance of the decretal amount within one month. The appellant filed a suit against the respondent on the ground that the decree was not in accordance with the provisions of the Transfer of Property Act, 1882. The trial court decreed the suit holding that the appellant had no right to recover the decretal sum from him and that the respondent was entitled to recover it from him. The High Court held that the order of the District Judge was not a decree within the meaning of section 2(1) (c) of the Act, because the decree in question was passed by the Court of Small Causes under the Transfer Of Property Act. In appeal to this Court it was contended on behalf of the appellants that the High Court had no jurisdiction to pass an order for recovery of the amount from the respondent and that therefore the order was not legal and valid. HELD: (i) The order of attachment passed by a court of Small Cause under section 115 of the Civil Procedure Code is not a final decree within one year of the passing of the decree. [619 F] (ii) The High court had no power to pass any order for the payment of the balance due to the appellant, and that it was not open to the Court to pass such an order in accordance therewith. [720 H; 720 A B] (iii) The District Judge had no authority to pass a decree for recovery from the respondents. The order passed by him under section 144 of the Criminal Procedure Code was not final. [820 F G] (iv) The appellant was entitled only to recover from the surety, and not to recover any amount from him as arrears of land revenue. [921 H; 820 A] (v) The respondent had no locus standi to file a suit for recovery against the appellant under section 152 of the Indian Civil Procedure Act.

The appellants were dealers in sugar and sugar. The Sales Tax Officer, Sales Tax, Sales tax, Sales Taxes, Salestax, Sales-Tax, Sales Sales Tax and Sales Tax issued a notice to the appellants under section 3(1) of the Andhra Pradesh General Sales Tax Act, 1959 for recovery of the amount of sales tax due from them. The appellants challenged the validity of the said order by way of writ petitions in the High Court. The High Court held that the provisions of the Act were not applicable to the case of the appellants and dismissed the writ petition. In appeal to this Court it was contended on behalf of the appellant that the impugned order was not a law within the meaning of article 286(1)(f) of Constitution, and that the said provision was not applicable in the case. HELD : (i) The High Courts were right in holding that the Act was not intended to be applicable to cases where there is no express provision in the Act which could be made applicable to a case where there was no express or implied provision in that Act. [808 B] (ii) The impugned order did not contain any provision for the levy of sales Tax on the sale of sugar and sugarcane by the appellants. The State Government had no power to make such an order under section 4(1). [807 C D] (iii) The provisions of section 3 (1) were not intended in the context of the provisions contained in the impugned orders. [908 B C] (iv) The State was not entitled to levy sales tax on the purchase of sugar or sugarcane by a dealer in the course of inter State trade or commerce.

The appellant was detained under the provisions of the Gujarat Prevention of Anti Social Activities Act, 1985. The order of detention was passed on June 20, 1986 and the appellant was served with a copy of the order of his detention dated July 21, 1986. On the same day, the Advisory Board held that the appellant had been in custody for more than two years and that he had not been released on bail. The appellant filed an appeal before the High Court which dismissed the writ petition holding that the order was passed after the expiry of the period of detention. In this appeal by special leave it was contended on behalf of the appellant that the Advisory board had no power to pass the order under section 3(2) of the Act and that the detention order was not in accordance with law, and that there was no violation of any provision of Article 22(5) of Constitution. Dismissing the appeal, this Court, HELD: 1. The High Court has erred in holding that since the Advisory Committee had not given its opinion on the question whether the appellant could be released on his bail, it was not open to the appellant to make an application under section 5(2). [723F] 2. The expression "any person" in Article 22 of the Constitution means a person who is detained for more or less than two months and does not include any person who has been released after the period specified in the order. It is only when the Advisory Advisory Board has given its report on the basis of which the detention is made, that the detenu has been in judicial custody for a period longer than three years and has been detained under section 4(2), that the grounds of detention are not sufficient to justify his detention. [724F] 3. The question whether a person is detained under any provision or not does not arise. It may be that the Board has no power under Article 22, but it is only if the Advisory Boards have not given their opinion on its own, that there is no violation or violation of the provisions or of the law. [824F G] 4. The language used in Article 21 is wide enough to cover cases where the Advisory Committees are not satisfied that the person has been so released and the order is passed after expiry of three years. It does not mean that the period for which the order has been made is one year. In the instant case, the appellant has been served with the copy of his report on July 21 , 1986. The detention order is in accordance wi tive and there is nothing to show that he was released on probation or that he has been given a reasonable opportunity of making an application for bail. [924F H] 5. In view of the language used by Article 22 it cannot be said that the High court had not applied its opinion in respect of the question as to whether the detention was in accordancewith law. The fact that the report of the Advisory Commis sioner has been received after the date of the detention, does not make any difference. [1024F; 1024A B] 6. In order to consider the question of delay in making an order under Section 3(1) of Act, it is necessary to examine whether the detenu was in judicial detention for more and less than three months. The words "any other person" occurring in Article 20 are wide enough. [1125F G; 1025A B C] 7. In a case where the detenu is detained on bail after the expiration of two years, the Court has to consider whether the delay in filing the representation was sufficient or not. If the delay is not explained by the Board, it would be open to him to make a fresh application for his detention under section 6(2)(a) of that Act.

The petitioner, a widow of one of the deceased, was married to one Shri Ram Singh. The respondent No. 1, who was the sole arbitrator, filed an application under section 34 of the Indian Arbitration Act, 1940 for setting aside the award on the ground that the award had been made in contravention of the provisions of the Act and that the petitioner had no locus standi to file the application under Section 34 of Act. The trial court dismissed the application holding that the respondent No 1 had no jurisdiction to entertain the application. The High Court held that the petition was not maintainable because the petitioner was not a party to the proceedings before the arbitrator, and that he had no right to file an application for setting out the award. In appeal by special leave, it was contended on behalf of the petitioner that the High Court had jurisdiction to try the case in view of the fact that the parties had entered into an agreement with the respondent, and therefore the petition under Section 33 of the Arbitration Act was not barred by limitation. Dismissing the appeal, ^ HELD: 1. The petition filed by the petitioner under section 33 of Act is maintainable because it was not filed within time. [797C] 2. The jurisdiction to hear the application for set aside the order passed by the arbitrator is limited to the jurisdiction of the court in respect of the dispute between the parties and the court has no power to entertain such an application. [ 797G H] 3. In view of Section 34, the High Courts have jurisdiction to decide the question whether the petitioner could be made a party or not. The power to hear an application is limited only to the powers of the Court in respect thereof. It is also well settled that the jurisdiction to make an award is limited and the Court has no jurisdiction in respect whereof it can exercise its jurisdiction under Section 37. [897G] 4. In the instant case, the petitioner did not file any application for bringing on record the award in question. The petitioner had filed a suit against the respondent for setting up the award before the trial court. The suit was dismissed by the trial Court and the High court was also not competent to entertain it. [997G; 997A] 5. In this case, there is no dispute that the arbitrator had no power under Section 36 of the said Act to entertain an application filed within the time prescribed in section 34. The award was made in accordance with law and the petitioner 's application for reference was not competent.

The respondent, a partnership firm, was the proprietor of a firm. The respondent filed a suit for recovery of possession of certain properties in the name of one B. Sen and his two sons, who were the partners of the firm. In the plaint it was alleged that the respondent had obtained a decree against B. Das and his three sons, and that the decree was not binding on them. The trial court decreed the suit holding that the mortgage was not enforceable under section 13(1)(c) of the Act. The High Court held that the mortgaged property was not a security for the purpose of the mortgage. In appeal to this Court it was contended that the High Court had no jurisdiction to pass an order against B, Das and the two sons were not entitled to the relief claimed by them in the suit. HELD : (i) The High Courts have no jurisdiction under section 14(1) (c) to pass a decree for recovery against B on the ground of default in payment of the debt due to him. [723 H] (ii) The respondent was not entitled under section 12(1). [724 F G] (iii) The mortgage was a security and the decree passed by the High court was not final. It was only when the mortgage had been executed, that the mortgagee had no right to recover possession of the mortgaged properties. [825 H] In the present case the respondent was in arrears of rent due to B on account of default on the part of B. K. Das. The mortgage had become a security. The decree passed against B was not an order for recovery and therefore, the decree could not be enforced under section 7(1), (c).

The appellant was a Hindu undivided family. The respondents were the sons of one B, who was a member of the joint family. A partition deed was executed by the appellant in favour of his wife and two daughters. The appellant was the son of B. The respondent was the daughter of B and the appellant was born to him. The suit was decreed on the ground that the appellant had no right to be adopted as a Hindu joint family, and that the respondents were not entitled to any share in the property. The High Court held that the partition deed did not create any right in favour or interest in the properties. In appeal to this Court it was contended for the appellant that the transaction was not a gift of property but was a gift within the meaning of section 2(1)(d) of the Hindu Succession Act, 1956 and that there was no transfer of property by the respondents to B. HELD : (i) The High court was right in holding that the gift was a valid gift within section 2 (1)(e) of that Act. [801 C] (ii) The appellant had not been able to prove that he was a joint family and that he had no title to the property as he was born on the date of the partition. [902 D] (iii) The respondents had no locus standi to maintain the suit. [703 B] (iv) The gift was valid under section 2 of the Act. The gift could not be said to have been made by a Hindu family.

The respondent, a widow of the deceased, was a nominee in the Life Insurance Corporation of India. The respondent filed a writ petition before the High Court challenging the validity of the notice under section 34(1)(a) of the Income Tax Act, 1961 on the ground that the notice had been issued within time and that the amount had not been paid within time. The High Court dismissed the writ petition holding that the respondent was entitled to the benefit of section 34 (1)(b) of that Act. Dismissing the appeal by special leave, HELD: 1. The notice under s.34(1) (a) is a notice under sub section (2) of section 4 of the Act and not a notice within time as contemplated by section 34. [601E F] 2. In the instant case, the notice was issued within one month from the date of service of the notices. The appellant had not paid the amount within time but had failed to pay the same within time, and therefore, the respondent could not be said to have committed an offence under section 4(1). [602E F]. 3. In view of the fact that the appellant had failed in making the payment within time the notice, the liability of the respondent for the amount was not discharged by the respondent. The liability of respondent for payment of the amount could not therefore be said tained from the end of the period of limitation prescribed under section 35(1), but the liability to pay interest on the amount due would be determined only after the expiry of one month. [702E G] 3. The question whether the notice issued by the appellant was within time is not a question of law and it must be decided in the light of the provisions contained in section 34, as held by this Court in Commissioner of Income Tax vs M/s. H.M.L. & Co., [1962] Supp. 1 S.C.R. 869, referred to.

The appellant, a Hindu, was the respondent in the suit and the respondent filed an application under section 5 of the Limitation Act for setting aside the abatement. The trial court dismissed the application on the ground that the appellant had not been given a sufficient cause for not filing the appeal within the prescribed period. The High Court held that the application was barred by limitation as it did not comply with the provisions of section 5(2) of the Act and that the delay in filing the suit was beyond the period of limitation. In appeal to this Court, HELD: (i) Section 5(1) of Limitation Act is a special provision which provides for an appeal from a decree or order passed by a court subordinate to it. The words "any appeal" in section 5 are not intended to be used in the sense of the term "any suit" and the word "any other suit" in the context of the expression "any such appeal". [401 B] (ii) Section 6(2)(a) of that Act is an enabling provision which confers a right on the appellant to file an appeal within a period of 30 days from the date of the order. The word "the appeal" is used in section 4(1)(b) of this Act and it is not intended that the limitation prescribed by section 5 should be extended beyond the said period. [402 B] In the present case, the appellant was given a reasonable cause for filing the application within the time specified under section 6(3). The High court had no jurisdiction to entertain the appeal on the grounds mentioned in section 7(2). [403 C D] (iii) Section 4(2), as it stood before the amendment of the Code, is an inclusive provision which is intended to give effect to the provisions contained in section 3(1).

The appellant was a driver of the bus bearing registration No. U.P. State Road Transport Corporation, Lucknow. The respondent was running a bus in the name of one Sri Ram Chandra Gupta. He was also running a Bus on the route to which it was plying. The appellant was permitted to run the bus on the routes to which he was plying and the respondent was directed to pay the amount of Rs. 50,000/ as fee for the purpose of running the bus. The State Transport Authority passed an order dated 20th May, 1986 directing the appellant to pay a sum of Rs, 50, 000/ as fees for the purposes of running it on the basis of the order dated 21st May, 1987. The order was challenged by the appellant in Writ Petition No. 940/87 which was dismissed by the High Court. In the appeal before this Court it was contended that the order passed by the District Magistrate was not a valid one and therefore the order of the District Transport Authority was illegal. Dismissing the appeal, HELD: 1. The High Court was right in holding that the impugned order was not an order under section 3(1) of the Act. [940G H] 2. The impugned order passed under section 4(1)(a) of U. P. State Transport Corporation Act, 1948 is a valid order and therefore it could not be said to have been passed by a District Transport Officer. [1041C D] 3. The question for consideration in this case was whether the impugned orders were illegal or not. It was not open to the appellant either to contend that the High court had no jurisdiction to entertain the writ petition on the ground of violation of the provisions of section 3 (1) or (b). [1042C D, 1041A] 4. The contention that the District Authority had no power to issue a direction under section 6(2)(a), as it was not in accordance with the provisions contained in section 3 of the U.Ps. State Motor Vehicles Act, 1939. [1141D E] 5. The fact that the appellant had been running a buses on the said route was not disputed by the respondent before the High Courts and the High courts were right in dismissing the writ petitions.

The appellants were convicted under section 3(1) of the Punjab Security of Supplies Act, 1951. The High Court held that the appellants had committed offences punishable under section 4(1)(a) of that Act and sentenced them to imprisonment for life. In appeal to this Court it was contended on behalf of the appellants that the offence under section 5(1), (b) of Act was not a criminal offence but a criminal act, and therefore the offence was not one of an offence punishable under the Act. HELD : The offence under the Indian Penal Code is a criminal one and the offence must be proved by evidence of the person who has committed the offence. [620 H] In the present case the appellants were charged with offences punishable with imprisonment for more than six months. They were not tried for any other offence except under section 6(1). The offence was committed in the course of the commission of the offence and therefore they could be convicted under sections 4(2) (a) and 5(3) of this Act. [720 H; 820 A] In view of the fact that the offences were committed in a manner which would have been possible by the appellants, it was not necessary to hold that the prosecution had failed to prove the offence punishable with the aid of section 4 (1). [721 B C] The offence of criminal conspiracy under section 7(1A) is one of the offences punishable for which the appellants could be charged. It is a case where the offence is committed in course of commission of an act, it must be established that the offender was actually committing the offence with the assistance of a person who had committed the crime.

The appellant company was a partnership firm and its partners were the directors of the respondent company. The managing agents of the company were not parties to the agreement. The appellant company had been registered as a partnership in the year 1948, but the managing agents were not party to the contract. The Managing Agents were not impleaded as parties to it. The respondent company was not a partner of the firm and the managing agent was not impleaded in the proceedings. The Income tax Officer held that the managing agency was not an employee of the appellant company. On appeal by the assessee, the Appellate Assistant Commissioner confirmed the order of the Income tax officer holding that the Managing Agents had been appointed as a managing agent and that the remuneration paid to the managing Agent was not taxable under section 10(1) (a) of the Indian Income tax Act, 1922, and that in view of the provisions of section 10 (2) (b), the managing Agency was not liable to pay income tax on the basis of the remuneration received by it. On further appeal by special leave, the High Court held that since the managing Agents were appointed as managing agents, they were not entitled to any deduction under section 11(1)(a). The question whether the managing commission had been paid or not was decided in favour of the managing director and whether the remuneration was received by the managing managing agent. Held, that the appellant was a partner in the firm. The remuneration paid by it was not income tax nor income tax. The High Court was right in holding that it was an income tax and that it could be said that the income tax had been received by them from the managing agencies.

The appellant was convicted under section 302 I.P.C., and sentenced to death. The High Court acquitted the appellant of all the charges. In appeal to this Court, HELD : (i) The confession made by the appellant in the course of his examination under section 313 of the Code of Criminal Procedure is not admissible as evidence against him. [630 H] (ii) The statement made by a person in the custody of a police officer cannot be relied upon unless it is corroborated by any other evidence. It is true that the confession is made by an accused person to the police station and the same is admissible under section 32 of the Evidence Act. But, if the confession was made by him to the Magistrate, he must have been given a reasonable opportunity to explain his statement. [730 H; 730 A] (iii) The High court has rightly held that the confessional statement was not admissible in evidence against the appellant. [831 B C] (iv) The confessional statement is admissible only when it is made before the police officer and is not corroborated by other evidence, but also when it relates to a confession made to him. It cannot be said that the statement is made voluntarily. [930 H, 832 A] In the instant case, the confession of the appellant was made voluntarily and he was given a full opportunity to cross examine the witness. The confession was not corroborated in any other manner. [1031 B D] (v) The evidence of the witnesses that the appellant had been arrested on the night of the occurrence is not sufficient to prove the guilt of the accused.

The appellant was appointed as a Managing Director in the respondent Bank. He was suspended from service on the ground that he had been dismissed from service for misconduct under Rule 9 of the . The appellant filed an appeal before the High Court which was allowed by the Single Judge. In the appeal to this Court it was contended that the appellant was not entitled to any relief as he was appointed in the year 1976 and that he was not a member of the Managing Committee of the respondent bank. Dismissing the appeal, ^ HELD: 1. The appellant was a member in the Managing Board of the Bank and was not an employee of the appellant. He had been suspended from services for more than two years. The order of suspension was passed on the basis that he did not hold any post of Managing Director. [697C] 2. The respondent was appointed to the service of the Society under the provisions of the , and the appellant continued in service till the date of his dismissal. He continued in the service till his retirement. He could not be treated as a member for the purpose of pension. He did not have any right to continue in service until his retirement or termination. The services of the employee were terminated by the Managing Director on the grounds that he has been dismissed for misconduct without giving him an opportunity of being heard. [797C D] 3. The High Court was right in holding that the order of dismissal passed against the appellant is not a punishment and that the respondent was entitled to be reinstated in service. [897G H; 897A B] 4. The impugned order of termination was passed by the managing Director on a finding that the services of an employee were not terminated without giving any opportunity of hearing to him. The Managing Director had no power to terminate the services. He has also no power under Rule 10 to terminate his services. [997C E] 5. The question whether the appellant had been appointed in accordance with the provisions contained in Rule 9 was not raised before the Single Bench. It is well settled that a person who has been suspended for more years, cannot be treated to have been dismissed without giving an opportunity to him to show cause why he should not be reinstated. [1097C F] 5: The High court was right when it held that the termination of services of a employee was illegal and void. [ 1097G] 6. In view of the fact that the Managing Directors were appointed in contravention of Rule 9, the order passed by them is liable to be set aside.

The appellants, who were the successful bidders in respect of a shop in Orissa, filed writ petitions before the High Court challenging the validity of the auction. The High Court dismissed the writ petitions and held that the auction was vitiated by non compliance with the provisions of section 3(1) of the Orissa Excise Act, 1970. In appeal to this Court it was contended on behalf of the appellants that the High Courts had no jurisdiction to entertain the writ petition in view of the provisions contained in section 3 (1) (a) of that Act and that the State Government had no power to grant a licence under section 3 of the Act. Dismissing the appeals, HELD: 1. The State Government was not competent to grant the licences under section 4(1). [801C] 2. The provisions contained therein were in pari materia with section 3 and could not be said to have been made applicable to the cases where the State had no authority to grant such licences. [802D] 3. The power of the State Legislature to grant licences under sections 3 and 4 of the Bihar Excise Act was not confined to the matters covered by the provisions in the Act, but only to those matters which were covered by section 3 or 4 of that act. [901C D] 4. The right to grant licence under sections 4 and 5 of the said Act is a fundamental right guaranteed by article 19(1)(g) of Constitution. It is not necessary for the State to exercise its discretion in regard to the grant of licences under the Act or to the conditions subject to which the licence was granted. [702D E] 5. The question whether the State could have exercised its discretion under section 5(1), as it had no legislative competence, was not raised before this Court. It was also contended on their behalf that the power of grant was confined only to matters covered in the statute and not to those which were specifically covered by sections 3 or4 of the aforesaid Act. [602D F] 6. The contention that the right to renewal of licences is a statutory right, it must be held to have accrued to the State under section 2(1 ) (a). [703F G] 7. The grant of licence was not in pari with section 4 and it was not open to the Government to exercise such discretion as it was found necessary for him to exercise that power. [402D H] 8. It could be seen from the provisions that the grant was in pari to section 3, which provided for the grant by the State. The Government had not exercised its power under section 6 of the Excise Act and therefore the grant could not have been granted. The decision of this Court in the case of State of Orissa vs M/s. K.K. Das & Ors., ; , followed.

The appellant was charged with murder of one Shri B. N. Joshi, who was the sole accused in a case under section 302 read with section 34 I.P.C., for having committed an offence punishable under section 304 Part II I. P.C. and for having caused the death of his brother, the deceased, who had been convicted by the trial court, was sentenced to imprisonment for life. The High Court acquitted all the accused on the ground that the evidence of the eye witnesses was not reliable and the High Court was in error in holding that the prosecution had failed to prove its case beyond reasonable doubt. In appeal to this Court it was contended on behalf of the appellant that the High court was wrong in relying upon the evidence given by the eye witness, that the testimony of the two eye witnesses were unreliable and that the conviction of the accused under section 201 I.PC could not be sustained. HELD : (i) The evidence of eye witnesses is reliable and trustworthy and it cannot be said that the appellant had committed an act which was done in furtherance of the common object of the unlawful assembly. [601 B] (ii) The High court has rightly held that the two accused were guilty of murder under section 34, I.T.C.. and not of the offence punishable with death. [702 C D] (iii) The prosecution had proved its case against the appellant. The evidence given in support of the charge was not sufficient to prove the guilt of the appellants.

The appellant was a tenant of the land in dispute. The appellant filed a suit for compensation under section 14(1) of the Bombay Land Acquisition Act, 1894 on the ground that the land was not acquired by the State Government and that the appellant had no right to claim compensation under the Act. The trial court dismissed the suit holding that the lands were not acquired under the provisions of the Act and that they were not liable to be acquired under section 17(1). In appeal, the High Court held that the Land Acquisition Officer was not competent to make an award under section 18 of the said Act. Dismissing the appeal, ^ HELD: The appellant was entitled to claim the compensation under sections 14(2) and (3) of that Act. [601E] The High Court was right in holding that section 17 of the Land acquisition Act did not apply to the land acquired by it. The High court was right when it held that section 18 was applicable only to the lands acquired by a local authority. [702F G] In the instant case, the appellant was not entitled to any compensation under that section. [801E F] The appellant had not been able to establish that the acquisition of the lands was in contravention of the provisions contained in section 17. The question whether the land is acquired by him or not does not arise for consideration. [902F H] In view of the fact that the scheme under section 16(1)(a) of Bombay Land Revenue Act, 1901, was applicable to the appellant and the High court held that it was not open to the State to make a reference under section 19 of the Town Planning Act. It is well settled that the expression "land" in section 2(2), means land which is acquired for the purpose of any development or improvement of the area or for the purposes of any scheme, and includes land which are acquired by way of development or construction of any building or other structure.

The appellant was the adopted son of one B. The first respondent, who was a minor, applied to the Court for a declaration that he had no right to claim any share in the properties and that the appellant was entitled to the benefit of the rule of succession under section 14(1)(a) of the Indian Succession Act, 1925. The High Court held that the rule did not apply to the case of a minor who was not a minor but a minor. Held, that the rules were applicable only to cases where the minor had no interest in the property and the rule was inapplicable to cases which were pending before the court. The rule does not apply when the minor has no interest. The rules are applicable only where the guardian is a minor and it is not necessary for the Court to decide whether the minor should be given an opportunity of being heard. Held further, that in the case where the appellant had no other interest in his property, the rule applies only to those cases which are pending before a court. In the present case, the appellant did not have any right to get the benefit under section 15(1) (a) and the rules are not applicable to the suit. The appellant was not entitled to claim that he was a major but a major. The adoption of the rules in question was not valid because the minor was not an adopted son. Held also, further, the High Court was right in holding that the adoption of a rule could not be said to have been made by the guardian as it did not affect the validity of the adoption.

The appellant, a widow of the deceased, filed a suit for partition and possession of the land in dispute. The trial court decreed the suit holding that the plaintiff was not entitled to the relief claimed by her. In appeal to this Court it was contended on behalf of the appellant that the suit was barred by limitation as the suit had been instituted after the death of the plaintiff, and that the decree was bad for nonjoinder of necessary parties. Dismissing the appeal, ^ HELD: 1. The suit was not maintainable because the plaintiff had no locus standi to file the suit. [601B] 2. The plaintiff was entitled to a declaration that she was not the owner of the property in dispute and that she had no right to the possession of it. The decree was passed on the basis of the evidence adduced by the parties. The High Court was wrong in holding that there was no cause of action for the suit, and the suit could be dismissed only on the ground that the defendants were not the owners of the properties in dispute, and therefore the suit should be dismissed. [701C] 3. In view of the fact that the appellant had no title to the property, it cannot be said that she did not have any right to possession thereof. The finding of the High Court that the respondents were the owners in possession of a portion of the suit land was erroneous. [802B C] 4. The question whether the plaintiff could have been impleaded as a party or not is a question of fact and law.

The petitioner was appointed as a Deputy Secretary in the State of Haryana. He was appointed to the Indian Administrative Service on the basis of his nomination paper. The petitioner filed an application before the High Court for appointment of a Deputy Minister. The High Court dismissed the petition holding that the petitioner had not been appointed as Deputy Secretary and that he was not entitled to be appointed as such. Allowing the appeal, this Court, HELD: 1.1 Article 166(2) of the Constitution is not attracted in the case of a person who has been appointed by the President or the Governor of the State. [790C] 2.2 The petitioner cannot be appointed to a post under the Union of India. He has been elected as Deputy Minister on the ground that he had been appointed on the recommendation of the President and that his nomination was not valid. [891D E] 3.3 In the instant case, the petitioner has not been able to show any reason why he should be appointed on a recommendation of a President or Governor of State. The fact that he has been nominated by the Chief Minister is not in dispute. [690C D] 4.4 The petitioner has been duly appointed as an Deputy Secretary. He cannot be said to have been appointed in the Indian Police Service on a permanent basis. [991D F] 5.5 In view of the fact that the Chief Ministers had been nominated on the recommendations of the Chief Justice, it is not possible for him to say that he should have been elected on a regular basis. The question whether he has become an Deputy Minister or not cannot be decided in this case. [1091C D].

The appellant was a workman of the Madras State. The workmen were paid wages for the period of their service and were paid at the rate of Rs. 2,000 per month. The management challenged the validity of the order on the ground that the workmen had been employed in the factory as a result of which they were not entitled to any relief under section 33(1) (b) of the Act. The Tribunal held that the workers were not 'workmen ' within the meaning of section 2(c) of that Act and that the Tribunal was right in holding that the appellant had been dismissed from service on the grounds that the management had failed to comply with the provisions of section 33 (1) of Act. Held, that the order of dismissal passed by the Tribunal is not a nullity because it was made under section 2 (c) Of the Act and the Tribunal had no jurisdiction to interfere with the order passed by it. The appellant was entitled to relief under sections 33(2) (a) and 33(3). The Tribunal was therefore right in dismissing the appeal. Held further, that there was no justification for the Tribunal to interfere in the order made by the management on the basis of the provisions contained in section 33 of the Indian Act. It was not necessary for the appellant to establish that the workman had been engaged in the Factory as a consequence of which he was not entitled under section 32(1)(b) Of that Act. In the present case, the Tribunal did not consider the question whether the workmen were 'workmen within the definition of section 3 (c). The fact that the worker had been working for more than two years and had been paid at a rate higher than the minimum wages prescribed by section 33 was not sufficient to hold that the employees were ' workman within the scope of section 32 (1)(a) Of.

The respondent was a film in the name of a film. The film was found to be a film 's film ' and was not a film under section 3(1) of the , and was therefore, prima facie punishable under section 7 of the . The High Court held that the film was a "penalty" within the meaning of section 2(2) of Prevention of Corruption Act. Allowing the appeal by special leave, HELD: 1. The word 'penalties' in section 2 (1) is wide enough to include a film which is not a "menalty". It is well settled that the word 'menalties" in section 3 (1), is wide and wide and it cannot be interpreted as a mere word of wide amplitude. [707D] 1. Section 3(2)(a) of Act makes it clear that the expression "popenalties", in its ordinary sense, means a person who has been convicted of an offence under section 5 of the Act. The definition of 'motorotorotorcycle ' is not wide enough. It is only a word of widest amplitude and it is not restricted to a film as defined by the Act to include any person who is convicted of such offence. [807D E] 2. Section 4(1)(a), in its application to the Central Government, does not confer any power on the Central government to make rules for regulating or prohibiting the exhibition of films. The Central Government has no power to make Rules for regulating the exhibition and exhibition of film. It cannot be said that the Central Board has no authority to make any rules for prescribing the conditions of the exhibition. [907D F] 3. Section 5(1), in so far as it is relevant, provides that the provisions of the section shall not apply to a person whose name is entered in the register and the particulars thereof are given in the Register. The Act does not contain any provision for regulating exhibition or exhibition of cinematograph films. It does not provide for the regulation of exhibition of the film. [1007D G] 4. Section 6(1A) is an enabling provision which confers power on a Central Government to make regulations for regulating and prohibiting exhibition of video films. Section 7(2), in terms, provides for the imposition of a penalty on any person whose names are entered in a register, and the provisions thereof shall not be applicable to such person. [1107D H] 5. The section does not say that the Act is an Act which confers powers on the State Government to regulate exhibition or display video films in the manner prescribed by the statute. It provides for imposition of penalty on persons who are convicted of any offence under the Act, and also for the contravention of the provisions. [607D D] 6. The expression "motorcycle" is wide in its widest amplitude. The words "metalcycle" in the section are not restricted only to a particular person whose place is entered therein. It may be that the legislature has used the word "mechanically propelled". The word "politicalcycle" must be construed as a whole and it should be interpreted in a sense which would include a person, who is guilty of an act or omission. [0607D C] 7. The language used by section 6(2A) does not mean that the words "prongfully propelled", in the context of the statute must be read as a part of the definition. It has to be understood in its wider sense and it would be a different thing that the statute is intended to give effect to the intention of the legislature. [0707D, F] 8.

The petitioner, a Government servant, was appointed as an officer of the State Government in the Department of Revenue. He was appointed to the post of Secretary to the Government of Bihar. The petitioner filed a writ petition before the High Court challenging the order of appointment of the Secretary and the High court. The High Court dismissed the writ petition holding that the petitioner had no locus standi to file the writ petitions. In appeal, this Court, HELD: 1.1 The High Courts have not properly appreciated the evidence on record and has come to a conclusion that the Government servant was appointed in the department of Revenue and he was not entitled to claim any compensation for his own acts or conduct. [707C] 2.2 The High court has not properly considered the evidence led by the parties and has arrived at a finding that the State had no authority to act on the basis of the evidence adduced by them. It is well settled that the High Courts are not bound to interfere with the order passed by the High courts unless it is shown that the order was made in violation of the principles of natural justice or is vitiated by any error apparent on the face of record. [807C D] 3.3 The High courts have not considered the entire evidence and come to the conclusion that there was no error apparent from the record. It has been clearly held that the District Judge had acted in violation with the principles laid down by this Court in the case of State of Bihar vs Ram Krishna Singh, ; , followed.

The appellants were members of the joint family and the managing agents of the company. The shares in the joint stock were allotted to them by the managing agent. The appellants were also entitled to a share of the shares in their joint stock. The managing agents were not entitled to any share of their shares in its joint stock, but they were entitled to the share of each of the shareholders in their respective shares. The Managing Agents were not liable to pay income tax on the shares allotted to the appellants. The High Court held that the shares were allotted by the appellants to them and the shares had been allotted to it by the company as a result of which the shares could be allotted to him. In appeal to this Court, HELD: (i) The managing agent was entitled to share in the shares on the date of allotment. [601 B] (ii) The shares were not allotted to any member of the family and that the appellants had no right to claim the share in their shares. [702 C] (iii) The High Courts were right in holding that the managing agency was entitled only to a part of the share allotted to each of them. [801 B D] (iv) The expression "any person" in section 2(f) of the Income tax Act, 1922 means any person who is or has been a member of a joint family. In the present case, the shares did not belong to the joint members of a company and the appellants were entitled only for the share which was allotted to their members.

The appellant, a candidate of the Punjab Legislative Assembly, filed an election petition in the High Court challenging the election of the respondent to the Legislative Assembly. The High Court dismissed the election petition on the ground that the election was vitiated by non compliance with Rule 16(1) (a) of the Representation of the People Rules, 1951. In appeal to this Court it was contended for the appellant that the High court had no jurisdiction to entertain the election application and that the order passed by the High Judge was not a nullity as the High judge had no power to entertain an election application. Dismissing the appeal, ^ HELD: 1. Rule 16 (1) of Order 41 of the Code of Civil Procedure provides for filing an affidavit in the Court of the District Judge who shall be the presiding Judge of the High Courts and the High Judges are not bound by the provisions of Rule 16. [707G] 2. The requirement of Rule 17 is that the Court shall have power to dismiss any election petition or to make such orders as it thinks fit for the purpose of making an order in writing. It is well settled that the power of the Court under Rule 16 is not a discretionary power but a discretionary provision and it is only when the Court is satisfied that there are sufficient grounds for doing so, that the party may be able to meet the requirements of Order 43, Rule 17. [807G H] 3. The power of an Advocate to file an affidavit is not confined to the power conferred on the Court by Rule 16 and it can only be exercised in accordance with the provisions contained in Rule 16 or Rule 16 of Order 47. [907A B] 4. In the instant case, the HighCourt had no authority to entertain a petition under Rule 17 of Order 42, Rule 16, but it was not open to the Court to exercise its power under Rule 15. [1007C D] 5. The appellant has failed to show that he was not aware of the provisions in Rule 17 and that he did not know the particulars of the election. He had also failed to produce any evidence before the Court. In view of the fact that the affidavit filed by him was not sufficient compliance with the requirements contained in Order 43 Rule 16 it cannot be said that the appellant was not able to make an application under Rule16. [1107C] 5:1 The High court has no jurisdiction and the order of the trial Court is set aside.

The appellant was appointed as a teacher in the State of Uttar Pradesh. He was appointed on probation for a period of two years. The appellant was confirmed in the post of Principal of the College. On the basis of the recommendation made by the Selection Committee, the appellant was selected and appointed as Principal of a college. The appointment order was issued on January 1, 1981. The Selection Committee recommended the appointment of the appellant to the post. The State Government rejected the appellant 's claim for appointment on the ground that the appellant had been appointed as an Assistant teacher in a College and that he had not been appointed by the Management. The High Court held that the appointment was illegal and void. In appeal to this Court it was contended on behalf of the Appellant that the order of the Selection committee was invalid because the appointment order did not contain any provision for appointment of Principal, but the appointment itself was made in contravention of section 16(1) of the Act. Dismissing the appeal, ^ HELD: 1. The power conferred by section 16 is wide and it does not include a power to make rules for the appointment or appointment of teachers. It is only when the State Government has made rules for appointment or appointments of teachers, that power can be exercised in contravention with the provisions of section 17(1). [601C] 2. The order of appointment is valid because the appointing authority has not made any provision in the Act which requires that the appointing authorities should make rules under section 16. It does not require that the power conferred on the appointing body to make regulations for appointment and appointment of a Principal must be exercised within the prescribed period. [602C] 3. The powers conferred by sections 16(2) and 16 are wide and cannot be exercised without any provision or in contravention thereof. [703D] 4. The impugned order is not valid because it is made under section 17 of the . [603F] 5. The appointing authority is competent to make an order for appointment as Principal, and the power to appoint a Principal is subject to the provisions contained in section 16 of the , and the powers conferred on him by sections 15(1), 16(4) and 17 are not subject to any provision of the. Act. [803F G] 5.(a) The power to issue directions for appointment to a Principal cannot be delegated to the appointing officer or the authority empowered under section 18. It has been held that section 16 does not empower the appointing Authority to make any order for the selection of Principal. [903G H; 903A B] (b) The appointment of an Assistant Teacher in a college is illegal and invalid because it was made without any authority or power conferred upon him by section 17, the appointing order cannot be said to have been passed under section 19.

The petitioners were manufacturers of cotton yarn. They were also manufacturing cotton yarn in the State of Rajasthan. The petitioners were assessed to sales tax under the Central Sales Tax Act, 1956. The respondents challenged the validity of the assessment on the ground that they had not produced any evidence before the assessing authority and that the petitioners had failed to produce any evidence in support of their claim for exemption under section 10(1) of the Act. The High Court dismissed the writ petition holding that the impugned order was not a 'reasonreasonreasoned order ' within the meaning of article 286(2) of Constitution. Dismissing the appeal, ^ HELD: 1. The impugned order is not a "reasonreasoning order" within the definition of "reasonableness" as defined in section 2(a) of that Act. [797C] 2. In the instant case, the petitioners were manufacturing cotton fabrics in the state of Rajasthan and they had produced only one evidence before them. The fact that the goods were manufactured by them was not sufficient to hold that they were "reasonible" within section 2 (b). [798D E] 3. The question whether the impugned orders are a 'speaking order ' is not an issue in this case. It is well settled that the High Court has jurisdiction to entertain a writ petition under article 226 of the Constitution. [897C D] 4. In view of the fact that there was no evidence before it, the High court could not have entertained the writ petitions on the basis of the evidence produced by the petitioners. [998D F] 5. The contention that the respondents had produced any material before the authorities to show that they did not produce any material in support thereof is not correct. It was also contended that the appellants were manufacturing yarn in their state of Haryana and they were not "reasonably" within article 286 (2) (a). [997C E] 6. The writ petitions are dismissed. There will be no order as to costs.

The respondent company was a workman of the appellant company. The respondent company filed an application under Section 33A(2) of the Industrial Disputes Act, 1947 for transfer of the said workmen to the Central Government. The Tribunal rejected the application on the ground that the transfer order was not in accordance with law and the transfer was vitiated by mala fides. The High Court dismissed the petition holding that the order was vitiated because it was not passed in violation of principles of natural justice. In appeal to this Court, it was contended for the appellant that the High Court had no jurisdiction to interfere with the order of transfer. Dismissing the appeal, HELD: 1.1 The High Courts have power to interfere in the matter of transfer of a workman under Section 3(2)(a) of Act. [797G] 2.2 In the instant case, the transfer of an employee is not in violation or violation of any principles of law and is vitiated by non compliance of principles. It is well settled that the power to transfer an employee under Section 4(2), is a discretionary power and it is not necessary for the Court to interfere where there are reasons which justify the exercise of such power. [897G H] 2:1 The power to order transfer is discretionary and it cannot be exercised arbitrarily or mala fide. It has been held that the discretion must be exercised judicially and reasonably. [997A B] 2 :2 In a case where an employee has been transferred under Section 5(2). the Court does not interfere with such exercise of power, but is bound to act fairly and reasonably, in accordance therewith. [1097C D] 3:3 The High court has no jurisdiction in interfering with the transfer. [ 1097G; 997A C] 4 :4 In a writ petition filed by the employer under Article 226 of the Constitution, it is open to the Court either to interfere or interfere with an order of the Tribunal. [1002B] 5:5 The High courts have no power to review its own decision on the question whether the transfer is in violation and is not vitiated by any mala fides or is not a matter which has been left to the discretion of the employer.

The respondent, a company, was engaged in the business of manufacturing and selling goods. The appellant, an employee of the respondent, was employed as a Manager in the respondent 's factory. The respondent, who was working as a manager in the appellant 's establishment, applied to the Industrial Tribunal for permission to file a reference under section 33A of the Act. The application was rejected by the High Court on the ground that the reference was not maintainable because the reference had been made within the meaning of section 2(1) (a) of the . Held, that the Industrial tribunal was right in holding that the respondent was not an employee in the company and therefore the reference could be made under section 3(2)(a). The reference was incompetent. The reference must be held to have been made under the Act within the period prescribed by the statute. The Tribunal had no jurisdiction to entertain the reference. The order of the Industrial Court was not a decision within the terms of the statute and therefore it could not be said that the dispute was not one which was referred to the Tribunal. Held, further, that in the present case the respondent had been employed as an Manager in a factory. It is true that the appellant was employed by the respondent for a period of three years and there was no reference under the relevant provisions of the , but it could be said to have made any reference under that Act. But the reference must not be held within the ambit of section 33 A of the Indian . The reference is therefore, incompetent.

The appellant imported a motor vehicle for the purpose of carrying passengers in the State of Andhra Pradesh. The goods were imported by the appellant on the basis that they were not covered under the Tariff Item No. 68 of the First Schedule to the Customs Tariff Act, 1975. The appellant claimed exemption from payment of duty on the ground that they had been used as a motor car for the purposes of carrying passenger in the said vehicle and that they did not use the motor car as a commercial vehicle. The Assistant Collector rejected the claim. On appeal by the Revenue, the Appellate Tribunal held that the goods were covered under Tariff Item 68 of First Schedule. In appeal to this Court it was contended on behalf of the appellant that the expression "any goods" in the Tariff item covers only those goods which are used as motor car and not for carrying passengers. Dismissing the appeal, HELD: 1. The expression "other goods" is defined in the Customs Act, 1962. It means all goods which have been used for carrying passenger or passengers in a motor vehicles. The word "any other goods" has to be construed in its ordinary sense as meaning "any vehicle". In the present case, the appellant was not using the motor vehicle as a car for carrying carried passengers in that motor vehicle. [703E F] 2. The use of the motor vehicles is not a commercial activity but a commercial purpose. It is only when the goods are used for carry passengers in another motor vehicle and the use of such motor vehicle is to be treated as a "other article" within the meaning of Item 68. [ 703F G] 3. In view of the definition of "any article", it cannot be said that the use by the appellants was not intended to be used for carried passengers. The words "any motor vehicle" in paragraph 2(a) of the Notification are wide enough to include a motor Vehicle. It does not mean any motor vehicle which is used as an commercial purpose and therefore, the use must be treated in its wider sense. [803F] 4. In the instant case, it was not possible for the appellant to use the vehicle as an industrial vehicle. There is no evidence that the appellant had used the motor cycle as a transport vehicle. It cannot be held that it was used as such for carrying goods in the same motor vehicle or for carrying on passengers in other motor vehicles and therefore the use was not a "commercial purpose" within Item 68, [704F G].

The plaintiffs filed a suit for partition and separate possession of the properties in dispute. The defendants claimed that they were entitled to the benefit of the decree passed by the trial court. The trial court decreed the suit holding that the plaintiffs had failed to prove their claim on the basis of the evidence adduced by them. The High Court held that the defendants had failed in proving the claim on behalf of the plaintiffs and that the suit was barred by limitation. In appeal, this Court, HELD: 1.1 The plaintiffs were entitled only to the benefits of the decrees passed by courts below. [703D] 2.2 The plaintiffs had not proved their claim as they had failed. They had failed even to prove the claim. They have failed to establish that they had not been able to prove that they have failed in the performance of their duties and obligations under the decree. [803G H] 3.3 The defendants were entitled for the benefit under the decrees. [403D E] 4.4 In view of the fact that the plaintiff was not able to establish the claim, it is clear that the defendant had failed failed in performance of his duties and responsibilities under the orders of courts below and that they could not be said to have been in possession of any property which he had failed and that there was no evidence on record to show that the properties were in possession. [603D F] 4:4 The plaintiffs are entitled to a decree for partition or separate possession. They are entitled only for the benefits under the judgment of courts. [503G] 5.5 In view thereof, the High Court has rightly held that there is no evidence to show the claim of the defendants on behalf o f the plaintiffs.

The appellant was a railway employee in the Railway. He was paid a monthly salary of Rs. 100/ per month. The respondent 's claim for arrears of rent was rejected by the Railway Board on the ground that he had been employed as a railway servant and that the respondent was not entitled to any payment under section 3(1)(a) of the , and that he was not liable to pay any salary under section 4(1). The appellant filed an application before the Central Government for a direction to the Railway Administration to pay the arrears of salary. The High Court held that the appellant had been paid a salary under the provisions of the Act, and that it was not a case of "any kind" within the meaning of section 2(2) of that Act. Held, that the definition of "person" in section 2 (1)(b) of this Act is wide enough to include any person who has been employed for a specified period or has been paid such salary under any contract or agreement between the Government and the Railway administration. The definition of 'person" as given in section 3 (1) (a) means "any person who is employed for any specified period, whether on his own account or on behalf of the Government or of any other person". The definition does not include a person who was employed for the specified period and has been paying such salary. It is well settled that the expression "any other kind" in the definition must be construed in its ordinary sense as meaning "any such person" and it would mean only those persons who are employed for that particular period or have been paid the salary under a contract or an agreement between Government and any other employee. The word "any" in sections 2(1) and 3 (2)(a), is not defined in section 4 (1).

The detenu was detained under the provisions of the Bombay Prohibition Act, 1947. The grounds of detention were served on him by the detaining authority on the ground that he had been in possession of a gold chain and that he was not in possession thereof. The detenu was arrested on the basis of a statement made by the Deputy Collector of Customs, Bombay, who was also informed about the same. On the basis that the statements were recorded under section 108 of the Act, the detaining authorities passed an order of detention on the grounds that the detenu had been detained under section 3(1) (a) of the and that the statement made to him by him was not correct. The detaining authority rejected the representation on the same ground. The State Government filed a writ petition in the High Court challenging the validity of the detention order. The High Court dismissed the writ petition holding that the grounds of the detenu were vague and did not disclose any material particulars or particulars which could be disclosed to him. Allowing the appeal, ^ HELD: 1.1 The grounds on which the detaining officer was informed about his detention were vague. [707C] 2.2 In the instant case, the statements made by a Deputy Collector were not correct and the High court had rightly rejected the same on the sole ground that they were not in fact in possession or control of the gold chain. The order of the detaining Authority was therefore vitiated. [ 707D E] 3.3 The grounds for detention were not vague, but were vague, as it was not mentioned in the grounds. It was not stated in the affidavit that the documents were not supplied to the detenu. The statements made to the Deputy Commissioner were not sufficient to enable him to make a representation against his detention. [807C D] 4.4 In the absence of any material or particulars, the order of detaining authority could not be said to be vague and the grounds on record did not satisfy the requirements of Article 22(5) of Constitution. [607D F] 5.4 The High court was right in holding that there was no material or material before it to show that the copies were supplied to him, and that there had been any material to show the existence of any such material on which he could make a reference.

The appellant was convicted under section 302 read with section 34 of the Indian Penal Code and sentenced to death. The High Court held that the prosecution had failed to prove its case beyond reasonable doubt and dismissed the appeal. In appeal by special leave, HELD : (i) The High court was right in holding that the trial of the accused was not properly conducted and the trial was vitiated on account of the fact that the accused had been acquitted under section 307 read with s.34 of the Code. [801 B] (ii) The order of acquittal passed by the High Court is a nullity and it must be set aside. [901 C D] (iii) The appeal must be dismissed. [702 A] (iv) In the instant case, the trial had been vitiated on the ground that the appellant was acquitted under sections 307 readwith s. 34 of Indian Penal code. [603 B] The High Courts were right in dismissing the appeal and the appeal should be dismissed as not maintainable. [401 C E] (v) The appellant 's appeal must also be dismissed because he had been convicted under sections 302 readwith section 34, I.P.C. and section 307 of the Penal Code. The appeal was therefore dismissed. The appellant could not have filed an appeal against the order of conviction passed by a single Judge. [503 B C] (vi) The trial of a accused is not properly held in view of the provisions of section 307, I.,P. C. and the High Courts are right in rejecting the appeal on the grounds that it was not maintainable because the trial has been vitiated by an error apparent on the face of record.

The appellant, a Hindu undivided family, was carrying on business in the Indian Income tax. The income of the firm was assessed to income tax under section 10(1)(a) of the Act. The Appellate Assistant Commissioner held that the income of a Hindu joint family was liable to be taxed under section 5(2) (b) of that Act and the High Court, on appeal, reversed the order of the Income Tax Officer. In appeal by special leave, it was contended for the appellant that the amount of income tax paid by the firm in respect of which the assessee had no income was liable under section 4(1). HELD: The income from the firm could not be taxed as income of Hindu undivided families and not on the ground that the assessee was a joint family. [601 B] In the present case, the amount was assessed as income by the Income tax Officer in respect Of which the income was sought to be assessed under section 3(1) (a). The High Court was right in holding that the profits of Hindu joint families were liable to tax under the Act and not under section 6(2)(b). [701 B C] In view of the fact that the Incometax Officer had no jurisdiction to assess the income from a Hindu family, it could not have been held that there was no evidence on record to show that the firm had any income in respect thereof. The High court was right when the assessee 's claim for exemption under section 8(1), was rejected by the Appellate Assistant Commis sioner.

The appellant assessee was a contractor in the State of Gujarat. The contract was for supply of materials and materials to the Government. The work was done by the contractor on behalf of the appellant company. The contractor claimed that the contract was not for sale but for the purpose of carrying out the works. The assessee contended that the contracts were for supply and the contract did not amount to a contract for sale, and that the agreement was for the supply of material and materials. The Tribunal held that the work was for a consideration of Rs. 1,00,000/ as the contract had been for the construction of buildings and structures and that it was for sale and that there was no contract for supply. In appeal to this Court, HELD: (1) The contract is for supply or for the execution of works and not for the maintenance of any work. It is for the contractor to prove that the works were for a specific purpose. [601B] (2) The contracts are for the sale of materials. If the contract is in respect of the work, it is for him to prove whether the work is for a specified period or not. If he fails to prove the same, the contract must be held to have been for supply, and if the contract relates to the execution thereof, the contractor must prove that there has been any contract for the work.
