[701B C] (3) The agreement is for sale of material materials and material. It does not contain a stipulation in the contract that the contractor shall be entitled to the benefit of the contract.

The petitioner was a member of the Legislative Assembly of Jammu and Kashmir. He was elected as President of India on the ground that he had been disqualified for being chosen as a President of the Union territory under Article 342(1)(a) of the Constitution. The petitioner challenged the validity of the impugned Act by filing a writ petition in the High Court which was dismissed by the High court. In this petition it was contended on behalf of the petitioner that the impugned Ordinance had been passed without jurisdiction and that the said Ordinance had not been passed as required by Article 342 (1)(b) of Constitution. Dismissing the petition, ^ HELD: The impugned Act had been enacted in exercise of its powers under article 342(2) of Part I of the constitution. It was not necessary to provide for a period of three years from the date of the publication of the Ordinance. [690E] In the instant case the Ordinance had come into force on January 1, 1975 and the impugned ordinance had been issued without jurisdiction. The Act had no application to the present case because it had been made in exercise thereof by the President of Jammu & Kashmir. It is not necessary that the Ordinance should be passed without any authority of law. [790E F] In view of the fact that the petitioner was disqualified for having chosen as an President of Union territory, the impugned order dated January 1. 1975 was passed without giving him a reasonable opportunity to show cause why he should not be removed from his office. The impugned Ordinance was passed in exercise whereof the powers under Article 368 were exercised by the Governor of Jammu And Kashmir.

The appellant was a Hindu temple. The respondent filed an application under section 4 of the Madras Hindu Religious and Charitable Endowments Act, 1950 for a declaration that the appellant was entitled to the benefit of the provisions of the Act as he had been in possession of the property. The trial court dismissed the application holding that the suit was not maintainable. In appeal by special leave it was contended on behalf of the appellant that the High Court was right in holding that there was no evidence to show that the respondent was in possession and that the property was acquired for a public purpose and that, therefore, the appellant could not be said to have acquired any title to the property as he was in actual possession. Held, further, that the question whether the appellant had acquired any right of ownership or interest in the property is not a question of fact. The High Court did not consider the question of law involved in the appeal and the High court was right when it held that the plaintiff was entitled only to the relief claimed by him. The appellant could have filed an appeal against the order of the trial court. Held further, further that the appeal was maintainable because the appellant 's suit was barred by limitation. The question whether a suit was properly instituted or not is a question which arises for consideration in this Court. The appeal must be decided on merits. The decision of the High Courts in the present case was based on the evidence adduced before it and the trial Court had rightly held that there were no evidence on record to show what was the property acquired by the appellant.

The appellant company was a permanent employee of the respondent company. The appellant company claimed that the appellant company had been paid wages for the period from 1st April, 1956 to 31st March, 1956 and that the workmen were entitled to the same wages as they were entitled under the provisions of the Act. The Tribunal held that the employees were entitled only to the wages which were paid by them in the year of their retirement. In appeal to this Court it was contended on behalf of the appellant that the respondents had been paying wages for a period of three years and that there was no evidence to show that they were paid wages as per the provisions. Held, that the Tribunal was right in holding that the appellants were entitled by the provisions contained in the Act and that they had not been paid any wages as it was paid in the month of March, 1955. The respondents were entitled for the same benefits as they had been receiving wages as their employees. Held further, that there is no evidence on record to show what was paid to them in respect of the period between 1st May, 1956, and 31st December, 1956. The question whether the appellant was entitled to any wages or not does not arise for consideration in this appeal. The fact that the dispute arose out of a reference made by the Tribunal under section 33A of the , does not make any difference. Held also, further, on behalf, that it is not necessary to refer to the question as to whether the workmen are entitled to wages or wages as the case may be.

The respondent was a Government servant in the Indian Railway. He was appointed as a Chief Accounts Officer of the Indian Railways and was paid a sum of Rs. 2,000/ . The respondent filed an application under section 125 of the Code of Civil Procedure for execution of the decree against him on the ground that he had been paid a full amount of money due to him in respect of his account. The respondent contended that the amount was not payable by the respondent and that the respondent was entitled to recover the amount from the respondent. Held, that the High Court was right in holding that the order of attachment passed against the respondent under section 126 of the Act was not a decree for money due under the Indian Civil Procedure Code. The High Court had no jurisdiction to pass an order for payment of money to the respondent on account of the amount due to the appellant in respect thereof. The order of the High court was not vitiated by any error apparent on the face of the record. The appeal must be dismissed. Held: (i) The order passed against him under section 127 of the Civil Procedure code is a decree which has been made by the Court of competent jurisdiction and it is not open to the Court to pass such an order as it thinks fit. (ii) The High court had no power to pass any order for the payment of the money due in respect whereof the respondent had paid a part of the debt due to it in respect thereto. (iii) The decree passed against respondent under sections 126 and 127 of Indian Civil procedure Code is not a final decree which can be enforced by the court of competent authority. (iv) The amount due under section 128 of the Criminal Procedure Code is a money due for the respondent, but the amount paid by the appellant to the Bank in respect o the account was not paid by him in pursuance of the order passed by the High. Court. (v) The respondent had no right to recover any amount from him in accordance with the provisions of section 126 or 127 of that Act.

The appellant was a workman of the respondent, who was working as an Assistant in the Industrial Security Force. The management of the appellant 's services terminated the services of the workmen on the ground that he had been guilty of misconduct and that the termination of service was illegal. The Labour Court held that the dismissal order was not justified because the management did not discharge its duties under the relevant rules, and that it was not a case where the management had failed to discharge its duty under the rules. In appeal to this Court, HELD : (1) The termination of services of an employee is illegal and void. [601 B] (2) The order of dismissal does not suffer from any infirmity or illegality. The order does not satisfy the test of reasonableness. It is a case of violation of principles of natural justice. In the instant case, the management was not guilty of any misconduct. The termination was illegal because it was an act of misconduct. [701 B C] (3) The dismissal order did not suffer on account of any fault or illegality in the conduct of the management. [802 D] (4) The Labour Appellate Tribunal had no jurisdiction to interfere with the order of termination and that there was no violation of the principles of Natural justice. [903 A] (5) The High Court was right in holding that the order was illegal, because it did not satisfy any test of reasonable classification. [1001 B D] In the present case, there was a breach of the rules and the termination was invalid.

The petitioners, who were the doctors of the respondent State, filed a writ petition in the High Court challenging the validity of the medical examination report and the medical reports. The High Court dismissed the writ petition holding that the medical report was not properly considered by the Medical Council and that the Medical Committee had no jurisdiction to examine the medical records. Allowing the appeal, this Court, HELD: 1.1 The medical report is a statutory one and it cannot be said that the State Government has acted in accordance with law or has acted arbitrarily or without any reasonable basis. [601D] 2.2 The medical reports are not conclusive as to whether the medical authorities have acted in violation of the provisions of article 14 of the Constitution. [702F] 3.3 The medical opinion is a part of the report and it is not open to the State to examine any medical records or to examine it on its own. [801D E] 4.4 In the instant case, the medical opinion was not based on any material before the Medical Board. It is not possible for the State authorities to examine whether the Medical Officer had acted in a manner which would cause serious injury to the patient. The Medical Committee has no jurisdiction under article 226 of the constitution to examine such medical records and to examine them on its merits. [901D F] 4:4 In view of the fact that the report was made by the medical board, it is clear that the said medical opinion had been duly considered by it. [1001F G] 5.5 The Medical Council has not acted in any manner which could cause serious injuries to the patients. It has also not been shown that the doctors have acted arbitrarily and without any lawful basis. The medical Committee has not taken into consideration the medical record of the patient, nor has it been shown by the State that the treatment was done by the doctors.

The Assam Legislative Assembly of Assam was constituted under the Assam Legislative Council Act, 1947. The Assam Legislative Board of Secondary Education Act, 1948 was enacted by the Assam Legislature in exercise of its powers conferred on it by section 3(1) of the Assam Panchayat Act, 1946. Section 4(2) of that Act provides for the constitution of a Committee to be constituted under section 5A of the Act. Section 6 provides for constitution of the Committee and the procedure to be followed in the meeting. The members of the Board were elected by the members of a committee. The petitioners challenged the validity of the said Act on the ground that the Act was not applicable to them as they had been elected by members of that committee. They also contended that the provisions of section 6(1)(a) of Assam Act, 1949 are ultra vires and void. The petition was opposed by the respondents contending that the impugned Act is violative of Article 14 of the Constitution and that the said provision is not applicable in the present case as it has been passed without any authority of law. The Court held that the members who were elected under section 6A of Assam Panchayat (Amendment) Act, 1984 are not entitled to be elected by a member of the committee. In the appeal before this Court it was contended on behalf of the petitioners that the decision of the High Court in the case of Assam Legislative Boards is erroneous and that they have been given retrospective effect from the date of the impugned notification. Dismissing the petition, HELD: 1. The Act has been enacted by Parliament to provide for the establishment of a Board to be called the Assam State Legislature. It is not possible to say that the Assam Act was applicable to the members belonging to the Assam Assembly. [797C] 2. The impugned Act has no application to the present cases. The object of the legislation is to ensure that the elected members are elected by them in accordance with the provisions contained in section 6 A of the General Clauses Act, 1897. It does not mean that the election of a member should be held on the date when the Act came into force. [ 797C D] 3. The question whether the impugned legislation is valid or not is not one which can be decided by the appropriate authority under the Act and the decision in the instant case is not covered by Article 14. [897F G] 4. The provisions of the Ordinance are ultra ultra vires. [ 897G H; 997A B] 5. The State Government has been given power to make rules for the purpose of carrying out the objects of the State Legislature and the manner in which it is passed. It has also been provided that the State Government may make rules under section 4 A of Assam Ordinance. [997C E] 6. The power conferred on the State Governments under section 3A of Act is not confined to the power of the appropriate authorities under the said section. [1097G] 7. The Constitution Bench in Assam Legislative Councils has held that there was no provision for the appointment of a members of an Advisory Board and the same could be done only by the State Govt. under the provisions. It also held that it is not open to the appropriate Government to make any rules under the Ordinance. The decision of this Court in Assam Assam Legislative council cannot be said to have been taken on the basis of the decisions of this court in Assam Council for the purposes of carrying on the objects and reasons.

The appellants were married to one Ram Chandra, who was the daughter of Ram Chandra. The marriage was performed on January 1, 1945 and the appellants were born in the year 1944. On July 2, 1945, the appellants executed a will dated June 30, 1945 in favour of Ram Chander. After the death of Ram Kumar, the respondents filed a suit for partition of the properties. The trial court decreed the suit holding that the appellants had failed to prove their case beyond reasonable doubt and dismissed the suit. In appeal to this Court it was contended on behalf of the appellants that the will dated July 30, 1946 was not valid because the will was executed in favour Of Ram Chandra and the will did not create any right or interest in the property. Held, that the document was a gift within the meaning of section 2(1)(d) of the Hindu Succession Act, 1956, and the High Court was right in holding that it was not a gift under section 2 (1)(e) of that Act. The document was not intended to create any interest in property but was intended to be used as a gift for the purpose of maintenance of the family. It was not necessary for the appellants to prove that the deed was a valid one and could not be acted upon by the respondents. Held further, that it is not necessary to prove the case beyond doubt that the testator had failed in his capacity as a daughter of the deceased. The High Court erred in holding the document as a whole and held that it did not amount to gift within section 2 of the Act.

The appellant, a candidate of the Punjab State Legislative Assembly, was declared elected as a candidate for election to the Legislative Assembly. The election petition filed by him was dismissed by the High Court on the ground that he had been guilty of corrupt practice under section 123(3) of the Representation of the People Act, 1951. In appeal to this Court it was contended that the appellant had not been convicted of any corrupt practice and that the corrupt practice was committed in furtherance of the prospects of the election. Dismissing the appeal, ^ HELD: 1. The High Court was right in holding that the election petition was not maintainable because the appellant was guilty of the corrupt practices under section 124(3). [707G] 2. In view of the fact that the respondent had been convicted for the corrupt corrupt practice committed by him in furtherance to the prospects, the High court was right to hold that the returned candidate was guilty and that he was guilty. [708C D] 3. The appellant was not guilty of any offence under section 3(1) (a) of Act. [807G H] 4. In the instant case, the appellant did not have been convicted by the trial court for the alleged corrupt practice. He had been acquitted by the Trial Court on a finding that he has been guilty and sentenced to imprisonment for life. [908C E] 5. The conviction of the appellant under section 7(1)(a) (b) of Punjab Act is set aside. The respondent shall be entitled to the benefit of section 123 (3).

The appellant, a Forest Officer, was appointed as a Forest officer in the State of Haryana. He was transferred to the Forest Department. The respondent challenged the transfer order on the ground that he had no jurisdiction to entertain the application under section 33(2) of the , and that the High Court had no power to entertain it. The High Court dismissed the petition holding that the appellant was not a Forest Officers, and that he was not an officer in State of Punjab. Dismissing the appeal, ^ HELD: 1.1 The High court has jurisdiction to hear the application on merits. It is well settled that the jurisdiction of the High Courts under Article 226 of the Constitution is not confined to the jurisdiction which is conferred by the Act or the Rules made thereunder. [603E F] 2.2 In the instant case, the appellant had no locus standi to file the application for transfer of his petition. The appellant was a Forest Department and he was also an officer of State Government. He has been transferred from one State to another. He is not a person in the service of the State. [703E G] 3.3 In the present case, there is no material on record to show that the respondent had any locus standi or locus standi. The fact that the petitioner was an officer and was not made a party to the proceedings before the High court does not make out a case for transfer. [803F] 4.4 In view of the fact that he has been posted in the Forest department, it is not possible to hold that the order of transfer was mala fide or was passed mala fide.

The appellant was a tenant of the land in dispute. The respondents were granted a lease of the lands on the ground that they had no right to hold the land as a lessee. The appellant filed a suit for possession of the said lands and claimed damages for the period from 1st April, 1945 to 31st March, 1945. The trial court decreed the suit holding that the appellant was not entitled to the relief of possession. The High Court held that the lease was not a lease within the meaning of section 2(1)(d) of the Bombay Rents, Hotel and Lodging House Rates Control Act, 1947. Held, that the provisions of section 3(1) (d) were applicable only to cases where the lease had been terminated by notice under section 106 of the Transfer of Property Act, 1882. The words "any person" in section 2 (1)(e) are not intended to be used in a particular case. The word "any other person" is defined in section 3 (2) (a) and not to include any person who has been granted a licence under the Bombay Rent Control Act. The expression "any such person" means any person whose interest in the land is affected by the grant of a licence or under the provisions contained in the Bombay Tenancy Act, 1948. The term "any persons" in the section includes any person whom he is entitled to a licence. The definition of "any class" in sections 2(2) and 3 (1) of that Act does not include any class of persons who are entitled to any licence under section 105 of the Act. It is well settled that the word "person" means a person whose interests are affected by grant of licence or as a result of an order made by the court in writing under section 107 of the Code of Civil Procedure, 1908. The language used in section 106(1), therefore, clearly indicates that the words "the person who is entitled under section 108(1). must be construed in its ordinary sense and not in its popular sense. It does not mean a person who was entitled to an licence under sections 2 (2)(d), but only means a tenant whose interest is affected. The meaning of the word 'any other class" is that the person who had been granted the licence must have been given a licence for the whole or any part of the area in which he was granted the lease. It cannot be said that the expression "the persons who were entitled under the Act" in sub section (1), means a landlord whose interest was affected by such grant and not a tenant who had become entitled to such licence.

The appellant was employed as a contractor in the respondent 's factory. He was suspended by an order dated May 3, 1968. The respondents were dismissed from service on the ground that the enquiry officer had not given any reasons for his dismissal. The appellant challenged the validity of the order of dismissal and the High Court held that the order was vitiated because it was violative of article 14 of the Constitution. In appeal to this Court it was contended that the High court was in error in holding that the termination of the services of the respondents amounted to violation of article 311(2) of the constitution as it had been passed without giving any reasons and that the dismissal order was bad because it had not been passed on the basis of the enquiry report. Dismissing the appeal, ^ HELD: 1. The High Court was in wrong in holding the termination order as it was passed without affording any reasons to support the findings of the Enquiry officer. [723C] 2. The order of punishment is bad because the enquiry has been held by the Enquiry Officer and the report of the Inquiry Officer is not based on any evidence or material which may be considered by him in the light of the principles laid down in article 311 (2). [724F G] 3. The enquiry officer has to give reasons for its dismissal. He must have given reasons for the order. If he has given reasons, he cannot be said to have acted arbitrarily and without giving reasons. [825C D] 4. The termination of services of a workman is not in accordance with law. It is only when the enquiry is held by an officer that the misconduct is proved that the workman has been guilty of misconduct or that the employer has given reason for his removal. If the enquiry itself is held to be vitiated on account of some material which would be considered, it will be open to the employer to take a decision in the matter. [925C] 5. The award of punishment does not contain any reasons as to why the termination was not passed without hearing him. It has been made clear that the reasons for such dismissal are not sufficient to justify the order and the order is bad. [1025F G; 1025A B] 6. The Tribunal has to consider whether the enquiry was vitiated on the grounds of misconduct and the evidence adduced by the parties before it can be said that the report was based on some material. If it is found that the findings are not based upon any material, it would be open for the employer either to take such a decision or to pass an order in accordance therewith.

The respondents were tenants of the land in question. The respondents filed a suit for possession of the lands on the ground that they had been cultivating the same by virtue of a lease granted to them under the Kerala Land Reforms Act, 1950. The trial court decreed the suit holding that the respondents had not acquired any right to hold the land as defined in section 2(1) of the Act and that the appellants had no right to continue in possession of it. The High Court held that the appellant had no title to the lands in question and that they were cultivating the land on the date of the suit. In appeal by special leave, the Court, HELD: 1. Section 2(2) of that Act provides for a lease of land in respect of which a lease is granted under section 3 or sub section (1). The right to possession is not an absolute right but an absolute one. [601B C] 2. The right of the landlord to hold land as a tenant under section 4 is a statutory right and it cannot be said that he had acquired any rights in respect thereof. [702C D] 3. Section 5 of the Kerala Act provides that a lease shall not be granted unless the lessee has been given an opportunity of being heard. The provisions of section 5 are intended to confer a right on the landlord under section 5(1). [703F G] 4. In the instant case, the respondents were cultivating land in the year 1969 and they had acquired no right of possession. They had not been able to prove that they have acquired any title to it. They were not entitled to continue as tenants under section 6. The appellants had not produced any evidence to show that they did not possess any right of ownership. [803F] 5. Section 6 provides for the grant of a right of occupancy in respect whereof a lease has been granted by the Government or the State Government. The appellant was entitled to possession of land on his date of commencement of the Madras Land Reforms (Amendment) Act, 1969.

The appellant was found in possession of a gold chain and was found to be smuggled. The appellant was arrested on the basis of a statement made by him under section 108 of the Customs Act, 1962. He was arrested and detained in custody for a period of six months. On the same day he was remanded to judicial custody. The Magistrate held that the appellant had failed to prove his case beyond reasonable doubt. In appeal to this Court it was contended on behalf of the appellant that the prosecution had failed in proving the case beyond all reasonable doubts and that the burden of proof was not on the appellant to establish his case. Dismissing the appeal, ^ HELD: The prosecution had proved the case against the appellant. [601C] In the instant case, the appellant was a person who had imported gold chain from Bombay to Bombay. He had been found in the possession of the gold chain. There was no evidence that he had imported the gold ornaments from Bombay and had not taken any steps for the recovery of the same. The prosecution failed to establish that the gold was smuggled into India. [701C D] In view of the fact that the goods were seized from Bombay, it could not be said that the contraband was smuggled in India. The burden of proving that the smuggled goods had been smuggled into the country was on the accused. [802D E] In order to prove the case, it must be proved that the seized gold was brought into India by the appellant and the appellant did not take any steps to recover the same from the appellant, but he failed to do so. The onus of proving the fact was on him to establish the case.

The appellants, who were members of the Association of the respondent company, filed a suit for recovery of certain sums due to them from the respondent. The trial court decreed the suit holding that the appellants had no right to claim any relief against the respondent and dismissed the suit. In appeal to this Court it was contended on behalf of the appellants that the suit was barred by limitation as the appellants were not members of a Association of a company, and that the suits were barred by time as they were members in a company. Held, that the plaintiffs had no locus standi to file the suit against them. The suit was not barred by the limitation as it was filed within the period prescribed under section 5(1) of the Act. The appellants were entitled to claim relief against them on the ground that they were not member of a association of persons. Held further, that there was no bar in the suit for the recovery of any sums due from the appellants to the respondent, and the suit must be dismissed. The plaintiffs had not been able to establish that they had no cause of action against them, and therefore the suit could not be dismissed on the grounds that they did not fall within the purview of section 5 (1) (a). Held, further, further that the provisions of section 4(1)(a) of Act were attracted only when a person is a member of an association of individuals. The right to sue for recovery against a member in a firm can be exercised by the court only if it is satisfied that he was not members in the company.

The respondents were prosecuted for offences under section 120B, I.P.C., and the trial was commenced on the basis of a complaint filed by one Ram Kumar Singh against the respondents. The High Court dismissed the petition holding that the offence under section 5(1)(d) of the Prevention of Corruption Act is not made out in the course of investigation and that the offences under sections 120B and 120B are not made punishable with imprisonment for life, and that there was no evidence to show that the respondents had committed any offence under the provisions of the Act. The State appealed to this Court by special leave. Dismissing the appeal, HELD: 1.1 Section 5(2) of Prevention of 1988 is a penal provision which provides for punishment for offences punishable with death or imprisonment for a term not exceeding one year but does not provide for punishment in respect of any offence punishable with life or imprisonment. The provisions of section 5 (3) are intended to be used in the context of the criminal proceedings and the purpose of the said section is to prevent abuse of process of court or otherwise to secure justice. [797C] 2.2 Section 5 (1)(a) of that Act provides for the punishment of an offence punishable under section 4(1) of this Act. It does not contemplate any punishment in cases where a person has been convicted of an offences punishable under the Act and is sentenced to imprisonment for more than one year. The object of the section is that if the offence is committed with the consent or connivance of, or is attributable to, any neglect on the part of, any director or manager of the company, such director or Manager shall be deemed to have committed an offence under this Act and shall be liable to be proceeded against accordingly. [897C D] 2(a) The provisions in section 5 are intended only to prevent the abuse of the process of Court or otherwise. It is not possible to say that the words "any director or master" used in section 4 (1) are meant only to bring out a case where the offence has been committed with consent or knowledge, and also to prevent any abuse of power or connivance on the person concerned. [997C E] 2.(b) The word "any offence" is not intended to include an offence which is punishable with fine but does include an act which is done with the intention of causing such injury. It has been held that the expression "any Director or master", in section 3(1), is wide enough to cover a case of criminal offences and it would be appropriate if the offender is found guilty of an act committed with a view to prevent him from committing an offence. [1097C F] 2 (c) The words "other director or servant" used by section 4 are intended not to include any person who has been prosecuted for an offence other than an offence specified in section 6(1). [1099F G] 3.(d) The expression "other Director or manager" used under section 6 (1), in the sense of a criminal offence, is wide and wide enough. It would be sufficient if the words are intended by the legislature to cover only those offences which are punishable with the punishment for an act done with a intention of committing an act. [ 1099F H] 4(e) The High court has not committed any error in holding that there is no evidence on record to show what was the offence committed with respect to which the offence had been committed.

The appellant was convicted for an offence under section 302 read with section 34 I.P.C., and sentenced to undergo imprisonment for life. The High Court dismissed the appeal of the appellant on the ground that he had been in custody since May, 1973 and that he was not released on bail. Allowing the appeal, ^ HELD: 1.1 The High Courts have power to grant bail to a person who is already in jail or is already undergoing sentence for life, but does not exercise their discretion under section 439(2) of the Code of Criminal Procedure. [797C] 2.2 The High court has power to refuse bail even if it is satisfied that there are reasonable grounds for believing that he is likely to commit an offence. In the instant case, the petitioner was in jail and was released on Bail. He was not in custody till May, 1974. His detention was not approved by the High Court. The petitioner was already in custody. [897C D] 3.3 The High courts have power under section 437(1) of Code of Civil Procedure to grant a bail even though he is already already in prison. In view of the fact that the petitioner has been released on his Bail, it would be appropriate for the High Courts to grant the bail to the petitioner on the same terms as those applicable to him. [997C E] 4.4 The High power under Section 439(1)(a) is not confined to a case where the accused is already released on a bail. It is only when the court has reason to believe that he has been in jail, it may refuse bail to such person. [1097D F] 5.5 In view thereof, the High court was right in refusing bail to any person who has been arrested and detained under section 167(2).

The respondent assessee was a registered dealer in the Indian Income tax Act, 1922. The appellant was assessed to income tax under section 10(1) of the Indian Incometax Act, 1961. The Income tax Officer held that the appellant had not been able to establish his case and dismissed the application for exemption. On appeal by the assessee the Appellate Assistant Commissioner set aside the order of the Appellate Tribunal and remanded the matter to the High Court for fresh decision. In appeal to this Court it was contended on behalf of the Revenue that the Appellate 'Tribunal had no jurisdiction to decide the question as to whether the appellant was entitled to exemption under section 11(1). Held, further, that the High court was in error in holding that the assessee was not able to prove his case. The Appellate Tribunal was right in holding the assessee guilty of an offence under section 12(1)(a) and (b) of Indian Income Tax Act, 1947. The High Court was in wrong doing so. Held, that on a proper construction of the provisions of section 11A it could not be said that the Tribunal had no power to decide whether the assessee had been able able to show his case or not. The Tribunal was therefore right in rejecting the application under section 13(1), and the High 's order was set aside. Held further, further that the appeal must be allowed. The question of law raised by the appellant before this Court was not a question of fact and could not have been decided on merits. Held also, further. (i) The Tribunal had jurisdiction to deal with the question of limitation as it did not decide the questions of law. (ii) The High court had no authority to interfere with the order passed by the Appellate Authority under section 16(1); and that the order was based on a correct appreciation of evidence.

The respondent, a Minister of the State of Punjab, was appointed as Chief Minister in the Punjab Government. The respondent filed a writ petition before the High Court challenging the order of appointment of the Chief Minister and the High court. The High Court dismissed the writ petition holding that the allegations made against him were not true and that the respondent had no locus standi to file the writ petitions. In appeal to this Court it was contended on behalf of the appellant that the High Courts had no jurisdiction to entertain the writ application. Dismissing the appeal, HELD: 1. The order of the High Judge is set aside and the writ applications are dismissed. [620H; 720A] 2. The allegations made in the writ affidavit do not constitute any offence or cognizable offence. It is only when the allegations are found to be true that the petitioner has no locus to file a writ application, it would be open to the High High Court to entertain such an application if there is a prima facie case for the same. [720B] 3. The petition should be dismissed on the ground of mala fide or malafide. [820C] 4. In the instant case, the allegations in the affidavit do constitute any cognizable offence and no investigation has been made out. [920D] 5. The allegation that the Chief Ministers had taken a decision to appoint the Chief Secretary was not correct. [1020F] 6. The petitioner is entitled to be considered for appointment as Chief Secretary.

The respondent was the tenant of a building in which he had been carrying on business. The appellant filed an application under section 125 of the Code of Criminal Procedure for the recovery of possession of the property from the respondent. The Magistrate rejected the application and held that the respondent was not entitled to any protection under section 126(1) of the Indian Penal Code, because it was a tenant in respect of the land which had been leased by him to the appellant. The High Court dismissed the application holding that the appellant was not liable to pay rent for the period from April 1, 1961 to March 31, 1961 and that the property was liable to be attached under section 127(1). In appeal to this Court it was contended on behalf of the appellant that the provisions of section 126 (1) were not applicable to the case in hand. HELD : The provisions of the Act were not intended to apply to a case where the property had been let for a period exceeding one year and the property could be attached only under section 128(1), but it was not necessary to refer to the provisions in the Act. [601 B] In the instant case, the respondent had no right to recover possession of any property from him under section 135(1)(a) of that Act. The respondent was a lessee and therefore he could not be prosecuted for the offence under section 132(1A). [602 C D] The provisions in section 126 were not attracted to the facts of the case. The provisions contained in section 127 (1A) were intended to be applicable only to cases where the land had been sold for a certain period and not to cases which could have been prosecuted under section 133(1B).

The appellant company was engaged in the business of manufacturing and selling goods. The respondent company was a dealer in the State of Rajasthan. He was employed as a dealer under the State Government. The appellant company claimed that he was not a workman within the meaning of section 2(h) of the Industrial Disputes Act, 1947. The Tribunal held that the appellant company had been engaged in manufacturing and supplying goods to the respondent company. The High Court dismissed the appeal holding that the respondent was not an employee within the definition of 'workman ' as defined in section 2 (h) and therefore he was entitled to be reinstated. In this appeal by special leave, it was contended on behalf of the appellant that the word 'workman" used in section 3(h), is wide enough to include a workman who has been engaged for the purpose of manufacturing or supplying goods. Dismissing the appeal, HELD: 1. The definition of "workman" as given in section 4 (h), does not cover an employee who has engaged for manufacturing or selling goods and therefore it cannot be said that he had been employed for the purposes of manufacturing, supplying goods by him. [797C] 2. The word ' workman ' is wide and it can only mean a person who has employed for manufacturing, selling, supplying or supplying any goods to another. It does not include a person engaged in manufacture or supplying or supply goods to others. The expression "workman ' means an employee of the company. [897C D] 3. The term ' workman is defined in the Act and it includes a person employed for carrying on the business or supplying such goods to any other person. It is not necessary that the definition should be read as a whole. The words used in the definition must include a worker who has worked for the last several years. [997C E] 4. The question whether an employee is an employer within the purview of section 3 (h).

The respondent company was a tenant of the land in dispute. The State Government issued a notice under section 80(1) of the Madhya Pradesh Land Revenue Code, 1959 to the effect that the land was not liable to be leased for any period prior to the date of the notice. The respondent Company filed a suit against the State Government and the Collector of Indore for eviction of the respondent company from the land. The trial court decreed the suit holding that the lease was not a lease within the meaning of section 2(1)(c) of Madhya Pradesh Tenancy Act, 1948. The High Court held that the respondent had no right to hold the land as it stood prior to its amendment in 1956 and that the State had no power to grant the lease. In appeal by special leave, the appellant contended that the High Court was wrong in holding that section 2 (1)(d) of Act was applicable only to the land which was not leased for a period prior thereto. Dismissing the appeal, this Court, HELD: 1. The term "lease" used in section 2 of the Act is not defined in the Act. It is well settled that the word "lease ' means any person who has been granted a lease under section 3(1). [797C] 2. In the instant case, the respondent was a lessee and was not entitled to hold land as he had no rights to hold it prior to his amendment in 1959. The lease was for a term of five years. The period of five year was not taken into account by the State. The appellant could not be said to have been granted the lease on the ground that the period of lease was beyond the period prescribed under section 2. [799C] 3. In view of the fact that the appellant had no title to the lands in dispute, the High court was right in holding the land for a long time and that it was not open to the State to grant a lease on that ground. [897F] 4. The question whether the respondent could be said as lessee or not is not a question of fact.

The appellant was a tenant of the land in question. The State Government issued a notification under section 4(1) of the Act on March 31, 1965, for the acquisition of lands for the purpose of cultivation and for the purposes of cultivation. The respondents challenged the validity of the notification on the ground that it was ultra vires the Constitution as it violated article 14 of the Constitution. The High Court held that the notification was ultra ultra vires article 14 and that the State Government had no power to make a law under article 31(1). In appeal to this Court, HELD : (i) The notification issued under section 3(1)(a) of that Act was ultra violative of article 14. [808 B] (ii) The impugned notification was not ultra vires Article 14 and was therefore void. [908 C D] (iii) The State Legislature had no legislative competence to make the law in respect of lands which were acquired for the public purpose. The notification was valid because it was issued under the Act. The Act did not provide for any provision for acquisition of land for the benefit of the persons who were entitled to compensation under article 14 or for payment of compensation under that article. [1008 C] (iv) The High court was right in holding that the impugned notification could be ultra vires because it had been issued under a statute which was not within the competence of the State Legislature. [1108 D] In the instant case, the notification issued by the State under section 6(1), was valid and the notification could not be said to have been issued without any authority of law. The impugned notifications were therefore ultra vires. [1208 C E] (v) The validity of section 3 (1)(b) of Act was upheld by this Court in State of Orissa vs M/s. K.K. Das & Ors., ; , followed.

The appellants, who were the sons of one Ram Singh, filed a suit for possession of certain properties in the Court of the Subordinate Judge, Bombay. The trial court decreed the suit holding that the appellants had no right to possession of the properties on the ground that they were not entitled to the benefit of the provisions of section 14(1)(c) of the Hindu Succession Act, 1956. The High Court held that the appellant was entitled to a decree for possession in respect of the property on the grounds (i) that the respondents had no title to the properties and that the suit was barred by limitation as it was not maintainable under article 136 of the Constitution; (ii) that they had no locus standi to file the suit. The appellants appealed to this Court. HELD : (1) The High Courts have held that in view of the decision of this Court in Ram Singh 's case, the right to property is a fundamental right and it cannot be said that the right of the appellant to possession was not a fundamental one. [601 B] (2) The right to the property is an essential part of the right which has been conferred by article 14(3). It is only when the right is conferred, the rights are absolute and have no relation to the right. [702 C D] (3) The question whether a person who has acquired title to his property under the will or under the Will or under any other law for the time being in force, is not a matter of discretion. It is not necessary that the rights conferred by the will are absolute or conditional and must be held to have been conferred on the person who had acquired title. [802 C] (4) The expression "any right" in article 14 means a right which is conferred by a statute, but does not include a right to a property which has vested in the person whose interest is affected by the grant of a decree or order. It cannot be disputed that the question whether the right was absolute or not depends upon the nature and character of the rights. [902 C E] (5) The words "any other right" are wide enough to include a claim for possession, but it does not mean a right in respect thereof.

The appellant company was a Company incorporated under the Companies Act, 1956. The Company filed a suit against the respondents for recovery of certain amounts due to it from the Company. The respondents contended that the Company had no right to claim any relief in respect of the said shares and that the company had no locus standi to file the suit. The trial court dismissed the suit holding that the appellant was not entitled to claim the reliefs claimed by him. In appeal, the High Court held that the order of the Company was illegal and void as it was not a nullity. Dismissing the appeal, ^ HELD: 1.1 The Company had been appointed as a Director of the company in accordance with the provisions of the Companies (Court) Act, 1961. [703E] 2.2 In the instant case, the Company has been appointed by the Government under section 3(3)(a) of the Act and the Company is not entitled for any relief claimed by it. The order of appointment was made in accordance to the provisions contained in the Companies Companies (Amendment) Act. 1961. The High Court had no jurisdiction to entertain the suit on the ground that the Government had no power to appoint a Director as a director. [803E F] 2:3 In the present case, it is not disputed that the respondents were appointed by Government under the provisions in the Company 's Act and they were also appointed by it under section 4(3) of that Act. The Government had only power to make an order for appointment of a Director. [903E G] 2 :4 In the absence of any express provision in the Act, the Government could not have made an order under section 5(3). [904F] 2.:5 In the case of a company which is a Company, it was only a company and not a company. The power to direct appointment of Director as an director was conferred on the Government by section 3 (3) (a) (b) (c) (d) (e) (f) (g) (h) (i) (j) (k) (l) (m) (n) (o) (p) (q) of section 5 (1) (iii) (x) (xiii) (xiv) (xv) (xvi) (xvii) (xviii) (xii) (viii) (ix) (xi) (vii) (xx) (xix) (xxii) (xxx) (xxiv) (xxv) (xxvi) (xxvii) (XIII) (xxiii) (XII) (XIV) (XV) (XI) L.R. 8 I.A. No. 9 of 1984 decided on 20th May, 1984. The appellant was appointed as Director under section 6(3), and the Government made an appointment under section 7(3); and the respondents had no authority to appoint the Director under that section. [603E H] 2.(xiii) In the circumstances, the order passed by the High court is set aside and the company is directed to be reinstated in service with effect from the date of the order. The appellants shall be entitled to all the benefits which accrued to them under the Act.

The appellant, a consumer of electricity, was carrying on business in the State of Andhra Pradesh. The Board issued a notice to the appellant under section 126(1) of the Electricity Act, 2003 for recovery of arrears of energy charges from the consumers. The appellant filed objections before the Board contending that the Board had no power to recover the arrears of electricity charges from its consumers. It was contended on behalf of the appellant that the State Government has not been able to recover any arrears of the electricity charges. Dismissing the appeals, ^ HELD: 1.1 The Act is a self contained provision and it does not provide for any other purpose. [601D] 2.2 The Act provides for the payment of arrears by the consumer in respect of the supply of electricity to the consumers at the rate of Rs.5 per month. The Act has been enacted with a view to ensuring that the dues are paid within three months from the date of the commencement of the Act. It is not possible to say that the Act does not contain any provision for payment of the arrears. [701D E] 2:3 The Act does provide for payment by the consumers in respect thereof at the rates specified in the Schedule to the Act, and it provides for payment on the basis of the rate at which the dues were paid. It does not contemplate payment of any arrears or charges. The provisions of the statute are intended to be construed as a whole and not merely to give effect to the provisions of any other law. [801D F] 2(a) The Act, therefore, is not meant for payment in respect whereof the dues have been paid. The object of the legislation is to ensure that the consumers are paid the arrears or Charges. It has also been provided for payment to the consumer at the same rate. The purpose of the enactment is to provide for the recovery of the dues from its customers and to make payment on such basis. [901D G] 2.(b) The provisions in the Act are intended not to be interpreted as a part of the general law but to give retrospective effect to any provision which may be made by the legislature or the State Legislature. It cannot be said that the provisions in respect to the supply and distribution of electricity are meant for the benefit of consumers who have paid the dues. [1001D, E] 3(c) The Board has not given any reasons for the same. [ 1001F G] 4(d) The power conferred on the State under section 127(1)(a) is to make a provision for recovery in respect only of the amount which is due and payable by the licensee.

The petitioners were appointed as Assistant Director of the Indian Institute of Research and Development in the Ministry of Finance. The Central Government issued a notification dated 4th March, 1973, inviting applications for promotion to the post of Deputy Director of Research. The petitioners challenged the said notification on the ground that the Central Government had no power to make any recruitment to the posts of Deputy Directors of the Institute. The Tribunal held that the petitioners were not entitled to the benefit of the said notifications. On appeal by special leave, the Court, HELD: 1.1 The petitioners are not entitled for the benefit under the said Notifications. They are entitled to claim the benefit as they have been appointed in the Department of Research, and they are entitled only to the benefits which are available to them under the rules. [620B C] 2.2 The petitioners were entitled to be considered for promotion on the basis of their seniority in the cadre of Deputy Secretaries of the Ministry. They were not eligible for the same. Their claim was rejected by the Central Administrative Tribunal. The State Government has not challenged the validity of the notification. [720C D] 3.3 The petitioners have been working as Deputy Secretaries in the Indian Council of Research in the Institute of research and Development. They have been denied the benefit on the grounds that they are not eligible to be promoted on the post. They cannot claim the same benefits as they were entitled for. [820F G] 4.4 The petitioners, who are working as Assistant Secretaries in Indian Council, are entitled for equal pay for equal work. Their grievance is that the State Government had not taken any decision on their representations. They should have been given the benefit which they have already received. [920G H] 5.5 The petitioners cannot claim that they were appointed to the said posts as Deputy Secretary of the Department. They can also be denied the same benefit as those who are in service of the Government. Their contention is that they have not been promoted on their own account and that they should have given them the benefits.

The appellant was a workman of the respondent, who was employed as a daily wage worker in the State of Maharashtra. He was dismissed from service on the ground that he had been dismissed from services under section 25(1) (b) of the , and that the order of dismissal passed by the Labour Court was not justified. The appellant filed an application before the Labour Appellate Tribunal for setting aside the order, but the same was rejected by the High Court. In appeal to this Court it was contended on behalf of the appellant that the Labour court had no jurisdiction to set aside the orders of dismissal and that there was no power under section 26(1)(b) to issue a direction to the employer to reinstate him in service. HELD : (i) The order of termination passed by an employer is not a judicial order but a judicial act. It is a judicial function and it is not for the Court to decide whether the order is a speaking one or not. [620 H] (ii) The High Court was right in holding that the termination of service of the workman was illegal. [720 A B] (iii) The Labour Court had no power to set set aside an order of reinstatement and that it was not open to the appellant to challenge the order on the grounds that it did not comply with the requirements of section 25 (1)(a). [721 C D] (iv) The provisions of section 26 (1) are not intended to be used in a particular case. It does not mean that the power conferred by section 26 is not confined to an administrative order but only to an executive order. [820 A] (v) The power conferred on the Labour Courts under section 27(1), is not restricted to an industrial dispute. The power of the Labour Commissioner under section 28(1). is not limited to an Industrial dispute. It can be exercised by a court of law in exercise of its powers under section 29(1); and it cannot be said that the jurisdiction conferred on it by section 27 (1), was confined only to a matter which is outside the scope of the power.

The appellants, who were tenants of the respondents, filed a suit for eviction on the ground that they had been in possession of the premises in question. The trial court decreed the suit holding that the appellants had not been in occupation of the property in question and that the respondents had failed to prove that they were in occupation thereof. The appellate court held that the appellant was in occupation and that he was in possession thereof. On appeal, the High Court reversed the finding of the trial court and dismissed the appeal. In this appeal by special leave it was contended on behalf of the appellants that the suit was barred by limitation as the respondents were not in occupation or possession of any premises in dispute. Dismissing the appeal, HELD: 1. The High Court had no jurisdiction to entertain a suit under section 14(1)(a) of the Bihar Buildings (Lease and Rent Control) Act, 1960. [703E] 2. The appellants ' case was that they are in occupation as tenants of a company which is a statutory tenant and the respondents have not been able to prove their claim. They were in possession and control of the company. Their tenancy was terminated by the respondent on the basis of an agreement entered into between them. The respondents had no right to evict the appellants from the premises. [803E F] 3. The suit was filed for eviction of the appellant on the grounds that they have been in continuous occupation of a building and that they did not possess any right to continue in possession as tenants. They are entitled to protection under section 13(1) (a). [704F G] 4. In the instant case, the respondents are in possession since the appellants were in actual occupation of their premises. The appellant 's suit was decreed by the trial Court on the finding that they failed to establish their claim and that there was no legal right to remain in occupation. [603E G] 5. The question whether the respondents could be evicted under section 15(1), is not a matter for determination before the court. It is well settled that the jurisdiction of the court is limited to the jurisdiction which is conferred on it by the Code of Civil Procedure and the High Courts are not bound to entertain such an application.

The appellant, a member of the Society, was elected as a member by the Society. The appellant filed an application under section 83 of the Code of Civil Procedure for setting aside the election of the appellant and for setting up a new society. The trial court dismissed the application on the ground that the appellant had not been elected as member of a Society. On appeal, the High Court set aside the order of the trial court and directed the trial judge to proceed with the suit in accordance with law. In appeal by special leave, it was contended for the appellant that the High court had no jurisdiction to entertain the application under Section 83 of Code of Criminal Procedure because the appellant did not file an application for setting out a new Society. Dismissing the appeal, this Court, HELD: 1. The High Court has no power to set aside an order passed by the trial Judge on the basis of the compromise arrived at between the parties and that the compromise was not binding upon the parties. [723C] 2.1 In the instant case, the appellant was elected only as a Member of the society. He had not filed any application for bringing a new Co operative Society in the year 1973. The compromise was entered into by the appellant on the date of the filing of the application and the appellant 's name was mentioned in the compromise. The respondent had no right to file an appeal against the order passed in his favour. [823C D] 2:2. In view of the fact that the trial Court had not taken any decision on the question whether the appellant could be brought as a party or not, it cannot be said that the suit was barred by limitation. The appeal is dismissed. [923D E] 3.1 The High court has no jurisdiction in the matter and the High Courts have no power under section 84 of the Act to entertain an application filed for setting setting aside a compromise. [1023C F] 2 :2. The question whether a party can be brought on record is not a mixed question of law and fact. It is well settled that the court has inherent jurisdiction in a matter which is not capable of being decided by a court of appeal. In the present case, it is not disputed that the respondent had filed an affidavit before the trial courts in support of his claim for settingup a new co operative Society. [1123C E] 2(a) The High Courts had no power or jurisdiction to set up a fresh Co operative society in accordancewith law. [1223F G] 3:3. In order to decide whether a particular co operative society is brought on the record, it has to be shown that the parties have entered into compromise and the parties are not entitled to file any application under Order 41 Rule 27 of the Civil Procedure Code. [1323C C] 4.4 The High courts have no jurisdiction or power to entertain a suit in respect of a co operative Societies. [1423F H] 5.5 In view thereof, the appeal is allowed and the order dated 11.6.1973 passed by both the trial Courts is set aside.

The appellant was convicted of an offence under section 3(1) (a) read with section 5 of the Indian Security Act, 1947. The High Court held that the provisions of the Ordinance were not applicable to the State of Bombay and that the Ordinance had been passed in exercise of its powers under section 4 of the Act. In appeal to this Court it was contended on behalf of the appellant that the Act was a law made by Parliament and the Ordinance was a valid law and therefore, the Ordinance could not be said to have been passed without the previous sanction of the State Government. Held, that the impugned Ordinance was not a law which had been repealed by the Ordinance and the Act could not have been extended to the Union territory of India as it stood before the Constitution (Fourth Amendment) Act, 1950. The Ordinance was an Act made by the Parliament with retrospective effect from the date of its commencement and therefore the Ordinance must be deemed to have come into force on the date when the Ordinance came into force. Held further that the repeal of the ordinance by the amending Act by the Amending Act by which the Ordinance became effective would not affect the operation of the law made under section 5(1)(a) of the Constitution. The repeal of that Ordinance by the Amendment Act was not retrospective in operation and therefore it could not affect that Ordinance. Held also, further, that there was no valid law for the State to pass any such Ordinance. The fact that the amending Ordinance had come into effect on the 1st day of April, 1950, did not make any difference between the repeal and the repeal by the Act by a subsequent amendment in the Constitution and the repealing Act by reason of which it came into operation was not valid law. Held: (i) The Ordinance could be deemed only to have retrospective operation when the amending ordinance had come in force on 1st April, 1949, and therefore no question of the repeal would arise. (ii) The repeal by a Amending Act was an act done with retrospective operation and it was not necessary for the Legislature to pass such Ordinance as it thought fit. (iii) The amending Act did not affect any previous law made in exercise Of its powers conferred on it under section 6 of the General Clauses Act, 1897.

The appellants were convicted under section 302 read with section 34 I.P.C. and sentenced to death for life. The High Court acquitted the appellants of all charges. In appeal by special leave, it was contended on behalf of the appellants that the sentence imposed by the trial court was excessive and unreasonable as the High Court had not considered the evidence in its proper perspective and that the High court had not properly appreciated the evidence and arrived at a correct conclusion. Dismissing the appeal, ^ HELD: 1. The conviction of the appellant under section 307 read with Section 34 I P.C., is based on the fact that the appellants were guilty of murder and the sentence of death imposed by him was excessive. [601D] 2. The sentence of life imprisonment is not excessive but it is a matter of discretion to be exercised in a case where the court has found that the accused had committed an offence under section 304 Part I I. P. C. and that there is no reason why the sentence should be reduced to death. [701D E] 3. The Court has not considered any evidence on record which was not properly considered by the High Courts in its correct perspective and arrived a finding of fact. [802E F] 4. In the instant case, the appellants had been convicted under Section 302 readwith section 34 IPC and sentenced for life for the offence under Section 304 Part II I. p. C., and sentenced them to death under section 201 read with sections 34 I and 201 readwith Section 34 of the Indian Penal Code. [902E G] 5. The question whether the sentence awarded by the Sessions Court is excessive or unreasonable is not a matter for consideration in the present case. [1001F] 6. In view of the fact, the High courts have not considered all the relevant aspects and come to a correct finding that the appellant was guilty of the murder and sentenced him to death, it cannot be said that the conviction under section 34 of I.T.C is excessive. The appellants are entitled to the benefit of doubt. [1101E F].

The appellant was promoted as Assistant Commissioner of Income tax, and he was promoted to the post of Deputy Commissioner. The appellant was reverted to his original post. He filed a suit for recovery of certain amounts from him. The trial court dismissed the suit holding that the charges were not proved. In appeal to this Court it was contended on behalf of the appellant that the High Court had no jurisdiction to interfere with the order of dismissal passed by the disciplinary authority and that the order was vitiated by an error apparent on the face of record. HELD: (i) The High Court was right in holding that there was a mistake apparent on record which could not be said to have been committed by the appellant. [619 D] (ii) The order of the disciplinary officer was based on no evidence and it was not open to the appellant to raise any objection at the time when the order had been passed. [720 H; 720 A] (iii) The appellant had failed to prove that he had been reverted to the original post, and that there were no reasons for the High court to interfere in the order. [820 B C] (iv) The finding of the High Courts was not based on any evidence or material which could be said against the appellant, but it was based only on a consideration of the evidence adduced by the parties. [920 D] In the instant case, the appellant had been dismissed from service and he had failed in his defence to prove the charges. The High court was right when it held that there had been a mistake which could have been said against him. [1020 B] (v) The findings of the trial court were based on some evidence or materials which could only be said not against the applicant.

The appellants entered into contracts with the State of Orissa for sale of foreign liquor and export of foreign goods. The appellants were also entitled to the benefit of the contract. They claimed that they were not liable to pay sales tax on the ground that they had no right to sell foreign liquor. The Sales Tax Officer rejected the claim holding that the contract was a contract of sale and that the contracts were not a contract for sale. On appeal, the High Court held that the appellants were entitled to exemption under section 3(1) (a) of the . In appeal by special leave, it was contended on behalf of the appellants that the sales were not in the nature of export of goods and that they could not be said to have been made for sale in the course of inter State trade or commerce. Dismissing the appeals, HELD: 1. The contracts are not a contracts for sale but are in the form of contract for export of liquor. [630H] 2. The contract is a contract relating to inter State sales and the contract is one for sale and the contracts are made for export. It is not a transaction of sale. In the present case, the appellants have no right or title to sell the foreign liquor in question. They were not entitled to claim exemption under the contract as they had not been able to sell it in the manner prescribed by the contract and that their contracts were also not in accordance with the contract for the sale. [730H; 730A] 3. The High Court was right in holding that there is no contract of export. [831C D] 4. In view of the fact that the goods are not in a state of interState trade or business, it cannot be said that they are not liable for sales tax. [932D E] 5. The State of Andhra Pradesh vs M/s. T.M.F. Ltd., ; , referred to.

The appellant was appointed as a Labourer in the respondent 's services on January 1, 1974. He was terminated from service on March 31, 1975. The termination of his services was challenged by the appellant before the Industrial Court which dismissed the claim of the appellant and held that he had been retrenched for want of sufficient cause for not making an application within the period specified in section 33(1) of the Act. The Labour Court held that the termination of service was illegal and set aside the order of termination. In appeal to this Court it was contended on behalf of the respondent that the appellant had been terminated from services under section 33 (1) (b) of Delhi Industrial Relations Act, 1958. Dismissing the appeal, ^ HELD: 1. The appellant was not entitled to any relief in view of the provisions of section 33 of the Delhi Industrial Disputes Act, 1947. [630G] 2. The order of dismissal is a valid one and it does not affect the validity of the termination. It is well settled that the employer has to prove that he has been retrenched by reason of the fact that he was not in service on the date of his termination. If the employer fails to prove the fact of the retrenchment, then the employer cannot be held to have committed an error of law in holding that the workman had been dismissed from service for want Of sufficient cause. [730G H] 3. The employer has a right to terminate the services of a workman on the ground of his being retrenched by reasons of the nature mentioned in section 31(1). If the termination is illegal, it would be open to the employer to terminate his services without giving him an opportunity of showing cause why he should not be dismissed from services. [830G; 830A] 4. The workman has a statutory right to continue in service for a period of three years and if he has not been so retrenched, he will be entitled to reinstatement.

The appellant was appointed as a Settlement Officer in the year 1960. He was confirmed by the Deputy Commissioner on the ground that he had been dismissed from service for misconduct under r. 3(1) of the Punjab Civil Services (Classification, Control and Appeal) Rules, 1965. The appellant challenged the order of termination on the grounds: (i) that the order terminating his services was illegal; (ii) that it was not a punishment which could be imposed on him by an order of dismissal; (iii) that there was no evidence to show that he was dismissed from services for misconduct in the years 1960 and 1960. Held, that the termination of service was illegal because the appellant had been terminated without giving any opportunity to the appellant to show cause why his services should not be terminated. The order terminating the services of a Government servant was not an order which could only be passed by the Settlement Officer under r, 3(2) of Rules, but it was merely a punishment inflicted on him in accordance with the rules and regulations of the State. The termination of services was not illegal because it was made without giving opportunity to him to showcause why his service should not terminated. Held further, that there could be no evidence for the termination, but the order was not passed by an authority under r., 3(3) of Rule, but was a punishment simpliciter. The High Court was right in holding that the appellant was dismissed on the basis of the enquiry report and that it had been proved that he did not have any opportunity of showing cause against the termination.

The petitioner was appointed as a Lecturer in the Government of Jammu and Kashmir. He was promoted to the post of Assistant Professor on the basis of his seniority in the State of Jammu. The State Government issued a notification dated March 1, 1970 under section 3(1) of the Jammu and Srinagar Public Service Commission Act, 1971, inviting applications for promotion to the posts of Assistant Professors. The petitioner challenged the said notification by filing a writ petition in the High Court which was dismissed on the ground that the notification did not contain any provision for selection of candidates for promotion. In appeal to this Court it was contended on behalf of the State that the impugned notification was invalid because it was issued without jurisdiction and that the Government had no power to make any recommendation for promotion, and that it was not open to the Government to make a recommendation for appointment to the said post. Dismissing the appeal, ^ HELD: The High Court was right in holding that the State Government had acted in accordance with the provisions of section 3 (1) (a) of Act, and therefore the impugned order was invalid. [723C] In the instant case, the notification dated April 1, 1969 was issued by the Government under section 4(1). The notification dated May 1, 1971 was issued on March 1. 1970. It is not open for the State to make an application for appointment of a person for promotion in the post. [823C D] In view of the fact that the High Courts had taken into consideration the relevant provisions of the Act and the rules framed thereunder, it cannot be said that the decision of the Government was arbitrary or unreasonable.

The petitioner was a member of the Indian Legislative Assembly. The petitioner challenged the validity of the Act on the ground that it violated article 19(1)(f) and (g) of the Constitution. The petition was dismissed by the High Court. In appeal to this Court, HELD : (i) The impugned Act is not a law which has been passed by Parliament or by any State Legislature. It is not open to the petitioner to challenge the validity on the grounds that it violates article 19 (1)(g). [690 E F] (ii) Article 19(2) of Constitution is not an independent provision and is not subject to any restrictions imposed by Part III of the Seventh Schedule to the Constitution, but is subject to the restrictions imposed in Part III. The impugned provisions are not inconsistent with article 19. [691 G H; 790 A] (iii) Article 20(1) of that Constitution does not apply to a particular case. It does not affect the validity or validity of any law which is passed by the Parliament or the State Legislature, as the case may be. The provisions of Part III are not subject only to the limitations imposed by article 19 but also to the extent of the restrictions on the exercise of the power conferred by Part IV. [790 E G] (iv) Article 21(1), in so far as it is inconsistent with the fundamental rights guaranteed under articles 19 and 19, are concerned, does not violate article 19 or any of them. The Constitution has no application to the present case because the impugned Act was passed by a State Legislature and the impugned provisions were not subject matter of any restrictions on his exercise of power conferred upon him by Part II. [890 E H] (v) Article 31(1A) is an independent one and does not confer any right on the petitioner under article 19, because it is not inconsistent therewith with the provisions of the articles. The Act has no bearing on the question whether the impugned provision was in contravention of article 19 nor is it a law passed by any Legislature which is competent to pass such orders as may be necessary for the purpose of carrying out the purposes of the said Act. [990 E] (vi) Article 14 of the constitution does not provide for any restriction on the freedom of speech and expression guaranteed under article 21(2). The impugned provision is in contravention with article 20(2), because it has no nexus with the right to freedom of trade or commerce.

The appellants were appointed as Assistant Teachers in the College of Education, Orissa. The Government of Orissa issued a notification dated March 1, 1971 under Rule 3(1) of the Rules for the recruitment of teachers to the teaching posts of Assistant Teachers. The said notification was published on April 1, 1970. The respondents challenged the validity of the said notification by filing writ petitions before the High Court. The High Court dismissed the writ petition holding that the Government had no power to appoint a teacher in the college of Education. In appeal to this Court it was contended for the appellants that the impugned notification was not issued under Rule 4(1). Dismissing the appeals, HELD: 1. The impugned notification is not an administrative order and is not a statutory one. It is only a statutory provision which requires that the appointment should be made by the State Government in accordance with the rules. [601D] 2. The State Government has no power under Rule 5(1), to appoint any teacher in a college of educational or other public sector, but it cannot be said that the appointments were made by way of promotion. It was not open to the State to appoint such teachers as Assistant Teacher in the colleges of educational institutions. [701D E] 3. The notification dated April 1. 1971 is not issued in accordancewith the rules and the Government has power under rule 4(2). [702F G] 4. The appellants were entitled to be appointed as a teacher on the basis of their seniority in the teaching post. They are entitled to claim the same benefits as they had been appointed by way o fication. [801D F] 5. The contention that the notification dated May 1, 1969 was issued under rule 3(2) is not correct. It cannot be disputed that the appellants were not appointed as teachers in the educational institutions of educational and other public Sector. They have no right to claim any benefit as they were appointed by the Government on April 2, 1970 and their seniority should be determined according to the rules governing their service. [901D G] 6. The question whether the impugned notifications dated May 3, 1971 are valid or not is a matter of fact to be decided in the light of the decision of this Court in State of Orissa vs Dr. B.K. Sinha & Ors., ; , followed.

The appellants, who were the Transport operators of a private bus, filed an application before the Regional Transport Authority under section 68(1) of the U.P. Motor Vehicles Act, 1939 for grant of permits to them on the ground that they had been granted permits by the Regional transport Authority in accordance with the provisions of the Act and that the Regional Regional Transport Authorities were not justified in granting permits to the appellants. The Regional Transport Officer rejected the application holding that the permits granted by the State Transport Appellate Tribunal were valid and the permits were valid. The appellants filed a writ petition before the High Court challenging the validity of the permits on the grounds that they were not valid and that they could not be granted permits under section 69(1). The High Court dismissed the writ petition. In appeal to this Court it was contended for the appellants that the State Government had no power to grant permits to any person who has been granted permit under section 70(1), and that there was no power in granting a permit to any other person who is not a Transport operator under section 71(1)(a) of that Act. Dismissing the appeal, ^ HELD: 1. The State Government has no power under section 73(1A) to grant a permit for a stage carriage or a stage carriages on the route which is not covered by the provisions in section 68 (1). [703 B] 2. The High court was right in holding that there is no power of granting permits under Section 70(2)(a), and therefore, the Regional Authority could not grant permits under sections 69(3) and 70(4) of this Act. [704 C D] 3. The scheme of the Regional Planning Authority under Section 68(2A) is a statutory scheme and it is not open to the Regional Development Authority to grant permit to a person who was granted permits in accordance therewith. [803 B C] 4. The object of the scheme is to give a permit only to persons who have been granted a permit under Section 69(4). If the Regional Officer has no authority to grant the permit, it would be open to him to grant such permits. [904 D E] 5.
