The power conferred on the Regional Manager under section 67(1 A) is not confined to a stage stage carriage. It is only when the Regional Director has no jurisdiction to grant or refuse the permit. If the State Authority has no such authority, it cannot be said that there are no other persons who can grant permits in favour of any person whose permits have been cancelled under section 72(1 B). [903 C D E; 904 A] 5: The Regional Regional Officer is not justified to grant an permit.

The appellant, a widow of the deceased, was the son of his father. The respondent 's father died in 1951 and the appellant was the adopted son of the appellant. He filed a suit for partition against the appellant on the ground that he had no right to property in the property. The trial court decreed the suit holding that the appellant had no title to the property and that the property was not ancestral property, but was ancestral property. In appeal to this Court it was contended that the High Court was wrong in holding that a Hindu law could not be applied to a case where the property is ancestral property and the property has been partitioned by metes and bounds and the suit was barred by limitation. Held, that the question whether a Hindu Law can be applied for the purpose of determining the question as to whether a particular property is joint or not, does not arise in the present case. The High Court had no jurisdiction to decide the question on the basis of the evidence adduced before it and the finding of fact recorded by the trial court was erroneous. The appellant could not have been allowed to raise this contention. Held further, that in a suit under article 226 of the Constitution the High Courts should not interfere with the findings of fact arrived at by the courts below. In the present appeal the appellant has no right or title to property and he had only a right to the properties. The question whether the property in dispute was ancestral or not is a question of law which can be decided on the evidence led before it.

The appellants were tried for offences under section 302 read with section 34 of the Indian Penal Code and sentenced to death. The High Court acquitted all the appellants but convicted them on the ground that they had committed the offence of murder. In appeal to this Court it was contended that the appellants had not committed the murder of the deceased and that the conviction of the appellants under section 307 read with Section 34 of Indian Penal code was illegal as the appellants were guilty of the offence under section 304 Part I I.P.C. and they were liable to be convicted under section 201 read with sections 34 and 201 readwith section 34, I. P.C., and that they were not liable to any punishment under section 306 read with s 34, Indian Penal Procedure Code. HELD : (i) The appellants had committed an offence of culpable homicide not amounting to murder but amounting to culpable homicide amounting to death within the meaning of section 300, I..P. C. [401 B] (ii) The conviction of all the three appellants under sections 302 and 201 was illegal and they could be convicted only under section 34 read with Sections 34 and201 read with ss 34 and 202. [501 B D] (iii) The High court had rightly held that the offence punishable under section 303 was not committed by the appellants and that it was not proved that the act of the appellant was done in furtherance of the common intention of the accused persons. [602 C E] (iv) The prosecution case was that on the date of occurrence the appellants ' assembly armed with deadly weapons had taken place and they had been guilty of murder under section 300 read with 34, IPC. It was not established that the acts of the two appellants were done in pursuance of common intention.

The appellant was the adopted son of one Ram Singh. The respondent filed a suit for partition and separate possession of his property in the Court of Civil Judge, Amritsar. The trial court decreed the suit holding that the appellant had failed to prove the adoption of the deceased Ram Singh as a result of which he was entitled to succeed. In appeal to this Court it was contended on behalf of the appellant that the adoption was not valid and the adoption did not amount to adoption of a Hindu female. Held, that the High Court was right in holding that there was no adoption of any Hindu female in the absence of any evidence to show that the adopted daughter had been adopted by her. The High Court erred in holding the adoption as invalid. The appellant could not be said to have failed to establish the adoption. The adoption was valid and it was not open to the appellant to prove that the son had been taken into consideration for the purpose of adoption. Held further, that there is no evidence to prove adoption of Hindu female by the adopted child. The fact that the father had been given a right to succeed in the property does not make any difference between the adoption and the adopted adopted daughter. The evidence of the adopted wife clearly shows that the respondent was adopted by his adopted son as a adopted son. The finding of the High court that the deceased was adopted in adoption is correct. The question whether the adoption had been valid or not is no longer res integra. The courts below have rightly held that the evidence of adopted son was not sufficient to prove it.

The respondent, a company, was the owner of certain properties in Calcutta. The respondent filed a suit for the recovery of the amount due under the deed and for the refund of the money paid by him to the respondent. The trial court held that the respondent had no right to sue for the amount claimed by him as his agent. On appeal the High Court held that section 5(1) of the Act was not applicable to the case in which the respondent was a partner, and that the suit was barred by limitation. In appeal to this Court it was contended on behalf of the appellant that the provisions of the deed were not applicable in the case of a firm which had been registered under the Indian Partnership Act, 1932, and as such the suit could not be dismissed. Held: (i) The respondent was not entitled to sue in respect of the properties in question as his agents were not liable to pay any duty on the property in Calcutta, and the suit must fail. (ii) The High Court was right in holding that section 4(1)(a) of Act was applicable only to the cases where the respondent could be sued for the purpose of the instrument. (iii) The provisions of section 5 (1)(b) of that Act were not attracted to the present case, and therefore the suit should fail. Held, further, that the High Courts were right in coming to the conclusion that the deed was not a registered document. (iv) The question whether the respondent 's agent was liable to be sued was not one which arose for consideration before this Court. (v) The decision of the High court on the question whether section 5 of the Indian partnership Act, 1931, applied only to cases where there were no rules or regulations governing the subject matter of the transaction and not to cases in which it could be said that the instrument was a registered instrument.

The appellant was a company carrying on business in the State of Bombay. The Income tax Officer assessed the income of the assessee under section 10(1)(c) of the Indian Income tax Act, 1922, for the assessment year 1949 50. The High Court held that the income had been assessed to income tax under section 11(2)(c). In appeal by special leave it was contended on behalf of the appellant that the High Court was in error in holding that the profits were not liable to be assessed to tax under the Indian Incometax Act, 1961, and that the Income tax officer had no jurisdiction to assess the profits. Held, that the provisions of section 10 (1)(b) of that Act were applicable only to the assessment years 1949 50 and 1949 51. The question whether the profits should be assessed in respect of the year 1949 51 was not a question of law involved in this case. The expression "any other person" in the context of the present case means "any person who is liable to pay income tax for the year 1950 51, or any other person who has been assessed under section 12(2) of this Act". In the present cases the profits had been determined by the Income Tax Officer on the basis of the profits which were assessed in the hands of the company. The profits were assessed as income from the previous year 1949 52 and the profits could be assessed only after the assessment was made. The fact that the assessee had not filed any return under section 8(1) (c) did not make any claim for deduction under section 9(2).

The petitioner, a contractor, was awarded a contract for construction of a building in the State of Karnataka. The work was completed on 31.3.1988 and the work was to be completed within 30 days from the date of the contract. The petitioner submitted his tender along with the documents. The respondent 's tender was rejected by the State Government on the ground that the work had been completed within the stipulated time, and that the contract was not in accordance with the terms of the tender. The writ petition filed by the appellant was dismissed by a Single Judge of the High Court. In appeal to this Court it was contended for the appellant that the respondent 'tenders were not entitled to any relief under Article 226 of the Constitution. Dismissing the appeal, HELD: 1.1 The contract was in accordance wi tive and the contract had been in accordance to the terms and conditions of the work. It is well settled that the contracts are in accordance and the terms are not in conformity with the conditions of a tender. [797C] 2.2 In the instant case, the contract did not contain any specific condition for the completion of the works. The contract had not been completed beyond 30 days. The appellant was entitled to the relief under article 226 of Constitution. [ 797F G] 3.3 The respondent had not filed any writ petition challenging the validity of the said tender. It was not open to the appellant to challenge the validity or legality of the same. [897C D] 4.4 In the absence of any specific provision in the contract, it cannot be said that the appellant had been given a reasonable opportunity to show cause why he should not be awarded the relief. [997F H] 5.5 The respondent was not entitled for any relief as claimed by him. He had not produced any material before the Court to show that the works were completed within 15 days from receipt of the notice.

The appellant was a tenant of the land in dispute. The Custodian issued a notice under section 5(1) of the Punjab Land Revenue Act, 1953 to the appellant on the ground that he had no jurisdiction to pass an order for possession of the property. The appellant filed a petition under article 226 of the Constitution challenging the validity of the said order and also prayed for a writ of certiorari quashing the order of the Custodian. The High Court held that the order was not in accordance with law and therefore the order passed by the Custodian was invalid. In appeal to this Court, HELD : (i) The order of Custodian is not in conformity with the provisions of section 5 of the Act. It is a well settled principle of law that an order made under section 4(1), must be deemed to have been made under the Act and it must be held to have become final. [630 H] (ii) The power conferred on the Custodian under section 6(1)(a) of Act, was not confined to a matter which is within the competence of the Central Government or the State Government. It could only be exercised by an order passed under section 3(1). If the order is made under that section it must have become operative and the order cannot be deemed as valid. [730 H; 730 A] (iii) The provisions of the Ordinance are not intended to confer a power on the Central or the Government to pass such orders as may be necessary for the purpose of making an order under section 8(1); but they must be construed in relation to the matters which are within the powers conferred by the Act, and that it is only when the order has been made. The power to pass a order under the Ordinance is not confined only to a reference to a question which is outside the competence or authority of the Government. [830 B] (iv) The powers conferred on an Custodian under the provisions are not confined merely to a particular matter which are covered by the provisions, but also to a decision which has been taken in appeal or revision. It cannot be said that the power conferred by section 6 is confined only with respect to matters which fall within the scope of the powers delegated to him under the statute. [930 B C] (v) The words "any order" in section 5 are not meant to confer any power on an authority subordinate to it. It must be understood in relation thereto that the powers exercisable by a person subordinate to him are confined only in respect of matters which come within the purview of the statute and not in relation thereof. [1030 B D] (vi) The impugned order was passed under the authority of section 6 of the General Clauses Act, 1897, and it could not be said to have any effect on the power of the State Legislature to pass the order under that Act.

The appellant, a partnership firm, was engaged in the business of manufacturing and selling goods. The respondents were employed as a dealer under the Bombay Shops and Establishments Act, 1947. The appellant claimed bonus on the basis that the appellant had paid bonus to the workers for the period 1965 1965 to 1965. The Tribunal held that the workmen were entitled to bonus on account of the fact that they were not entitled to any bonus in respect of their wages. In appeal to this Court it was contended that the bonus was payable only when the workmen had paid the bonus and not when the workers had paid them. Dismissing the appeal, ^ HELD: The bonus is payable only if the workmen have paid the same. The bonus has been paid by the employer in respect thereof. The claim for bonus is based on a mere presumption that it is payable at the time of making the bonus. [615H; 716A] In the instant case, the appellant was not entitled either to bonus or if the workers were not paid the wages were paid at the relevant time. The workmen had not paid any bonus at the earlier stage. The fact that the workers have paid their bonus at a later stage does not make it clear that they are not entitled for bonus. The question whether the workmen are entitled to claim bonus is one of law and must be decided on the facts of each case. [716A B] In view of the provisions of section 2(1) of the Act, the bonus payable by the appellant in respect whereof the workers paid their wages cannot be said to have been paid at a subsequent stage.

The Punjab Civil Service (Judicial Branch) Rules, 1975 were amended by the Punjab Government of India (Amendment) Act, 1976. Rule 3 of the Punjab Civil Services (Judicial Division) Rules was amended by Haryana Government Notification dated January 1, 1977. The petitioners who were appointed as Additional District Judges in the Punjab Judicial Service on the basis of their seniority in the cadre of Additional District Judge were promoted to the post of Additional Sessions Judges on the ground that they had been regularly appointed as Assistant District Judges on January 1. 1976 and that they were not entitled to any promotion from the date of their confirmation. The respondents challenged the validity of the said amendment by filing a writ petition in the High Court which was dismissed by the High court. In the appeal to this Court it was contended for the petitioners that the amendment made by the Haryana Government (Amendment Act, 1977) was retrospective and that the amended rules were not retrospective in nature; that the amendments made by Haryana Act No. 1 of 1976 were prospective in nature and that since the amended Rules were retrospective in character, the amended rule could not be applied to the case of the petitioners as they had already been appointed as Deputy District Judges after the amendment of 1976. Dismissing the writ petition, ^ HELD: The High Court was right in holding that the rules were retrospective retrospectively and that their seniority was governed by the amended Rule. [601B] In the instant case, the amendment was prospective in character and the amended provisions were retrospective only when the amended provision was retrospective in operation.

The appellants were appointed as Assistant Engineers in the Andhra Pradesh State Administrative Service. The respondents were promoted to the post of Assistant Engineers on the basis of seniority list prepared by the Government of India. They challenged the validity of the said order before the Tribunal. The Tribunal held that the said seniority list was not applicable to the appellants and directed the State Government to consider the case of the appellants for promotion to the posts of Assistant Engineer in the State Administrative Services. The High Court dismissed the writ petition holding that the appellants were entitled to be promoted to that post. Dismissing the appeal, this Court, HELD: 1.1 The State Government has power to make rules for recruitment of Assistant Officers in the cadre of Assistant Executive Engineers and the State Public Service. [703E] 2.2 In the instant case, the State Legislature had framed a scheme for promotion of Assistant officers in the service of the State Civil Services. It is not possible to say that the State has power under the said Act to make Rules for recruitment to the cadre. The State Legislature has power and it cannot be said that the rules are applicable to all the posts. [803E F] 2(a) In the present case, there was no provision in the Act for promotion from the post to the Assistant Executive Engineer. The appellants were not appointed as Junior Engineers on a regular basis. They were appointed to the said cadre. They have been promoted to such post. They are entitled to get their seniority list published by the State. [903E G] 3(b) In view of the provisions contained in the Rules, the Government has no power to appoint Assistant Engineers as Junior Engineer on regular basis and they cannot be appointed to that cadre. [1003F] 4(c) The State is not entitled to make any rules for promotion in the said posts. They cannot be denied the right to be considered for promotion under the Rules.

The appellant was a tenant of the land in dispute. The mortgage was executed by the respondent on June 30, 1946. The appellant filed a suit for possession against the respondent and his father. The trial court decreed the suit holding that the mortgage was not a lease within the meaning of section 2(1)(d) of the Transfer of Property Act, 1882. The High Court held that the mortgagee had no right to sell the property in dispute and that the mortgagor had no title to the property. In appeal to this Court it was contended on behalf of the appellant that the mortgaged property was a lease for a period of three years and that it was not an lease within section 2 (1)(e) of Act, 1908. Held, that the suit was not maintainable because the mortgagee was in possession of the property as a lessee and had no interest in the property and therefore the mortgage could not be said to have been created by the mortgagor. The mortgagee was entitled to sell it in his favour. The right to transfer the mortgaged properties was not available to the mortgagor, but was only an interest which could be exercised by the mortgagee in the absence of a lease. Held further that the plaintiff had no locus standi to file the suit for redemption of the mortgage and the mortgagee 's right to redeem the mortgage in his own favour was not affected because the mortgage did not exist. The mortgagor was entitled under section 2 of Act. The mortgaged property could be sold by the defendant on the ground that he had no rights to sell or to transfer it in favour of the plaintiff.

The respondent, a contractor, was appointed as an arbitrator under the provisions of the Arbitration Act, 1940. The respondent filed a suit for specific performance of his contract and claimed that he had no right to claim any amount from the date of the appointment of the arbitrator. The trial court dismissed the suit holding that the respondent had no locus standi to file the suit. The High Court held that the arbitration agreement was not valid and the respondent was entitled to claim the amount from time to time. In appeal, this Court, HELD: 1.1 The arbitration agreement is a contract of service and it is not a contract for service. It is a contractual contract. The contract is one of service. The terms of the contract are not intended to be construed as an agreement of service but merely by reference to the date on which the appointment is made. [797C] 2.2 In the instant case, the respondent has no right or claim to any amount in respect of the work done by him. The dispute between the parties was one relating to the contract and the other relating to contract. It was not a contractual agreement but a contract which was not for service, and therefore, the arbitration clause cannot be invoked. [ 797C D] 2:3 In the present case, there is no dispute that the contract was for service and the contract had been for service of the respondent. The question whether the respondent could claim any right or privilege under the contract does not arise. [697D E] 3.1 In the absence of any such agreement, it cannot be said that the petitioner has no locus to file a suit. [ 697F G] 2 :3 The arbitration clause in the agreement is not intended for service by reference and the arbitration is governed by the provisions contained in section 9 of the Act. It does not contemplate any right of action or privilege. The arbitration is a statutory contract and it cannot create a bar to the jurisdiction of the court to entertain the suit, unless there is an express provision in that clause. [97F] 2(a) In the case of a dispute relating to a contract, the question whether a party has locus standi would arise only if the parties have not been able to file any such claim. The arbitrator has no jurisdiction to entertain it. [98G H; 98A B] 3:3 The respondent has not filed any claim in respect thereof. The petitioner has not challenged the validity of the arbitration proceedings and the High Court has rightly held that there is a bar for the jurisdiction under section 9 to entertain such an application. [99B C] 4.4 In the light of the provisions in the Act, the arbitrator has power to entertain any claim which is for service or not. The jurisdiction of court is limited to the question as to whether the arbitration was valid and whether the petitioner had locus standi. [1999G H] 5.5 The respondent cannot be permitted to file an application under section 8 of the . The High Courts have rightly held in favour of the petitioner.

The appellants were the tenants of the lands in dispute. The respondents filed a suit for recovery of possession of the land on the ground that they had no right to recover possession of it. The trial court decreed the suit holding that the appellants had no title to the property and that the decree was not properly passed. The High Court held that the suit was barred by limitation. In appeal to this Court, HELD : (i) The High Courts were in error in holding that section 5(1)(a) of the Bihar Land Reforms Act, 1950, did not apply to the proceedings under the Act. [619 D] (ii) The provisions of section 5 (1)(b) of that Act are applicable to a proceeding under the Code of Civil Procedure and the decree is not properly executed. [720 F G] (iii) The appellants had not been able to prove that they were entitled to recover the possession of their lands on the basis of the decree. They had no locus standi to file the suit. [819 E] (iv) The question whether the decree in question was a nullity or not is a matter which can be determined by the Court under section 5 of the Act and it must be decided only after the decree has been passed. [920 F H] (v) The jurisdiction of the court to entertain a suit under the provisions of the Code is limited to the determination of the question whether a decree was properly passed or not.

The appellants, who were appointed as Assistant Engineers in the Indian Administrative Service (Recruitment) Rules, 1985, filed a writ petition before the High Court challenging the validity of the said Rules. The High Court dismissed the writ petition holding that the Rules framed under Article 309 of the Constitution are not applicable to the case of direct recruits and promotees. In appeal by special leave, it was contended on behalf of the appellants that the impugned Rules do not apply to the cases of direct recruitee Engineers in Indian Administrative Services (Recruitment), Rules, 1987 and that the said Rule does not apply in the case where direct recruits are appointed as a direct recruitor Engineers in India. Dismissing the appeal, this Court, HELD: 1.1 The High Courts have held that the provisions of Article 309 do not provide for any relaxation of the requirement of the proviso to Article 309. [703F] 2.2 In the instant case, the Rules do provide for a relaxation of requirement of Rule 3(a) of the Central Civil Services (Appointment and Conditions of Service) Regulations, 1985. The said Rules do indicate that the relaxation is not applicable in the cases where direct recruitees are appointed to the Indian Service. [803F G] 2.(a) In the case in hand, the relaxation has been given only to those who have been appointed as direct recruits but they have been selected by the Central Government. The relaxation has also been given to those whose services were terminated and not to those of the direct recruiters. [903G H; 903A] 3.(b) In view of the fact that the proviso does not provide any relaxation in the requirement, it is not necessary for us to go into the question whether the relaxation was applicable in case of promotees or direct recruits. The question whether a direct recruits can be appointed as an direct recruiter Engineers in Central Administrative Service cannot be decided by this Court. [1003G] 3(c) In order to give effect to the said proviso, it has been held that in the absence of any provision in the Rules, the provisions contained in the proviso are not attracted and the relaxation given is only to persons who have already been appointed to Indian Administrative service. The proviso does indicate that if a direct recruitment is made by promotion from one source or another, the same would be applicable to those persons who had already been promoted as an Assistant Engineer in Central Civil Service. It is also clear that the requirement for the relaxation of Rule 4(a)(i) is not attracted.

The appellant was detained under section 3(1) of the , on the ground that he had been detained for more than one year. The grounds of detention were vague and indefinite, as it was not a case of detention. The detenu 's representation to the Advisory Board was rejected by the Central Government. The Board rejected the representation. The appellant filed an appeal before the Central Excise & Customs (Appeals) against the order of detention on the grounds that the Advisory board had no power to pass any order under section 8(1)(a) of that Act, and that the detenu ' had not been given a reasonable opportunity to make his representation. It was contended on behalf of the appellant that the Board had no authority to pass an order under Section 8(2) of this Act, because it had no jurisdiction to pass such an order. Dismissing the appeal, ^ HELD: 1. The detention order is vitiated by mala fides and is liable to be quashed. [797C] 2. The detaining authority has power to make an order for detention of a person under section 4(1). If the Advisory Advisory Board had not made any such order, it would have no jurisdiction in the matter. [ 797G H] 3. The power conferred on the Central Board by Article 22(5) is wide and wide and it cannot be exercised arbitrarily or without any authority of law. It is a well settled principle that the power to detain a person is not absolute but is subject to the limitations imposed by Article 21. [897C D] 4. The expression "any order" in Article 22 means an order made under section 9(1), and it does not mean an order which is made under Section 11 of the Act. It has no power or authority to make a detention order. [697G] 5. The word "any other order" used in Article 21 is wide enough to include an order of preventive detention, but it cannot mean that an order can be made under Article 22. [997C E] 6. In the instant case, the Advisory Boards had not taken any decision on the representation made by the detenu. The Advisory Board has not taken into consideration the relevant circumstances and the grounds of the detention were not vague and definite. It could have taken into account the relevant facts and circumstances of the case. [1097C F] 7. In view of the fact that the appellant had been released on bail, it cannot now be said that the order was made under the provisions of Article 22 of the Constitution.

The respondent company was a company carrying on business in the State of West Bengal. The company was served with notices under section 4(1) (a) of the Act to show cause why the property should not be sold for a period of one year from the date of the notice. The respondents contended that the property was acquired by the Government and the property had been delivered to the respondent on August 31, 1946. Held, that the order of requisition under section 6(1)(a) (b) of Act was not valid because it was passed in contravention of the provisions of the West Bengal Land Acquisition Act, 1894. The order of the requisition was not vitiated by any error apparent on the face of the record and was therefore liable to be set aside. Held further, that there was no error apparent in the order. The property was delivered to respondent on September 31, 1947. The Government had no power to make a requisition under r. 6(2) (c). The order was not made by the Central Government under r., 6(3) (d). The property could not be taken possession of by the company as it was in the possession of the Government. The respondent was not entitled to claim compensation for the property. Held also, that r. 5(1), (c) and (d) were not applicable to the case because the property did not belong to the Government, and the order was made under r, 6(4). The question whether the property belonged to the government or not does not arise in the present case.

The assessee company was a registered company carrying on business in the manufacture of its products. The assessee company had been assessed to tax under section 3(1)(a) of the Income Tax Act, 1922. The Income Tax Officer held that the assessee company did not fall within the purview of the expression "any other person" as defined in section 2(2) of that Act and that the said amount was liable to be included in the income of the assessee. On appeal by the assessee, the Appellate Assistant Commissioner confirmed the order of the Appellate Tribunal. The High Court held that since the assessee had not been assessed under section 4(1) of 1922 Act, the Income tax Officer could not have proceeded with the assessment on the ground that the amount was not included in his income. In this appeal by special leave it was contended for the Revenue that the expression 'any other persons" as used in section 3 (2) (a) (i) of 1961 Act means "any person". Dismissing the appeal, ^ HELD: 1. The word "any such person" is not defined in the Act. It is only a definition which has been given in the statute. [703E] 2. In the instant case, the assessee was not liable to pay tax under the head "any of the persons". The expression "other persons" used in the section is not confined to "any specified person". The word 'any such" is defined in that definition. It has been defined in a statute which is used in its ordinary sense and includes "any class or classes of persons". In the present case, it was not shown that the word "other person" used by the appellant in section 4 (1) (b) (ii) of 1962 Act had been used in any other manner. [ 703E F] 3. The expression 'other persons", in section 5(1), is a definition and includes all specified persons. It does not include any specified person. In view of the language used in that section, it cannot be said that the words "any" are used in their ordinary sense. [803F G] 4. The question whether the word 'other person ' in section 6(1A) (iii) of 1963 Act is a matter which has to be considered by the Incometax Officer under section 5 (2). [704E F].

The Railway Board, in exercise of its powers under Article 309 of the Constitution, issued a notification dated 30.1.1990 inviting applications for recruitment to the post of Assistant Engineers (Civil) and Junior Engineer (Civil). The Railway Board issued a circular dated 15.2.1990 providing that the Railway Board should consider the cases of all the candidates who had been appointed as Assistant Engineers in the Railways on the basis of their length of service, and that the seniority of the candidates should be determined according to the rules governing the field. The Railway Administration issued a letter dated 30th March, 1990 to the Railway Administration stating that the vacancies arising out of the said recruitment were not filled up by direct recruitment. The railway administration issued a Circular dated 15th March. 1990 providing that in case of any vacancy arising out or arising out from the said selection, the Railway administration should consider all the eligible candidates for appointment as Assistant Engineer (Electrical) and Senior Engineers (Electrical). The Board also directed that the candidates selected for the post would be considered for appointment to the posts of Assistant Engineer. The Board further directed that in the event of any vacancies arising on or after the date of their initial appointment, the seniority should be fixed according to rules governing such vacancies. The petitioners challenged the said order before the High Court by way of writ petitions. The High Court dismissed the writ petition holding that the Railways had not acted upon the recommendations made by the Railway Recruitment Board and that there was no justification for the Railway Authorities to consider the case of all those candidates who were appointed as Junior Engineers (Mechanical) and Assistant Engineer, and directed that their seniority should also be fixed in accordance with rules governing their field. In the appeal to this Court it was contended on behalf of the petitioners that the High Courts had erred in holding that there is no justification in the Railway authorities to consider all those eligible candidates who have been appointed by direct Recruitment, and therefore, the decision of the Railway Selection Board was not correct. Dismissing the appeals, ^ HELD: 1. The Railways had acted upon their own recommendations and had acted on their own discretion. They were bound to follow the same procedure as they were in fact acting on their behalf. [703E] 2. The decision of Railway Recruitment Commission is based on a different set of facts and not on law. It is well settled that the decision in the case before it is based upon a different principle, cannot be said to have been arrived at by the High court. [ 703F G] 3. In view of the fact that the railway administration had acted in accordance to the provisions of the rules, the Railways were not entitled to any relief. [803E F] 4. The question whether the Railway Service Rules were applicable to the case on hand is a matter which has to be decided by the appropriate authority. [ 803F H] 5. In order to decide the question whether a particular post of Junior Engineers was filled up, it must be held that the posts in question were filled up and the Railway Services (Electrical), which had been filled up on the ground that the said posts were filled by direct recruits. The principle of seniority is not applicable to cases where there are vacancies arising in the said cadre. [903F] 5:1 In the instant case, the railway authorities have acted upon a wrong approach and have acted arbitrarily and without any basis. They have acted on the same footing as they had been made in accordance therewith. The respondents have no right to claim that the post was filled by promotion from the date when the Railway Staff (Electrical ) were appointed. [1003F, G] 2:2 In the present case, there is nothing in the rules which indicate that the recruitment of Assistant Officers and Junior Engineers are made on the recommendation of the Board.

The appellant was convicted of the offence under section 302 read with section 34 I.P.C., and sentenced to imprisonment for life. The High Court held that the appellant had no right to be tried by a Special Judge, West Bengal, in view of the fact that the offences were committed by him exclusively within the State of West Bengal and that the trial was vitiated by an error apparent on the face of the record. In appeal to this Court it was contended that the High Court was wrong in holding that the offence was committed by a person exclusively within his State, and that section 34(1) (b) of the Act was not applicable to the case because the appellant was not a member of the West Bengal State, as he had been convicted of an offence under the Act. Held, that the provisions of the Ordinance were not applicable in the case of a person who is not a resident within the territory of West West Bengal. The question whether the offences committed by the appellant were committed exclusively within its State was not decided by this Court in the present case. The appellant was entitled to be convicted under section 34 (1) of that Act, and the High court was right in holding the appellant guilty of an act which was committed in contravention of the provisions contained in the Ordinance. Held further, that section 35(1)(b) was not attracted to the cases of a State Government or a State within the meaning of article 19(2) of Constitution. The Act was enacted by the Legislature of West Tripura and it was not necessary for the High Courts to decide whether the offence committed by an accused person exclusively outside the State was one which could be said to have been committed in violation of the fundamental rights guaranteed under article 19 (1)(a). Held, further, also that section 36(1), as amended by Act No. 1 of 1956, was not intended to be a law within the purview of article 21 (2) and that it was only when the Act came into force, that it could be held that section 37(1A) (c) was applicable to cases where there was an error in the face or the face, of the records. The provisions contained therein were not intended for the purpose of the legislation.

The appellants were convicted under section 302 I.P.C., and sentenced to life imprisonment for the offence of murder, and sentenced them to death. The High Court acquitted all the accused on the ground that they had been falsely implicated in the case and that the evidence of P.W. 1 was not reliable. In appeal by special leave it was contended on behalf of the appellants that the prosecution has failed to prove its case beyond reasonable doubt and that there was no evidence to show that the appellants were guilty of murder. Dismissing the appeals, ^ HELD: The High court had rightly convicted all the appellants under section 307 I. P.C. and sentenced each of them to life. [601D] In the instant case, the prosecution failed to establish its case against the appellants. The evidence of the P.Ws. 1 and 2 was not corroborated by any other evidence. The prosecution has not proved that they were armed with weapons. The appellants had been armed with deadly weapons. They have been falsely involved in the murder of one Ram Chandra. There is no evidence on record to show the presence of the accused at the time of occurrence. [701D E] In view of the fact that the deceased was a member of the family of the deceased and there was nothing to show any intention to cause the death of the appellant. The fact that he had been assaulted by the appellants is not sufficient to prove the case against them. [802E F] In order to establish the case, it must be established that the accused were armed in the commission of murder and they have been guilty of the offence under section 304 I.T.C..

The appellant was appointed as a conductor in the State of Karnataka. The services of the respondent were terminated by the Labour Court on the ground that it had been terminated without giving him an opportunity to show cause why he should not be dismissed from service. The Labour Court held that the termination of the services of a workman was illegal and void. The High Court, however, held that there was no evidence to show that the workman was guilty of misconduct or misconduct. In appeal to this Court it was contended on behalf of the appellant that the services were terminated without affording him an adequate opportunity to prove his case. Dismissing the appeal, ^ HELD: 1.1 The termination of service of a employee is not illegal and invalid because the employer has not given any reasons for terminating the services. [601C] 2.2 The termination is illegal and bad because it is not in accordance with law. It is not necessary to prove that the employer had given reasons for termination of services. The employer has to show what reasons he was guilty or misconduct, but the employer must show that there were no reasons for the termination. [701C D] 2:3 The termination does not amount to retrenchment within the meaning of section 2(s) of the Act. It does not mean that the employee is guilty of any misconduct or misbehaviour. The workman has to prove the fact that he was a workman in the service of the Corporation. [802D E] 2 :4 The employer must prove that there had been no evidence on record to show the reasons for retrenchment. If the employer fails to prove its case, it is open to him to prove what reasons the termination has been done. [903F G] 2(a) The employer cannot be held guilty of an misconduct or inefficiency. It may also prove that he had given reason for termination. But if the employer does not prove that a workman has been guilty of such misconduct, it must show the reason for retrenchment and the employer is entitled to take into account the reasons which are recorded in writing. [1003F] 2.(b) The termination was illegal because the employee was guilty and was therefore, liable to be dismissed. [1103G H; 1003A B] (c) The workman had not given reasons why he did not give reasons for his termination. He has also not given reason why he could not be held responsible for the misconduct or incapacity. [ 1103F F] 2 (a) In the instant case, the employer was guilty in the absence of any evidence to prove such a fact. The appellant had not produced any evidence on which the termination was founded. [1203G] 3(b) It is true that the Labour court has held that it was not open to the employer to prove any fact on which it could be inferred that the workmen were guilty of the misconduct. But, in the instant cases, the Labour Judge had held that since the employer did not adduce evidence to establish that the employees were guilty for misconduct or negligence, he was liable to termination. The Industrial Court has also held that even if the workman had given a reason for terminating his services, it could not have been said that there is no evidence of any such fact on record which would show that he did so.

The assessee was a dealer in the State of West Bengal. The Sales Tax Officer, after considering the evidence on record held that the sales were not taxable under the provisions of the Act and that the sale was not taxable within the meaning of section 2(f) of the . The High Court set aside the order of the Sales Tax officer and remanded the case to the assessing authority for fresh decision. In appeal by special leave, it was contended on behalf of the assessee that the Sales tax Officer had no jurisdiction to pass an order under Section 5 of the West Bengal Sales Tax Act, 1948. Dismissing the appeal, this Court, HELD: 1. The sales were taxable under section 2 (f) and not under the Act. [707D] 2. The sale was taxable under Section 2(g) of that Act. The assessee was not a dealer within the definition of "dealer" as defined in section 2 of the said Act. It was not an inter se transfer of property by the assessee to the Sales Officer. The transfer of the property was not covered by the provisions contained in the Act, and therefore the sales could not be taxed under the said provision. [807D E] 3. The High court was right in holding that the transfer of a property by an assessee to another person is not taxable as it was not within the purview of section 5(f). [706E F] 4. In view of the fact that the assessee had no locus standi to file an application under Section 6 of the East Bengal Sales tax Act, 1947, the sales in question were liable to be taxed.

The appellant was a director of the company. He was convicted under section 120B read with section 34 I.P.C. and sentenced to imprisonment for life. The High Court acquitted him on the ground that he had been guilty of an offence under section 5(1)(d) of the , and that the prosecution had failed to prove that the appellant had committed a breach of trust and that he was not liable to be punished under section 13(2) read with s.34 I. P.C., and that there was no evidence on record to show that the company had committed any breach of the trust, and that it was not guilty of any offence under sections 5(3)(d), 6(1) and 7(1). The High court acquitted him. In appeal to this Court by special leave, HELD : (i) The prosecution had proved that the appellants had committed an offence of cheating and forgery in respect of the shares of the Company. It was not necessary for the prosecution to prove the fact that the Directors were guilty of a breach or of trust. [723 B] (ii) The evidence on the record showed that the Company had taken the shares in the company and that they had taken it out of the funds of the Bank. There was no material on the basis of which the High Court could not have held that the transactions were made by the Directors in the course of their business. [823 B C] (iii) The High Courts were right in holding that the transaction was made by a company and it was only when the Directors had taken them out of their funds, that they were guilty.

The appellants were appointed as Assistant Engineers in the State of Gujarat. They were promoted to the Indian Administrative Service on the basis of their seniority in the cadre of Assistant Engineers. The appellants were promoted as Assistant Engineer on the ground that they had been appointed as Deputy Engineers on the same date and that they were not entitled to any salary for the period of their service. The respondents challenged the validity of the order of the State Government on the grounds: (i) that the State was competent to make an order in respect of the posts of Assistant Engineer, (ii) that there was no provision in the rules for the appointment of Assistant Commissioners on the post of Assistant Collectors and (iii) that they could not be appointed as Additional Collectors on the posts which were held by them on the date when they were appointed. The High Court dismissed the petition holding that the order was invalid because it was made under section 16(1)(a) of the Bombay Civil Services (Classification, Control and Appeal) Rules, 1957. In appeal to this Court, HELD : (i ) The State Government had no power to make any order in regard to the posts held by the appellants on the said date. [419 F] (ii ) The High Courts were right in holding that there is no provision for the recruitment of Assistant Secretaries and that the appointment was made on the strength of the rules framed under section 17(1) (a). [420 A B] (iii ) The order of appointment was invalid as it was not made under the rules. The State had no authority to make such an order.

The petitioners, who were dealers in cotton and cotton, challenged the validity of the Punjab Agricultural Produce Tax Act, 1961 (Act No. III of 1962) on the ground that they had not been registered under the Punjab Sales Tax Act as they did not fall within the purview of the Act. The High Court dismissed the writ petitions holding that the provisions of section 3(1)(a) and (b) of the Central Sales Tax (Amendment) Act, 1968 were ultra vires the Constitution. In appeal to this Court it was contended on behalf of the petitioners that the impugned Act was not a law within the meaning of article 286(2) of Schedule I of the Constitution and that the said Act was violative of article 301 of the constitution. Dismissing the appeals, ^ HELD: (1) The impugned Act is a law which has been enacted by Parliament under Entry 54 of List II of the Seventh Schedule to the Constitution, and therefore it cannot be said that the Act was ultra vires. [790 F] (2) The provisions of the impugned Acts are not violative of articles 301 and 304(a). The impugned Acts do not violate article 301 nor are they violative of Articles 301 and 303 of the Indian Constitution. [ 790 G H; 890 A B] (3) The Act is not a tax within the scope of Entry 54. It is only a tax which is imposed on the dealer in cotton or cotton, that is to say, the tax is imposed by the State under Entry 53.

The first respondent, a co proprietor of the first respondent and his brother, filed a suit for recovery of the amount due from him. The first respondent contended that the mortgage was not a mortgage but a mortgage in respect of which he had no right to claim any interest on the mortgage. The trial court decreed the suit holding that the mortgaged property was a mortgage within the meaning of section 2(1) of the Madras General Clauses Act, 1897 and that the decree passed by the first appellate court was not binding on the parties. On appeal, the High Court held that the mortgagee had no title to the property in question. The High Court also held that there was no right in the mortgagor to claim interest on mortgage. In appeal to this Court it was contended for the appellants that the High Courts were wrong in holding that a mortgage could not be enforced against the mortgagor, and that as the mortgaged properties were not a mortgaged property within the definition of section 3(1), the decree could not have been enforced against him. HELD: (i) The mortgage was a sale within the purview of section 4(1). [723 B] (ii) The High Courts had no jurisdiction to entertain the suit for specific performance of an agreement between the parties and the mortgagee. It is well settled that the right of redemption is not a decree in respect which the mortgagor has no right or interest. But it is only a mortgage, but a decree which can be enforced by the mortgagor against the mortgagee who has no title.

The appellants were the tenants of a hotel. The suit was decreed by the trial court on the ground that the suit was not maintainable as it had been filed within the period prescribed under section 14(1) of the Bombay Rents, Hotel and Lodging House Rates Control Act, 1947. The appellants challenged the decree in the High Court on the grounds: (i) that the provisions of the Act were applicable to the suit; (ii) that there was no bar for the suit being filed within a period of three years from the date of the institution of the suit and (iii) that section 14 of the said Act had not been applied to the case. The High Court held that the appellants were entitled to the protection of section 14, because they were tenants of the hotel. In appeal by special leave it was contended on behalf of the appellants that the High court was in error in holding that the plaintiffs were tenants within the meaning of section 2(1)(c) of Bombay Rents and Lodging Houses Rates Control (Control) Act, 1946. Held: (per Sinha, J.) that the jurisdiction of the civil courts to entertain a suit under the Bombay Rent Act is not barred by limitation as it has been filed after the institution thereof. The provisions of section 15 are applicable to a suit instituted within the time prescribed under the Act and the suit must be dismissed on the basis of the provisions contained in the Act. (per Das, J., dissenting) that even if the suit is not maintainable, the civil court would have jurisdiction to entertain such a suit.

The appellant was a director of the respondent company. The respondent was appointed as a director in the company. He was appointed to the company on the basis of a resolution passed by the company and his appointment was confirmed by the High Court. In appeal to this Court, HELD : (i) The word "company" used in section 2(c) means a company which is not a company within the meaning of that term. It does not mean any company which has been appointed as an director under the Act. [619 B] (ii) The words "company", in section 3(b) means any company who is appointed as such by the Central Government or the State Government or any other authority, and includes a company whose appointment is confirmed by a resolution of the company, but does not include a company in which it has been constituted. [719 B C] (iii) The expression "company " means any person who is employed for the purpose of carrying on the business of the Company. It is only when the words are used in the Act that the word "Company" is used in that section. If the words "any company which was appointed by the State or the Central Govt. are used, it would be a company as defined in section 617 of the Companies Act. The expression 'company " includes any person whose appointment has been confirmed by an order of the High court. [819 B D] (iv) The term "company ' means any body corporate which is appointed by or under the provisions of this Act. It cannot be said that the words used in sections 3(c), 4(b), 5(b)(ii) and 5(a)(iii) are not intended to be used in a company for carrying on business of a Company. [919 B E] (v) The definition of "company' is wide enough to include a body corporate, but it does not cover any body or body which has become a director under section 617. It would be an act done by the person who was appointed in that behalf. The word 'company" is wide and it cannot be used as a term of office. [1019 B F] (vi) The proviso to section 3 of the Act does not exclude a body or entity which has ceased to exist, but only refers to a body body corporate. It merely means a body which is a company. It may be a body of persons who are appointed by it and it is not an act of oppression. [ 1019 B G] (vii) The language used in sub section (b) of section 3 does not indicate that the term "Company " includes a body other than a company, and it does only mean a body constituted under the Companies. It also means a person who has ceased or is deemed to have been appointed by a company to be a director for carrying out the business. The words used are wide enough and it can not be said to exclude a person whose name has ceased.

The respondent landlord filed a suit for eviction of the appellants on the ground that the premises in question were not let out to the appellant and that the respondent was not a tenant within the meaning of Section 2(1)(d) of the Tamil Nadu Buildings (Lease, Rent & Eviction) Act, 1960. The Trial Court decreed the suit holding that the appellants had no right to continue the business as a tenant under the provisions of the Act. The High Court held that the appellant was not entitled to continue in the business and that he was not liable to be evicted from the premises. In appeal by special leave, it was contended on behalf of the respondent that the suit was barred by limitation because the appellants were not tenants within the definition of Section 3(1) (d) read with section 2(2)(d). Dismissing the appeal, this Court, HELD: 1. The provisions of Section 13(1), (e) and (f) of Act are not applicable to a case where the premises are let out by the landlord for a period exceeding six months or more. [703E] 2. In view of the fact that the landlord was not in occupation of the premises, the respondent cannot be evicted under the Act because he had no other option but to continue his business as tenant under Section 13 (1) readwith section 13(2). [704F G] 3. The appellants were tenants within a period of six months and they were also liable to eviction under the Rent & Control Act. [803E F] 4. In the instant case, the premises were let out for a long time and that there was no evidence on record to show that the shop in question was let out as a result of which the respondent had been evicted from his premises. The appellant was therefore not entitled for eviction under Section 14(1). [804E F; 803F G].

The Andhra Pradesh Land Reforms Act, 1961 was enacted by the State Legislature in exercise of its powers under section 3(1) of the Andhra Pradesh Ceiling on Agricultural Holdings (Amendment) Act, 1976. Section 4(2) of that Act provides for the acquisition of land for a public purpose and for the purposes of this Act. The Act provided for the transfer of land to the Central Government or the State Government. Section 5(3) provides that the Central Legislature shall have power to make laws for the purpose of carrying into effect the provisions of this section. Section 6(4) provides for acquisition of lands for a specified period and for matters connected therewith. The Central Government, after consultation with the Central Board of Revenue, issued a notification under section 4(1). The petitioners challenged the validity of the notification on the ground that it was not in accordance with the provisions contained in section 5(2), and that the Act did not provide for acquisition by the Central or State Government, and that it had no power to acquire land for any specified period. The High Court dismissed the writ petitions holding that the notification was invalid because the Act was not passed under section 6(3). In appeal to this Court it was contended on behalf of the petitioners that the provisions in section 4 (2) were ultra vires the Constitution and that, therefore, the Act could not be said to have been passed by the Parliament. Dismissing the appeals, ^ HELD: 1. The notification issued under section 5 (3) is valid because the Central legislature had no legislative competence to make any law for the time being in force. [797C] 2.1 The notification was valid and could not therefore be said that it did not contain any provision of a law for acquisition or requisitioning of land. It was, therefore not open to the Parliament to enact a law which was passed by Parliament under section 7(3), and the Act cannot be said in contravention of the provisions made in section 6 (2). [798C D] 2:1 The Act is a self contained provision for acquisition and requisitioning of lands. It is not possible to say that the legislature has legislative competence, but it must have legislative competence. The legislature has power to legislate on the subject of legislation. The Legislature cannot be permitted to make law in respect of land which is not covered by the provisions. [897C D; 897F] 2(a) The Act does not provide that the State shall have the power to take action under section 8(3)(b). The legislature can also legislate on any subject of the legislation. It cannot be contended that the Legislature has legislative power to enact laws in respect thereof. [997C E] (b) The notification is valid and must be held to be invalid because it is not inconsistent with the Act. [1097F G] 2.(c) The legislature is competent to legislate for the same purpose. It can also make a law in relation to land which are not covered under section 9(3); and (d) The State Legislature has power under section 10(3A). [998C E F] 3.2 The Act cannot, therefore be held invalid because, it is inconsistent with section 6 of the Act, it does not contain a provision for the imposition of any tax on land which was not covered within the provisions and that is, therefore. valid.

The respondent company was a company in which the workmen were employed. The workmen were paid wages for the period of their service and were paid compensation for the same. The company filed an application under section 33A of the , to the Industrial Tribunal, Calcutta, praying that the workmen should be dismissed from service on the ground that they had been guilty of misconduct or negligence in the discharge of their duties as a result of which they were not entitled to any relief. The Tribunal held that the workman was guilty of professional misconduct and that the dismissal was illegal. In appeal to this Court it was contended for the appellants that the order of dismissal was bad because the workmen had been dismissed from services without giving them an opportunity to explain their case, and that there was no evidence on record to show that they were guilty of any misconduct or misconduct. Held, that the Tribunal was right in holding that the termination of the service of the workmen was illegal as it was not a punishment for misconduct or inefficiency. The order of discharge was bad as it had been passed without giving him an opportunity of being heard. The Industrial Tribunal was therefore right in dismissing the workmen from service. The question whether the dismissal of the workman could be said to have been made without giving any opportunity to them was not decided by the Tribunal. Held: (i) that the finding of the Tribunal that the respondent company had been discharged from service, was correct and must be upheld. (ii) that there were no evidence to show what was the misconduct or misbehaviour on the part of the company in discharge of its duties as an employer. The fact that the management had not given any opportunity of hearing to the workmen did not make any reference to the Tribunal for adjudication.

The appellant, a teacher of the University, was appointed as a Principal in the University. The Selection Committee recommended the names of the candidates for appointment to the post of Principal. The appellant filed an appeal before the High Court which dismissed the writ petition. In the appeal by special leave it was contended on behalf of the appellant that the Selection Committee had no power to appoint any person as Principal, and that the selection committee had no jurisdiction to appoint a person as a teacher in the College. Dismissing the appeal, this Court, HELD: 1.1 The Selection Committees had no authority to appoint an officer as Principal. [636D] 2.2 The Selection Board has no power under section 16(3) of the Act to appoint such persons as Principal and the Selection committee is empowered to appoint them as Principal in accordance with the provisions of the Statutes. [737C D] 3.1 In the instant case, the Selection Committees have no power or authority to make appointments to the posts of Principal and Selection Committee. The selection committee has no jurisdiction under section 17(3). [736D E] 2:2 The High Court was right in holding that the appointment of the appellants as Principal was not a Principal but a Principal. It is well settled that the power conferred on the Selection Board under section 18(3)(a) of Act is not confined to the appointment by the Selection Selection Committee and it cannot be said that the appointments were made by the selection Selection Selection Selection Committees. [836D F] 2 :2 The selection Committee has no authority either to appoint the appellants in accordancewith the provisions contained in section 16 (3)(b) of Rajasthan University Act, 1956 or to appoint persons as a result of the selection. [937C E] 3:3 The Selection Selection Board is empowered by law to appoint teachers as Principal on the basis of the recommendations made by it. [1036D G] 4.1 If the Selection Commis sioner has power to make appointment of teachers as a principal, it cannot mean that the appointing authority has no powers to make selection for appointment as Principal or Selection Committee in accordance therewith. [1137C F] 5:2 In the present case, there is no provision in the Act empowering the Selection https://hcservices.ecourts.gov.in/hcservices/ Selection Committee to appoint candidates as Principal by the State Government. The High court has not committed any error of law or fact in holding the selection for appointments to posts of teachers. [1237C] 5.2 In view of the provisions made in section 18 (3) and (4) of 1956, the selection of the respondents as Principal is a Principal and selection committee.

The petitioners, who were members of the Municipal Corporation of Bombay, applied for a writ of mandamus directing the respondents to construct a building on the land in question. The respondent No. 1, who was the owner of the land, filed a petition under article 226 of the Constitution challenging the validity of the order of the State Government dated March 31, 1964, and prayed that the action taken by the Municipal Commissioner be quashed. The petitioners contended that the State Legislature had no power to make rules for the purpose of carrying out the purposes of the Act and that the provisions of the Bombay Town Planning Act, 1958 were not applicable to the land which was in the possession of the petitioners. The High Court dismissed the petition holding that the impugned order was invalid because it was passed without jurisdiction and that it was not open to the State to make a rule for the purposes specified in section 3(1) of the said Act. In appeal to this Court, HELD: (i) The provisions of section 3 of the Maharashtra Town Planning (Amendment) Act, 1964 are not applicable in the case of land which is in the occupation of the owner or occupier of the building. [601 B] (ii) The impugned order passed by the State was invalid as it had been passed without authority and that no power could be exercised under section 3. It was open to a person aggrieved by an order of a competent authority under section 4 to make an application for permission to construct the building on a land which he is entitled to do under section 6. The impugned orders were not valid because the petitioners had not been able to establish that they were in occupation of any land or building on that land. [701 B C] (iii) The State Government was competent to make the rules for carrying out its purposes and it could not be said that the petitioners were in possession of any such land or buildings on the date of the publication of the notification under section 5. It is open to an authority to make such rules as may be prescribed by the Act. [801 B D] (iv) The power conferred on the State under section 7 is not confined to the power of making rules for carry out the purpose and it is only when the rules are made, that power can be exercised in accordance with the provisions contained in section 6, that the power could not have been exercised in contravention of the provisions. [901 B E] (v) The petitioners were entitled to a permission under section 8(1). They had no right to carry out any development or construction on the said land. They had also no right of carrying on the development or work on the same land and they could not claim that they had been in occupation thereof. [1001 B F] (vi) The order of sanction was passed by a competent officer under section 10(1), and the petitioners ' right to make any application for the permission was also subject to the provisions mentioned in section 11.

The appellant, a resident of India, was the owner of certain lands in Bombay. The State of Bombay acquired certain rights and privileges of the Government of India under the Indian Independence Act, 1947. In the year 1965, the Union of India issued a notification under section 4(1) of the Indian Tariff Act, 1948 to the effect that the said land was not included within the territories of India. The appellant challenged the validity of the said notification on the ground that it was not an 'State ' within the meaning of article 31A of the Constitution and that the Union had no authority to make any award under section 3(1). The High Court held that the notification was not a 'State' within the territory of India and that it could not be made applicable to the territories in Bombay, and that therefore the said decision was not binding on the State. In appeal to this Court, HELD : (i) The notification issued under section 5(1)(a) of that Act was not valid because the notification did not specify any particular area within the territorial jurisdiction of India as it was a 'state ' within which the State could make an award under the said Act. [808 B] (ii) The Union had not made any reference to the High Court for the determination of the question whether the notification issued by the Government under section 6(1), was valid or not. It was not open to the Union to raise a contention that the Notification was invalid because it did not contain any reference in respect of the area within which it could make the award. [908 B C] (iii) The High Courts were right in holding that the notifications issued by Government under the Act were valid and the notification could not have been made applicable only to the areas within the jurisdiction of the State, but also to the territory outside India. [1008 D E] (iv) The award was invalid as it did no mention any area within its territorial jurisdiction. [1108 B D] (v) The State had not taken any objection that the award was valid because it was made in respect thereof and that there was no reference to any area outside India, and therefore the notification under article 31 A could not apply to the area outside the territorial limits of India within which such area was included.

The appellant was a lessee of the land in question. The mortgage deed was executed by the mortgagee on November 1, 1932 and the mortgagor was to pay the amount due under the mortgage deed. The mortgagee filed a suit for recovery of possession of the mortgaged property from the mortgagor. The trial court decreed the suit holding that the mortgage was not a mortgage within the meaning of section 2(d) of the Transfer of Property Act, 1882. On appeal by the mortgagor the High Court held that the mortgagee had no right to recover possession of any mortgaged property and that the mortgagor had no title to the mortgaged land. The High Court dismissed the suit on the ground that the plaintiff was not entitled to recover the amount from the mortgagee. In appeal to this Court it was contended for the appellant that the suit was barred by limitation as the mortgage in question was a mortgage of immovable property within the definition of section 3(d)(i) of Act, 1908 and the suit had been filed beyond the period of limitation prescribed under section 2 (d)(ii). Held, that the mortgaged properties were not a mortgaged property within section 3 (d) (iii) of that Act. The plaintiff was entitled to recovery of the amount by way of interest from the defendant. The suit was therefore barred by time as the mortgagee was not in possession of such mortgaged property. The mortgagor had not been able to prove that he had no interest in the mortgaged lands. The defendants were not entitled under section 3 of the Act. Held, further, that a mortgage in favour of a mortgagee was a sale within the scope of section 5(d).

The appellants were employed in the respondent State of Maharashtra. They were paid tax on their vehicles. The appellants were also paid tax at the rate of Rs. 1,000 per month. The respondents were not paid tax under section 3(1) of the Bombay Sales Tax Act, 1948. The appellant 's appeals against the orders of the Assistant Commissioner and the High Court were dismissed by the Supreme Court. In this appeal by special leave it was contended on behalf of the appellants that the provisions of the Maharashtra Sales Tax (Amendment) Act, 1976 are not applicable to the facts of the case. Dismissing the appeals, ^ HELD: 1. The definition of "goods" in section 2(1)(a) of that Act is wide enough to include goods which are used for the purpose of carrying on or carrying on of any activity in relation to which they are carried on. [723F] 2. The word "goods", in section 3 (1)(b) means goods which have been used for carrying on any activity for carrying passengers or carrying passengers. It is not necessary that a person who has been employed in a particular place must be deemed to be a 'person" within the meaning of section 2 (1) (a). The definition does not include goods used for earning passengers or carry passengers. [823F G] 3. The expression "goods used for any purpose" is wide and it cannot be said that the word "any other person" in the definition would mean a person employed in an industry. It must be understood in its ordinary sense as to include all goods which were used for a purpose connected with the carrying on by or carrying of any business. [923F H] 4. The words "any person" are wide enough and it is not possible to hold that the expression "any such person" has been used in the context of the definition. [1024A B] 5. The High Court was right in holding that the definition of 'goods ' in section 1 (1), as amended by the Maharashtra Act, must be read in its entirety and it should be interpreted in its proper sense. [1125C D] 6. In view of the fact that the appellants were not employed in any other place for carrying out the activity of carrying passengers, the High court was right to hold the view that the words "other person" used in section 4 (1). [1026F G].

The respondent was a licensee of the appellant 's premises in which he was working as a cinema theatre. He applied for renewal of his licence on the ground that he had been running a cinema hall under the Madhya Pradesh Municipal Corporation Act, 1956. The application was rejected by the District Magistrate and the order of the District Collector was confirmed by the State Government. The respondent filed an appeal before the High Court which allowed the appeal holding that the licence was valid and the licence could not be granted to him on the grounds specified in section 3(1) of the Act. In appeal to this Court it was contended for the appellants that the licensing authority had no power to grant a licence under section 3 (1) (a) of Act, and that the order passed by the licensing authorities was without jurisdiction. Dismissing the appeal, ^ HELD: The High Court was right in holding that an application for renewal is not maintainable because it is not a matter of policy or public policy. [630C] In the instant case, the licence had been granted to the respondent on the basis of the licence and the licensing order was valid. It was not a licence granted under section 4(1). The licence was granted to a cinema theatres in the State of Madhya Pradesh. The licence could only be granted only if it was granted by the competent authority. [730C D] In view of the fact that the respondent had been working as an cinema theatre, the licensing Authority had no jurisdiction to grant the licence.

The appellants entered into a contract with the respondent for mining of coal in the State of Mysore. The appellants agreed to sell the coal to the respondent on the terms and conditions mentioned therein. The respondent agreed to execute the contract. The appellant agreed to do so. The respondents agreed to accept the offer of the appellant. The agreement was signed by the parties. The parties agreed that the contract should be terminated with effect from the date of the agreement. The suit was decreed in favour of the appellants and the appellants filed a second appeal before the High Court. The High Court held that the agreement was not binding on the parties and dismissed the suit. In appeal to this Court, HELD : (i) The agreement did not contain any condition for the grant of the lease. It was not a contract which was binding on both parties. [619 F] (ii) The terms of the contract were not binding upon the parties but only a condition for grant of a lease. The terms in the contract did not indicate that the parties had agreed to the contract and the contract was binding upon them. [720 H; 720 A] (iii) The contract was not enforceable on the ground that the terms of contract were binding on all parties. It is true that the conditions mentioned in the agreement were not fulfilled by the appellants but only an express condition for granting a lease, but it was not so. But the conditions contained therein did not apply to the case of the respondent. [820 B] (iv) The appellant had agreed that he would be entitled to the grant or renewal of the leases. The contract did contain any stipulation for the renewal of a mining lease.

The appellants were prosecuted under section 3(1) of the Bihar Prevention of Food Adulteration Act, 1954. The prosecution was dismissed by the High Court on the ground that the appellants had not been able to establish their case against them and that they had not committed any offence under section 4(1). In appeal to this Court it was contended that the provisions of section 3 (1) were ultra vires the Constitution as they contravened article 14 of the Constitution. HELD : The High Court was right in holding that the impugned provision was ultra vires article 14. [801 B] The impugned provision is not violative of article 14 and is therefore void. [901 C D] In the instant case, the appellants were not able to prove their case on the basis of the allegations made against them. They had not established their case. They did not establish that they were guilty of any offence punishable under section 5(1)(a) of Act. The High court was right when it held that the offences under section 6 (1)(b) of Bihar Prevention Of Food Adulteration Rules, 1954 are not attracted. [701 B C] In view of the fact that the prosecution had failed to establish that the offence under the Act was committed by the appellants and that the complaint against them was not maintainable. The appellants were therefore entitled to the benefit of article 19. [601 D E] The High Courts were right in taking a contrary view. The impugned order of the High court is set aside and the appeal is allowed.

The appellants, who were manufacturing sugar in the State of Karnataka, filed writ petitions before the High Court challenging the validity of the said order. The High Court dismissed the writ petitions holding that the State Government had no power to grant exemption from payment of sales tax on the sale of sugar by the State. In appeal to this Court it was contended that the impugned order was not a law within the meaning of section 2(f) of the Karnataka Sales Tax Act, 1957 and therefore the said orders were not valid. Dismissing the appeals, ^ HELD: 1. The State Government has no power under section 3(f). It is well settled that the power conferred by section 3 (f) can be exercised only in respect of a particular commodity or class of goods. [703E] 2.1 In the instant case, the State had no authority to grant the exemption from sales tax. The impugned order did not contain any provision for granting exemption from Sales Tax on the sales of sugar. It was not open to the appellants to contend that the said power could be exercised in respect only in cases where the State has not been able to show that the same was not intended to be used as a unit or class thereof. [ 703E F] 2:2 The impugned orders were, therefore, valid and are liable to be set aside. [803F] 3:3 In the present case, it is clear from the order of the High court that the exemption granted by the Government was not in respect respect of any particular commodity.
