It is also well settled law that the notification issued under section 4(f), which was issued on April 1, 1977, was not an order of exemption from tax on sale of goods and therefore no exemption could be granted to the appellant.

The appellants were convicted under section 302 read with Section 34 I.P.C. and sentenced to life imprisonment for the offence under section 304 Part II I. P.C., and sentenced them to life life imprisonment. The High Court acquitted all the accused on the ground that they were not guilty of murder and that they had been falsely implicated in the case. Dismissing the appeal, this Court, HELD: 1.1 Section 34 is a special provision which provides for an offence of murder. It is well settled that the word 'person ' includes any person who is in possession of property or any part thereof. The expression 'person' has to be understood in its ordinary sense and not in its popular sense. [703F] 2.2 Section 34 does not confer a special right on the accused to commit an offence under Section 302 readwith Section 34. In the instant case, the appellants were guilty of the murder. They were rightly convicted for the offences under section 307 read with section 34 I I.T. and they were also liable to be punished under section 201 I.PC. [ 703F G] 2:3 The appellants were not charged with the offence of causing death of the deceased. They had been convicted for an murder punishable under Section 304 Part I I I..P. C. and were sentenced to imprisonment for life. [803G H; 803A B] 3.1 In view of the fact that the appellants had been acquitted by the High Court, the conviction of the appellants under section 34 is not sustainable. The appellants are entitled to be convicted under Section 201 I.. P. C., and they are also liable for the same. [903G] 2 :3 There was no evidence on record to show that the deceased was in possession or any portion thereof. They have been convicted under Sections 302 read together with section 149 I. T.P., and their conviction under Section 34 of the Indian Penal Code is set aside. [1003B C] 4.2 The appellants, who were armed with a knife, had been charged with murder punishable with death under Section 307 readwith section 34 IPC. They are also convicted under sections 302 read along with section 201I.P.. and sentenced each of them to imprisonment.

The assessee was a registered dealer in the assessment year 1965 67. The Income tax Officer, who assessed the income of the assessee for the assessment years 1964 67 to 1967 68 on the basis that the assessee had not acquired any right or interest in the property and that the transfer of the property was made by the assessee to the assessee. The assessee filed a return under section 10(1) of the Income tax Act, 1961 for the year 1965 65. The Assessing Officer rejected the return and held that the sale of the house was not an asset within the meaning of section 2 (c) of that Act. On appeal the Appellate Assistant Commissioner confirmed the order of the assessing officer. In appeal to this Court it was contended on behalf of the Revenue that the transaction in question was a transfer of property and therefore, the transfer was not a transfer within the definition of section 5(1)(a) of Income tax act, 1961. Dismissing the appeal, ^ HELD: (i) The transfer of a house is an asset which has been transferred by the transferor to the transferor and the transferee is entitled to claim the benefit of section 10 (1)(b). [601 B] (ii) The transaction in dispute was a sale of property within the scope of section 9(2) of Act. It is not necessary that the transferor must have acquired any interest or interest therein. The transfer must be made by a transferee to the transferee and it must be held that such transfer must have been made by him to the parent. [602 B] In the instant case, the assessee was not entitled to the benefit under section 9 (1) (a). [701 C] (iii) The sale of house in question is a transfer which has not been effected by the transferee. It was not necessary for the assessee that the property should have been transferred from the transferor. [702 B D] (iv) The assessee had acquired any rights or interest as it was not competent to transfer the property to the owner. [801 C E] (v) The High Court was right in holding that the transfers were made by an assessee to a transferee and that there was no transfer of such right or interests therein.

The appellant was charged with the offence under section 7(1) (d) of the Prevention of Food Adulteration Act, 1954. The prosecution case was that on the date of the incident the appellant had been selling a sample of 'B ' and 'C ' in the market. The appellant was convicted for having committed an offence under sections 7(2), 8(1)(d) and 8(3) (e) of Prevention of Adulteration Act. The High Court, however, held that the prosecution case did not fall within the definition of "B ' as defined in section 2(f) of Act. In appeal to this Court it was contended on behalf of the appellant that the appellant was guilty under section 8(2) (g) of that Act and that the offence was committed by him only after he had been charged with an offence punishable under section 3(1). Dismissing the appeal, ^ HELD: The prosecution has not proved that the sample was sold in the Market. It is true that the Food Inspector had found the sample to be adulterated. But it is true, that the report of the Food Analyst shows that the food was adulterated. The Food Inspector did not find any evidence to show that the samples were adulterated. [601 B] In the instant case, the appellant has been convicted under section 13(1), read with section 8 (2) of this Act and he had not been charged for having sold the sample in the shop. The fact that the complainant was a manufacturer of 'C " is not sufficient to hold that the quantity of the sample which was adulterated was adulterated is not enough to hold the appellant guilty under sections 13(3), 8, 9, 10, 11, 12 and 13 of the Act.

The appellant was a member of the Municipal Board, Jabalpur. He filed an application for leave to appeal against the order of dismissal passed by the Collector of Jabalpur. The appellant 's suit was dismissed on the ground that he had not been served with the notice of dismissal and that the order was bad in law. The High Court held that the appellant had failed to comply with the requirements of Article 311(2) of the Constitution, and that he was entitled to be heard in the appeal. In appeal by special leave, this Court, HELD: 1.1 The High Courts have jurisdiction to entertain a suit for damages or for damages. [797C] 2.2 The High court has no power to entertain an application under Article 311 of the constitution. It is not open to the High Court to exercise its discretion in regard to the question whether the order passed by it was bad, because it was not within the competence of the High Courts to entertain such a suit. [897C D] 2:1 The power of the appellate authority under Article 227 is discretionary and is not discretionary. It has been held that it is discretionary. In the instant case, the High court had no jurisdiction to decide the question as to whether the appellant was entitled for leave in appeal. [997D E] 3:2 The power conferred on the appellate authorities under Article 226 of the is discretionary, and the High courts have no jurisdiction in the matter. It cannot be said that the High Power has been exercised by the appellate court in exercise of its discretion under Article 136. [1097C F] 4:3 In the present case, it was open to a High Court under Article 133 to entertain the application under article 227 of the. Constitution. The power is discretionary only when the appellate or revisional authority exercises its discretion and has exercised its discretion properly in regard thereto.

The appellant, a Hindu undivided family, was the sole proprietor of a joint family. The appellant claimed that he had no right to sue for partition and that he was entitled to be impleaded as a party to the suit. The trial court decreed the suit on the ground that the appellant had not been impleaded as an party to it. On appeal by special leave, HELD : (i) The High Court was in error in holding that the decree of the trial court was erroneous and that the High Court had no jurisdiction to entertain the appeal. [601 B] (ii) The appellant 's case was that he did not have any right to be brought on record as a necessary party to an appeal. He did not claim that he could be impleaded in the suit because he did so. The High court was wrong in holding the decree for partition. [702 C D] (iii) The decree of partition was erroneous. It was not open to the appellant to raise any objection before the trial judge that the appeal was barred by limitation. [801 B C] (iv) The appellate court had no power to entertain a suit on its own. The appellate judge was in right in holding it as a proper party and the High court could not have entertained the appeal on the basis of the evidence adduced before him. [902 D E] (v) The trial judge was wrong when he did it. [1001 B D] In the instant case, the appellant ' had no locus standi to file the suit in view of the provisions contained in section 100 of the Code of Civil Procedure. He could not be impleaded on the grounds that he failed to establish his right to claim partition. The appeal was therefore dismissed.

The appellant was the respondent in a suit filed by the respondent for recovery of Rs. 1,000/ from the appellant and for a declaration that the decree passed by the District Judge was erroneous and illegal. The trial court dismissed the suit on the ground that the High Court had no jurisdiction to entertain the revision petition under section 115 C.P.C. The High Court held that the revision filed by him against the order of the District judge was not maintainable. In appeal, the High court reversed the order passed by it and allowed the revision application. In this appeal by special leave, it was contended on behalf of the appellant that the revisional jurisdiction under section 116 C. P.C., is a discretionary power conferred upon the High Courts under section 114 C.Ps. to entertain an revision petition in accordance with the provisions of the Code of Civil Procedure and the High courts have no jurisdiction in the matter of revision. Dismissing the appeal, ^ HELD: 1. The revisional jurisdiction of the High High Court under section 117 C.p.C is not a discretionary one but is a special power conferred by the Code. It is a general power which has been conferred upon it by the statute and is not an appellate court. [636B] 2. The power to entertain a revision petition is not confined to the exercise of jurisdiction under the Code, but is limited to the powers of the revisional court under section 100 C. p.C, and the power to decide such a question cannot be exercised by the High or the High. Court exercising its appellate jurisdiction under that section can interfere with the order made by it in revision. [736B D] 3. The jurisdiction of a civil court is limited only to the revisional powers which are conferred upon a civil Court under the provisions contained in the Code and not to the power of the civil courts under the Act. It has been held that when a revision filed against an order passed under section 97 C.R.P., is maintainable, it is open to the High and the trial court exercising its revisional jurisdiction cannot interfere with such orders. [836C D] 4. The powers conferred upon an appellate Court under Section 115 C C. & P. C. as well as the power conferred on a civil courts by section 115 of the Civil Procedure Code are not confined only to those powers which have been conferred on it by that section. [937E F] 5. In the instant case, the revisional power under section 104 C. C., is limited in respect of the revision petitions filed against the orders passed under Section 97 C C., and the revisional order passed thereunder cannot be interfered with by the appellate court unless it has been shown to have been passed under that provision or by the provisions in the Act that the trial Court had jurisdiction to try the suit.

The respondents were owners of land in the State of Rajasthan. The appellants filed a writ petition before the High Court challenging the validity of the notification dated March 1, 1984 issued under section 4(1) of the Land Acquisition Act, 1894 on the ground that the acquisition was illegal and void as it had been made without jurisdiction and that the respondents were not entitled to any relief in respect of the land. The High Court dismissed the writ petition holding that the appellants were not 'service providers ' within the meaning of section 2(1)(d) of that Act. Allowing the appeal, HELD: 1. The notification dated April 1, 1985 issued under the Land ( Acquisition and Acquisition) Act, 1984 was valid and the respondents had no right to any reliefs in respect thereof. [703 D] 2. The acquisition of land for a public purpose is not illegal and invalid as it has been made with the object of preventing the respondents from taking possession of the lands. It is only when the acquisition is made without authority or authority, that the land is required by law to be used for any purpose other than for which it is intended to be needed. [803 D E] 3. The respondents were entitled to the relief in the writ petitions. They had no locus standi to file the writ of mandamus against the appellants. They were not the owners of the property. They could not have been deprived of their right to the land under section 5(1). [704 G H] 4. The writ petition was dismissed by the High court on the basis that the notification issued under s.4(1), was valid as it did not contain any provision for the acquisition of the said lands. They are entitled to relief in accordance with law.

The appellant landlord filed a suit for eviction of the respondent tenant on the ground that the building was constructed in contravention of section 14(1)(a) of the U.P. Urban Buildings (Regulation of Letting, Rent and Eviction) Act, 1972 and that the appellant had not paid any rent for the period from 1st April, 1975 to 31st March, 1976. The trial court decreed the suit holding that the respondent was entitled to the benefit of section 13(1) (a) read with section 14 of the Act. The High Court held that the landlord had failed to pay the rent within the time specified in the proviso to section 14 and that he was not entitled to any relief under section 14. In appeal by special leave, it was contended on behalf of the appellant that the High Court erred in holding that since the building had been constructed in violation of the proviso, the tenant could not be evicted from the building unless he had paid the rent for that period and that therefore the appellant was entitled only to the relief under Section 14(2) (b). Dismissing the appeal, ^ HELD: 1. The appellant landlord had not filed any suit for recovery of possession of the building on the grounds that the tenant had failed in making payment of rent within time specified therein. [797C] 2. The proviso to Section 14 of Act is a general provision and it does not apply to cases where the tenant has paid the amount of rent for one or more months, but has paid such amount as may be prescribed by the landlord. It is well settled that in a case where the landlord has failed in paying the rent beyond time specified under the proviso the court can grant relief only if the tenant fails in making the payment within the period specified therein and the court has no jurisdiction to entertain the suit on the basis of the provisions contained in section 14 or section 14, as the case may be. [897C D] 3. The legislature has not intended that the court should have granted relief only when there is a specific provision in the Act which provides for the grant of relief under the Act and the Court has no power to grant relief under that proviso. [997D E] 4. In the instant case, the appellant landlord was entitled for the benefit under section 13 (1) readwith Section 14. The suit was barred by limitation as it did not contain any provision in section 15 of the Rent Act. [1097C F] 5. The question whether the appellant is entitled to relief under sections 14 and 14 of that Act is one which has been expressly provided for in the statute. It does not arise for consideration in this case.

The appellant company entered into an agreement with the respondent for construction of a building in the State of Bihar. The agreement was signed by the Chief Engineer, who was the Chief Executive Officer of the Government of Bihar on August 21, 1948. The appellant company was to be appointed as Superintending Engineer and the Chief Engineers were to be made parties to the agreement. On August 22, 1948, the Chief Engineering officer filed a suit for specific performance of contract. The trial court dismissed the suit holding that the contract was not in accordance with the terms of the contract and that the agreement was not valid. The High Court held that the appellant company had no right to sue for specific specific performance. On appeal by special leave, Held, that the arbitration agreement was valid and the contract could not be enforced under section 8(1) (a) of the Act. The contract was in accordance only with the conditions of the agreement and the terms thereof were not valid and therefore the contract had to be enforced. The arbitrator was right in holding that it was not a contract for the purpose of the arbitration. The award was not made under section 7(1)(a). The arbitrator could not have made an order under section 9(1), but he did not make an order for the enforcement of the terms and conditions of such agreement. Held, further, that in the absence of any express provision to the contrary, the contract must be enforced by the arbitrator. The arbitration agreement is valid and it cannot be said that the arbitrator was not competent to enforce the terms or conditions of a contract.

The respondent, a Public Works Department, was charged with offences under Sections 420 and 120B of the Indian Penal Code. The respondent was tried for an offence under Section 409 IPC. He was acquitted by the High Court on the ground that he had been guilty of criminal misconduct. The State Government filed a writ petition in the High court challenging the order of acquittal passed against him. The High Court dismissed the writ petition holding that the respondent was not entitled to any benefit of the provisions of Article 311(2) of the Constitution. In appeal by special leave, it was contended on behalf of the appellant that the High Courts had no jurisdiction to interfere with the order passed by the State Government under Rule 9 of the Punjab Civil Services (Classification, Control and Appeal) Rules, 1965. Dismissing the appeal, ^ HELD: 1. The impugned order of conviction is based on a finding of fact recorded by the trial court which is based upon a finding arrived at by the criminal court that the appellant was guilty of the offence under Rule 5 of the Civil Services Rules. [697E] 2. The order of dismissal passed against the respondent is not in accordance with law and is therefore, liable to be quashed. [797F G] 3. In view of the fact that the State government had no power to interfere in the matter of punishment under Rule 4 of the Criminal Services (Discipline and Appeal ) Rules, it cannot be said that the order was passed without giving any opportunity to the appellant to show cause why he should not be dismissed from service. [897F] 4. The question whether the impugned order is liable to suffer from any infirmity or illegality in the order under Rule 8 of the Rules is not a matter for consideration before this Court. It is well settled that the power of the State is not confined to punishment which is imposed on an employee but only to punishment inflicted on him by way of punishment. [997F H] 5. The power of compulsory retirement is not restricted to punishment imposed on a Government servant in respect of whom a charge sheet has been submitted or where there are allegations of misconduct, the order cannot be sustained. [1097G H] 6. In the instant case, the High courts have no jurisdiction under Rule 10 of the Code of Criminal Procedure to interfere or interfere with such order. The appellant was not given any opportunity of being heard in the criminal proceedings. He had been acquitted by a criminal court on the basis of a finding recorded by a civil court. [1197G] 7. In this case, it is not possible for the High High Court to interfere into the matter in exercise of its power under Rule 11 of the rules. The contention that the impugned orders are liable to face the trial is rejected.

The respondent company was a registered company under the Companies Act, 1956. The respondent company applied to the Income tax Officer for the assessment year 1949 50 and the Income Tax Officer rejected the claim of the respondent company on the ground that the income from the shares held by it was not taxable in the hands of the company. The Appellate Assistant Commissioner upheld the order of the Incometax Officer. On appeal, the High Court held that the dividend received by the respondent was a dividend received under section 3(1) (a) of the Act and that the profits earned by the company were not income from its business. In appeal to this Court it was contended on behalf of the appellant that the expression "any person" in section 2(1)(a) means any person who is or has been a member of a company, but does not include a person who holds shares in a company and includes a person holding shares in the company and that such dividend received from the company was not income within the meaning of section 2 (1)(b). HELD: The expression "other persons" in the context of section 3 (1) of that Act means any persons who hold shares in an company. It is well settled that the word "any other person" has to be construed in a narrow sense and it must be interpreted in a restricted manner so as to give effect to the intention of the legislature. The expression 'other persons", in the wider sense, includes persons holding shares or held by a company. [808 D E] In the instant case, the dividend paid by the appellant was not a dividend which could be taxed under section 10(1). The respondent Company had not been able to establish that the dividends received by it were income from it. The High Court was right in holding that the shares were not liable to tax under section 11(1), but was not liable for tax under the Income Act.

The appellant was convicted under section 7 of the Bombay Sales Tax Act, 1947. The High Court held that the goods were not liable to sales tax under the Bombay General Sales Tax Rules, 1947 and that the appellant had no right to sell them in the market. On appeal by special leave it was contended on behalf of the appellant that the High Court was wrong in holding that the sale was not liable for sales tax because the appellant was a dealer within the meaning of section 2(1) (c) of the Act and that he was not entitled to purchase the goods in the stock. Held, that the word "sale" used in section 2 (1) of that Act is wide enough to include a person who has been given possession of goods by him for the purpose of sale. The words "sale " are wide enough and must be construed accordingly. The word "transfer" in the context of the definition of "sale ' in section 3(1)(c) means a person whose possession is taken over by the person who is given possession or by any other person to whom the goods are delivered, but does not include a man who has no right of sale in the course of his business. The expression "sale in the ordinary sense of the term includes a person having a right to purchase goods for the purposes of sale and includes a man whose possession has been taken over. The definition of 'sale ' is wide and it must be interpreted accordingly. It is not possible to accept the contention that the words "transfer " in the normal sense of section 3 (1)(b) are wide, but they include only a person holding a right of purchase in the goods for which he has been delivered. The use of the word 'sale" in section 4(1), therefore, is not sufficient to hold that the expression " sale in any ordinary sense means a transfer of property by way of sale or by way or by means of sale, but only a transfer which is made by way and by way.

The respondent was charged with an offence under section 7(1)(d) of the Prevention of Corruption Act, 1947. The prosecution case was that on the date of the incident he had been in a position to pay Rs. 500/ as bribe for the purpose of obtaining a loan from the Government and that he had paid Rs. 200/ as advance to him. On the question whether the respondent was guilty of an offence punishable under section 8(1) (d) read with section 7 of the Act, HELD: The High Court was right in holding that the respondent had been guilty of any offence punishable by section 7 and that the prosecution had failed to prove that he was guilty for any offence under the Act. [601 B] In the instant case, the appellant was charged under section 3(1), read with Section 7 of Prevention of Money Laundering Act, 1972. The High court was right when it held that the appellant had been convicted for an offence which was punishable under the provisions of section 7. [702 C] The question whether a public servant is guilty of a criminal offence or not does not arise in this case. [803 D] In view of the fact that the Government had taken a decision to pay the amount of Rs. 100/ as gratification for the purposes of obtaining the loan, it was not necessary to decide whether the appellant should be prosecuted under section 6 of the said Act. The question is whether the High Court could have held that there was no evidence on record to show that the public servant had been charged with any offence.

The petitioners who were working as Assistant Engineers in the Railways, were appointed to the Railway Service on ad hoc basis. The petitioners were appointed on ad temporary basis and they were absorbed in the Railway service. They were also paid salary for the period of their engagement. Their services were regularised by the Railway Board. The respondents filed a writ petition before the High Court challenging the validity of the order of the Railway Administration dated 20th April, 1984. The High Court dismissed the writ petitions holding that the petitioners had been absorbed in service on adhoc basis and that they had not been absorbed as Assistant Engineer in the railways. In appeal to this Court it was contended that the Railway administration had no power to make any rules for the purpose of giving effect to the policy of the Central Government, and that the said rules were ultra vires the Constitution. Dismissing the writ petition, ^ HELD: 1. The Railway Administration has no power under Article 309 of the Constitution to make rules for recruitment of Assistant Engineers on ad permanent basis. [723C] 2. The Railways have no power or authority to make such rules for appointment of Assistant Engineer on ad regular basis. They are not entitled to any benefit of the policy. [823F G] 3. The scheme of the Railways is a statutory provision and it has been enacted in order to provide for the establishment of an Assistant Engineer. It is well settled that the employees who have been absorbed under the railways are entitled to the benefit of this policy. They cannot be denied the benefit on the ground that they have not been appointed as Assistant Executive Engineers on regular basis and their services were regularized by the Railways. [923C D] 4. The provisions of the rules are in addition to the general provisions of a statute which provide for recruitment and conditions of service of Assistant Executive Engineer. [1023F H] 5. In the instant case, the Railway authorities have not taken any steps to fill up the posts of Assistant Sub Engineers on temporary basis. Their claim is that they were appointed as Junior Engineers on daily wage basis. It has been clearly stated in the counter affidavit that the Railways had no authority to extend the benefit to them. The railway administration has no right to make appointments on ad interim basis. In view of the fact that the services of Assistant Assistant Engineer are not available, it is not possible for the Railway Authorities to fill the posts on ad Temporary basis. There is nothing in the rules which indicate that the temporary employees have been appointed on regular regular basis or on ad officiating basis. Therefore, the petitioners cannot be said to have been engaged as Assistant Sub Engineer on daily wages basis. If they are absorbed under a scheme of Central Government they will not be entitled to claim any benefit on ad adhoc basis. This is not a case where the Railway has no authority in making such appointments. [1123C E] 5.(a) The Railway Board has power to extend or extend the benefits of the scheme of regularisation of the temporary workmen on ad ad hoc appointment. [1223F] (b) The petitioners have been given the benefit under the scheme and they are entitled for the same.

The appellants, who were members of the Indian Trade Association, filed a writ petition in the High Court challenging the validity of the notification dated March 31, 1956. The High Court dismissed the petition holding that the notification was invalid because it was not issued under section 3(1) (a) of the , and that the provisions of the Act were ultra vires the powers conferred on the Central Government under section 4(2) (b) of that Act. In appeal to this Court, HELD : The notification dated April 31, 1957 was valid and could not be challenged in any court. The notification was issued under the Act only after the expiry of the period of three years from the date of the publication of the said notification. The validity of section 4 (1) was not questioned by the appellants. The provisions of section 3 (1)(a) were not ultra vires. The impugned notification did not contravene the provisions contained in section 3 and could be challenged only after expiry of three months from the publication thereof. The Act was a valid law and it was therefore void. [808 B] In the present case, the notification issued under that section was invalid as it was issued without jurisdiction. The appellants were not entitled to challenge the validity or validity of that notification. They had no right to challenge it on the ground that the impugned notification was ultra vires because the notification did neither contravene the fundamental rights guaranteed by article 19(1)(g) nor could it be challenged on the grounds that the Act was violative of article 19 (1).

The assessee company was a company carrying on business in the State of West Bengal. The income tax authorities assessed the income of the assessee company as dividend under section 10(1) (a) of the Income Tax Act, 1922. The Appellate Assistant Commissioner held that the income tax authority had no jurisdiction to assess the income for the year 1948 49 and that the amount of compensation was not liable to be included in the profits of the company. In appeal by special leave, the assessee contended that the amounts of compensation were not liable under section 11(1)(a) (b) of Act, 1961. The High Court held that there was no evidence on record to show that the assessee had any income from the assets of the Company and that it was not a dividend within the meaning of section 10 (1) of that Act. Dismissing the appeal, ^ HELD : (i) The amount of Rs. 1,00,000/ was liable to tax under section 12(1). [801 B] (ii) The High Courts were right in holding that the interest of the appellant company was not chargeable under section 23(2)(a), and that there could be no question of any deduction under section 24(1), because the amount was not included in profits of a company. [802 C D] (iii) The Income Tax Officer had no power to assess or reassess the income, but he did not do so. [703 B] In the instant case, the High Court was right in taking into consideration the fact that the dividend was not paid by the assessee and that this amount was received by the company from the company on the date of the order of assessment. [602 C] (iv) The income from which the dividend had been paid was not taxable under section 8(1A)(a).

The respondents were prosecuted under section 120B of the Indian Penal Code and the High Court dismissed their petition. In appeal to this Court it was contended that the expression "any material" in section 2(1) of the Act includes any material used for the purpose of carrying out or carrying out any of the purposes of the said Act, but does not include any material which is used for carrying out the purposes mentioned in section 3(1). Dismissing the appeal, ^ HELD: 1. The expression "other material" means any material intended for carrying on the business of the trade or commerce and includes any materials used for such purpose. [601D] 2. In the instant case, the respondents were not prosecuted under the Act. They had no right to be prosecuted under sections 120B and 120B. The prosecution was that they were using the said material for carrying the purposes specified in section 4(1)(a) of that Act. The High Court was wrong in holding that the word "any" used in section 5(1), as understood in the dictionary sense, means any materials which are used for making out or carry out the purpose mentioned in the definition. [701D E] 3. In view of the fact that the words "other materials" were used in the context of the definition, it was not necessary to hold that the said word was used in a dictionary sense. [802E F] 4. The question whether the expression 'any material used in Section 5(2) of this Act is a matter for determination by the Court under section 2 (1).

The appellant was convicted under section 302 I.P.C., and sentenced to death. The High Court acquitted the appellant of all the charges. In appeal to this Court it was contended on behalf of the State that the evidence of the eye witnesses was not reliable, because they were interested witnesses in the prosecution case, and that the High Court had rightly convicted him under section 304 I. P.C. and sentenced him to death under section 201 I. p. C. HELD : (i) The High court was right in holding that the appellant was guilty of the offence of murder. [838 B] (ii) The evidence of eye witnesses is not reliable because they are interested witnesses, but it is a matter of record which must be considered by the Court on its own merits and not on the basis of any other material. It is well settled that the Court should not interfere with the findings of fact recorded by the trial court unless there is some evidence to show that the accused had committed the offence. [938 B C] (iii) The finding of the High court is based on no evidence and it is not open to the High Courts to interfere with such findings except in accordance with law. [740 D E] (iv) The conviction of the appellant under section 307 I.T. P., is based solely on the evidence which has been accepted by the High Judge. It must be shown that the prosecution had failed to prove that the deceased was guilty for murder. The Court should have regard to the circumstances of each case and not to the facts of each particular case. [640 D] (v) The judgment of the trial Court is based only on the fact that the medical evidence was not consistent with the medical opinion, but on a proper appreciation of the evidence it must be held that the conviction of appellant under sections 302 I., P. C., and section 201 of the Indian Penal Code are based solely upon the evidence given by the eye witness.

The appellant company was a factory in Bihar. The appellant company, a company incorporated under the Companies Act, 1956, was a company registered under the . The appellant Company was a union of workmen and its employees were employed by it for the purpose of carrying on business as a factory. The company was also a company carrying on the business of manufacturing and selling goods. The workmen were employed in the factory at Bihar. It was alleged that the workmen had been working in the company for more than five years and that they had been employed in a factory for more number of months. The union contended before the Tribunal that the appellant Company had no right to carry on business in the said factory. On behalf of the appellant it was contended that the Tribunal had erred in holding that the workers were not workmen within the meaning of section 2(1)(d) of the Act and that the company was not a 'industry ' within the definition of section 3(2) (d) and that there was no dispute between the parties. Held, that the dispute between them was one of the two workmen and the appellant company had been referred to the Tribunal for adjudication. The Tribunal had rightly held that the employees were not workers within the purview of the definition. The question whether the workmen were workmen within a meaning of the section does not arise. The decision in the case of M/s. K. C. Mills Ltd., vs Union of India, [1962] Supp. 1 S.C.R. 841 and M/S. Carson & Co. vs Union Of India, ; , referred to.

The appellant firm was a Hindu undivided family and the respondent firm was dissolved by the Income tax Officer. The assessee 's firm was assessed to income tax under section 10(1) of the Indian Income tax Act, 1922. The Income tax officer held that the partnership was not a Hindu joint family and that the partners were entitled to the benefit of section 10 (1). In appeal to this Court it was contended on behalf of the appellant that the firm had no separate business in the firm and that there was no evidence to show that the partner was a member of the firm. Held, that the assessee ' firm was not liable to income income tax for the assessment year 1948 51, and that it was not entitled to claim the benefit under section 8(1). The Income Tax Officer held that there had been a partnership between the partners and the partners in the partnership. The High Court was of opinion that the business was not one of the partners but was one of them. Held: (i) The firm was an undivided family, and the partnership did not come into existence after the dissolution of the partnership by the assessee. The firm had a separate business and it was only a joint family. The partnership was a joint Hindu family and could not be said to have been dissolved by reason of the dissolution. The partners were not entitled under section 9(1), because they were members of the joint family, but were members thereof. (ii) The assessee firm had not been assessed to tax for that year. (iii) The Incometax Officer was right in holding that the income of the assessee firm was income from the partnership and that no question of law arose for determination by this Court.

The appellant was granted a permit under the Mysore Motor Vehicles Rules, 1939. The respondents were granted a certificate of fitness for the grant of a permit on the ground that they had not applied for the renewal of the permit. The appellant filed an appeal before the Appellate Authority which dismissed the appeal. The Appellate Authority held that the permit was valid and the permit could be renewed only after the expiry of the period of validity of the permits. The High Court allowed the appeal holding that the Regional Transport Officer had no jurisdiction to grant a certificate under section 9(2) of the Act. In appeal by special leave, it was contended on behalf of the appellant that the Appellate Tribunal had no power to grant the permit in respect of the route which was already notified by the State Government under section 3(1)(a) of Mysore Motor Vehicle Rules, 1938 and that the order of the Appellate authority was not valid. Dismissing the appeal, ^ HELD : (i) The Regional Transport Authority had no powers to grant an renewal of a permits in respect thereof. [630E] (ii) The High court was right in holding that section 9 of the Mysore Act did not apply to a permit issued under section 10(2)(a). [631C D] (iii) The order of a Regional Transport officer is valid and it could be granted only after expiry of a period of three years from the date of the grant. [732E F] (iv) The Appellate Tribunal was right when the permit had been issued under rule 9(1) of that Rules.

The appellant, a candidate of the respondent, was declared elected to the Legislative Assembly. The appellant challenged the election of the appellant on the ground that he had been guilty of corrupt practices under section 123(3) of the Representation of the People Act, 1951 and that the appellant had not been given an opportunity to explain his allegations against him in the election petition. The High Court held that the allegation was false and that it was not proved that the respondent had committed the corrupt practice within the meaning of section 123 (3). In appeal to this Court, HELD : (i) The appellant was guilty of the corrupt practices alleged by the respondent. The allegations were vague and did not constitute any offence under section 3(1)(a) of Act. [808 B] (ii) The allegation in the petition was that the first respondent had been given a fair opportunity to show cause against the election. The allegation was that he was guilty for corrupt practices, and that he acted as an agent of the candidate. The evidence of the witnesses showed that the second respondent had not committed any corrupt practice under section 124(3). [809 B] In the present case, the appellant was a member of the Legislative Council and was also a member in the Legislative assembly. He was also an agent for the first time. There was no allegation that he used any corrupt practices to commit the corrupt activities. The fact that the third respondent had acted as a agent of his candidate did not make any allegation against him. [909 B C] (iii) The allegations made by the appellant were vague, and did neither constitute any offences under section 4(1). [910 E F] (iv) The evidence showed that he took part in the conduct of the first appellant nor was there any allegation that the fourth respondent had used any criminal practice to commit any corrupt activity. The statement of the witness was not recorded by the police during the investigation and the evidence showed the commission of the offence. [1010 E] (v) The High court was right in holding that the allegations made against the appellant did not attract section 123 of the Act. The finding of the High Court that the corrupt conduct alleged by him was proved was erroneous.

The appellants filed a suit for recovery of possession of the property in dispute on the ground that the sale was not made within the period prescribed by section 58 of the Transfer of Property Act, 1882. The trial court decreed the suit holding that the decree holder had no right to sue for recovery and that the judgment debtor had no locus standi to file a suit under section 58(1) of the Act. The High Court held that the order passed by the District Judge was not in accordance with law and therefore the decreeholder could not be said to have been made within time. In appeal, this Court, HELD: 1. The judgment debtor has no right or title to sue on the basis of a sale deed executed by him. He is entitled to sue only for recovery. [797C] 2. The decree holder has no locus to file the suit under Section 58(2) of Act. [897D] 3. In view of the provisions contained in section 58, the decree holders cannot be said not to have any right or interest in the property. [997E F] 4. The order passed under section 59(1)(a) is a decree and it is not a decree. It is a judgment debtor who has no title to the property but he has no claim to sue. [1097D E] 5. In the instant case, the sale deed was executed by the respondent in favour of the appellants on the date of execution of the sale deeds. The sale deed did not contain any provision for the sale of the properties. The respondent had no title or interest to the said property. Therefore, the judgment debtors were entitled to recover possession of that property from the respondent. [1197E] 5:1 In view thereof, the High Court was right in holding that it was a decree which could be executed within time and therefore, the order of the District judge was not legal and valid.

The appellant, a candidate of the Kerala State Legislative Assembly, was elected as a candidate for the election to the Kerala Legislative Assembly. The election petition was contested by the first respondent and the first appellant. The first respondent challenged the election of the first Respondent on the ground that he had been falsely implicated in the case because he had not been given an opportunity to cross examine him. The High Court dismissed the Election Petition holding that the appellant had been guilty of corrupt practice under section 123(3) of the Representation of the People Act, 1951 and that the election petition had been filed without any reasonable cause. In appeal by special leave it was contended on behalf of the appellant that the first part of the election order was not a valid one and that it was not an election petition within the meaning of section 123 (3) and that there was no evidence to show that the second respondent had been given a reasonable opportunity to explain his case. Dismissing the appeal, this Court, HELD: 1. The expression "any person" in section 123 is used in the context in which it occurs. It is not necessary for the purpose of determining whether the first party has been guilty or not. In the present case, the first defendant had been acquitted by the trial court and the High Court was right in holding that he was guilty of the corrupt practice. [707B] 2. The appellant had not given any explanation as to why he had given a false statement before the Returning Officer. He had also not given a true copy of the statement made before him. In fact, he had stated that he did not know the name of the second defendant and his name was mentioned in the statement. [807C] 3. The evidence of the two witnesses clearly shows that the third respondent had given an incorrect statement before him and that he has been falsely involved in the alleged corrupt practice and that this statement was made before the returning officer. In view of the fact that the fourth respondent had not stated any name in the election record, it cannot be said that he knew the name and his names were mentioned in his statement. The second respondent has also not stated anything about the name or the name in which the first first party was named as the first candidate. [907C D] 4. In order to prove the allegation of corrupt practices under section 124(3), it is necessary to establish that the respondent had made a false declaration before him, and that in any event he has not given the true copy to the appellant. [1007G H] 5. The fact that there were no allegations against the first and second respondents was not denied by the appellant in his written statement. It was also not disputed that the statements of the third parties were made before them. The respondent had also stated that the statement of the fourth respondents was made after the returning officers. [ 1007C E] 6. In a case where the first witness has been examined, it is not possible to hold that he could be said to have given the false statement in his election petition. The statements of two witnesses were not recorded by the Returning officer and the same were not considered by the High court. [1107G] 7. It would be appropriate if the evidence of a witness is found to be reliable, but it is only when the first one witness has stated that there had been a false entry in his electoral roll before the returned officers. The statement of such witness was not recorded at all. [ 1107C F] 8. In any case, it would be open to the High Courts to hold an enquiry into the allegations made by the third party and come to the conclusion that the said statements were made after he had signed the electoral roll.

The respondent Corporation, a public limited company, was granted permission to construct a building on the land in question. The respondent Corporation filed an application before the Municipal Commissioner for permission to develop a building. The Municipal Commissioner rejected the application and directed the Municipal Corporation to grant permission to the respondent Corporation to construct the building on it. The appellant challenged the order of the Municipal Authority, which was dismissed by the High Court. In appeal to this Court it was contended that the Municipal Council had no power to grant the permission to a private limited company for construction of a building and that the permission granted by the Municipal Authorities was not valid as the permission was not in accordance with law. Dismissing the appeal, ^ HELD: 1. The High Court has erred in holding that the respondent corporation had no authority to grant such permission. [797C] 2.1 The Municipal Corporation is a statutory body and it cannot be said that the building was constructed on the plot of land in dispute. It is not necessary for the Municipal authorities to give any reasons for granting the permission. The fact that the land was acquired by the respondent, does not make out a case for grant of permission. In the instant case, the Municipal authority had no jurisdiction to grant a permission to an private limited corporation for construction on it and the Municipal Board has no power under section 7(1) of the Act to grant any permission. It cannot be disputed that the Corporation was not a statutory corporation. The question whether the respondent is a public company or a public body, does arise in the present case. [897C D] 2:2. In view of the fact that there was no material before the High court to show that the construction was constructed by the appellant. [997D E] 3.1. The Corporation has not produced any evidence to show whether the building is constructed on it or not. It has also not been shown that the plot in question was acquired for the purpose of construction of the building. In fact, the High Courts have failed to consider the relevant material before granting permission to respondent corporation for constructing a building in dispute and the High courts have failed in considering the relevant materials before granting the sanction. [1097C E] 2 :3. The order of this Court is set aside and the matter is remitted to the Municipal Administration to reconsider the matter afresh after giving an opportunity to the parties to lead evidence.

The appellant company was a registered industrial concern. The workmen were employed in the factory of the appellant company and were working as a casual labour. The employees were prosecuted for offences under section 25(1)(a) and (b) read with section 25A of the , and the charges were framed against them. The trial court acquitted all the employees. In appeal to this Court it was contended that the workmen had been guilty of misconduct and therefore they should be dismissed from service. Dismissing the appeals, ^ HELD: 1.1 The workmen have been guilty for misconduct and not for misconduct. They are not entitled to any relief under section 33(2) of the Act. [797C] 2.2 The workmen are not required to prove that they were employed as a regular labour. Their conduct is not only a matter of course but also a material irregularity in the conduct of the workmen. It is also necessary for the employer to establish that the workman was engaged in any other kind of work and that he had been continuously absent from duty without any reasonable cause. [897C D] 2:1 The employer has to prove the charges against the workmen and it must be proved that they have been employed as regular labour, and that the employer has failed to establish the charge against them for misconduct or not. [997D E] 2 :2 The employer is required to show cause why the workmen should not be dismissed for misconduct without reasonable cause and if so, the employer may prove that the employee was engaged on any other ground. If the employer fails to show that the employees were employed on any particular ground, it will be open to the employer either to establish or establish that they had been employed in any particular kind of job. [1097C E] 3:2 The burden of proving that the workers were employed for a period of three years is not on the employer but on the other hand, if the employer does not prove that there was no reasonable cause for the workman to establish a charge against the workman, it would be open for the employers to establish and establish that there has been any reasonable ground for the workmen to establish their charge. [ 1097C F] 3 :3 The employer must show that there is sufficient cause for action against the employee. If there are no reasonable grounds for the employees to establish such a charge, it may be open either to the employers or the employer, if he so desires, to establish his charge. The employer cannot prove that he has been employed on a particular ground. [1011A B] 4:4 The employer should show that he was engaged as a daily labour and not as a temporary labour. If it is proved that there were reasonable grounds to believe that the worker had been engaged in some other kind, it can be said that the management has failed in any manner of work or that the industrial concern has failed. [1002C] 5:5 The employer may establish that he is engaged on a specified ground and if the workmen are employed for more than three years, it cannot be said to be an unfair labour practice. If he fails to establish any reasonable grounds, it must show the reasons for the action taken by the employer in the matter. [1031C D; 1012A B C] 6:6 The employer shall not be liable to be dismissed on the ground of misconduct or breach of the terms of employment. [1023D E].

The assessee company was a registered firm carrying on business in the business of selling shares to its shareholders. The assessee company had purchased shares from its shareholders and sold it to its shareholder. The Income tax Officer held that the shares were not sold by the assessee company as the assessee was not entitled to the benefit of section 10(2) of the Indian Income Tax Act, 1922. On appeal the Appellate Assistant Commissioner confirmed the order of the Income tax officer holding that the sale of shares was not a sale within the meaning of section 2(1)(c) of that Act and that the assessee had no right to claim the benefit under section 10 (2). The High Court held that there was no evidence on record to show that the sales were made by the company in the course of inter se business. In appeal to this Court it was contended for the appellant that the Tribunal was wrong in holding that there is no evidence to show whether the sale was made by a company in its course of business or not and that there could be no question of law involved in the present case. HELD: (i) The High court was right in holding the sale as a result of the sale, and the Tribunal had rightly held that it was not open to the assessee to claim that the transaction was made for the purpose of carrying on the business. [707 B] (ii) The finding of the High Court that the transactions were made for a purpose other than that which the assessee could have claimed under section 11(2). [708 C E] (iii) The Tribunal had not considered the evidence on the record and held that in view of the evidence it was open to it to the Tribunal to come to its own conclusion. [ 707 B D] (iv) The decision of the Tribunal in the case of Commissioner of Income tax, Bombay vs M/s. K. C. Mills Ltd., , relied on.

The appellant was appointed as a District Judge of the Andhra Pradesh State. He was promoted to the post of District Judge, and he was confirmed in the year 1953. The appellant was suspended by the High Court on the ground that he had been dismissed from service for misconduct under r. 5(1) of the Rules. On appeal by special leave, Held, that the High court was right in holding that the appellant was not entitled to the protection of article 311 of the Constitution and that the order of suspension passed against him was illegal. The order of dismissal passed against the appellant could not be said to have been passed without giving him an opportunity of being heard. The High Court was right when it held that the dismissal was illegal, because the appellant had been guilty of misconduct under the Rules and that he was entitled to a protection of articles 311 of his Constitution. Held, further, that r. 4(1)(a) of Rules did not apply to the case of an officer who was dismissed from services for misconduct in accordance with r. 6(1). The High court had no jurisdiction to pass any order under r 5(2) of Rule 5(3), because it held the appellant guilty of professional misconduct under cl. (b) of r. 7(1), and that r, 5(4) was not applicable to the cases of an Officer who was removed from service by reason of his dismissal. The contention that r., 5(5) did not affect the validity of r, 6(3) was wholly untenable.

The respondent company was a Hindu undivided family and the appellant was a member of the joint family. The Income tax Officer, Bombay, held that the shares in question were not liable to income tax under section 10(1) (a) of the Indian Income tax Act, 1922. The Appellate Assistant Commissioner confirmed the order of assessment on the ground that the share in the shares was not liable for income tax as defined in section 2(f) of that Act and that the appellant had no right to claim the share of the share. On appeal by the respondent company, the Appellate Tribunal held that there was no transfer of shares in favour of the appellant and that it was not a transfer of the shares. The High Court, on appeal, reversed the order. In appeal to this Court, HELD: (i) The expression "any person" in section 10 (1) of this Act means a person who is a member or a member thereof. It does not include a person whose share has been transferred by the person who has been appointed as a member and has been paid a tax under the Indian Incometax Act, 1961. [601 B] (ii) The word "any other person" used in section 9(1)(a) means a member who is an individual or a person of a Hindu family. It includes a person holding any shares in his own name. In the present case, the appellant 's share was transferred by him to the respondent on the basis that he had no legal right to receive the share from the deceased. The question whether the share was liable for tax under this Act is not a question of law. [701 B C] (iii) The High Courts were in error in holding that the transfer of a share in his favour by the appellant to the deceased was not an transfer of property and that he was entitled to claim any share in it. [802 D] (iv) The provisions of section 10 are not applicable to the case of the respondent.

The appellant was a Ruler of Madhya Pradesh. He had been in possession of certain lands in Madhya Bharat and the State of Madhya Bharat. The appellant was an Ruler of Gwalior. His land was acquired by the State Government under the Madhya Bharat Abolition Act, 1950. The State Government issued a notification under section 4(1) of the Madhya Pradesh Abolition Act to the effect that the appellant had been given possession of the lands in the Madhya Madhya Bharat, and that the said land was not liable to be assessed to tax under the Act. The respondent filed an application before the High Court for quashing the order of the State. The High Court dismissed the petition holding that the land was liable to tax on the basis of a document which was produced by him in support of his claim that he had been granted possession of those lands and that it was not a 'estate ' within the meaning of article 31(1)(f) of Part III of the Constitution. The appeal was dismissed. In appeal to this Court, HELD: (i) The appellant had no right to claim the benefit of article 19(1). [801 F] (ii) The High Courts were right in holding that it had been a ' jagir ' within article 31 (1)(g) of Constitution. [802 G H] (iii) The expression "estate" in article 31 means an estate which is not liable for tax under article 31. [903 A B] (iv) The word "estate", in the context of article 366(f) means a person who has been granted a right to hold any land or part thereof on behalf of the Government, and includes a person whose land was held by him as such. [702 F G] (v) The definition of 'estate" is wide enough to include an estate in which he had acquired the rights under article 19 (1). It does not mean that it has been used for the purpose of the Act or any part thereof. [603 B C] (vi) The term "estate " means a thing which is liable to pay tax under section 3(1), but does not include an interest in the land.

The respondent, a retired employee of the Indian Forest Service, was transferred to the Indian Administrative Service on the ground that he had been posted in the Indian Army. He was transferred from one place to another and his wife was transferred by the Indian Police Service. The respondent filed a Writ Petition before the High Court challenging the transfer order. The High Court dismissed the Writ Petition holding that the transfer of the respondent was not justified. Hence this appeal by special leave. Allowing the appeal, ^ HELD: 1.1 The transfer of an employee is not a matter of policy and it is not open to the Tribunal to interfere with the transfer. [797C] 2.2 In the instant case, the transfer was made in accordance with the rules and regulations of the Central Government. It is not possible for the Tribunal or the Tribunal that the respondent had been transferred from another place to one place. The transfer order is a matter which is within the domain of the Administrative Tribunal. [897C D] 2:1 The High Courts have no jurisdiction to interfere in the transfer, but it has no power to interfere. In the absence of any statutory provision or statutory rules, the Tribunal cannot interfere with such transfer. It has no jurisdiction in the matter. [997D E] 2 :2 The High court has not properly appreciated the facts and circumstances of the case. [1097C F] 3:3 The High Powered Tribunal is not justified in interfering with the order of transfer. The Tribunal has no authority to interfere the order. [1197F G] 4.4 In the present case, there was no statutory rule or statutory regulations governing the transfer and the respondent has been transferred by transfer. Therefore, the order is not vitiated.

The appellants were convicted under Section 302 read with Section 34 I.P.C. and sentenced to life imprisonment for the offence under Section 304 Part II I. P.C., and sentenced them to undergo rigorous imprisonment for one year. The High Court acquitted all the accused persons, but reduced their sentence to three years rigorous imprisonment. In appeal by special leave, this Court, HELD: 1.1 The appellants were not guilty of any offence punishable under Section 34 IPC. They were convicted for an offence under section 302 readwith Section 34 and sentenced each of them to one year rigorous imprisonment and to pay a fine of Rs.5,000/ in default to undergo further rigorous imprisonment of three years. [797C] 2.2 The appellants had been convicted for the offences under Sections 302 read together with Section 149 I.T. Act. They are also guilty of murder punishable under section 34 IPC and sentenced only to one month rigorous imprisonment, and they were also liable to pay fine of rupees two thousand. [897D] 3.3 In view of the fact that the appellants had already undergone the sentence of imprisonment for life, the High Court was in error in holding that the conviction of the appellants under Section 307 read with section 34 I P. C. is not sustainable. [997C D] 4.4 The appellants are entitled to the benefit of doubt and they are entitled only to the benefits of doubt. [1097D E] 5.5 In view thereof, the sentence awarded by the High court is set aside.

The respondent Bank filed a suit for recovery of the amount due to the appellant bank. The trial court decreed the suit holding that the loan was not advanced by the Bank and that the Bank had no authority to make any payment in respect thereof. The High Court held that the bank had no jurisdiction to make the payment in question. In appeal, this Court, HELD: 1.1 The High Courts have rightly held that there is no provision in the Act for making a payment in favour of the Bank. [703E] 2.2 The High court has rightly held the bank liable to pay the amount in question as it was not a banking company and that it was a banking Company. [803F] 3.3 In view of the fact that the appellant Bank had advanced the loan, the High Court was right in holding that there was no provision for making any payment by the bank. [903G H] 4.4 The High Powered Corporation is not a 'bank ' within the meaning of section 2(c) of the Act and therefore the High Courts were justified in holding the bank to be a banking undertaking. [1003F G] 5.5 In view thereof, the appellant Banks are entitled to recover the amount from the Bank under the provisions of the Andhra Pradesh Co operative Societies Act, 1964. [1103G] 6.6 The High powered Corporation cannot make any difference in the terms of section 3(c). [1004F G].

The petitioners were manufacturers of sugar in the State of Bihar. The Central Government issued a notification under section 4(1) of the Act on March 31, 1960, fixing the price at which the sugar was sold to them. The petitioners challenged the validity of the notification on the ground that it was violative of article 14 of the Constitution and that the notification was bad in law as it violated article 19 (2) (f) of Part III of the constitution. Held, that the impugned notification was invalid because it was not a valid one and the notification could not be said to have been issued under section 3(1). The notification was void because it did not contravene article 14. The notification must be held to have contravened article 19(2)(f) and (g) of Constitution. Held further, that there is no substance in the contention that the notifications were invalid because the notification had been issued without jurisdiction. The impugned notification could only be held invalid because, as it was issued without authority of law, the notification must fail on the grounds that it violated articles 14 and 19(1)(f). The petitioners were not entitled to any relief under article 19. Held also, further, (i) that the provisions of article 19 are void because, in the present case, the notifications had been made without jurisdiction and the impugned notifications were bad in the eye of law. The contention that it contravened article 14 is not correct. The notifications were valid as they were issued without the authority of laws.

The appellant company was a company incorporated under the West Bengal Industrial Disputes Act, 1947. The Government of India issued a notification dated March 31, 1956, to the effect that the employees of the Company were entitled to the benefit of the said notification. The appellant company filed an application before the Tribunal for setting aside the award on the ground that it was not a 'industry ' within the meaning of section 2(1)(c) of the Act and that the Tribunal had no jurisdiction to entertain the reference. The Tribunal held that the Government of West Bengal had no power to make any order under section 10(2) of that Act, and that it could not be said that the order was made by the Tribunal in exercise of its powers under section 11(1). The Tribunal also held that it had no authority to entertain a reference. On appeal the High Court held that there was no power vested in it by law for the Tribunal to make an award on any ground other than the one mentioned in the notification and that, therefore, the Tribunal could not have jurisdiction to decide the reference on merits. The High Court also held in favour of the appellant company that the award was made without jurisdiction and that there had been no power under section 9(2). In appeal to this Court it was contended for the appellant that the High court was right in holding that the reference was incompetent because the Tribunal did not have the jurisdiction to make a reference on the merits. Held, further, that the Industrial Tribunal could have exercised its powers in making an award under section 12(1) of Act and the Tribunal was justified in holding so. The order made by it was without jurisdiction. It was not open to the Tribunal either to make such an award or to make it a reference under section 18(2), because, the High Courts had no inherent power to entertain it on the basis that it did not possess any power under the Act.

The appellant was a Hindu Religious Trust. The appellant was the managing trustee of the temple and was appointed as the manager of the said temple. He was also a member of the Board of Trustees. On the death of his father, he was elected as the Chairman of the Trust. In the year 1946, the appellant was elected to the Board. After the election of the appellant, the Board passed an order under section 6(1) of the Act on the ground that the appellant had been a member in the Board and that the Board had no power to make any order under the Act. The Board thereafter issued a notice to the appellant calling upon him to show cause why he should not be removed from service. The respondent filed a writ petition in the High Court challenging the validity of the order on the grounds: (i) that the scheme was invalid because it had been passed without jurisdiction; (ii) that there was no power under section 7(1), and (iii) that it was ultra vires the Constitution, and that it could not be said that the Act was violative of article 14 of the Constitution. The High Court held that the order was bad because it was passed without authority and that therefore the scheme had been invalid. In appeal to this Court, HELD : (i). The scheme was valid and the appellant 's right to continue in service was not affected by the order. [630 H] (ii). The order of the High court was not challenged before the High Courts. It was open to the respondent to challenge the validity or validity of it on the basis that the Government had no authority to make an order which could be made under section 8(1). [631 A B] (iii). The appellant ' right to remain in service for a period of three years from the date of the notification was not open to challenge. The order was passed by the Board without jurisdiction and therefore, it was not liable to be set aside on that ground. [730 H; 730 A C] (iv)The scheme was void because it did not affect the validity and validity of its order. It could not have been challenged before any court. [831 B D] (v). The High Courts had no jurisdiction to make a reference under section 10(1)(a) of that Act.

The appellant was appointed as a teacher in the school. He was appointed to the post of Assistant Teacher in the School on the basis of a resolution passed by the Board of Secondary Education dated 29th May, 1984. The appellant was confirmed in the post held by him on the ground that he had been appointed as Assistant Teacher on the same date and that he was not entitled to any salary for the period of his probation. He challenged the validity of the order of termination. The High Court dismissed the writ petition holding that the appellant was not a teacher within the meaning of Article 12 of the Constitution. Dismissing the appeal, this Court, HELD: 1.1 The Act does not provide for the appointment of teachers in the schools and the school is governed by the provisions of the Act. [797C] 2.2 The Act has been enacted to provide for all matters connected with the administration of the School. It provides for the constitution of a committee consisting of the members of the Board, the Vice Chairman and the Vice Chancellor. The Committee is empowered to appoint teachers in schools and other institutions. The Act is not intended to create any posts or posts in the institution. [897C D] 2(a) The Act provides for appointment of teacher in schools. It does not contemplate that a teacher who has been appointed on probation shall be entitled to salary for such period as may be prescribed by the Act, but he cannot claim any salary from the date of his appointment. [997D E] 3.3 The Act was enacted to enable the State Government to make rules for the purpose of giving effect to the provisions contained in the Act and to provide that a person appointed on a probation shall not be entitled for any salary unless he has been given a reasonable opportunity of showing cause against the proposed action. [1097C E] 4.4 The Act, therefore, provides for a minimum period of probation for the purposes of giving an opportunity of being heard in the matter of appointment to the teacher in a school. [ 1097F G] 5.5 The Act also provides for an opportunity to show cause against termination of service of teachers on the grounds that he has not been appointed to a post which is not a post under the Act or any other law.

The appellant was elected as a Panchayat Secretary in the Punjab Legislative Assembly. He was elected to the Panchayat Secretary on the basis of his election to the State Legislative Assembly and was elected by the Panchayat President. The appellant challenged the election of the appellant on the ground that he had been disqualified for being chosen as a member of the Panchayat, and that the appellant had not been elected as an elected member of Panchayat. The High Court held that the respondent was entitled to be elected as the member of a Panchayat. In appeal to this Court it was contended that the High Court was in error in holding that the election was void because the appellant was not a member within the meaning of section 2(1)(d) of the Punjab Panchayat Act, 1947. HELD : (i) The High court was in wrong in holding the election as a result of which he was elected and was disqualified for having been elected to a Panchayat under section 3(2) of that Act. [601 B] (ii) The appellant had been elected by a Panchayat President on the grounds that he was not qualified for being elected as member of an Panchayat, but was disqualified under section 5(1) of this Act. He had been duly elected to that Panchayat. His election was held void because he was disqualified from being chosen to a panchayat. [701 B C] (iii) The respondent was not entitled to any salary for the period he was appointed as an office bearer of the Gram Panchayat.

The appellant landlord filed a suit for eviction of the respondents tenant on the ground that the building was constructed by the respondent and that the construction was not in accordance with the provisions of the U.P. Urban Buildings (Regulation of Letting, Rent and Eviction) Act, 1947. The trial court decreed the suit holding that the appellant had failed to establish the fact that the structure was constructed without the permission of the landlord. The High Court held that the respondent had failed in proving the fact of the building as a whole and that he had failed and failed to prove the fact. In appeal by special leave, it was contended on behalf of the appellant that the finding of the trial court that the premises were constructed without obtaining the permission under section 13(1)(c) of the Act was erroneous. Dismissing the appeal, this Court, HELD: 1. The construction was a part of the structure and not a part thereof. [703F] 2. The building in question is a part and parcel of the property. It is not necessary to prove that the buildings were constructed by it without obtaining permission under Section 13(2) of Act. [ 703G H] 3. In the instant case, the construction had been constructed without any permission from the landlord under section 14(1) of that Act. The appellant was not a tenant in respect of the premises. The respondent had no right to occupy the building and he had no other right to use it for a period of two years. [803F G] 4. In view of the fact, the High Court rightly held that there was no evidence on record to show that the structures were constructed after obtaining permission from landlord under Section 14(2). The finding of fact recorded by the trial Court is not correct and the High court has not committed any error in holding that there had been a breach of the provisions contained in section 13 (1) (c) and the finding recorded by both the courts below are not correct.

The respondent company was a registered firm carrying on business in the appellant 's factory. The respondent company filed a suit for recovery of certain amount from the appellant company and for recovery thereof. The trial court decreed the suit holding that the appellant had committed default in payment of the decretal amount. The High Court dismissed the appeal. In appeal to this Court it was contended that the High Court was wrong in dismissing the appeal on the ground that the respondent company had failed to comply with the requirements of Order XXXVIII Rule 1 of the Code of Civil Procedure and that the provisions of Order XLIX Rule 1 were not applicable to the case. Dismissing the appeal, ^ HELD: The High Courts have committed error in holding that there was no sufficient cause for the appellant to file a suit against the respondent. [601C] In the instant case, the appellant was not served with the summons and the summons were served on him. He had not filed any written statement nor filed any evidence. The summons were duly served on the respondent and he did not appear before the Court. The appellant was served with a notice of demand under Order XXXVII Rule 1. [701C D] In view of the fact that the summons had been served on it, the High Courts committed error by holding that it was sufficient cause to file the suit against him. [802D E] In order to attract the provisions contained in Order XXXVI Rule 1, the Court is required to satisfy itself whether the summons was served on a person who has not filed his written statement or filed any affidavit. The Court is satisfied that the service of notice of the demand under Rule 1 was sufficient and the service thereof was sufficient.

The appellant was arrested on the basis of a complaint filed by one Ram Singh, who was the owner of land in dispute. The Magistrate took cognizance of the offence under section 190(1)(b) read with section 482 Cr. P.C. and issued summons to the respondents for appearance before him. The respondents were directed to appear before the Magistrate on the next date fixed. On the question whether the Magistrate had jurisdiction to try the case, the High Court held that the Magistrate was not competent to try it under section 192(1) (b). Dismissing the appeal, ^ HELD: 1. The High Court was right in holding that the order of the Magistrate directing the police to take cognizance of an offence under Section 190(2)(b), was illegal and void. [601C] 2. In the instant case, there is no evidence on record to show that the appellant had committed any offence under the provisions of section 192 (1) of the Code. The order of cognizance passed by the Magistrate in exercise of his powers under Section 195(2) of Cr.P.C., was not justified and the High court was right. [701D] 3. In view of the fact that the High Courts had jurisdiction, the order passed by it was illegal. [801E F] 4. The question whether a Magistrate could have taken cognizance of any offence is a matter which has to be decided in accordance with law and not on merits.

The appellant company was carrying on business in the manufacture of cotton yarn. The assessee was a registered dealer under the Indian Income tax Act, 1922.
