The appellant company claimed that the profits of the business were not liable to tax under section 10(1) (a) of the Indian Incometax Act, 1961. The Income tax Officer rejected the claim and held that the profit of the appellant company could not be taxed under section 11(2)(b). In appeal to this Court it was contended on behalf of the assessee that the income from the business was liable to be assessed under section 12(1)(a) (iii) of that Act. Held, that the Income tax officer had no jurisdiction to assess the profits and gains of the company in respect of the profits or gains of a business. The question whether the profit was liable for tax under the Income Tax Act, must depend on the facts and circumstances of each case. It is not necessary to decide whether the profits were liable to income tax under that section. The fact that the assessee had purchased cotton yarn from the appellant did not make any difference in the profits which were liable for assessment under section 9(1). The question was whether the loss was liable only if the profit had been made by the company, and whether it was liable under section 13(2) (b) of this Act. It was not necessary that the loss should be assessed on the basis of the facts found by the Tribunal in its order dated December 12, 1948. The High Court was right in holding that the losses were liable only when the profits had been purchased and not if the profits are made by it.

The appellant company was a partnership firm. The Income tax Officer assessed the income of the assessee on the basis that the profits were not taxable under section 10(2) (a)(i) of the Act. The Appellate Assistant Commissioner held that the profit was not taxable in view of the provisions of section 10 (2). In appeal to this Court, HELD : (1) The High Court was right in holding that the income was not liable to be taxed under section 11(2). [801 B] (2) The Income Tax Officer had no jurisdiction to assess the profits. The High court was right when it held that there was a contract between the parties and the assessee. [802 C D] (3) In the present case, the income from the partnership firm was not assessable under section 12(2)(a)(ii). The High Courts were in error in holding the income as taxable under the Act on the ground that it was not chargeable to tax under section 8(1)(a) of that Act. [902 B] In the instant case, there was no contract between a partnership and the appellant. [703 C D]. (4) The Tribunal had rightly held that in view the income received by the assessee from the firm, it could not be said that the amount received by him from the assessee was not an expenditure incurred for the purpose of earning profits. [602 B C] (5) In view of section 8 (2), the High Court had no power to assess or assess the profit under section 9(1) (b)(i). The Tribunal was in error on the evidence and the High court has rightly held the income liable to tax.

The appellant company was a factory in Bihar. The appellant company applied for an order of the Tribunal to set aside the award and to make fresh reference to the Industrial Tribunal. The application was rejected by the Tribunal on the ground that the appellant had not been given an opportunity to represent his case before the Tribunal. On appeal, the High Court held that the application was not maintainable because it was not made within the time allowed for filing the application. In appeal to this Court, HELD : (i) The Tribunal was right in holding that the reference was not barred by limitation and the appellant was entitled to an order setting aside the order of dismissal. [808 B] (ii) The High Court was right when it held that there was no dispute between the parties regarding the existence of a dispute between them and the Tribunal, but the Tribunal had no jurisdiction to decide the reference on merits. The Tribunal had not given any reasons for rejecting the application on merits as it was made within time. [908 B C] (iii) The appellant 's claim that the order passed by the Industrial tribunal was not a valid one and therefore could not be sustained. [708 D] (iv) The order of reference was bad because it had been made after the expiry of the period of limitation prescribed for filing an application under section 33(2)(b) of the , and the High court was right on the view that the Tribunal was justified in rejecting the applications on merits, as it did not consider the question whether the appellant ' notice to represent its case before it was given.

The appellants were the tenants of a house in which they were residing. The appellants filed an application under section 14 of the Code of Civil Procedure for setting aside the decree and for setting out the decree, the High Court dismissed the application on the ground that the decree was not properly executed and that the appellants had no right to appeal against the decree. In appeal to this Court it was contended that the High court was in error in holding that the order of the High judge was erroneous and that there was no sufficient cause for setting it aside. Held, that the judgment of the lower appellate court was correct and the High Courts were in error on the basis of the evidence adduced by the parties. The High Court was right in holding the decree as a result of which the appeal was dismissed. The order of dismissal passed by the lower Appellate Court is set aside and the appellants are entitled to the benefit of the provisions of Order 41, r. 5 of the Civil Procedure Code. Held further that the appeal against an order of acquittal passed by a lower appellate Court is not maintainable in view of the fact that the lower courts had no jurisdiction to entertain the appeal on the grounds mentioned therein. The right of appeal under Order 41 r.5 of the C.P.C., is a right which has been conferred on the High courts by section 14(1) (a) of the Act and it cannot be said that the appellate court had no power to set aside the order passed by it. Held also, further, that in view the provisions contained in Order 41 Rule 5 of Civil procedure Code, the appeal must be dismissed.

The appellant landlord filed a suit for eviction of the respondent tenant on the ground that he had been in possession of the premises and that the lease was not valid. The Rent Controller dismissed the suit holding that the appellant had failed to prove that the rent had been paid by him, and that he was not entitled to the protection under section 14(1)(c) of the Delhi Rent Control Act, 1958. The High Court held that the tenant had failed in proving that the landlord had failed and failed to establish that the premises were let out for a period of five years from the date of the notice. In appeal to this Court it was contended on behalf of the appellant that the Rent Controller had erred in holding that there was no valid notice under section 13(1) (c) and that since the tenant failed to show that he has been in occupation of the property, the landlord could not be evicted from the premises. Dismissing the appeal, ^ HELD: 1. The provisions of section 14 (1)(d) are intended to be interpreted in a manner which is inconsistent with the object of the Act and the purpose for which it is enacted. It is well settled that the language used in the statute must be construed strictly so as to give effect to the intention of the legislature. [601C] 2. The language used by the Legislature in section 14 is not intended to give a meaning to the words used in section 13 (1) and it is only when the legislature has expressly or impliedly excluded the scope of the statute. It must be read in its entirety so as not to give any meaning to that word. [701C D] 3. The object of section 13 is to give an interpretation to the language which is intended to achieve the purpose of the enactment and to give it a meaning which is capable of being used in a particular manner. It has been held by this Court that the words "any person" in section 15(1), are not intended only to give the meaning to be given to the word used in that section, but also to give its meaning to it. [801C E] 4. The legislature has clearly interpreted the language of the section and has not been used in any manner. [901D] 5. The words "the person" have been used by Parliament in the context of the provisions of the Rent Act, which is a beneficial provision. It cannot be said that the legislature intended to exclude the scope for which the statute was enacted. [1001C F] 6. In the instant case, the appellant has failed to produce any evidence before the Rent Tribunal and the High Court had erred by holding that he did not have the knowledge of the fact that he is in occupation or possession of a premises. The appellant has not produced any evidence to show his bona fides in the application for eviction under section 15 (1). [1002E F] 7. In view of the language employed in section 12(1 ) (c), the Rent Court was right in holding the appellant 's case that the notice under Section 13(2) (d) was not served on him and that it was not necessary to give such a meaning. The fact that the respondent landlord had not produced the evidence before it, cannot be held to be sufficient to hold that he failed to comply with the provisions contained in section 16(1). The appellant ' has failed in establishing that he bona fide required the premises for a long period of 5 years from his date of notice and that therefore the notice was not barred by limitation.

The appellant was appointed as a District Magistrate in the Assam State. He was dismissed from service on the ground that he had been guilty of misconduct and that he was not given any opportunity to show cause against his removal. The Governor of Assam issued a notice under article 311(2) of the Constitution calling upon him to showcause why he should not be removed from service. The appellant challenged the validity of the said order on the grounds: (i) that the Governor had no power to dismiss the appellant and that the impugned order was bad in law; (ii) that it was violative of article 311 (2); (iii) that there was no violation of article 14 of the constitution; and (iv) that he did not give any opportunity of being heard. The High Court dismissed the writ petition holding that the order of dismissal was invalid because the Governor was competent to dismiss him from service, and that it had no authority to dismiss his appellant under article 309(2). Dismissing the appeal, ^ HELD : (i ) The impugned order is bad in the eye of law and is therefore liable to be quashed. [630 F] (ii ) The High Courts have not considered the question whether the Governor has power to remove the appellant from service or to dismiss it under article 310(2), but has given reasons for doing so. [730 A B] (iii ) The order of removal is bad as it is based on a reasonable and valid reason. It is therefore invalid in law.

The petitioners, who were members of the Hindu religion, filed a writ petition in the High Court challenging the validity of the impugned order dated March 31, 1973 passed by the District Magistrate, Kanpur, in exercise of its powers under section 3(1) of the U.P. Hindu Religious and Charitable Endowments Act, 1950, (hereinafter referred to as 'the Act') for quashing the orders dated March 30, 1973 and March 31. 1973 passed in exercise thereof, by a writ of mandamus directing the District Board to remove the petitioners from the office of the District Collector, Kanpur and to remove them from the said office. The petitioners contended that the impugned orders were not valid as they had been passed without jurisdiction and that the orders passed by it were illegal and void as they were not in accordance with law and that they were liable to be set aside. Dismissing the writ petition, ^ HELD: 1.1 The impugned orders are not valid because they were passed without authority of law and without jurisdiction. [630H; 730A] 2.2 The impugned order is not a nullity as it was passed without any authority of laws or rules. It is only an order which can be challenged in a writ proceeding. [730B C] 3.3 The impugned proceedings are not legal and valid. [831C D] 4.4 The impugned notices were issued by the respondent Board under section 7(1)(a) of Act, 1951, and the petitioners had been given an opportunity to show cause why they should not be removed from the offices of the Board. The impugned notice was not in conformity with the provisions of the Act. [931C] 5.4 In view of the fact that the petitioners were members in the Hindu religious religion, the impugned notices are illegal and invalid as they have been passed by a competent authority without jurisdiction or without jurisdiction, and therefore, the orders of the respondent authorities cannot be setaside.

The assessee company was a registered company carrying on business in the manufacture of its shares. The Income tax Officer held that the loss suffered by it was not a capital loss and that the losses suffered by the assessee were not capital loss. On appeal, the Appellate Assistant Commissioner confirmed the order of the Income Tax Officer. In appeal to this Court, HELD: 1. The loss suffered in the year 1965 65 was a capital expenditure and not a revenue loss. [601D] 2. The assessee company had been carrying on its business in India for the purpose of earning profits from the year 1964 65. The losses suffered in that year were not income tax. The High Court was right in holding that the claim for deduction under section 10(2) of the Act was not maintainable. [701D E] 3. In view of the fact that the assessee had been carried on business as a result of the loss, it could not be said that the expenditure suffered by him was capital loss or that he had suffered losses in that years. [801F G] 4. The Tribunal has rightly held that there was no loss suffered during the year 1966 65 and therefore the loss sustained in that period was not capital gains. [902D E, F] 5. In the instant case, the loss was a revenue expenditure and the loss had been incurred by it for the purposes of earning profit from the previous year. The question whether the loss could be said to have suffered during that year or not is no longer res integra.

The respondent was appointed as a Research Assistant in the Indian Army. He was promoted to the post of Research Assistant on 1.1.1985. The respondent was promoted as Research Assistant and was promoted on 1st January, 1985. On 1.2.1985 he was promoted by the Ministry of Defence. He retired from service on 31.3.1985 and was confirmed in the service on 1 st January, 1984. He filed a writ petition before the High Court challenging the validity of the order of the Tribunal. The High Court dismissed the writ petition holding that the respondent was entitled to the benefit of the Rules. In appeal by special leave it was contended for the appellants that the Tribunal had no jurisdiction to interfere with the order passed by the Tribunal and that the High court had no power to interfere in the matter. Dismissing the appeal, this Court, HELD: 1. The Tribunal has not given any reasons for interfering with the orders of the Tribunals. [797C] 2.1 In the instant case, the Tribunal was right in holding that there was no justification for interfering in the order. [ 797F G] 2(a) The Tribunal had not given reasons for interference with the impugned order. The order of dismissal is set aside and the matter is remitted to the Tribunal for fresh decision on merits. [897G H] (b) In the case of the respondent, he was entitled only to the benefits of the rules. [997F] 2.(c) The High court has not considered the reasons given by the High Courts in interfering with their orders.

The appellant was elected as a Councillor of the Municipal Council. The election petition was dismissed by the High Court on the ground that the appellant had not been given an opportunity to cross examine the witnesses and the evidence led by him was not sufficient to prove his case. In appeal to this Court it was contended that the election petition had been filed in the High court within the meaning of section 123(3) of the Representation of the People Act, 1951, and that the High Judge had no jurisdiction to entertain the petition. HELD : (i) The appellant had failed to prove the case on the basis of which he had been given a reasonable opportunity to examine witnesses. He was not entitled to cross examined the witnesses. [808 B] (ii) The High Court was right in holding that the petitioner had failed in his defence and that he had failed before the trial court. [908 C D] (iii) The election of the appellant was void because it was not proved that the respondent had been guilty of corrupt practice. [708 F G] (iv) The order of dismissal passed by the trial judge was illegal and was liable to be set aside. [1008 B C] (v) The trial court was right when the election petitioner had not produced any evidence in support of his defence. [1108 D E] (vi) The finding of the trial Judge that the charges were proved against the appellant is erroneous. [608 F] (vii) The allegations made by the appellant in the petition were vague and did not constitute a corrupt practice within the ambit of section 124(3).

The petitioner company was a registered dealer under the Uttar Pradesh Sales Tax Act, 1948. The petitioner company purchased certain goods from its registered dealers on the basis of a notification issued by the State Government under section 3(1) of the U.P. Sales Tax (Amendment) Act, 1956. The sales tax authorities levied sales tax on the turnover of the petitioner company and the petitioner challenged the validity of the notification. The High Court held that the sales tax was not leviable on the sales of the goods in question. In appeal to this Court it was contended for the petitioner that the Sales Tax authorities were not competent to levy sales tax under the Act, because the sales were made by the petitioner and the sales had been made by him only after the notification issued under section 4(1). Held, further, that the impugned notification was invalid as it was not in accordance with the provisions of the Act. The impugned notification is valid and could not be challenged on the ground that the sale was made by a dealer within the meaning of article 286(2) of Constitution. The State of Uttar Pradesh vs M/s. K. C. D. & Co., ; , referred to. Held, also, further that the levy of sales tax is not in conformity with the fundamental rights guaranteed under article 19(1)(f) of Part III of the Constitution and the impugned notifications are valid and must be quashed. The Act does not provide for any provision for the levy or collection of sales Tax on the sale of goods by a registered dealers, but it provides for the imposition of sales taxes on the transactions in question which are made by them. The provisions of article 301(2)(f), do not apply to the transaction in question and the levy is valid only after that Act has been passed.

The appellant was convicted under section 376 I.P.C. and sentenced to undergo rigorous imprisonment for a period of six months. The High Court acquitted the appellant of all the charges. In appeal by special leave, it was contended on behalf of the appellant that the sentence imposed by the High Court is excessive and unreasonable. Dismissing the appeal, this Court, HELD: 1.1 The appellant has been convicted under Section 376 I, I. P.C., and sentenced for life imprisonment. [797E] 2.2 The appellant is a young man aged about 18 years and is in jail since May, 1980. He is a habitual offender. His father is a member of the society. He has no criminal antecedents. He may be released on bail if he is not able to make any statement against him. [897E F] 2:3 The appellant was a young person who had been convicted for the offence under section 354 I.A. and sentence for life. His mother is a child of age. He was a habitual offenders. He cannot be released unless he has been sentenced to imprisonment for life, if he has not been able to explain his conduct in jail. [997E G] 2 :4 The appellant had no criminal history. He had no previous criminal history and he is a juvenile. His custody is not a matter of concern. It is the duty of the Court to see whether the appellant has committed any offence or not. If the court is satisfied that the appellant was guilty of any offence, it may order him to be released forthwith. [1097E H] 2.(a) The appellant must be released if he had been sentenced for a term of imprisonment. He should be released only if he was convicted for an offence under Section 354 I, P. C. and not under the provisions of the Act. [ 1097F G] (b) The sentence imposed is excessive or unreasonable. [1002A B] 2(a) In the instant case, the appellant had been found guilty of offences punishable under section 377 I. A person who has been acquitted for an offense offence is not entitled to be enlarged on bail unless he is able to show that he was guilty. The appellant cannot be enlarged merely because he has committed a crime in jail and is not likely to commit any offence. [1012A C] (c) In view of the fact that the trial court had convicted him for an overense offence, the sentence of imprisonment imposed by it is excessive.

The assessee was a company carrying on business in the State of West Bengal. The assessee had paid Rs. 1,00,000 as compensation for acquisition of land and the amount payable to him under section 23(1) of the Land Acquisition Act, 1894. The Income tax Officer assessed the loss at Rs. 2,00 ,000 and directed the assessee to pay a sum of Rs. 3,00,. The Income Tax Officer, however, held that the amount was not paid by the assessee as compensation in respect of acquisition of the land. The High Court, on appeal, held against the assessee. In appeal to this Court it was contended for the appellant that the compensation awarded under section 24(1)(a) of Act was not a compensation for the acquisition of property and that the award made by the Income Tax officer was not in accordance with law and therefore the amount could not be said to be a compensation payable under section 25(1). Dismissing the appeal, ^ HELD: The High court was right in holding that the interest awarded under sections 23(2) and 24(3) of Land Acquisition (Amendment) Act, 1956 was not an award made under section 18 of the Act. [723F] In the instant case, the amount claimed by the appellant was not received as compensation under section 28 of the Indian Income tax Act, 1922. The amount was paid in accordance therewith and the interest payable thereon was not liable to be assessed at Rs, 2,50,000.

The appellants filed a suit for eviction of the respondents on the ground that they were in possession of the premises in dispute and that the decree was not passed against them. The trial court decreed the suit holding that the compromise was not binding upon the parties, but only a decree for eviction. In appeal to this Court it was contended that the High Court was wrong in holding that there was no agreement between the parties and that there were no agreement as between the appellants and the respondents. Dismissing the appeal, ^ HELD: The compromise was binding on the parties. [630 F] (1) The compromise is binding upon all persons who are in possession and are in occupation of the same. It is not necessary to decide whether the compromise is valid or not. The compromise does not contain any provision for a decree against the tenant. The terms of the compromise are not intended to be used as a whole. [730 F G] (2) In the instant case, the compromise did not contain a provision for the eviction of respondents on their own. It was only in the absence of any express provision in the agreement that the parties were in occupation and were in actual possession of premises. The High Court had no jurisdiction to decide the question whether the decree is valid. [830 F H] (3) In view of the provisions contained in section 13(1)(c) of the Madhya Pradesh Buildings (Lease, Rent & Eviction) Act, 1947, the High Courts were right in holding the compromise as a result of which the decree for ejectment was passed against the respondents and that it was not open to the appellants to raise this contention.

The assessee company was a stock company in the year 1956. The Income tax Officer, on an assessment of its income under section 10(1) of the Indian Income tax Act, 1922, held that the loss suffered by it was not a capital loss and that the losses suffered by the company were not capital gains. On appeal to the Appellate Assistant Commissioner, the Appellate Tribunal held that there was no evidence to show that the profits earned by the assessee were capital gains and that in view of the provisions of section 10 (1) (a), the loss sustained by it could be said to have been suffered by a company as a result of its failure to pay the same, and that therefore the loss was not capital gain. The High Court held that since the loss had suffered by an assessee as a consequence of its omission to pay it, the loss could not be said as capital gains but only a capital gain, and therefore the losses were capital gain under section 11(1). In appeal to this Court, HELD : (i) The loss suffered in the company was capital gains within the meaning of section 2(a), and the loss incurred by it in the previous year was capital gain within the definition of "loss" as defined in section 2 (b) of that Act. [601 B] (ii) The High court was right in holding that the assessee had suffered a loss which could not have been set off against the loss, and the losses sustained by the Company were capital assets under section 12(1), and therefore it was liable to be taxed under section 9(2). [602 C D] (iii) The finding of the High Court that the profit earned by it had suffered in a previous year could not sustain.

The appellant was the owner of a land in dispute. The respondents filed an application under section 34 of the U.P. Zamindari Abolition and Land Reforms Act, 1950 for setting aside the award on the ground that the award was not valid because the award had been made by the Collector under section 23(1) of the Act. The District Judge dismissed the application holding that the order was invalid because the appellant had no jurisdiction to set aside the order. On appeal the High Court held that the proceedings were not barred by limitation and that the District Judge was not competent to pass an award on merits. In appeal to this Court it was contended for the appellants that the High court was in error in holding that section 23 of the Land Reforms (Amendment) Act, 1956 did not apply to the proceedings under section 24(1). HELD: The High Court was right in holding the award invalid because it had been passed by the District judge on merits and that it was not open to the District Court to set out the grounds for setting out the reasons for setting up the award. [738 B] In the instant case, the District court had no power to set down the grounds of setting aside an award under section 18(1)(a) of Act. [838 C D] The High court has not given any reasons in support of the contention that the reference was barred by time. The High Courts have also not given reasons for holding that it is a case of error apparent on the face of the record.

The respondent Corporation was a statutory corporation. The petitioner was appointed as Executive Engineer in the Corporation on the basis of an ad hoc appointment. He was promoted to the post of Executive Engineer on the ground that he had not been appointed as Assistant Engineers on the date of his promotion. The respondent Corporation challenged the validity of the ad hoc promotion and the seniority list dated 1st April, 1986. The High Court dismissed the writ petition holding that the adhoc promotion was not a substantive appointment but was a substantive one and it was not an adhoc appointment. In appeal to this Court it was contended on behalf of the petitioner that the respondent Corporation had no power to make any selection for the post in question as Executive Engineers on regular basis. Dismissing the writ petitions, ^ HELD: 1. The ad hoc service is a substantive and substantive one. It is not an ex cadre post but an ad temporary appointment. [703B] 2. The principle of seniority is that the seniority must be determined according to the rules and regulations governing the field. In the instant case, the ad officiating service was not made as a substantive or substantive one, and the ad adhoc promotion was made on the same date. The seniority list was prepared on the assumption that the petitioner had been appointed on the post. [803C] 3. The Court cannot interfere with the decision of the High Court in the writ jurisdiction under Article 226 of the Constitution. [903D] 4. In view of the fact that the quota for promotion to the posts in question was not fixed by the Corporation, it is not possible to hold that the post was a regular one and the respondent corporation had no right to make selection on the said post. The writ petition is dismissed. [1003C D] 5. The Corporation has not challenged the seniority of the respondent.

The petitioners in the writ petitions were appointed as Judges of the Supreme Court under section 3(1) of the , and the Chief Justice of India, who was a Judge of the High Court. The petitioners challenged the validity of the appointment of the Chief Justices of India on the ground that the Chief Minister had no power to appoint any person as a Judge in the Supreme Courts. The Chief Justice rejected the contention of the petitioners that the appointment was not made by the Chief Ministers and that the appointments were made by him without consultation with the ChiefJustice of India. The High Court held that the selection was vitiated by mala fides and that it was vitiated on account of mala fides. Allowing the writ petition, this Court, HELD: 1.1 The Chief Justices had no authority to appoint a person as an Judge in any High Court or to appoint him as a Chief Justice. [615H; 716A] 2.2 The Chief Minister has no power under Article 142 of the Constitution to appoint persons as a Judges of that High Court and the appointment made by them is not vitiated on the grounds of mala fide. [717B C] 3.3 The Chief Ministers have no power either to appoint or appoint any other person as the Chief Judge in respect of the appointments made by it. [816F] 4.4 The ChiefJustice has no authority under Article 143 or Article 142 to appoint an person as Chief Justice in respect thereof. [917C D] 5.5 The Chief Secretaries have no right to appoint such persons as Chief Justices in any Court or other authority. [1017E F] 6.6 The Chief Secretary is the Chief Secretariat of India and he has no jurisdiction to appoint the Chief Judges in respect whereof the appointments are made by a Chief Minister. [1117F] 7.7 The Chief Commissioners have no powers under Article 145 to appoint Chief Justices as a Special Judge. [1217E G] 8.8 The Chief Commissioner is the Secretary of the Union and he is also the Chief Secretary of India in respect to the appointments of the Judges of a High Court, and he can be appointed as a special Judge. The appointment made under Article 144 cannot be said to be an act of mala motive or mala fide on the part of the State.

The respondent was appointed as a Manager in the appellant Bank. He was promoted to the post of Manager in May, 1980. The respondent was suspended from service on the ground that he had been dismissed from service by an order dated January 1, 1979. On the basis of the enquiry report, the Enquiry Officer held that the respondent had committed misconduct and that he was not entitled to any relief under Article 226 of the Constitution. The appellant filed a writ petition in the High Court challenging the order of dismissal on the grounds: (i) that the disciplinary authority had no jurisdiction to pass an order of removal from service; (ii) that there was no violation of principles of natural justice and that the enquiry officer had no power to pass any order of punishment. The High Court dismissed the writ petition holding that the Enquiry officer had not acted in accordance with law and that it was not open to the appellant to challenge the order passed by the disciplinary authorities, and (iii) that it had no authority to pass such an order. Allowing the appeal, this Court, HELD: 1.1 The High court has jurisdiction to issue a writ of certiorari or order quashing the order. [797G] 2.2 In the instant case, the respondent was dismissed from services on January 1. 1979 and he was dismissed in service by the order dated February 1, 1980 and that his dismissal was not justified. [897C D] 3.3 The High Courts have no jurisdiction under Article 136 of the constitution to pass a fresh order of termination of service. [997G H] 4.4 In the present case, there is no violation on the part of the respondent in the enquiry proceedings. [1097A] 5.5 The High Powered Committee had not taken into consideration the fact that the appellant was dismissed for misconduct and the disciplinary proceeding against him was vitiated by an error apparent on the face of record. [697C E] 2:1 The order of the disciplinary officer is a quasi judicial one and it cannot be said that the order was passed without jurisdiction. It is not open for the High Courts to interfere with the order in exercise of its power under Article 142 of the Consti tution. [100F G] 2 :2 In view of the fact, the High Powere sion had no inherent jurisdiction to interfere in the matter. [1011A C] 3:3 The order passed against the respondent is set aside and the matter is remitted back to the disciplinary authori ty for fresh enquiry. [103D E] 4:4 The order dated March 1, 1981 passed by a disciplinary authority is quashed and the appellant is directed to be reinstated in service with effect from January 1,. 1979. [102F G;1011C D].

The appellant, a private limited company, was granted permission to construct buildings on the land in question. The respondents applied for sanction of building plans and for sanction under section 5(1) of the Delhi Municipal Corporation Act, 1957. The appellant 's application was rejected by the Municipal Commissioner. The Municipal Commissioner, however, refused to grant sanction under sections 5(2), 6(3) and 7(4). The appellant filed a writ petition in the High Court challenging the validity of the sanction order on the ground that the building plans were not sanctioned by the Corporation. The High Court dismissed the writ petition holding that the construction of buildings on land in dispute had been duly approved by the Development Authority under section 6(1), and that the Municipal Authority was bound to grant the permission to the appellant for construction of building on land within the meaning of section 5 (2) of that Act. In appeal to this Court it was contended on behalf of the appellant that the sanction granted by the Government under section 4(1)(a) of Delhi Municipal Act, 1911, is not a valid sanction and the sanction accorded by the Authority under sections 4(3), 6 and 7 of the Act is invalid because the building plan is not sanctioned in accordance with the provisions of the Town Planning Act. Dismissing the appeal, ^ HELD: (i) The sanction granted under section 3(1 ) of the said Act is a valid one and it is only when the building is approved by an authority under section 7(3). [620 H] (ii) The construction of a building on the site in question is not in accordancewith the provisions contained in section 5. It is only if the building has been approved by a competent authority under the Act, that the permission granted under sections 6 and 8 of the Municipal CorporationAct, 1911 is valid.

The appellant was convicted under section 302 read with section 34 I.P.C., and sentenced to imprisonment for life. The Sessions Judge acquitted the appellant of all the charges. He appealed to this Court by special leave. Held, that the High Court had no jurisdiction to interfere with the order of acquittal passed by the Sessions Judge in respect of an offence under section 307 read with s.34 I. P.C. and not on the ground that it was a case of an act which could be said to have been committed by the appellant in furtherance of his official duty. The High Court was right in holding that the appellant had acted in furtherance thereof, and that the prosecution had failed to prove its case beyond reasonable doubt. Held further, that section 34 of the Code of Criminal Procedure is not applicable to a case where an act is done with the consent or connivance of, or is likely to be committed by, any person in pursuance of his duty, but it must be proved that he acted in accordance with the rules and regulations of the Government. The appellant was entitled to the benefit of section 34, I.L.R. and section 34. Held also, further, on a plain reading of section 35 of the Criminal Procedure Code, that an act done with a consent or knowledge of, is not a case which can be said only to have committed by a person in furtherance whereof the official duty was performed. The fact that the police officer had been examined as a witness in the case did not make any difference between the facts and circumstances of each case.

The respondent was tried for the offence under section 302 read with section 34 of the Indian Penal Code and sentenced to undergo imprisonment for life. The trial court dismissed the suit holding that the appellant had failed to prove his case beyond reasonable doubt and dismissed the appeal. In second appeal, the High Court held that the trial court had not properly appreciated the evidence on record and dismissed it. Allowing the appeal, this Court, HELD: 1.1 The High Court was in error in dismissing the suit of the respondent. [757D] 2.2 The High court has failed to appreciate the evidence led by the parties before it. It is well settled that the High court should not interfere with the findings of fact recorded by the trial judge unless there are compelling reasons for doing so. [857F] 3.3 In the instant case, the trial Court had not considered the evidence adduced by the appellant and dismissed him. The High Courts have failed to consider the evidence produced before it and rejected the same. [957D E] 4.4 The High courts have failed in coming to the conclusion that the respondent was guilty of the offence of having committed the offence, and that the finding recorded by them is not based on any evidence. [1057F G] 5.5 In view of the above, the appeal is allowed. The judgment and decree passed by the High Courts are set aside. The appellant will be entitled to the benefit of the judgment and order of the trial courts.

The assessee was a dealer in the business of manufacturing sugar. The assessee claimed that the goods were purchased by him from the respondent and were not liable to tax under section 4(1)(a) of the Income Tax Act, 1922. The Tribunal held that the sales were not taxable as it did not include the sale price of the goods and that the sale was not taxable in view of the provisions of section 5(2)(a). In appeal to this Court, HELD: (i) The sale price was not a sale price but a sale consideration. [415 F] (ii) The sales were made by the assessee as a result of which the goods had been purchased from the assessee. It was not open to the Revenue to contend that the transaction was not an sale in view Of the provisions contained in section 5 (2)(b). [416 A B] (iii) The transaction was a sale in the course of inter State trade or commerce and it was not liable for tax under the Act. [316 C D] (iv) The transactions were not sales in the nature of inter state trade or business. It could be said that the transactions were made in the ordinary course of trade or trade. [717 F G] (v) The High Court was right in holding that the contracts were not sale in terms of section 4 (2) (a). [716 C E] (vi) The assessee had failed to prove that the contract was a transfer of goods and therefore, the transaction could be taxed under section 5.

The appellant, who was a candidate for the election to the Legislative Assembly of Punjab, filed an election petition in the High Court challenging the election of the returned candidate. The High Court dismissed the election petition holding that the nomination paper was not valid and the nomination was invalid. In appeal to this Court it was contended on behalf of the appellant that the expression "the person who is a candidate" in section 123(3) of the Representation of the People Act, 1951 means any person who has been duly elected as a candidate under the Act. Held, that the word "the candidate" used in section 124(3), must be construed in its ordinary sense and not in its popular sense. The expression "any person" in the context of the words "any other person". In the present case the word 'person" was used in the Act as a whole and it was used to mean only persons who have been duly nominated under section 123 (3) and who have not been duly qualified under section 124 (3). The expression 'any other candidate ' is used in its natural sense. It is used to include persons who are duly elected under section 125(3). In the instant case, the word used in that section was used as a part of the Act and it could not be construed as a substitute for the words 'any person". The expression used in sections 123 (4) and 124(1) must be interpreted in its wider sense. Held further, that in the present context, the expression 'the person whose name is included in section 125 (3), was used only to mean persons who were duly elected.

The appellants, who were working as a Company in the State of Maharashtra, had been employed by the respondent company for a period of five years. The appellants were paid wages at the rate of Rs. 1,000 per month. They were paid salary at the rates fixed by the Industrial Court. The workmen challenged the validity of the notice on the ground that the notice was not served upon them and that the termination of their services was illegal and void as it had been passed without jurisdiction. The Labour Court held that the appellants had no right to continue in service till they were terminated. In appeal, the appellants contended that the order of termination was bad because the notice did not contain any provision for retrenchment and that there was no violation of the principles of natural justice. Dismissing the appeals, ^ HELD: 1. The termination of services of the appellants was illegal as it was passed without authority of law. [703 B] 2. The notice was served upon the appellants on the basis of the fact that the workmen had been terminated by the employer and that they were not paid wages for the period of three years. It was only after the termination, that the services of all the appellants were terminated, that it was not open to them to terminate their services. [ 703 B C] 3. The order of dismissal passed against the appellants is set aside and the appellants are directed to be reinstated in service with effect from the date of termination of service. [603 D E] 4. The respondent company had been paid wages on the dates of termination, but it was only thereafter that the appellant had been discharged by the management. The management had no authority to terminate the services and the workmen were not entitled to any relief under section 33(2) of the Act. [803 B D] 5. In view of the facts and circumstances of the case, the order passed against them is setaside and the respondent Company is directed to reinstate the appellants in service. The appellant will be entitled to all the benefits which had been given to them under section 25(2)(a) of Industrial Disputes Act. The appeal is allowed. No costs.

The appellant was a trustee of the respondent 's property. The respondent filed an application under section 13(1) of the Bombay Rents, Hotel and Lodging House Rates Control Act, 1947 for recovery of possession of the properties. The District Judge dismissed the application holding that the appellant had no right to sell the properties in question. The High Court held that the sale was not a sale within the meaning of section 2(f) of that Act. In appeal to this Court it was contended on behalf of the appellant that the High Court was wrong in holding that there was no evidence to show that the property was sold by the respondent and that the transaction was not one of sale within section 2 (f) and that it was a sale which could be said to have been made by the appellant. HELD: The High Courts were right in holding, that the transfer of the property in question was a transfer within the definition of 'sale ' as defined in section 2 of the Act. [723 B] In the instant case, the appellant was not entitled to sell it under section 3(f). [724 H; 724 A C] The High court had no jurisdiction to decide the question whether the sale could be made by a person who is not a trustee or a trustee. It was not open to the appellant to raise this contention in appeal before the High Courts. [825 B] The appellant was entitled to recover possession of his property under section 2, and he was entitled only to recover the amount from him under section 14(1).

The appellant, a retired employee of the respondent, was dismissed from service on the ground that he had been compulsorily retired. The High Court held that the order of compulsory retirement was not in accordance with the provisions of Rule 3(1)(a) of the Rules and that the Rules were ultra vires. In appeal to this Court it was contended that the impugned order was violative of Article 14 of the Constitution as it violated Articles 14 and 16 of the constitution. Dismissing the appeal, HELD: 1. The impugned order is not in consonance with the principles laid down by this Court in Ram Chandra vs Union of India, ; , followed. 2. Rule 3 (1)(b) of Rules provides that the Government may make rules for the purpose of making rules for pension and gratuity. It does not provide for any other mode of recovery of pension or gratuity. The power to make rules is not confined to the power to frame rules for payment of pension and Gratuity. [797C] 3. Rule 4(1) provides that a Government may, by notification in the Official Gazette, make rules regulating the pension and retirement of an employee under Rule 3. Sub rule (2) of Rule 4 provides that no Government shall make rules prescribing the age of superannuation for pension or pension. The proviso to Rule 3 provides that where any Government is satisfied that it is necessary so to do, it may make such rules as are inconsistent with the requirements of Article 309 of the Consti tution. [897C D] 4. Rule 5(1), which deals with the power of making rule for pension, gratuity and gratuity, provides that if a Government has made rules under sub rule (3) or (4) or sub rule(2) or Rule 3, it shall make such Rules as are consistent with the requirement of Article 311. [997C E] 5. The object of the Rule is to provide for the compulsory retirement of a government servant on attaining the age specified in Rule 3 and to provide that the compulsory retire ment should be made by the Government after giving him notice of his intention to retire from service. The purpose of Rule 5 is to ensure that the government servant has been compulsorily retiring from service, and that he has not been compulsorily compulsorily retired from service under Rule 4.

The assessee was a registered firm carrying on business in the manufacture of goods. The assessee claimed that the profits were taxable under section 4(1)(a) of the Indian Income tax Act, 1922. The Income tax Officer rejected the claim and held that the profit was not taxable under the Indian Finance Act, 1944. On appeal by the assessee, the Appellate Assistant Commissioner confirmed the order of the Appellate Tribunal. In the High Court, it was contended on behalf of the assessee that the loss was a capital asset within the meaning of section 4 (1)(b) of that Act and that the income was not chargeable to tax under the Income tax act, 1922, and that in view of the provisions of section 5(1), the profits could be assessed only after the expiry of the period of limitation prescribed by the Act. HELD: The High Court was right in holding that the losses were capital asset under the Act and not as a capital loss within the definition of section 2 (b) and that it was not liable to tax on the profits which were taxable at the time when the business was carried on. [790 F] In the instant case, the assessee had not been able to show that the total income was taxable under that Act. The High court was right to hold that the assessee was entitled to the benefit of section 6(1) (a). [791 A B] Commissioner of Income tax vs M/s. K. C. D. & Co., , referred to.

The petitioner was appointed as Assistant Engineer in the Kerala Public Service Commission. He was selected for the post of Assistant Engineer. The Commission recommended that the selection should be made by the Public Service commission. The Government, however, directed that the appointment should be done by the Commission on the basis of the seniority list prepared by the Selection Committee. The petitioner filed a writ petition in the High Court challenging the order of the High court. The High Court dismissed the writ petition holding that the appointments were not made by promotion and that the Public Services Commission had no power to make any appointment, and that it was not necessary for the Public service Commission to appoint any person as Assistant Engineers. In appeal to this Court it was contended on behalf of the petitioner that the Government had no authority to make an order directing the Public Public Service Commissions to appoint a person as a Assistant Engineer, and therefore the High Courts were in error in holding that there was no power under section 5(1) (a) of the Kerala State Civil Services (Classification, Control and Appeal) Rules, 1965. Dismissing the appeal, ^ HELD: 1. The Public Service Tribunal had no jurisdiction to make appointments on the ground that the Commission had not made any order directing that the candidates should be appointed as a Junior Engineer. [601B] 2. The State Government has power under clause (a), to appoint persons who have been appointed as Junior Engineers, and the High Power Committee has no power or authority to direct appointment of persons who are appointed as such. [702C D] 3. The power under sub clause (b) is not confined to the appointment of a person on the recommendation of the Commission. It is only when the Commission decides that the appointing authority should be consulted, it is open to the Public Commission to make a fresh order directing appointment of such persons as Assistant Executive Engineer. If the Government has not made an order, it would be open to any person to make such appointments as Assistant Superintending Engineers. [802C] 4. The order of appointment of the petitioners was not in accordance with the rules and regulations of the Public services Commission. [903D E] 5. The orders of appointment were passed by the High courts on the recommendations of the Selection Committees. The petitioners have been given a right to be appointed to the post. They are entitled to be considered for appointment as Assistant Assistant Executive Engineers. Their appointments are not in conformity with the Rules and regulations.

The appellant, a partner of the firm, was a partner in the firm. The partnership deed was executed on May 19, 1979 and the plaintiff was appointed as a partner. The suit was dismissed by the trial court on the ground that the plaintiff had no locus standi to file the suit. The High Court held that the suit was barred by limitation. In appeal to this Court it was contended for the appellant that the plaint was not maintainable because the plaintiff has no locus to file it. Dismissing the appeal, ^ HELD: 1.1 The suit is barred by time and the suit is not maintainable. [603 D] 2.2 The suit must be dismissed on the basis of the pleadings in the plaint. [703 G] 3.3 In the instant case, the plaintiff is a partner and he has no right to file any suit. He has no cause of action to file a suit. [803 A B] 4.4 The suit filed by the plaintiff for specific performance of his duties under the partnership deed is not barred by law. [903 D E] 5.5 In the present case, there was no pleading that the defendant had any right to sue. The plaintiff has not been able to prove that he had any cause of actions to file such a suit and that the relief claimed in the suit cannot be granted. [09E F] 2:1 The plaintiff is not entitled to claim any relief as prayed for by him. [1003 A C] 3:2 In the absence of pleading, it is not open to the plaintiff to raise this contention.

The appellants, who were manufacturers of sugar in the State of Madhya Pradesh, challenged the validity of the notification dated 5.8.1982 by a writ petition in the High Court. The High Court dismissed the writ petitions holding that the notification was not valid and the exemption granted to them under section 3(1) (a) of the Madhya Pradesh Sales Tax Act, 1958 was not applicable to the case of the appellants. In appeal to this Court it was contended on behalf of the State that the exemption was not available only to the manufacturers who were registered with the State Government but also to the manufacturer who had been registered with them under the Madhya Bharat Sales Tax (Amendment) Act, 1981 and that the benefit of the exemption could be extended to the manufacturing unit. Dismissing the appeals, this Court, HELD: 1.1 The notification dated 4.8..1982 was not a valid one and it is only for the manufacturer to obtain the benefit under section 6(1)(a) and the notification issued thereunder. [740B] 2.2 The exemption granted by the State in respect of the manufacturing units cannot be extended merely because the manufacturer has been registered under the Act. [ 740C D] 3.3 The exemption is not available to the manufacture unit only if it is a manufacturing unit and not for the manufacturing process. It is only when the manufacturer is registered with that State, he can obtain the exemption from payment of tax on the basis of the certificate issued by the Government. [841D E] 4.4 The notification issued under section 5(1), which was valid in respect thereof, cannot be said to have been issued without the prior approval of the Government and the same is not a mere declaration of the fact that the manufacturer had been granted exemption from tax on his basis.

The Delhi High Court in its judgment dated May 20, 1979, held that the seniority of the officers appointed to the Delhi High Courts under Rule 5(1) of the Delhi Subordinate Services Rules, 1954 was not a rule made by the Delhi Judicial Service (Judicial Branch) Rules, 1955. The Delhi High court in its order dated May 19, 1979 directed the Delhi Civil Service (Administrative Branch) to prepare a list of officers appointed by the Government from time to time for recruitment to the service of the State Civil Services and to make appointments on the basis of seniority in the cadre of District Judges. The respondents challenged the validity of the said order before the High Court which dismissed the writ petition. In appeal to this Court it was contended that the Delhi Rules were not applicable to the posts of District Judge, and that the rules made by them were ultra vires the provisions of Article 309 of the Constitution. Dismissing the appeals, ^ HELD: 1. The rules framed under Rule 4(1)(a) of Delhi Subordinate Service Rules, 1953 are not applicable in the case of the direct recruits appointed to a service of a State Civil Service and that they are governed by the rules framed by the High Courts. [697E] 2. The rule is ultra vires Article 309 and is therefore void. [797F G] 3. Rule 4 (1)(b) of Haryana Subordinate Services (Judicial Division) Rules 1955 provides for recruitment of officers to the Service of District judges in the State of Delhi. Rule 5 (1) provides that the appointments of officers shall be made by direct recruitment on the recommendation of the High court and the appointments made by promotion on the recommendations of the District Judge shall be subject to the provisions contained in the rules. The Rules do not provide for recruitment by direct recruits. [897F] 4. Rule 6(1), which provides that a person appointed to any service of State Civil services shall be eligible for appointment to the post of District judge, and if he is appointed to such service he shall be entitled to be appointed to that service on the ground of seniority. The proviso to Rule 5 of Delhi Rules, 1956, provides that in case of direct recruits recruited by promotion from the Service, the persons appointed to each service of any State Civil service shall be deemed to have been appointed to another service of that State Civil and not to such other service as may be determined by the Governor. [997F H] 5. Rule 7(1A) provides for appointment by direct recruit on the strength of seniority, and the persons recruited to the said Service shall be considered for appointment in accordance with the rules and the rules shall be applicable to such persons. The provisions contained therein are not inconsistent with the provisions in the Rules. [1097F F] 6. Rule 8(1B) provides a procedure for recruitment on direct recruits, and it is provided that the persons selected by promotion shall be appointed by direct appointment on the same basis as if they were appointed to different service of which they were recruited. The procedure prescribed in Rule 7 (1A), which requires that the person appointed by promotion should be appointed on the posts specified in the rule. The method of recruitment is to be followed by the method of selection and not by direct appointments. The mode of recruitment, however, does not require that the candidates selected by direct Recruitment should be considered as if their names were included in the list of the service. [1197F; 1197A] 7. Rule 9(1C) provides the procedure for appointment on a post of State Judicial Service. Rule 10(2B) is also made applicable to persons appointed by transfer from one cadre to another. The manner of recruitment and promotion are to be governed by rule 8(3B).

The appellant firm was a partnership firm. The partners of the firm were assessed to income tax under section 10(1) (a)(i) of the Income Tax Act, 1922. The Income Tax Officer held that the firm had been dissolved by the order of assessment and that the assessment was not barred by limitation. On appeal, the Appellate Assistant Commissioner confirmed the order but upheld the order. In appeal to this Court it was contended on behalf of the appellant that the order passed by the Income tax Officer under section 11(1)(a) (i) (ii) of Act No. XIV of 1951 was not a valid order and therefore the order could not be sustained. HELD : The High Court was in error in holding that the income tax officer had no jurisdiction to pass an order under section 16(1). [703 B] In the instant case, the Incometax Officer had no power to pass any order under sub section (3) of section 16. The order passed under sub s.(3) was not valid and therefore it could not have been made by the Appellate Tribunal. The High court was in wrong error in setting aside the order under s.16(1), but the High Court had no occasion to interfere with the order, because, the order was not one of assessment or reassessment. [704 B] The High Courts were right in holding the order as valid and valid. [603 C] In view of the fact that the Income ' Officer had jurisdiction to make an order for the assessment of income tax, it could be said that the Appellate Commissioner had no authority to pass such an order.

The appellant, a Hindu undivided family, was the adopted son of one P. C. who died in 1936. The appellant claimed that he had no right to sue for partition and that the suit was barred by section 14(1)(a) of the Madras Hindu Religious Endowments Act, 1950. The trial court decreed the suit on the ground that the appellant had not been able to establish his claim as a joint family property within the meaning of section 2(2) of that Act. On appeal the High Court held that the plaintiff was entitled to sue in respect of the properties mentioned in the plaint and that he was entitled only to sue under section 14 (1)(b). The High Court also held that there was no bar for the appellant to sue as a separate suit. In appeal to this Court it was contended on behalf of the appellant that the High court had jurisdiction to entertain the suit, and that in view of the provisions of section 14 of the Act the High Courts were not competent to entertain such a suit. Held: (i) The High court was right in holding that the plaint was barred under section 15(1) (a) as it stood before the amendment of the Indian Limitation Act, 1908. (ii) The appellant had no locus standi to file the suit and that there could be no question of jurisdiction on the basis of the decision of this Court in P.C. vs R. C., [1955] 1 S.C., page 818, referred to. (iii) The suit was not barred by article 14(2)(a). The appellant was entitled under section 9(1), (b) as he had not filed his written statement and that it was not competent for the High courts to entertain a suit as it was barred in view, the provisions contained in section 14 were applicable. (iv) The plaint was not maintainable because the appellant was not able to prove his claim. (v) The trial Court was right when the appellant did not file his written statements and that no question was raised for the first time before the High judge. (vi) The appeal must be dismissed as barred by limitation. (vii) The plaintiff had no cause of action in respect thereof, and the suit could not be dismissed on the grounds mentioned in section 9 (1). (viii) The court was not right in rejecting the plaint. (ix) The courts were right in dismissing the suit merely because the High Judge had jurisdiction under section 13(2), (a). (x) The Court was not entitled to entertain it as a preliminary issue and that, therefore, the appellant could not have filed his Written statement.

The appellant, a public limited company, was granted permission to construct a building on the ground that it had been constructed without obtaining necessary permission from the Municipal Authority. The respondent No. 1, who was the owner of the building, applied for permission to erect a building in the area of Delhi. The Chief Executive Officer, Delhi Development Authority, by his order dated November 6, 1987, rejected the application and directed the appellant to construct the building on that ground. On appeal, the High Court held that the building had been built without obtaining requisite permission from it. In the appeal to this Court, it was contended for the appellant that the construction of a building was not permissible in law as the building was constructed without the sanction of the Municipal authority and the permission granted by the Municipal Authorities was illegal. Dismissing the appeal, HELD: 1. The High Court was right in holding that the permission was valid and the building could be used only after obtaining necessary permissions from the Chief Executive Authority. [799C] 2.1 The High Courts were right in coming to the conclusion that the buildings had been erected without obtaining prior permission from a Municipal authority. [899F] 2:2. The construction of the buildings was not justified because the building did not have any sanction for the purpose of construction of building. It was also held that it was necessary to obtain necessary permissions and permission from all the authorities concerned. [999G H; 999A B] 3.1 In the instant case, the building in question had been used without obtaining permission from any authority. The building was built without the approval of the Chief Officer. It is not possible for the Municipal authorities to obtain permission from them. [1099C D] 2 :2.1 There is no doubt that the Building in question was constructed on the basis of a sanctioned plan and the construction was not permitted by the Chief Engineer. The Municipal Authority had no authority to grant permission to the appellant. It could not have granted permission for the building. [ 1099A C] 3:2 The High court was right when it held that there was no sanction in respect of the construction. In view of the fact that the constructions were constructed without prior permission, the Municipal Council had no jurisdiction to grant the permission. [1199C E] 4.2 The building in dispute was a public street and the Municipal Committee had no power to grant such permission. The appellant could not be permitted to construct any building on it. [ 1199A D] 5:3 The High Power Committee had not given any reasons for refusing permission to carry out the construction, but had given reasons for rejecting the application. [1299C F] 4:4 The High power of granting permission was not a statutory power and it could not therefore be said that the Municipal Officer had no discretion in granting permission to a person who had applied for the same. [ 1299A] 5.3 In the absence of any such reasons, the appellant could have granted the permission to build a building without obtaining the requisite permissions from all authorities concerned, but the High Power Committees had not taken into consideration the relevant factors and the circumstances of the case. [699C G] 4 :4 The Municipal Committee was right to grant sanction for construction of buildings on the grounds that it did not require prior permission to establish a building. The decision of the High power Committee in granting approval to the building would be arbitrary and unreasonable. [599F H; 699A, G] 5(a) The High Powers Committee had also not given reasons as to why the building should not be constructed without sanction of any authority or authority. It did not give any reasons as regards the construction which was in violation of the provisions of the Act.

The appellant, a Hindu undivided family, was the sole proprietor of a business in which he had been carrying on business. The respondent, who was the son of the deceased, filed a suit for partition and separate possession of his business. In the plaint it was alleged that the appellant had not paid any money to the respondent as required by section 7(1) of the Bombay Hindu undivided Family Courts Act, 1947, and that he had no right to claim the amount of Rs. 1,000/ . The trial court decreed the suit holding that the respondent was a partner in the business of the appellant and that the suit was barred by limitation. On appeal the High Court held that the compromise decree was not binding on the parties and that it was not open to the parties to claim any amount as required under section 7 (1) (a). The High Court also held that there was no dispute between the parties regarding the liability of the respondent to pay the amount due to him. In appeal to this Court, HELD : (i) The compromise decree is binding on both parties and it is not open for the parties in the suit to claim that the agreement was not a compromise decree. [619 D] (ii) The High court had no jurisdiction to try the suit as it was filed within the period of limitation prescribed by section 8(1). The compromise was not final and binding on all parties. It is open to both parties to raise their contentions before the Court. [720 F G] (iii) In a suit under section 13 of the Act, the court has no jurisdiction in respect of the dispute between them. The compromise is final and conclusive. The decree is therefore binding on each party.

The appellant was convicted under section 3(1) of the Bombay Factories Act, 1948. The High Court held that the word "building" in section 2(1)(a) of that Act did not include a building or structure which is used for the purpose of carrying out any work or operation. Held, that the words "building", in section 3 (1)(b) of this Act were wide enough to cover a building and structure which was used for carrying out the work or operations. The word " buildings" in the definition of "building". In the present case, the word 'building" was used in the sense of "any building" as defined in section 4(1). Held, further, that in view of the definition given in section 5 (1) (a), the word used in section 6 (1A) of Act did include a buildings or structure used for any purpose other than the purpose for which it was used. The words "any such building" were wide and could not be construed as including a building used for a purpose other as the purpose was for carrying on the work. Held further, further that the expression "building " is used in relation to any building or structures used for purposes connected with the business of the factory. The definition of 'building ' in section 1 (1), therefore, clearly indicates that the term "building ' means a building which is intended for the use of the purpose specified in section 7(1A). Held further that in the present context, the expression 'building " includes any building used as a building for the purposes of carrying on any work. The expression "any buildings" was not defined in the Act and therefore, the definition could not have been given to the word in section 10 (1).

The respondent was appointed as a Junior Engineer in the Department of Higher Education on January 1, 1960. He was promoted to the post of Assistant Director of Technical Education on July 31, 1960 and he was promoted as Assistant Director on June 30, 1960, but his seniority was not fixed at the time of his appointment. The respondent challenged the validity of the order dated August 31, 1961 by way of a writ petition in the High Court which was dismissed by the High court. In appeal to this Court it was contended that the respondent had been promoted as Junior Engineer on July 1, 1959 and he had not been given any opportunity of showing cause against his promotion. HELD: The respondent was entitled to be considered for promotion to the posts of Assistant Directors in the department of Higher education on the basis of seniority list prepared by the Government. [601 B C] In the instant case, the respondent was promoted on July 30, 1961 and he could not be given any chance of showing showing cause why his promotion should not be cancelled. The High Court had rightly held that the order of the Government dated August 1, 1961 was illegal and void. [702 D] The respondent 's claim to be senior to him was rejected by the State Government on the ground that he had been given a chance of being promoted as Senior Engineer on June 31, 1959. The State Government was not justified in rejecting his claim for promotion. [801 B] In view of the fact that the State had taken a decision to consider the case of the respondent for promotion on July 29, 1960 it could not have been said that he was given a right of promotion to that post.

The petitioner was a minor in the United States of America. The petitioner applied for a writ of mandamus directing the respondents to appoint a guardian of a child under the provisions of the Indian Adoptions and Maintenance Act, 1956. The High Court dismissed the petition holding that the petitioner had no right to be appointed as guardian of the child. In appeal to this Court it was contended on behalf of the petitioner that the order of the High Court is not correct and that the impugned order is liable to be set aside. Dismissing the writ petition, ^ HELD: 1. The order of appointment of a guardian under the Act is not a valid one and is therefore liable to set aside the order. [601D] 2. The impugned order does not suffer from any infirmity or illegality in the order passed by the High court. It is well settled that the Court has no power to make an order for the appointment of guardian under section 3 of the Act. If the Court is satisfied that the child is a minor, it may order the guardian to be given an opportunity to show cause why the child should not be appointed. [701D E] 3. The Court cannot act as a court of appeal unless there are compelling reasons for doing so. [801E F] 4. In the instant case, the petitioner was not a minor and was not entitled to be considered for appointment under section 16 of the . [602F G] 5. The question whether the order is valid or not is not one which requires consideration in the present case. It has been held by this Court that the court should have regard to the circumstances of each case.

The appellant company was a registered company carrying on business in the manufacture of its products. The company had paid bonus to its employees for the year 1965 65, but the company did not pay any bonus for the years 1965 66 and 1964 67. The workmen claimed that the bonus payable by them was not paid by the company as it was not liable to be deducted from the profits of the company. The Tribunal held that the claim of the workmen was not justified. In appeal to this Court, HELD : (1) The bonus payable under the Act is a part of the profits and gains of the business of the Company and therefore, the bonus paid by them cannot be deducted in computing the profits. [601 B] (2) The Tribunal has rightly held that there was no evidence on record to show that the workmen were not entitled to any bonus. [702 C D] (3) The claim of bonus payable to the workmen is not justified because it is a matter of fact and law which has to be decided by the Tribunal. [803 B] In the instant case, the Tribunal had rightly held in its award that the amount paid by it was a part and parcel of profits and therefore the bonus claimed by the workmen cannot be said to have been deducted from their profits. The claim for bonus is not based on any evidence. [902 C E] (4) The question whether the bonus was payable under section 10(2)(b) or section 10 (3)(c) is a question of fact.

The appellant was appointed as a Tax Assistant in the Tamil Nadu State Sales Tax Department. He was promoted to the post of Tax Assistant on January 1, 1971. The appellant was promoted as Tax Assistant and was promoted on January 31, 1971 by an order dated March 2, 1971, which was confirmed by the Government. On December 14, 1971 the Government issued a notification under Rule 3(1) of the Tamil Pradesh Sales Tax Rules, 1959, calling upon the appellant to show cause why he should not be reverted to his substantive post in the service of the State Government. The said order was challenged before the High Court by special leave. Dismissing the appeal, ^ HELD: 1. The impugned order is based on a misappreciation of the evidence and the reasons given by the authorities below for holding that the appellant had been promoted as an Tax Assistant. [630B] 2. The order of reversion is based upon a mis appraisal of the record and the findings recorded by the authority below are not based on any misappreciation or misappreciation. It is well settled that the order of promotion is based solely on misappreciation, misappreciation and misappreciation but it is based only on mis appreciation of evidence and no error apparent on the face of the records. [730C] 3. The High Court was right in holding that there was a mis appreciation or mis appraisal on the record. [831E] 4. The Government had not considered the appellant 's case as an officer in the State Sales tax Department. [932F G] 5. The Tribunal has rightly held that the impugned order of transfer is based primarily on mis misappreciation which is based entirely on mis appraisal and mis appreciation.

The appellants, who were the operators of a transport bus, challenged the validity of the scheme on the ground that they had no right to carry on their business in the State of Andhra Pradesh. The High Court held that the scheme was not valid and the scheme could not be validly made under section 3(1) of the Act. In appeal to this Court it was contended for the appellants that the schemes were invalid because the scheme did not provide for the grant of permits to the operators in the transport bus. HELD: The scheme was valid and there was no justification for the State Government to make any order under section 4(1). [601 B] In the instant case, the scheme had been made by the Transport Authority in exercise of its powers under section 5(1), and that it was not a valid scheme. It was only after the scheme came into force that the permits were granted to the appellants. The State Government could make any such order under sub section (2) of section 3, but it did not do so. [602 B] The scheme had not been made in exercise Of its powers conferred by sub section(1)(a) of r. 4 of the Andhra Pradesh Transport Corporation Act, 1964. It is only after a scheme came to be passed that the Regional Transport Authority was bound to make an order under r.4. [702 B C] The State Transport Authority had no power to make a scheme in exercise thereof. The Regional Transport Authorities were therefore bound to give reasons for its decision.

The appellant company was registered under the Indian Sales Tax Act, 1947. The Sales Tax Officer issued a notice to the appellant on the ground that the sales were not taxable within the meaning of section 2(f) of the Act and that the appellant had failed to disclose the particulars of the goods in respect of which the sales had been made. The appellant filed an application under article 226 of the Constitution for quashing the order of assessment. The High Court held that the notice was not a valid one and accordingly the order was invalid. In appeal by special leave, HELD: (i) The words "any person" in section 2 (f) are wide enough to include a dealer who has been registered under section 3(f). [703 B] (ii) The word "any other person" is wide enough and it cannot be said that the words "other person" are wide. It is not necessary for the High Court to consider whether the words 'other person", in section 3 (f), are wide, but they must include a person who has made an application for registration under section 4(1) of that Act. [704 B] The word 'any other persons" in the proviso to section 5(1)(a) is not restricted to a dealer whose turnover is assessed to tax under the Act. It does not mean that the word "other persons" must include only a person whose turnover has been assessed to sales tax under section 6(1). [804 B C] (iii) The expression "any dealer" in sub section (2) of section 5 (1)(b) is wide and it can be said to include any person who is registered under that Act or not.

The petitioners were convicted of offences under sections 302 and 201 read with section 34 I.P.C. and sentenced to death for life. The petitioners challenged the order of the High Court in a writ petition before this Court. Dismissing the writ petitions, ^ HELD: 1. The High Court has not properly appreciated the evidence on record and the reasons given by the trial court while rejecting the application for bail. [797C] 2. The State Government is entitled to consider the question of grant of bail in a case where there are serious allegations against the accused persons, including the petitioners, who have been convicted of an offence under section 302 read with Section 34 I P.C., and the court has not taken into consideration the reasons recorded by the High Courts while rejecting their application for grant of anticipatory bail. The Court is entitled only to consider whether the reasons are sufficient or not. [897D] 3. The object of granting bail is to enable the accused to be heard in a particular case, and if it is satisfied that there are special circumstances which may justify the grant of such bail, it would be open to the court to take into consideration all relevant factors including the nature of the offence and the circumstances of each case.
