[997C D] 4. The purpose of granting anticipatory bail is not to enable a person who has been convicted for an offence committed under section 201 readwith section 34. It is only when the court is satisfied, that there is special circumstances justifying grant of regular bail, that the accused are entitled to be released on bail. If the court finds that there exists special circumstances in which the accused is charged with an offence, it may refuse to grant anticipatory bail to such person. [1097C E] 5. The court has to consider all relevant aspects and come to a conclusion whether the accused have been guilty of any offence or not, and whether the court should be satisfied that the evidence is sufficient or reasonable. If there are other circumstances which justify the granting of anticipatory relief, it will be open for the court in the first instance to take appropriate action against the person who is convicted for the offence committed by him under section 307 read with sections 34 I I P and section 34, if the court considers that the reasons mentioned in the order are sufficient.

The appellant was the tenant of a land in the State of Bombay. The respondent landlord filed an application under section 14(1) (a) of the Bombay Tenancy and Agricultural Lands Act, 1948 for eviction of the appellant on the ground that he had not been evicted from the land in question. The application was rejected by the Assistant Collector on the grounds: (i) that the tenant had no right to continue in possession of the land; (ii) that section 14 (1) of that Act did not apply to a landlord who had not applied for the grant of the lease; and (iii) that it was not applicable to a tenant who had applied for a renewal of the tenancy. The appellant filed an appeal before the High Court which held that the application was barred by limitation. Held, that section 15(1)(a) did not affect the right of the landlord to continue the possession of land in accordance with the provisions of the Act and the proviso to section 14 of the said Act. The proviso to sub section (2) of section 14 does not apply only to a person who had been evicted under the Act but also to a non tenant who has applied for renewal of his tenancy. It is well settled that the right to terminate the tenancy is an exception and it is not necessary that the landlord should be given a notice of termination of the service of the tenant. The words "any person" in section 14 are wide enough to include a person whose services have been terminated under the provisions or the proviso thereto. The word "any other person" has no application to a tenancy which is terminated under section 15 (1).

The petitioners were the owners of certain property in which they had been declared as evacuee properties. The Custodian issued a notice under section 5 of the Act to the petitioners on the ground that they had no right to hold any such property. The petitioners challenged the validity of the notice on the grounds, inter alia, (i) that the petitioners were not entitled to hold the property in question; (ii) that there was no valid order for the acquisition of their property under section 6 of the . Held, that the order of the Custodian was not a nullity and the order passed by the Custodian could not be sustained. The order of dismissal was not an order of adjudication and therefore the petitioners had no locus standi to file the petition. The orders of the authorities were not vitiated because they were not made under section 7 of the , as it was not open to them to challenge the validity or legality of the order. Held, further, that there could be no valid notice for the purpose of the proceedings under section 4 of the ; and (iii) that in view of the provisions of section 5, the Custodian had no jurisdiction to entertain the petition because the petitioners did not have any right to claim the property under the Act. The fact that the Custodian has no right or title to the property was not sufficient to hold that the property had been acquired by them under the provisions. Held further, further that the orders of dismissal were not valid and the petitioners could not claim the right of the property as they had not been declared evacuee properties under section 3 of the : Held, also, that section 5 did not apply to the proceedings before the Custodian under section 8 of the but only a proceeding under section 9 of the was not maintainable. The provisions of sections 5 and 6 were not applicable to the case in which the petitioners have no right.

The assessee company was carrying on business in the manufacture of sugar and sugar. The assessee company had a business in its own name and style as an agent of the Company. The business was carried on by it for the purpose of manufacturing sugar. In the year 1953, the assessee company paid Rs. 1,50,000/ to the assessee for the purchase of sugar from the Company and received Rs. 2,50 ,000/ . The assessee claimed that the amount of Rs. 3,50,. as commission was not payable by it in respect of the said business. The Income tax Officer rejected the claim on the ground that the assessee had paid Rs, 1,00,000 as commission to its agent and that the amounts were not payable under the agreement between the Company as the commission was received by it from the company. The Appellate Assistant Commissioner held that the commission received by the assessee was not a commission received in respect thereof and that it was not liable to be taxed under section 10(2) of the Income tax Act, 1922. In appeal to this Court, HELD : (i) The commission received from the assessee is a commission paid by the company for the manufacture and sale of sugar. It is not a receipt received by its agent. The commission is received in the name of the assessee but it is received by him as commission received on behalf of the company and the commission is paid to the agent. [723 B] (ii) The amount received by way of commission received is a part of the profits of the business. It does not include any profit or loss arising from the business of the firm. The receipt is not an income but it must be treated as a receipt for the purposes of section 10. [824 F G] (iii) The assessee was entitled to deduction under section 11(2).

The appellant company was a registered company carrying on business in the manufacture of its products. The Income tax Officer, who assessed the income of the assessee, held that the profits of the company were not taxable under section 10(1)(c) of the Indian Income Tax Act, 1922. The Appellate Assistant Commissioner rejected the application and held that it was not a case of appeal or revision against the order of the Appellate Assistant Commissioners. On appeal by special leave, the appellant contended that the High Court was in error in holding that the application for reference to the High court under section 66(1) of Income Tax Rules, 1922 was not maintainable as the application was not barred by limitation and that the Tribunal had no jurisdiction to entertain the application. Dismissing the appeal, ^ HELD: The High Court has rightly held that there was a case in which the application could be entertained. [630E] In the instant case, the application of the appellant for reference under section 11(1A) of Indian Income tax Act, 1961 was not within the meaning of section 10 (1A). [631C D] The High court has rightly rejected the contention that the order passed by the Appellate Tribunal was a judgment within the ambit of section 66 (1B) of that Act. [732E F] In view of the fact that the appellant company had not filed any application under section 16(1), it is not open to the Appellate Commissioner to entertain such an application for the purpose of determining the question whether the application should be entertained or not.

The plaintiff filed a suit for the recovery of possession of certain lands in dispute. The defendants claimed that they were entitled to the benefit of the rent and that they had no right to claim the same. The trial court decreed the suit holding that the defendants were not entitled to any relief under the rent Act, and that the plaintiffs were entitled only to the relief under section 14(1)(f) of the Bengal Land Revenue Code, 1908. The High Court held that the plaintiff was entitled to a decree for possession of the lands in question. Held, that the suit was barred by limitation. The plaintiff had not proved his title to the lands and the defendants had no title to it. The suit was not barred by time. The plaintiffs were not bound by the rent rules. The defendant could not be said to have been in possession of those lands. The burden of proving that the defendant was in possession or control of the land was on the plaintiff. The onus was on him to prove his title. The presumption of adverse possession is not available to the defendants. The mere fact that the burden of proof is on the plaintiffs and the burden is on them to prove it. In the present case, the defendants did not establish their title to those lands in suit. The plea of adverse ownership was not raised by the defendants but only a plea of hostile possession. The evidence of the defendants was not sufficient to prove that they are entitled to relief under article 14(2) (f). The burden was on them. The fact that they did not produce any evidence to establish their claim was not established. The question whether the plaintiff had proved his adverse possession or not was a question of law. Held further, that in the absence of any evidence it could be said that the onus was discharged by the defendant.

The appellant was the owner of a land in suit for specific performance of contract. The plaintiff filed a suit for declaration that the sale deed dated March 31, 1960 was void and inoperative. The trial court decreed the suit holding that the plaintiff had no right to sue for specific specific performance. The High Court held that the suit was barred by limitation as it was not maintainable in view of section 14(1) of the Bombay Tenancy Act, 1948. In appeal to this Court it was contended on behalf of the appellant that the civil court had jurisdiction to entertain a suit under section 14 of the Act and that the Civil Court had no jurisdiction to try the suit. Dismissing the appeal, ^ HELD: 1. The civil court has jurisdiction to decide the question whether the plaintiff was entitled to sue in respect of specific performance or not. [601C] 2.1 In view of the provisions of section 15(1), the civil courts have jurisdiction to adjudicate upon the dispute between the parties and the civil Court has no jurisdiction, but it is only when the civil Courts have jurisdiction, they are competent to decide such a question. The Civil Court has jurisdiction in respect thereof. [701C D] 2:2. In view, the civil suit was not barred by time as it had been filed within the period of limitation prescribed under section 15 (1) and the Civil Courts have no jurisdiction. [802D E] 3.3. The suit is barred by the provisions contained in section 14 (1). It is not a suit within the meaning of section 2(a), but it has to be decided on its own merits. [903F G] 4.4. In the instant case, the plaintiff filed an application under section 16(1)(b) for the grant of a decree for specific Performance of contract and the suit is not barred under section 13 (1)(c). The civil Court had jurisdiction in the matter. The appellant was not entitled to file any suit within time as the civil forum has no power to entertain the suit, it cannot be said that the land in dispute was purchased by him from the plaintiff for a consideration of Rs. 1,00,000/ and the sale was void. [1003F] 5:4. The jurisdiction of the Civil court is not limited to the civil proceedings. It is only where the civil tribunal has jurisdiction, it can decide the dispute in accordance with law.

The assessee company was carrying on business in the manufacture of cement and cement. The assessee company had a manufacturing unit at Calcutta. The manufacturing unit was carrying out its business in India. The business was carried on by it for the purpose of manufacturing cement and steel. The Income tax Officer, who held that the manufacturing unit could not be carried on in India as it was engaged in the production of cement. On appeal, the Appellate Assistant Commissioner confirmed the order of the Income tax officer holding that the assessee company did not carry on its business within the meaning of section 2(f) of the Act. The Tribunal held that there was no manufacturing unit in India and the manufacturing units were carried on outside India. In the appeal to this Court it was contended for the Revenue that the business was not carried on within the definition of "business" as defined in section 2 (f) (g) of that Act. Dismissing the appeal, HELD: 1. The word "business", in the context of the expression "business". is used in the sense of a term which means a business or activity which is carried on for the purposes of manufacturing manufacturing cement. It is not necessary to refer to the definition as defined by section 2 of the Indian Income tax Act, 1922. [619B] 1.1 The word 'business" has been used in section 3(f). In the context it is used to mean a business which is carrying on for its own purpose and is carried out in India or any part thereof. It means a manufacturing undertaking which carries on the business of manufacturing, manufacturing, selling, supplying or producing cement. [719D] 1:2 The word used in sub section (1) of section 3 of the said Act has been defined in the definition. In this context it would be necessary to have a meaning which is not defined in that Act but in the same sense it is not possible to say what is meant by the term "business " and" as used in that clause. [819D E] 1.:3 The word business means a trade or business which carries with its own business, but does not include any activity carried on or incidental to the carrying on of the business. It has been held that it is only when the manufacturing process is carried upon by it and the production is carried in India, that the production was carried out within the scope of the definition and therefore the word "resid tive" would be used in this context. [919D F] 1.(a) The expression "resides" in sub clause (1), means a person who carries on business for the manufacture or sale of cement, manufacturing or producing any cement. In other words it is also not necessary that the activity carried out by it should be carried out as a result of the carrying out of the trade or commerce. [1019D G] 1(b) The word in sub cl (1)(a) of clause (c) of sub section(1) must be construed in its ordinary sense and not in any way restricted to the business carried on. It does not mean a manufacturing activity carried by it. In such a case, the production must be carried in the course of carrying out the business or commerce but only when it is carried into the course or activities carried on with the aid of power, it must be held that its activity carried in by it is carrying out as an activity carried upon in India which carries the business in a manufacturing process. [1119D H] 1 (c). The word is used for the production and manufacture of goods carried on at the time when the production takes place. It cannot be said to mean only a manufacturing industry carried on, or carried on without the aid or power.

The appellants were the owners of a temple in Madras. They were granted a lease of lands in the year 1950 to the temple. The appellants filed a suit for possession of the lands on the ground that they were not entitled to the benefit of section 4(1) (a) of the Madras Estates Abolition Act, 1953. The trial court decreed the suit holding that the appellants were not 'suited ' within the meaning of section 2(g) of that Act and that the plaintiffs were not "suited" within the definition of section 3(2)(b). The High Court held that the defendants were entitled to a decree for possession in respect of lands on their own. In appeal to this Court, HELD : (i) The appellants were entitled only to a permanent injunction restraining the respondents from interfering with the possession of lands and not to dispossess them from the lands. [630 F] (ii) The High court was right in holding that section 4 (1)(b) of Madras Estates Estates Abolition Rules, 1953 did not apply to the suit for eviction under section 4 of the Act. [731 A B] (iii) The plaintiffs were entitled for a permanent relief and they were entitled under section 5(1)(a). [732 C D] (iv) The defendants were not tenants in the lands in dispute. They had no right to continue in possession of land on their behalf. [833 E F] In the present case, the plaintiffs had been granted a permanent status and they had no rights to continue the same.

The appellant Municipal Corporation of Indore, was assessed to tax under the Madhya Pradesh Municipalities Act, 1950. The respondents were assessed to pay tax on the basis of the rates fixed by the Municipal Corporation in respect of certain buildings. The Municipal Corporation passed a resolution dated March 20, 1954, which was published in the Gazette on April 1, 1954. The appellant Municipal corporation challenged the validity of the said resolution and the High Court dismissed the appeal. In appeal to this Court it was contended that the Municipal Commissioner had no jurisdiction to pass the order under section 3(2) of the Act as he did not have the power to pass such orders under section 4(1). HELD: The High Court was right in holding that the rates were fixed by a municipal council and the rates prescribed by the municipal council were not fixed by it. [601 F] In the instant case, the Municipal Committee had no power to levy tax on buildings. It is true that the municipal committee had no authority to pass any order under sections 4(2), 5(1) and 5(3). The High court was right when the rates are fixed by an municipal council. But it could not be said that the rate fixed by section 4 (1) was a reasonable one. [701 F G] In view of the fact that the appellant Municipal Committee was assessed under section 6(2)(a), the Municipal Board had no powers to levy any tax on building. The High Courts were right in coming to the conclusion that the assessment made by the Corporation was not unreasonable and could not have been challenged.

The assessee company was carrying on business in the manufacture of sugar. The assessee company sold its goods to the assessee for a price of Rs. 1,50,000 and the price paid by it was Rs. 2,50. The sale price was Rs, 2,00,000. The sales were made at the instance of the assessee company and the sale price had been taken at the time of sale. The price was not taken at a later stage. The Income tax Officer held that the sale was not in the course of business but was in the nature of trade or business. On appeal by the assessee, the Appellate Assistant Commissioner confirmed the order of the Income tax officer and dismissed the appeal. In appeal to this Court, HELD : (i) The sale was in a way connected with the manufacture and sale of sugar and not in any other manner connected with that manufacture. It is not possible to hold that the sales were in the character of trade. [601 B] (ii) The sales are in the same nature as trade or commerce, but it must be held to have been in the way connected therewith. In the present case, the sale of goods was in fact a trade or industry. It was not possible for the assessee to hold the sale at a subsequent stage. [701 B C] (iii) The transaction was in an ordinary course of trade and business. The transaction did not take place in the sense that it was a sale of property. In such circumstances, the sales could not be said to have taken place in a particular manner.
